articles.title: AWS achieves Spain’s national Limited Distribution (Difusión Limitada) and NATO Restricted accreditation in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region
articles.context: With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe...
articles.full_text:
Spanish version »

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is pleased to announce that AWS has achieved Spain’s national Limited Distribution (“Difusión Limitada”) and NATO Restricted accreditation for the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation was granted by the Spanish Delegated Authority for the Security of Classified Information, the Secretary of State Director of Spain’s Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). The Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) and the Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS) are working bodies of the CNI, which audited AWS against the CCN-STIC-004 policy and the applicable ONS requirements.

With this milestone, AWS becomes the first cloud provider to be accredited under NATO Restricted level, and the first to be accredited for Difusión Limitada in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region. In Spain, this was a double achievement: AWS first met the national Difusión Limitada requirements and then, in addition to this national methodology, achieved the NATO Restricted accreditation by incorporating the requirements of NATO Directive 32. This demonstrates our continued commitment to helping the public sector, defense, and NATO-affiliated customers run sensitive workloads in the cloud while meeting the highest applicable national and international security requirements.

What this covers

The Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation by the CNI confirms that the AWS system in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region meets the procedural and security requirements for handling classified information up to the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted level.

What is Spain’s classified information framework?

Spain’s framework for protecting national classified information is administered by the ONS and the CCN, under the CNI. In 2026, Spain established the framework that enables handling of Difusión Limitada information in the commercial public cloud, under which this accreditation was granted. The accreditation builds on the AWS ENS High certification and the CCN’s IT Product and Service Catalogue (CPSTIC) qualifications. The scope of the accreditation covers the CPSTIC-qualified services and all AWS services certified under ENS High (see the list of AWS services in scope for ENS High). Only the services within this scope that are qualified or certified under the CCN framework (CPSTIC and ENS High) and run in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region can be used for Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted workloads.

What is NATO Restricted?

NATO Directive 32 establishes the security requirements for handling NATO Restricted information in public cloud, and is the directive referenced by Spain’s CCN-STIC-004 policy.

Why this matters to customers

Public sector and defense organizations in Spain can use the AWS Europe (Spain) Region for national Difusión Limitada classified workloads and for NATO Restricted workloads. Under the shared responsibility model, customers that want to process classified information in the AWS Europe (Spain) Region engage the CCN and ONS to accredit their own systems, building on the AWS accreditation.

How to get started

National security and defense customers may build on the AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) to design a cloud architecture for their sensitive workloads. Accreditation documentation is available to eligible customers through AWS Artifact. Customers can also work with their AWS account teams to understand how the Difusión Limitada and NATO Restricted accreditation, and TSE-SE apply to their use cases.

To learn more about AWS compliance in Spain, see the AWS ENS compliance page and the AWS Compliance Programs page.

For more details see AWS NATO Restricted and Difusión Limitada for AWS Europe (Spain) Region web page

Spanish version

AWS obtiene la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted en la Región AWS Europa (España)

Amazon Web Services (AWS) se complace en anunciar que ha obtenido la acreditación nacional de España “Difusión Limitada” y la acreditación NATO Restricted para la Región AWS Europa (España). La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted ha sido concedida por la Autoridad Delegada para la Seguridad de la Información Clasificada de España, la Secretaria de Estado Directora del Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI). El Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN), y la Oficina Nacional de Seguridad (ONS), son órganos de trabajo del CNI, que auditaron a AWS conforme a la política CCN-STIC-004 y a los requisitos aplicables de la ONS.

Con este hito, AWS se convierte en el primer proveedor cloud acreditado en el nivel NATO Restricted, y en el primero acreditado para Difusión Limitada en la Región AWS Europa (España). En España ha sido un doble logro: AWS cumplió primero los requisitos nacionales de Difusión Limitada y, sobre esta metodología nacional, obtuvo la acreditación NATO Restricted incorporando los requisitos de la Directiva 32 de la OTAN. Esto demuestra nuestro compromiso continuo de ayudar al sector público, a la defensa y a los clientes vinculados a la OTAN a ejecutar cargas de trabajo sensibles en la nube cumpliendo los requisitos de seguridad nacionales e internacionales más exigentes aplicables.

Qué abarca

La acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted del CNI confirma que el sistema de AWS en la Región AWS Europa (España) cumple los requisitos procedimentales y de seguridad para tratar información clasificada hasta el nivel Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted.

¿Cuál es el marco español de información clasificada?

El marco español de protección de la información clasificada nacional lo administran la ONS y el CCN, bajo el CNI. En 2026, España estableció el marco que permite tratar información Difusión Limitada en la nube pública comercial, en virtud del cual se ha concedido esta acreditación. La acreditación se basa en la certificación ENS categoría Alta de AWS y en las cualificaciones del Catálogo de Productos y Servicios de Seguridad TIC (CPSTIC) del CCN. El alcance de la acreditación incluye los servicios cualificados en CPSTIC y todos los servicios de AWS certificados en el ENS categoría Alta (consulte la lista de servicios de AWS en el alcance del ENS categoría Alta). Solo pueden utilizarse para cargas de trabajo Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted los servicios de este alcance cualificados o certificados en el marco del CCN (CPSTIC y ENS categoría Alta) que se ejecuten en la Región AWS Europa (España).

¿Qué es NATO Restricted?

La Directiva 32 de la OTAN establece los requisitos de seguridad para tratar información NATO Restricted en la nube pública, y es la directiva a la que hace referencia la política española CCN-STIC-004.

Por qué es importante para los clientes

Las organizaciones del sector público y de defensa en España pueden utilizar la Región AWS Europa (España) para cargas de trabajo clasificadas nacionales Difusión Limitada, así como para cargas de trabajo NATO Restricted. Conforme al modelo de responsabilidad compartida, los clientes que quieran tratar información clasificada en la Región AWS Europa (España) deben dirigirse al CCN y a la ONS para acreditar sus propios sistemas, apoyándose en la acreditación de AWS.

Cómo empezar

Los clientes de seguridad nacional y defensa pueden apoyarse en AWS Trusted Secure Enclave, Sensitive Edition (TSE-SE) para diseñar una arquitectura cloud para sus cargas de trabajo sensibles. La documentación de la acreditación está disponible para los clientes elegibles a través de AWS Artifact. Los clientes también pueden trabajar con sus equipos de cuenta de AWS para entender cómo se aplican a sus casos de uso la acreditación Difusión Limitada y NATO Restricted y TSE-SE.

Para más información sobre el cumplimiento de AWS en España, consulte la página de cumplimiento ENS de AWS y la página de Programas de cumplimiento de AWS.

Para más detalles, consulte la página web de AWS sobre NATO Restricted y Difusión Limitada para la Región AWS Europa (España)

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below. If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support.

Borja Larrumbide

Borja is a Security Assurance Manager for AWS in Iberia. He has a bachelor’s degree in computer science from Boston University (USA) and has worked in companies such as Microsoft and BBVA in different roles and sectors. Borja is a seasoned security assurance practitioner with many years of experience engaging key stakeholders at national and international levels. His areas of interest include security, privacy, risk management, and compliance.

articles.context: But researchers at Stony Brook University found that it was enough time for a bot to test a cloud access key they’d deliberately left inside a publicly available software package

In this article

A bot tested an AWS key just 7.86 seconds after researchers published it

Attackers used up about $60 in prepaid OpenAI and Anthropic credit

If you accidentally publish a key, revoke it and check your account for unexpected usage and charges

Eight seconds is barely enough time to notice a mistake, let alone fix it.

But researchers at Stony Brook University found that it was enough time for a bot to test a cloud access key they’d deliberately left inside a publicly available software package. The fastest observed use came just 7.86 seconds after publication.

You don’t need a company cloud account to have a key worth stealing. If you’ve created an API key for an AI service and used it in an app or script, someone who gets hold of it can run up charges on your account. OpenAI warns that they could also use up your quote and interrupt your service.

To see who was collecting those secrets, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis set up honeypots, or decoys that let researchers monitor what happens when someone takes the bait. Over four months, they published 300 honeypot images across eight public registries. The bait included working access keys for Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, and Anthropic. Each key was tied to monitoring, so any use would show up in the provider’s logs.

The researchers didn’t advertise the images anywhere, but they were still downloaded tens of thousands of times.

Most of the early activity looked like bots checking whether the keys worked. Nearly every bot that tested an AWS key began with GetCallerIdentity, essentially a “who am I?” request that tells an attacker whether a key is live. About half the IP addresses researchers saw scanning for AWS keys stopped after that initial check. Only around 6% went on to sustained use of account resources.

A key that passes that check can still be sold on or used later. In the AI-service tests, the OpenAI keys sat quiet for weeks before someone used one to burn through the remaining balance in under 24 hours. The researchers offered an explanation:

“We speculate that the wait phase reflects validated keys being resold and held idle until a buyer eventually uses them.”

The researchers loaded about $60 in total onto their OpenAI and Anthropic accounts, and attackers used up all of it.

How to stay safe

The researchers published honeypot container images on Docker Hub and seven other registries, then shared their findings with Docker. According to the paper, Docker acknowledged the disclosure, and its security team was reviewing the findings.

The number of probing bots and their speed is something developers should worry about. If you use cloud or AI services, a few precautions can help keep your keys safe:

Keep secrets out of what you share. Don’t put keys in code, public repositories, or container images.

Scan before you publish. A bot can find an exposed key within seconds, so a check after publication is too late. The researchers also recommend that registries scan images as they’re uploaded.

Limit what each key can do. In the second round of tests, every OpenAI and Anthropic key that attackers used to burn through credits had unrestricted permissions. No restricted key was used that way. The scanners appear to check permissions first, so a narrowly scoped key gives them less to work with. A narrowly scoped key can only perform specific actions or access particular resources.

Prefer short-lived credentials. AWS recommends using temporary credentials instead of long-term access keys wherever possible.

Set spending limits and alerts. Check whether your provider’s budget setting just sends an alert or sets a hard limit on what you can spend.

If you’ve already published a key, treat it as compromised, even if it was public for only a minute. Revoke it and replace it. Then review account activity and charges.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection catches suspicious activity before it becomes a problem.

articles.title: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
articles.context: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an...
articles.full_text: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes. It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine. “What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.” Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one. Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET. 'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking' OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work. “Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.” That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing. The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t). After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works. The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems. “It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.” 'No blocklist would have helped' In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit. It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then. The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.” While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein. “No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.” Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds. “Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

articles.title: Iran-Aligned Volant Manticore Uses IPFS-Based KuboShell Backdoor in Espionage Campaigns
articles.context: The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in...
articles.full_text:
A previously undocumented Iran-aligned cyber espionage group called Volant Manticore has targeted telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure in Cyprus.

Central to the group's operations is a backdoor called KuboShell that uses the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) and deploys Homa, a post-compromise framework that's a reimplementation of MuddyWater's MuddyC2Go. Evidence indicates that the threat actor has been operational since late August 2025.

Also delivered alongside these tools are Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) programs like MeshCentral and NetLock RMM. In tandem, the group has been observed orchestrating credential harvesting campaigns to harvest email and corporate credentials of some of the impersonated organizations.

The use of legitimate RMM tools for persistent access has been a hallmark of the MuddyWater group, although the adversary has since also increasingly deployed its own malware in attacks. Both MuddyWater and Volant Manticore are assessed to be affiliated with Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).

"While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster," Check Point said in an analysis published today. "Volant Manticore's targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments."

This assessment is based on the use of an older MuddyWater framework and its playbook, while diverging from established modus operandi over time to incorporate its own attack methods like credential-harvesting campaigns. The targeting of Cyprus, a country that does not align with MuddyWater's targeting patterns, and the use of separate infrastructure points to a group that pursues its own strategic objectives.

Attack chains have been found to leverage artificial intelligence (AI)-generated personas in bogus CVs to trick targets into clicking on a link to download the complete resume, resulting in the deployment of KuboShell on the victim's system. The activity is said to have been aimed at a Cyprus-based airline that operates flights between Cyprus and Israel.

This includes a shift toward Saudi Arabian healthcare entities, coinciding with escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

"This fits the MOIS's track record of targeting hospitals and healthcare providers through cyber operations during military conflicts, in some cases attempting to disrupt their operations," the cybersecurity company said.

As recently as September 2026, the group has been found to launch a phishing campaign against Saudi targets, distributing the backdoor and N-able RMM through two different healthcare-themed ZIP archives named "AI_Healthcare_Seminar.zip" and "Ai_Healthcare_Seminar_Online.zip," respectively. Some of the emails have been sent from a compromised account belonging to a private hospital in Saudi Arabia.

A Windows backdoor, KuboShell, uses IPFS for C2 and relies on Pinata to facilitate file transfer over the peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing network.

"On startup, KuboShell checks whether it has administrator privileges. If not, it tries to relaunch itself with higher privileges, which triggers a User Account Control (UAC) prompt," Check Point explained.

"KuboShell retrieves the MAC address of the machine's first network adapter and uses it as a unique identifier for each victim. It then registers the host by uploading a file containing hi, saved to C:\Users\Public\<MAC>.log, using a hard-coded Pinata access token."

Once registered, KuboShell checks Pinata for a command file named <MAC>.txt, and if the file exists, looks up the file’s IPFS identifier and downloads its contents through Pinata's public gateway. The downloaded content is executed via PowerShell in a hidden window. The results of the execution are saved in a file named "C:\Users\Public\<MAC>re.txt" and uploaded back to the server.

It's worth noting that the backdoor is not responsible for capturing the output. Rather, the results are returned only if the received command writes them to the text file. KuboShell then checks for a new command every 60 seconds.

Analysis indicates that KuboShell is primarily used to run basic reconnaissance commands and assess the compromised environment before downloading and executing a more capable backdoor, which includes the modular Homa Framework. This involves a three-stage process -

PowerShell stager, which contacts a hard-coded IP address ("185.205.187[.]109:8000") to fetch a PowerShell loader and execute it in memory

PowerShell loader, which decodes and launches a JavaScript backdoor

JavaScript Backdoor, which implements a continuous C2 loop to receive and execute PowerShell, SSH, and "cmd.exe" commands

It's suspected that the third-stage backdoor is used to execute additional modules, although the precise nature of those components is presently unknown.

"We assess that Homa's client is a JavaScript reimplementation of the older MuddyC2Go client, potentially allowing Volant Manticore to retain the more complex server-side component with minimal modifications, thereby reducing development time and resources," Check Point said.

The post-compromise framework has also been distributed via a macro-enabled Microsoft Word document called "MilitaryHeritageProposal.doc" that's believed to have targeted a Cypriot defense-related government entity. Enabling the content triggers the execution of a VBA backdoor that serves as a conduit for running follow-up payloads or commands using "cmd.exe."

"Volant Manticore shows how Iran's cyber ecosystem continues to reshape itself," Check Point concluded. "What appears to be a group of former MuddyWater operators now operates independently, pairing legacy MuddyWater tooling with new implants of their own while pursuing a regional focus that has until now drawn little attention."

"If MuddyC2Go is the latest MuddyWater framework Volant Manticore's operators had access to, the split may have happened around 2023 as MuddyWater replaced MuddyC2Go with DarkBeatC2 in late 2023.

articles.title: VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities
articles.context: Broadcom on Tuesday announced the release of patches for 23 vulnerabilities across multiple VMware products, including critical-severity flaws in ESX and vCenter
articles.full_text:
Broadcom on Tuesday announced the release of patches for 23 vulnerabilities across multiple VMware products, including critical-severity flaws in ESX and vCenter.

The vCenter patches resolve seven bugs, including a critical authentication bypass issue in the VMware Directory Service tracked as CVE-2026-123903 (CVSS score of 9.8).

Additionally, the fixes target three denial-of-service (DoS) issues in the VMware Directory Service, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS).

The ESX updates resolve seven security issues as well, including three critical-severity weaknesses leading to code execution on the host.

CVE-2026-123910 and CVE-2026-123911 (CVSS score of 9.8) are heap out-of-bounds write and use-after-free flaws in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123912 (CVSS score of 9.3) is an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the XHCI USB controller that requires local administrative privileges on a virtual machine.

An attacker “may exploit this issue to execute code as the virtual machine’s VMX process running on the host. On ESX, the exploitation is contained within the VMX sandbox whereas, on Workstation and Fusion, this may lead to code execution on the machine where Workstation or Fusion is installed,” Broadcom explains.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The remaining four include a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a DoS vulnerability in guest RPC, a security bypass in the host configuration store, and a signature verification bypass.

Broadcom also patched eight flaws in Avi Load Balancer that could lead to code execution with root privileges, privilege escalation to root, command execution, password hash leaks, access to the routing management interface and other resources, and unintended file access, and one in VMware Tools leading to DoS.

According to Broadcom, some of the issues were resolved with the vCenter updates released last week. vCenter version 8.0 U3m contained the fixes, and customers who applied it do not need to update again. vCenter 9.1.x deployments, however, as well as ESX, VMware Tools, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer instances, need to be updated.

“Patches are cumulative, so the updates listed in this advisory also contain the fixes from VMSA-2026-0009 when they are newer than the fixed versions listed in VMSA-2026-0009. However, this advisory does not mention the SDDC Manager updates from VMSA-2026-0009; please ensure you are handling those,” the company notes.

Broadcom makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild, but it’s not uncommon for the company to not warn about exploitation in its public advisories.

On Tuesday, Broadcom also updated its advisory on Node2Shell to add VMware Cloud Foundation version 9.1.2 to the list of fixed releases.

articles.title: ShinyHunters claims to return after FBI arrests, uses old PGP keys as proof
articles.context: The new Tor site, launched on November 23, contains messages in both Russian and English announcing the group's return, distancing itself from alleged impostors, and denouncing...
articles.full_text:
The ShinyHunters extortion gang claims to have returned in posts on a new data leak site after a series of arrests over the past two months targeting alleged members.

The new Tor site, launched on November 23, contains messages in both Russian and English announcing the group's return, distancing itself from alleged impostors, and denouncing a former member who was reportedly arrested and is cooperating with law enforcement.

The site also includes two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys dating back to 2020, including one previously used to authenticate communications with BleepingComputer in August 2025.

BleepingComputer confirmed that both messages were signed using known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang, confirming that the new operators have access to private signing keys historically used by the group.

However, these keys do not confirm whether the individuals behind the new operation are the same people who previously controlled the group, as the keys have circulated among numerous people.

The announcement follows a series of law enforcement operations targeting alleged ShinyHunters members after the group claimed to have breached FBI systems in September using an Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability.

Later that month, Dutch police confirmed the arrest of a 24-year-old Amsterdam man suspected of involvement with ShinyHunters, who was identified in media reports as Pepijn van der Stap, previously known online as Umbreon.

In early October, another alleged ShinyHunters member known as Rey or Saif was reportedly detained in Jordan and is cooperating with law enforcement. Around the same time, Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky was arrested in Pennsylvania in an extortion investigation reportedly linked to ShinyHunters.

After the arrests, ShinyHunters' main representative, who had regularly communicated with BleepingComputer and other media outlets, abruptly stopped responding, and their Telegram account was deleted. Soon after, the group's data leak site went offline.

In the new statement, the purported ShinyHunters operators say they are returning after months of rumors and misinformation circulated about the group.

"We’re finally back. A lot has happened recently, and there’s still plenty going on right now," reads the English announcement.

"To be honest, there’s just too much nonsense going on. Everyone’s telling different stories, but no one is really explaining what’s been happening over the last few months."

The operators of the new data leak site say they will communicate exclusively through the Exploit hacking forum account, which they claim to have controlled since 2020, and through the new Tor site.

The statement also addresses the reported arrest of a hacker and ShinyHunters member known as Rey, Dedale, or Saif, who was reportedly detained in Jordan in late September.

According to the announcement, Rey previously collaborated with ShinyHunters but began operating independently, creating Telegram channels without the group's approval.

"As far as we know, he has already been arrested and is now "actively cooperating" with the authorities," reads the English message.

"We already rotated the PGP key that Rey used for DLS, since it has most likely been compromised."

The message also mocks two other individuals reportedly tied to the ShinyHunters investigation, Umbreon and Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky, referring to their arrests.

"It was a pleasure working with you. And it’s truly a shame that our guys got caught because of such silly mistakes, ones that could easily have been avoided if you fools hadn’t gotten involved with the wrong people," reads the post.

The operators say they plan to launch a new CDN for hosting stolen data and will no longer use any of the existing backup servers.

Old PGP keys used to authenticate new site

To attempt to prove their legitimacy, the operators published two verification messages signed using historical ShinyHunters PGP keys created in January and August 2020.

The keys have the following fingerprints:

ShinyHunters RaidForums PGP key: 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3

ShinyHunters Empire Market PGP key: 828537C15F43F135A8317153CD16A1660CC7CE51

BleepingComputer verified that both messages were signed using these known PGP keys associated with the ShinyHunters extortion gang.

PGP uses a pair of cryptographic keys: a public key that anyone can access and use to verify a message or data, and a private key used to create signatures. The private key must be kept secret to prevent others from impersonating the key's owner.

BleepingComputer previously verified a message received from ShinyHunters on August 26, 2025, using the 1FC4D0B1DEE914BB05B57FABF1F1B98A51C989B3 public key.

Successful verification of the November message with that same public key shows that whoever signed it had access to the same private signing key used in the earlier communications, linking it to the ShinyHunters operation behind the widespread data theft attacks in 2026.

However, both historical keys were revoked in March 2026, when ShinyHunters announced a replacement PGP key with the fingerprint F4953411767DE71BEDCDABCB76F4E26F7A20978A.

At the time, the group used both 2020 keys to authenticate the replacement and stated that the older keys would no longer be used for communications.

Despite this, the November 23 announcement once again uses the two revoked 2020 keys to authenticate another new PGP key, 27DA9D5B183247CADFC322880ABC63E30F73822E.

However, none of the November messages examined by BleepingComputer were signed using the March 2026 replacement key, leaving it unclear whether the new operators also have access to that private key.

Because it was rumored that numerous people had the original 2020 keys, these unfortunately do not prove with certainty that the ShinyHunters group has returned or that the brand has not been revived by imposters.

articles.title: New Inception Extortion Brand Tied to SSO Vishing Campaign
articles.context: ReversingLabs found the lure sites were web-only and used legal-themed lookalike domains, so the campaign never had to pass through email filters
articles.full_text:
Okta and ReversingLabs have linked a new data-extortion brand called Inception to a voice phishing campaign that targeted single sign-on (SSO) credentials and used stolen access to take data.

Okta Threat Intelligence researchers Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels and ReversingLabs researcher Robert Simmons detailed the activity in separate reports published November 23.

Okta's report focused on the operators behind the campaign, while ReversingLabs' analysis mapped the infrastructure that tied it to Inception.

A Likely Rebrand After ShinyHunters Arrests

Okta tracked the operators as O-UNC-053, a cluster at work since March 2026. It had previously associated the group with the ShinyHunters data leak site, where companies it had gone after were listed from March to September.

Okta said it did not know precisely how the two were connected, though the link "may have involved an agreement" between the cluster and the site's operators.

After two people allegedly tied to ShinyHunters were arrested in September, the gang's leak site went offline, and Okta saw no O-UNC-053 targets published on any leak site until Inception appeared on November 16. Okta found that targets appearing on Inception had been preceded by O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.

Okta said the cluster had "very likely changed their brand affiliation" but could not determine with high confidence whether O-UNC-053 operated the Inception data leak site itself or partnered with another extortion group.

The company was also unable to validate whether the published data was authentic. ReversingLabs counted seven claimed victims by November 21, which it treated as unverified claims.

Read more on ShinyHunters: Net Closes Around ShinyHunters with Another FBI Arrest

How the Vishing Campaign Works

The attacks relied on vishing, with callers posing as support staff and pressuring employees to reset passwords through fake sign-in pages. The campaign captured usernames and passwords before seeking additional multifactor authentication (MFA) factors, including one-time codes or push approvals.

ReversingLabs found the lure sites were web-only and used legal-themed lookalike domains, so the campaign never had to pass through email filters. It confirmed the phishing kit itself on 21 domains and attributed 41 more to the operation at a high confidence level and four at a medium level. Most mimicked Okta sign-in pages, though the kit adapted to other identity providers.

Okta noted that the kit could not get past phishing-resistant authentication. The two companies' advice included passkeys or FIDO2 security keys, checks on a caller's identity before help desks reset passwords or MFA and limiting sensitive applications to managed devices.

ReversingLabs also advised checking DNS, proxy and identity logs going back to October 21 for signs of the campaign.

articles.title: European Commission confirms data theft in EU Academy breach
articles.context: The European Commission, the European Union's main executive body, has confirmed that attackers breached its EU Academy online learning hub and stole the personal data of an...
articles.full_text:
The European Commission, the European Union's main executive body, has confirmed that attackers breached its EU Academy online learning hub and stole the personal data of an undisclosed number of users.

This follows the Commission's Thursday disclosure that hackers breached its systems on October 22 using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing framework, causing service disruptions that also affected its internal Sysper HR platform.

"As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several ​applications and most of them have since been restored. The investigation is still ongoing," spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters at the time. "We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings as they come. We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole."

While the Commission said it hasn't received a ransom demand and has yet to attribute the attack, Regnier confirmed in a Monday press briefing that the attackers also breached the EU Academy platform, used to learn more about EU policies and follow EU online courses.

Regnier also confirmed a data leak following the EU Academy incident, which is still under investigation and has affected users' personal information, including their names and email addresses.

"And as a precautionary measure, given that the fact that there is a data leak that is confirmed including names and email addresses,today there was a message to all users on the EU academy website," he added. "This is definitely a cyber attack, a cyber campaign that was targeted against the Commission via an AI assisted tool. When it comes to the attribution, we would need the investigation to be concluded to be able to find out who is behind this."

The Commission has also published a notice on the EU Academy website about this cybersecurity incident, informing users that public access to the platform has been disabled and warning them to be suspicious of unsolicited emails or messages that may be part of potential phishing attacks.

The European Commission disclosed another data breach in February after discovering on January 30 that a mobile device management platform used to manage staff devices had been compromised.

More recently, it disclosed an additional incident on March 27 after BleepingComputer reached out for confirmation that the Commission's Amazon cloud environment had been breached. The EU's Cybersecurity Service (CERT-EU) later attributed the March cloud hack to the TeamPCP threat group and said the resulting breach exposed the data of at least 29 other Union entities.

These recent security breaches follow the Commission's January 20 proposal for new cybersecurity legislation to strengthen defenses against cybercrime groups and state-backed actors targeting Europe's critical infrastructure.

articles.title: Police disrupt 57 illegal streaming services with 7.3 million visits
articles.context: Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss
articles.full_text:
Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries have disrupted 57 illegal streaming services that operated hundreds of websites and drew over 7.3 million visits each year.

Such illegal IPTV services offer access to television channels, live sports, and movies without permission from the copyright owners for a small monthly fee.

According to the European Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance (AAPA) trade association, legitimate service providers lose around €4.83 billion annually as roughly 60 million people in Europe use illegal platforms for streaming content.

"The operation resulted in the disruption of 57 illegal IPTV services and the identification of 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, with a combined annual traffic of more than 7.3 million visits. Investigators have so far traced over EUR 26 million in cryptocurrency transactions, with further analysis ongoing," Europol said in a Tuesday press release.

"The operation targeted a criminal market worth billions of euros annually, in which illegal streaming providers sell unauthorised access to premium television channels, live sports and films, often collecting subscription payments through cryptocurrency."

As part of this joint action, which also involved Europol, the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO), INTERPOL, and AAPA, the investigators also partnered with crypto industry experts from Binance, Coinbase, and Chainalysis to trace cryptocurrency payments and identify the financial networks powering these illegal IPTV services.

They did this by looking for links between the illegal IPTV services, crypto wallets, financial transactions, and the individuals who control these services, who used the wallets to receive and transfer payments, making it easier to move money between countries and hide the origin of their profits.

Europol and the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) joined forces in 2016 to create the Intellectual Property Crime Coordinated Coalition (IPC3), which operates within Europol and targets counterfeiting and online and offline piracy.

In June, another major international operation coordinated by Bulgaria with Europol's support, dubbed "Operation KRATOS 2," resulted in the removal of more than 27,000 illegal streaming URLs, the shutdown of nine organized crime groups, and 29 arrests.

That followed Operation KRATOS, another international anti-piracy operation carried out in summer 2024, which shut down a massive illegal streaming network with over 22 million users worldwide.

Earlier this year, in January, Europol, Eurojust, and Interpol also coordinated Operation Switch Off, a global law enforcement action that led to the seizure of three industrial-scale illegal IPTV services.

More recently, in May, Italian authorities dismantled the CINEMAGOAL piracy platform, which provided illegal access to many online streaming platforms, including Netflix, Spotify, and Disney+.

articles.title: From Vulnerability Noise to Resilience: Rethinking Security in the AI Era
articles.context: A high or critical Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score can command attention, but the business question is whether the vulnerable code is relevant and exploitable...
articles.full_text:
Written by: George Manuelian, Chief Strategy Officer, RapidFort

The modern software stack has become an iceberg. The application code customers and security teams see at the surface is only a small portion of what is being shipped. Beneath it sit operating systems, frameworks, libraries, packages, and transitive dependencies, with much of it drawn from open source or third parties.

As AI accelerates software development, that hidden complexity has become an even more critical security challenge.

For business and technology leaders, the question is no longer simply how many vulnerabilities exist. It is where does meaningful risk live, which vulnerabilities can be exploited in our environment, and how we can reduce that risk without turning developers into full-time vulnerability managers.

The answer requires a fundamental shift from vulnerability accumulation to continuous software resilience.

First step: Recognizing composition of modern software

The typical containerized stack is layers of base operating system software, packages, libraries, language frameworks and dependencies, and the application itself. The application a company writes may represent only a small portion of what it ultimately ships.

That is important because vulnerabilities multiply. A vulnerable package in a base image is not necessarily one vulnerability in practice; it can be replicated across every application and container that uses that image.

In light of this, executives should ask a different question of their security programs: How much of the reported risk is relevant to the way our software operates? Traditional scanning frequently identifies the presence of a vulnerable component without establishing whether that component is loaded, executing, reachable or exposed.

A software bill of materials (SBOM) identifies what exists; a runtime bill of materials (RBOM) can pinpoint what is actually being used. That distinction can dramatically reduce noise.

For example, in the real world from a customer, an NGINX image containing 152 packages and 48 CVEs had only 47 packages actually running in the application. More than 80% of the software was not being exercised. The lesson is not that every unused package is harmless, but that security teams need operational context before assigning remediation urgency.

This is also why severity alone has become an inadequate basis for prioritization. A high or critical Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) score can command attention, but the business question is whether the vulnerable code is relevant and exploitable in the environment.

There are four contextual factors increasingly shaping remediation decisions: Whether a vulnerability is exposed, whether it is a known exploited vulnerability, whether exploitation is automatable, and whether exploitation would have meaningful technical impact.

The shift from severity to exploitability and reachability is important because it changes the operating model. Instead of asking engineering teams to chase the largest number on a scanner dashboard, leaders should ask whether the organization has enough visibility to determine what is running, what is reachable, and what is exposed.

As a result, security becomes a business-risk exercise rather than a race to close tickets.

Eliminate Up to 99.9% of Container CVEs Without Code Changes

RapidFort Curated Images give your team 35,000+ near-zero CVE container images, rebuilt and hardened every 24 hours.

Swap in a hardened base image and remove exploitable vulnerabilities at the source, with no code, OS or pipeline changes.

Learn More

Hardening is the important next step

Hardening should not mean merely passing a configuration benchmark. It should also mean removing software and functionality that the application does not need

. Every unnecessary library, shell, package manager, build utility, or default component increases the amount of software that must be maintained and potentially gives an attacker additional tools if a container is compromised.

Runtime profiling is a proven approach for identifying these unused components and removing them systematically.

AI makes this discipline more important

AI-assisted development can rapidly generate code and pull in packages, but developers may not always know which dependencies were introduced or whether they remain necessary as the application evolves.

For example, a development environment in which developers may have to ask the AI system which Python version or packages were used because the model generated much of the implementation is a warning sign for governance.

Speed of development cannot come at the expense of knowing what is being shipped.

No one is going to slow AI development. The answer is to put security controls into the pipeline so developers do not have to perform every security task manually. Clean, curated base images; runtime profiling; removal of unused components; vulnerability context; and automated rebuilding can become repeatable parts of CI/CD.

The objective is to make the secure path the default path.

Introducing Zero Trust software architecture

Zero Trust has traditionally been associated with network access and identity. But when organizations continuously ingest open source and third-party software, they also need to question the software entering their environments.

Software should be verified, trusted components should be maintained in controlled registries, and the software should be continuously evaluated as it moves through development, testing and production – following the common principles of Zero Trust.

This represents a meaningful change in how software supply chain security should be managed. The goal should not be a perfect vulnerability dashboard.

The goal should be a development system that continuously produces software with less unnecessary code, fewer meaningful vulnerabilities, and a smaller attack surface.

For example, one customer reduced an initial 5,286 findings to three unresolved vulnerabilities within 48 hours by combining profiling, curated images, and removal of unused components.

The strategic lesson learned

Vulnerability remediation should become a manufacturing process, not a recurring emergency. If organizations wait until a scanner produces a massive backlog, they have already allowed complexity to become technical debt.

If instead they control what enters the software supply chain, understand what actually runs, prioritize based on reachability and impact, remove what is unnecessary, and continuously rebuild from cleaner components, security becomes part of software production itself.

This approach also changes the conversation between security and engineering. Developers should not be expected to fix every finding simply because a scanner found it. They need context, automation and a clear understanding of which risks require action.

Security leaders need visibility into runtime behavior and the ability to distinguish a theoretical exposure from a vulnerability that can actually affect the business.

The future of software security in the AI era

The future of software security belongs to organizations that manage complexity continuously. AI will accelerate development, it’s a given. Open source will remain foundational, that’s understood. Neither trend is going away, nor should it of course.

But both make it more important to establish disciplined software intake, strong supply-chain controls, runtime visibility, effective hardening, and automated remediation.

Ultimately, the objective is not simply to reduce the number of CVEs on a report. It is to build software that contains less unnecessary functionality, relies on cleaner components, exposes fewer opportunities to attackers, and can be continuously refreshed without overwhelming those responsible for delivering it

. Software supply chain security works best when profiling, verification, clean images, and removal of unused components are built directly into the pipeline.

The executive mandate for the AI era must stop treating vulnerability management as a downstream cleanup exercise. Build security into the way software is assembled, tested and deployed.

When continuous remediation becomes part of the normal development life cycle, organizations can move faster without accepting vulnerability volume as an unavoidable cost of innovation.
