articles.title: European Commission Uncovers Data Breach in Cyberattack Investigation
articles.context: The European Commission (EC) on Monday confirmed that a recently disclosed AI-assisted cyberattack resulted in the compromise of personal information
articles.full_text:
The European Commission (EC) on Monday confirmed that a recently disclosed AI-assisted cyberattack resulted in the compromise of personal information.

The attack, disclosed last week, prompted the temporary shutdown of several applications. At the time, the organization said it had found no evidence that personal information belonging to Commission staff had been compromised.

Spokesperson Thomas Regnier revealed during a press briefing on Monday that the investigation has since uncovered a data breach affecting EU Academy, an online learning platform used by people outside the EC to take courses and learn about European Union policies.

Compromised information includes names and email addresses of EU Academy users, but the full extent of the breach is still being investigated.

Access to EU Academy has been suspended during the investigation and the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) has been notified. Potentially affected individuals have not been informed directly.

“Important to keep in mind at this point in time that the exact scale of the data leak is still subject to the investigation, so there was no reach-out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency,” Regnier explained.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The cyberattack was detected on October 22 and the EC said last week that it had largely been contained. The spokesperson declined to comment on Monday on whether the incident was over, and said attribution could only be made once the investigation is concluded.

Euronews reported that the Commission suspects a China-backed threat group. According to the publication, the attack has yet to be fully contained.

The EC said the intrusion involved AI, but it did not publicly identify the tool leveraged by the hackers. According to Euronews, the suspected China link is based partly on the use of Artex, an AI-powered penetration testing framework with Chinese roots that has been widely used by threat actors.

articles.title: Cloudera helps enterprises deploy sovereign AI without proprietary lock-in
articles.context: Cloudera has announced Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty, a solution and partner ecosystem designed to give organizations jurisdictional, operational, and technical control...
articles.full_text:
Cloudera has announced Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty, a solution and partner ecosystem designed to give organizations jurisdictional, operational, and technical control across their data, cloud, and AI lifecycle.

Bringing together Cloudera Anywhere Cloud, Cloudera’s Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric, and natively integrated Mistral open-weight models and Mistral Forge, the solution enables organizations to deploy governed data and private AI across sovereign clouds, private data centers, and fully air-gapped environments.

Built on open standards and an open source foundation, Cloudera provides consistent governance and security across these environments while allowing organizations to determine where individual workloads run and adapt as regulatory, operational, and business requirements evolve without forced data migrations or proprietary lock-in.

Regulation, including privacy and data sovereignty requirements, is among the top three barriers to scaling AI, according to recent Cloudera research. Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty addresses this challenge by enabling organizations to:

Maintain verifiable sovereign control across data and AI with zero-trust access controls, policies, lineage, and governance that remain consistent across sovereign cloud and private infrastructure. This supports compliance readiness for requirements including the EU AI Act, DORA, CADA, NIS2, Seals Sovereignty Framework, and others globally.

Put sovereign AI into production securely by extending access and governance policies to the enterprise context that AI agents retrieve and use. Integrated Mistral open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling agentic workflows and local model customization while keeping sensitive enterprise intelligence within existing security boundaries.

Shift workloads as requirements change without costly data movement through Cloudera Anywhere Cloud’s hybrid and modular architecture, enabling compute to move across sovereign infrastructure providers and private data centers without refactoring applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data.

“AI moved sovereignty from a compliance question to an operational one,” said Patrick Moorhead, CEO and Chief Analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy.

“A company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on. Walling off sensitive workloads isn’t the answer; it just makes data and AI harder to manage. Cloudera has a long history in hybrid data management, and extending it to open-weight models across sovereign, on-prem, and public cloud is a logical step. The next step is how quickly customers get it into production.”

“Digital sovereignty has to be an architectural decision, not a compliance exercise after the fact,” said Sergio Gago, Chief Technology Officer at Cloudera.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change. We’re giving organizations a foundation they can build on for the long term, so they can adopt the next generation of AI without having to rethink their sovereignty strategy every time the technology evolves.”

Expanding the sovereign AI ecosystem

Building on its strategic partnership with Mistral, Cloudera is expanding customer choice through a growing network of sovereign cloud and implementation partners. Cloudera delivers an end-to-end, zero-trust approach to sovereign data and AI while giving customers the flexibility to combine sovereign deployments with other cloud and on-premises infrastructure.

This allows organizations to apply strict sovereignty controls where required without forcing the rest of their data estate into the same architecture or creating isolated security boundaries.

articles.title: Astelia blocks attack paths to vulnerabilities without waiting for patches
articles.context: Astelia has announced autonomous network mitigation, a new capability that defends against AI-driven exploits by blocking attack paths to reachable vulnerabilities at the...
articles.full_text:
Astelia has announced autonomous network mitigation, a new capability that defends against AI-driven exploits by blocking attack paths to reachable vulnerabilities at the network level. Organizations can now eliminate the 1% of vulnerabilities attackers can reach without waiting for a patch.

The mitigation workflow · 6 steps, 1 approval branch (Source: Astelia)

Frontier AI models have cut the time to exploit to almost zero. Manual triage and remediation can’t keep up, so organizations need to automate how they respond. Autonomous remediation has become the industry’s latest buzzword, but it isn’t a viable option for large enterprises, where every patch needs a change window so it doesn’t break important business processes. Often, there is no patch to apply at all because the vendor hasn’t released a fix yet, or, for older and end-of-life systems, never will.

Blocking threats at the network level avoids both problems and keeps pace with AI-driven exploits. Instead of changing the vulnerable system, Astelia blocks the path an attacker would use to reach it, automatically and within policies the organization sets, without waiting for a ticket or a change window. Nothing on the asset changes, so business-critical systems, including OT, stay online. It works whether or not a patch exists.

This approach is built on Astelia’s reachability analysis. Astelia maps the organization’s real network topology and uses agentic AI to analyze what each exploit requires. By correlating those exploit conditions with the topology, it determines which vulnerabilities attackers can reach, and through which paths. In one enterprise deployment, approximately 40 million vulnerabilities came down to fewer than 2,000 that were reachable.

For each reachable vulnerability, Astelia uses the same topology to find the most effective choke point on the attack path, then drives the mitigation there through the organization’s WAF or IPS/IDS. A single rule at that point protects every vulnerable server behind it, where patching would take one change per server. Because Astelia only mitigates paths it has proven reachable, it doesn’t add rules for exposure that doesn’t exist. Initial support covers WAF and IPS/IDS rules, with firewall rules planned.

Unlike a patch, which can break a system and can’t always be undone, every mitigation Astelia applies can be rolled back, so teams can act quickly without putting business operations at risk.

Each organization sets the guardrails. Through Astelia Agents, teams set up a dedicated autonomous network mitigation agent that applies mitigations on its own within the policies they define, and connect it to their other agents to respond to urgent threats such as zero-days and critical disclosures like the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws of October 2026, which left end-of-life PHP servers with no official fix.

Teams can require human approval for specific environments or actions, and every action is logged and auditable. Astelia’s analysis continues to run on read-only integrations, and mitigation actions use scoped permissions that each organization enables and controls.

“For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” said Alon Noy, CEO of Astelia. “That advice stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does. The same network data that tells us a vulnerability is reachable tells us where to cut it off, so we block it there automatically and the exposure is closed before an attacker can use it.”

articles.title: Signal blocks AI assistants from snooping on your encrypted messages
articles.context: Some may consider it very convenient for their mobile operating system's agentic AI features to use their ability to look at their screen to do something like add an event to...
articles.full_text:
Signal, the privacy-focused encrypted messaging app, has started blocking Apple and Google's AI assistants from snooping on users' private conversations.

Some may consider it very convenient for their mobile operating system's agentic AI features to use their ability to look at their screen to do something like add an event to their calendar. They may be happy for Onscreen Awareness for Apple's Siri and Google's Gemini Intelligence to answer questions and do tasks for them.

But it's far from welcome when the screen shows an encrypted conversation that was supposed to be private.

Once a message has been captured, it could end up in a locally-stored database or uploaded to a remote server - potentially putting everyone in the chat at risk.

Signal's president, Meredith Whittaker, said in a blog post that unless proper safeguards were in place, putting AI agents into operating systems was "an existential threat to privacy at the application layer."

If you are running iOS 27 on your iPhone, Signal now blocks screenshots inside the app - which means Siri cannot read message content from the screen. A new setting called "Block Siri AI" allows users to toggle the feature on or off.

Meanwhile, on Android, Signal attempts to look where it can for an AI assistant trying to read the screen and when it spots one, automatically turns on its existing "Screen security" setting.

There are repercussions, of course, for anyone on iOS who wants to sometimes take screenshots of their own conversations, perhaps for innocent reasons. You can switch the protection off, but - as Signal warns - doing that might expose your chats to AI agents.

Furthermore, Signal admits that its efforts do not prevent every method an AI agent might use to try to read messages being sent via the app.

There is also no protection yet for Mac users, because Signal says it cannot reliably block the taking of screenshots on macOS. For that reason, the best advice if you are using the Signal desktop app on your Mac is to add it to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri.

And, of course, you need to bear in mind that there are also third-party AI agents, such as Meta's Muse, which can access sensitive data through accessibility permissions that users are encouraged to grant during setup.

Signal has called on Microsoft, Apple, and Google to to give developers an easy, well-documented way to opt their apps out of sharing data with AI agents, and to publish better technical details of how their AI features access and process data.

It is worth bearing in mind that this issue is not unique to Signal - any app that handles sensitive information faces the same problem. The difference is that Signal is publicly trying to do something about it.

As Whittaker says, "Signal is the canary in the coal mine."

articles.title: Impact of AI on CVEs : PROTECTION STRATEGIES
articles.context: By combining an AI-discovered vulnerability in the libheif image-parsing library (CVE-2026-47178) with a Linux kernel privilege escalation exploit, we turned a single malformed...
articles.full_text:
For enterprise software development operations, AI now handles work that was once too hard or too costly to justify, from reverse engineering and debugging to building fuzzing harnesses. Recent high profile security incidents shows how far this goes:

AI agents escaping ChatGPT sandboxes through zero-day logic flaws

Claude models breaking out of test environments while surfacing critical zero-days.

Independent researchers using LLMs to find dozens of vulnerabilities in heavily audited codebases.

Higher Volume and Lower Quality CVEs

In the first blog of this series, we explained how AI is a multiplier for security research experts, resulting in faster bug discovery and PoC development, which leaves more time for deep architectural analysis. For novices, however, it means the ability to create a large volume of low-quality CVEs that increase response time and amplify triage noise.

Published CVEs are accelerating sharply reaching 75,000 in just the first nine months of 2026

Perhaps a more serious consequence of vulnerability research with AI is “democratization” of nation state capabilities. It used to take the resources of a nation state to launch sophisticated hacks such as 0-click smartphone attacks and unauthenticated RCEs (Remote Code Execution) on enterprise servers. Using AI, these and other attacks can be launched by smaller groups such as ransomware gangs and even individual malicious actors.

Real World Evidence

This year alone, we have had more than 10+ Linux LPE (Local Privilege Escalation) vulnerabilities and have also seen multiple RCEs in popular open-source packages that power the internet, such as PHP, Chrome and Redis.

Confirmed in-the-wild exploits across major open-source projects from 2023 to October 2026

The trajectory is clear: CISOs and security teams should prepare themselves for disclosure of high severity vulnerabilities in well-known industry components by professional and amateur security researchers on a monthly basis.

Example: JFrog’s Zero-Click Chain

Exploiting a malformed image tile to achieve zero-click remote code execution

To demonstrate how AI compresses weeks of advanced exploit development into a matter of hours, our research team built a full zero-click attack chain targeting everyday desktop software. By combining an AI-discovered vulnerability in the libheif image-parsing library (CVE-2026-47178) with a Linux kernel privilege escalation exploit, we turned a single malformed image file into complete root-level system takeover without a single click from the user.

Libheif – Malicious images as an infection vector

The danger of parser vulnerabilities are well documented, , especially those that parse untrusted input sent from an attacker without user interaction. Vulnerabilities like these have been used extensively by nation-states and PSOAs (private-sector offensive actors), as well as cybercriminals, to deploy malware on systems with minimal, and in some cases, no human interaction whatsoever.

CVE-2026-47178 – Heap out-of-bounds write to popping calc

Feeling inspired by how nation-state-grade spyware infects devices, often using format parsing as the initial access vector, we started researching libheif, which is a library implementing the parsing of the HEIF image format.

Exploit flow from a malformed image tile to heap corruption and control-flow hijack

CVE-2026-47178 is a heap out-of-bounds write in the UNCI decoder in libheif that allows an attacker to overwrite virtual function pointers on the heap, thus leading to remote code execution. Leveraging AI, we discovered the vulnerability within 2 hours, as opposed to the weeks of research it would take a professional using conventional methods.

It took us another 5 hours to turn it into a reliable exploit against Debian’s File Explorer, without user interaction.

Researching & Confirming our Findings

The research environment was quite straightforward: We compiled heif-dec, the library-bundled C++ binary for parsing HEIF images using libheif with AddressSanitizer, and instructed the AI to find a heap out-of-bounds write using static analysis only and confirm its hypothesis dynamically via a crash under ASAN.

AddressSanitizer crash report confirming a heap-buffer-overflow during image decoding

The ASAN essentially acts as a truth indicator (oracle). This result tells us immediately that the LLM did not hallucinate its finding, and the finding is an actionable, real vulnerability.

We may now proceed to developing the actual exploit:

Debugger output showing a crash due to an overwritten vtable pointer from a virtual function call

Through specific heap manipulation, a technique known as heap feng shui, we successfully overwrote a virtual function pointer, a C++ object data structure, granting us direct control over the instruction pointer and completing another critical milestone. The classic convention is to set the instruction pointer to 0x41414141, to demonstrate instruction pointer control.

The final stage is to turn our control flow hijack into code execution. By default the stack is non executable, so we must utilize gadgets, or useful pieces of code that already exist in the executable’s memory space, for our needs.

Since our target was the gnome file explorer, nautilus, we decided to take a look as to how it decodes these heif images, and noticed that it uses a binary called `libheif-thumbnailer`, a binary that’s similar to libheif-dec, which uses the libheif library, alongside other libraries.

The library that’s particularly important this time is libdav1d, which is another codec. The library provided a useful gadget, akin to a one_gadget, that allows us to run `system()` with our own string specified in the `rdi` register, which is just perfect.

Now, we can run any code that we want, but not as root, and that’s the next stage.

DirtyClone – Elevating Linux LPE privileges

Now that we have remote code execution, we can begin elevating our privileges. We previously disclosed an LPE in the Linux kernel as a result of an incomplete patch of the dirtyfrag vulnerability. We won’t go in depth into the details of how the exploit works, but you can more info our previous blog post.

Exploit chain turning a corrupted vtable pointer into arbitrary code execution

The following is a summary of the attack scenario:

An attacker, using a delivery mechanism such as a messaging app (different delivery mechanism than what we outlined here), or even just downloading the file unwittingly and just navigating to the directory where the file is stored via file manager, will cause remote code execution as root.

How Can JFrog Help?

SCA scanning often begins by matching component versions against public CVE records. While this identifies potentially vulnerable dependencies, it may also report issues that are not applicable to the way a specific application uses them.

JFrog Advanced Security’s Contextual Analysis goes beyond version matching. It examines source code, binaries, configurations, and dependency paths to decide whether the vulnerable conditions are actually present, and only then reports a CVE as Applicable.

Take CVE-2026-47178 in libheif. A version match would flag every artifact that contains an affected libheif. Contextual Analysis marks it Applicable only when both conditions are met:

libheif was compiled with -DWITH_UNCOMPRESSED_CODEC=ON

the application calls the vulnerable function heif_decode_image

In the scan below, JFrog Xray found both: libheif.so.1.19.8 built with the flag, and a reference to heif_decode_image in /app/heif_app. Each piece of evidence comes with its path, offset, and symbol, so teams can verify the verdict instead of trusting it blindly. When the evidence is incomplete, Xray returns Undetermined rather than a false positive.

Validating CVE applicability through binary, function-level, and configuration evidence.

JFrog Security Research and Severity Assessment

JFrog Xray is strengthened by CVE research and enrichment from the JFrog Security Research team. Rather than treating every CVE equally, the team focuses mainly on High and Critical CVEs. For these, researchers analyze real-world exploitability, assign a JFrog Severity Score, document the conditions that determine applicability, and provide actionable remediation or mitigation guidance.

When JFrog’s analysis differs from a public CVSS rating, Xray can present a separate JFrog Severity analysis based on technical evidence and likelihood of exploitation. This gives teams another signal for prioritization instead of requiring them to rely on a single external base score.

JFrog Advanced Security complements Xray’s research-backed enrichment with Contextual Analysis. According to JFrog’s internal statistics, Contextual Analysis covered an average of 80% of High and Critical CVEs in customer scans. The same data found that an average of 85% of High and Critical findings were marked as not applicable, helping teams focus remediation on a smaller set of relevant issues. Among the NVD CVEs reassessed by JFrog researchers in 2025, JFrog’s severity assessment was lower for 96% of those rated Critical and 65% of those rated High. Together, JFrog Advanced Security’s Contextual Analysis and Xray’s research-backed severity reassessment help teams reduce CVE noise and direct remediation toward vulnerabilities that represent the greatest threat to their applications.

Take Aways

AI is uncovering real vulnerabilities faster, but also increasing false reports, inflated scores, and pressure on already overloaded maintainers and security teams. As discovery outpaces validation and patching, CVE volume and severity alone are no longer enough to guide remediation. In the AI era, the challenge is not simply finding more vulnerabilities, but identifying which findings are real, reachable, and urgent. Combining vendor guidance with contextual analysis and research-backed severity helps teams focus their limited time on the vulnerabilities that pose genuine risk.

Speak to a JFrog security expert to find out how we can help you effectively manage CVEs in today’s challenging environment.

articles.title: McDonald's Japan data breach exposes customer location information
articles.context: Sejiyama found that attackers are now probing websites and APIs for access-control, configuration, and authentication weaknesses, and exploiting known (n-day) vulnerabilities to...
articles.full_text:
McDonald's Japan, the fast-food giant's Japanese subsidiary, has disclosed a data breach after attackers accessed a database containing sensitive information for users of the company's official smartphone app.

Founded in 1940, McDonald's is now a multinational fast-food chain that operates more than 40,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries and serves tens of millions of customers daily.

In a Friday statement, the company's Japanese subsidiary confirmed that threat actors gained access to its official app's database and said the exposed information includes the users' product purchase history, IP addresses, mobile device location data, and customer management IDs (which cannot be used to identify the customers' email addresses or member IDs).

McDonald's Japan also added that the exposed data doesn't include the affected customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, or credit card information.

While it has yet to reveal when it detected the attack or how many individuals had their data stolen, the company said a follow-up investigation found no service disruption or misuse of official apps as a result of the incident.

"We are working to invalidate any credentials used for unauthorized access, investigate the relevant systems, and report to the Personal Information Protection Commission," it said. "In addition, we will strive to strengthen security measures and prevent recurrence."

This isn't the first data breach to affect McDonald's in recent years, with the fast food giant disclosing a breach in June 2021 after attackers breached its systems and stole information belonging to employees and customers from the US, South Korea, and Taiwan.

In 2017, McDonald's also patched a cross-site scripting (XSS) security flaw that affected its official website and exposed customers' plain-text passwords.

Japanese companies under attack

Last month, Burger King Japan also disclosed a major data breach after attackers stole 11.18 million customer records that were later leaked online.

The two incidents affecting the two Japanese fast food chains add to a large wave of cyberattacks impacting high-profile Japanese companies since the start of the year, including Japan Airlines, entertainment system maker Daiichi Kosho, cloud and digital infrastructure firm IDC Frontier, Japanese publishing giant Nikkei, cloud and data center service provider Sakura Internet, taxi operator Nihon Kotsu, telecommunications giant KDDI, and many others.

Macnica researcher Yutaka Sejiyama has logged 288 cybersecurity incidents affecting Japanese organizations involving personal information theft or exposure since the start of the year.

Sejiyama found that attackers are now probing websites and APIs for access-control, configuration, and authentication weaknesses, and exploiting known (n-day) vulnerabilities to find other victims.

articles.title: Address AI Agent Risks or Face Action, FCA Warns Financial Firms
articles.context: The UK’s financial regulator has warned firms that they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action
articles.full_text:
The UK’s financial regulator has warned firms that they must address cybersecurity risks from the deployment of AI agents, or face regulatory action.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said that AI agents are being widely deployed in the financial services sector to improve productivity and convenience to customers.

“But these products can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive in relation to their finances and data,” the regulator noted.

Banks now using these AI agents to initiate transactions, move money and make investment decisions.

Without appropriate safeguards in place, such as strict access controls, agents have been observed taking dangerous actions such as gaining access to sensitive systems and data, even in pursuit of legitimate aims.

The FCA guidance, published on November 24, said that senior managers responsible for AI models deployed in a specific area of the business need to take “reasonable steps” to understand the risks arising from AI. This includes providing effective oversight and ensuring governance controls and escalation arrangements are appropriate for the risks.

Regulated financial organizations should consider any liabilities from accepting agent instructions and whether it is appropriate to accept payments instructed by an AI agent.

They should also help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

Responsibility for complying with regulatory obligations remains with senior managers and the organization as a whole, whether the firm deploys agentic AI themselves or relies on a third-party provider, the FCA emphasized.

Read now: Bank of England, FCA and Treasury Raise Alarm Over Frontier AI

“We expect you to demonstrate that you understand the systems you use, the degree of autonomy those systems have, the risks they create and the controls necessary to manage those risks in real time and in stress situations,” the authority wrote.

“We will assess the services firms provide through agentic products, including how they develop over time, to ensure they keep to regulatory requirements,” it continued.

Failure to adhere to existing regulatory requirements, including data protection laws, will see the FCA use its powers to sanction non-compliant organizations. These powers include imposing financial penalties, prohibiting individuals from carrying out regulated activities, public censure and prosecution.

The FCA added that it welcomes early engagement from those deploying agentic AI in their products and systems, and that it offers support services including testing whether these tools meet regulatory requirements.

articles.title: GTA 6 hacker sentenced to seven years and released the same day
articles.context: The Lapsus$ member who leaked footage of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) was sentenced to seven years in prison on Monday and released from custody on licence the same day, City of...
articles.full_text:
The Lapsus$ member who leaked footage of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) was sentenced to seven years in prison on Monday and released from custody on licence the same day, City of London Police announced.

Arion Kurtaj, 21, formerly of Oxfordshire, pleaded guilty to six charges, including fraud and computer misuse offences, at Woolwich Crown Court on 16 November. The court set a nine-year term and then took off two years for the time he had spent under a hospital order.

Hacking Rockstar from a hotel room

Kurtaj was on bail when he went after Rockstar Games. In September 2022 he had been moved to a hotel for his own protection. From there, according to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), he broke back into company networks using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a Fire Stick.

He took 90 gameplay videos of the unreleased game, posted them online under the name “TeaPotUberHacker” and threatened to leak the source code in an attempt to blackmail the developer.

Uber and Revolut were hit during the same period. Prosecutors said the Uber attack, in which Kurtaj stole and deleted data and sent a lewd image to employees, cost the company more than $2.8 million. At Revolut, he compromised data belonging to thousands of customers.

A year earlier he had gained remote access to systems at BT/EE. The CPS linked that intrusion to a jump in unauthorised SIM swaps at the telecoms provider in November 2021.

Lengthy investigation

Police worked with law enforcement agencies abroad and with private industry partners on the case, which covered hacks carried out between August 2020 and September 2022.

“This was a lengthy investigation which spanned a number of years and highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online,” said Detective Inspector Mike O’Sullivan of the force’s Cyber Crime Unit.

“That said, Kurtaj knew what he was doing when he carried out these crimes and has finally admitted his involvement,” he added.

O’Sullivan thanked the targeted companies, whose “willingness to work with law enforcement may have prevented other organisations becoming victims of the group’s activities.”

Four years in the courts

Kurtaj was first arrested in September 2022. Doctors found him unfit to stand trial, and in 2023, after a jury decided he had carried out the hacks, he was given an indefinite hospital order.

In January 2026 a court ruled that the order could be lifted, and the original charges were listed for trial. While on remand, Kurtaj was caught with a mobile phone in prison, which prosecutors said he used in March 2026 to send a mocking message to 999.

“We hope this case serves as a lesson that these types of acts will not be tolerated. Although cyber crime is borderless, we will seek to utilise the co-operation of partner agencies and international law enforcement to ensure that offenders are brought to justice no matter where they offend from,” O’Sullivan concluded.

articles.title: New Shirudo tool uses AI to shield unpatched Linux systems from exploits
articles.context: OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo that deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI and Cisco launched an open-source Linux security tool named Shirudo that deploys temporary runtime protections to block vulnerability exploitation while administrators prepare and roll out patches, without restarting services.

Shirudo leverages the eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) mechanism in Linux to monitor for suspicious activity and deploy targeted protections called "shields."

eBPF is a Linux technology that lets programs run in a controlled environment within the operating system's kernel without modifying its source code or requiring a restart.

It enables real-time monitoring of system and network activity, performance analysis, and enforcement of targeted security protections, making it an ideal operational basis for Shirudo.

Shirudo’s shields aim to block malicious behavior in a targeted way, leaving legitimate application operations undisturbed. OpenAI highlights four core capabilities for the tool:

Live protection: Blocks vulnerable code paths without restarting systems, letting operators assess shield impact before enforcing them.

AI-assisted defense: Enables agents to investigate vulnerabilities, develop shields, and validate their effectiveness, with deployment remaining under human control.

Trusted deployment: Uses cryptographic signatures, Linux's eBPF verifier, and kernel security controls to prevent unauthorized modifications.

Hardware-backed verification: Uses Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) to provide verifiable records of shields being loaded or removed.

OpenAI and Cisco researchers tested custom-generated shields and demonstrated that they could successfully block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without interrupting its operation.

Marcus Hutchins, principal threat researcher at managed detection and response company Expel, says that while there is "genuinely so much runtime exploit mitigation potential with eBPF," it may not be a good idea to let AI agents write rules that could impact the kernel.

He also noted that the tool's "capabilities are limited to Linux because Mac/Windows haven't implement the components needed to be effective."

Researchers at Isovalent, a cloud networking and security company acquired by Cisco in 2024, explain that "Shirudo is a rewrite of Tetragon," an open-source eBPF-based runtime security platform the company introduced in 2022, which also serves as the foundation for Cisco's existing Live Protect technology.

Shirudo is designed for agentic control plane, and a configurable degree of autonomy when it comes to deploying mitigations. Isovalent says the tool isn’t limited to eBPF and can also modify application or userspace runtime bytecode to extend protection where needed.

When a shield is deployed, they also provide operators with hit counts, giving them insight into attempted exploits and where defenses need strengthening.

The two companies plan to provide “ready-to-use” mitigations in the form of tested shields, along with vulnerability disclosures, until patching is possible. Shields will be distributed as cryptographically signed ‘.bee’ packages through an OCI registry.

Isovalent says that Shirudo can be activated through a command-line interface and doesn’t require a daemon to run permanently on the machine.

"The Shirudo project is only the beginning, but it already shows the true potential of combining agents as a workforce with machine interfaces to let agents output what they are best at: code," the researchers say.

They expect the tool to evolve and other projects to emerge around it, to the point of building self-defending that can run applications and agents side by side.

Shirudo is open-source (BSD + GPL) and comes with a quick-start guide as well as "getting started" documentation from Isovalent.

In a deep-dive webinar on December 15, OpenAI will provide a technical rundown of how the tool works and how it combines eBPF and artificial intelligence to detect and counter new attacks.

articles.title: VMware vCenter Hit by Another Critical 9.8-Rated Auth Bypass Flaw After Zero-Day Exploitation
articles.context: The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9
articles.full_text:
Broadcom has shipped patches to address 23 vulnerabilities impacting VMware ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, and Avi Load Balancer, including one critical bug that could be abused to bypass authentication.

The critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123903, is rated 9.8 out of 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system. It resides in the VMware Directory Service ("vmdir").

"A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system," Broadcom said in an advisory released today.

The company credited sglab of QiAnXin, Qi Qin (@LeoQ7_) of depthfirst, and VulTeam, XGTP from ThreatBook for independently reporting the flaw.

Also patched in vCenter are four high-severity flaws, including an arbitrary file write vulnerability while processing certain archives that could be exploited to achieve code execution on the appliance (CVE-2026-123904, CVSS score: 7.5).

The remaining three vulnerabilities relate to denial-of-service in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-123905, CVE-2026-123906, and CVE-2026-123907, CVSS scores: 7.5).

The issues have been addressed in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.2

VMware Cloud Foundation and VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0300

VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m

VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)

VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x - Fixed in 5.2.5

VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

The fixes arrive days after Broadcom shipped updates for CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), another authentication bypass flaw impacting the VMware Directory Service that was exploited as a zero-day by a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group called Armory Castle. VMware has noted that CVE-2026-123903 is a distinct issue and is not related to CVE-2026-123890.

While Broadcom makes no mention of any of the newly disclosed flaws as being exploited in the wild, it's essential that customers apply the updates for optimal protection.

articles.title: The Microsoft Outage Brought a Surge of Phishing Email
articles.context: 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports, across KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security (PhishER Plus and Defend)
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R, Jeewan Singh Jalal

When a service you rely on goes down, you look for answers, and attackers know it. After the Microsoft outage on Nov. 12, KnowBe4 Threat Lab observed a sharp rise in outage-related email.

Read on for what we found, what the lures looked like, and how to protect your organization.

Key Findings

The surge peaked on the second day of the outage. On Nov. 13, outage-related phishing emails reached about 468 times the Nov. 9 to Nov. 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports, across KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security (PhishER Plus and Defend).

The lures were built to look like Microsoft. The lures we reviewed used a held-messages notice, a fake security check, an Exchange service notice, and a Teams notification.

One lure cited Microsoft's real incident number. A correct incident number does not make an email genuine.

The goal appears to be sign-in access. All four emails appear designed to steal sign-in access, through credential harvesting or device code phishing.

What Happened in the Microsoft Outage?

On Thursday, Nov. 12, a global outage hit the networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services. According to Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report for incident MO1550821, dated Nov. 15, the incident ran from Nov. 12, 2026 to Nov. 13, 2026. It lasted nearly 24 hours and reached users around the world. Microsoft listed 14 affected services, including Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Copilot.

Exchange Online took the biggest hit. Most users could not reach their mailboxes, and email delivery was delayed for many. Microsoft said the outage came from a chain of events, not a single failure:

A hidden defect. A software fix deployed to the gateway servers in July contained a flaw that caused servers to stop responding under certain loads. It ran for more than three months without problems.

More load, less capacity. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams traffic moved to the gateway that also supports Exchange Online. At the same time, nearly 14% of server capacity was out of service for an unrelated reason.

A cascade. Servers that failed pushed traffic onto fewer healthy servers, which then failed too. At its lowest point, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive.

Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint could move away from the gateway and partly recovered sooner. Exchange Online could not, so email stayed disrupted. Recovery took longer because servers that returned to service were overwhelmed again by waiting traffic. Microsoft also extended the email delivery window so delayed messages were not returned as undeliverable. The report is preliminary, and a final report will follow.

How Big Was the Surge in Outage-Themed Phishing Emails?

Phishing activity followed the outage. The peak came on the second day, Nov. 13, when outage-related email reached about 468 times the Nov. 9 to 11 daily average in detections and about 187 times that average in user reports.

What Did the Outage Lures Look Like?

We reviewed sender and subject patterns across all matched emails, and the message body of four examples. The first two use the subject "Outage -" plus a random string. The other two use different subjects.

Lure

What it says

What it wants

Held messages

Copies a Microsoft notice. Cites Microsoft's real incident number for the Nov. 12 outage, lists the affected services, and says four messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours.

A click on "Restore Messages."

Fake security check

Claims to be from a support desk and says "1 security issue found on your account."

A click on "Take Action," the only button in the message.

Exchange service notice

Styled as Microsoft Support, with the subject "Action Required: Microsoft Exchange Service Interruption" and a date. Refers to "our recent server outage" and asks you to update your email to avoid further disruption.

A click on "Update Email Now," pushed by a red "ACTION REQUIRED NOW!" banner.

Teams notification

Looks like a Microsoft Planner task notification assigning you a document to review. The subject is "Due To Microsoft Error Early- Access Doc" plus a code. It presents itself as a workaround for the Microsoft error, with an access code to "enter when prompted" that expires in 30 minutes.

A click on "Open in browser" or "Open in Teams," then entering the code.

This lure cites Microsoft's real incident number and warns that held messages will be deleted within 24 hours. The deadline and the "Restore Messages" button are meant to push a quick click.

This lure states that it comes from a "support desk" rather than Microsoft and claims "1 security issue found on your account." It has a single button, "Take Action," so there is only one place to click.

The Exchange notice has odd wording, such as "We've detect a refresh issue," which is a sign it is not genuine.

This lure imitates a Planner task notification and offers a "workaround" for the Microsoft error.

Why Do These Lures Work?

They match what people expect during an outage.

The failure was real. Mail delivery did fail, so a warning about held messages sounds plausible.

A security check feels natural. Users are already checking their accounts.

A Teams notice sounds like a sensible workaround. Email is down, so another route-in seems reasonable.

All four emails appear designed to steal your sign-in access, through credential harvesting or device code phishing.

How Can You Stay Vigilant?

Outages make people more willing to click. Build these habits before the next one:

Go to the source. Check Microsoft's official service status page or your IT team's usual channel. Do not rely on a link in an email. A real incident number can appear in a fake notice, so a correct number does not prove an email is genuine.

Treat sign-in prompts and deadlines with care. A request to "restore messages" or log in to "restore access" is more believable when services are failing. Never enter a sign-in code from an email or a Teams notice unless you started that sign-in yourself. Open the service directly instead.

Verify new contact details. Confirm any change in contact details sent during an outage with a contact you already know.

Look for odd subjects and wording. Random strings, typos, urgent red warnings, and unfamiliar senders are all signs to pause.

Question workarounds. Be wary of any message that offers another way in while Microsoft is down, such as a task, a document, or a Teams link. Confirm it with your IT team.

Report, don't click. If an email looks wrong, use your report button instead of clicking. Your security team can then spot the attack early and act on it.

Security teams should also watch for newly seen domains that send large volumes in a short time.

How Does KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security Help?

You cannot stop an outage. You can limit what attackers gain from one.

KnowBe4 Email & Collaboration Security brings together KnowBe4 Defend (inbound email and messaging security), KnowBe4 Prevent (outbound email security), and PhishER Plus (incident response).

In this event, Defend detected outage-themed phishing emails as threats. PhishER helps your team act on what users report: it classifies reported messages, gives reporters instant feedback, and lets you remediate threats across every inbox with one click.

Training closes the gap. Security Awareness Training and Real-Time Coaching help your users spot urgent, outage-themed lures before they click.

Be Ready Before the Next Outage

Outages end. The habits you build for them endure. Start by asking your team one question today: where would you check first if email went down?

For real-time updates and ongoing phishing threat intelligence, follow KnowBe4 Threat Lab on X: @Kb4Threatlabs

articles.title: Chinese Open-Weight AI Models Top Closed Ones at Vulnerability Discovery in New Test
articles.context: In addition, the Israeli company specified that cost figures covered only the four exploitation agents and exclude discovery, browser use, reporting, advisor calls and other...
articles.full_text:
Additionally, A Security found that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost a fraction of what other models required, at $0.81 per validated finding, when the closed models cost between $9.54 (for Gemini 3.8 Flash) and $31.85 (GPT 5.6 Sol).

GLM 5.3, however, was not as cost-efficient, at $10.49 per validated finding, slightly more than the cheapest closed model.

Study Caveats: Cost Scope and Provider Variables Complicate the Results

While the A Security test is another example showing a rising interest in Chinese open-weight AI models, the results of the study, released on November 23, do not mean these models are always better, or cheaper, at finding vulnerabilities.

In addition, the Israeli company specified that cost figures covered only the four exploitation agents and exclude discovery, browser use, reporting, advisor calls and other orchestration costs, partly because advisor configurations varied across runs. A full scan would cost more, and costs will vary by setup.

The pricing basis also differs: GLM 5.3 was priced at its official token rates, while the other models used recorded provider spend. DeepSeek ran on a pinned provider route after earlier runs through another provider had heavy fallback, and timings reflect the specific inference providers and configurations used, so they should not be read as fixed model-level speed rankings.

DeepSeek also drifted the most, reporting findings outside its assigned lead on at least 4.5% of leads, versus under 2.5% for the other models. While A Security researchers noted that such considerations matter little for attackers, it raises scope-control concerns for defenders, as an agent straying from its lead could touch assets outside an engagement's authorized scope.

Image credits: Tomas Ragina / Nick Livyi / Shutterstock.com

In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. articles.title: U.S. CISA adds N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
articles.context: According to Amazon, the attackers used autonomous AI agents running the open-source Cairn framework to discover and exploit the zero-day
articles.full_text:
U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added N-able MailAssure and Project MONAI vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog:

CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

The first flaw is CVE-2026-133968 (CVSS score of 9.8), a critical path traversal vulnerability in Project MONAI’s MONAI Label. It affects versions up to 0.8.5 and allows unauthenticated remote attackers to access files outside the intended directory through the image parameter in the PUT /datastore/image endpoint. Successful exploitation can also lead to remote code execution, potentially allowing attackers to take control of the affected server. The vulnerability has been exploited in the wild since September 2026, before its public disclosure on November 20.

Amazon Threat Intelligence linked the exploitation to a Chinese-nexus threat actor, with moderate confidence. According to Amazon, the attackers used autonomous AI agents running the open-source Cairn framework to discover and exploit the zero-day. The agents reportedly gained root access to a university server and later used the vulnerability to target another university network. Amazon has not identified a specific threat group. The vulnerability was fixed in MONAI Label 0.8.6.

The second flaw is CVE-2026-134624 (CVSS score of 9.3), a critical Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts). The flaw affects versions earlier than 20261121.1943 and exists in the LDAP synchronisation connection check performed when a relay is configured. It does not properly restrict the destination of the connection, allowing an authenticated API user with sufficient privileges to make the vulnerable server connect to arbitrary internal IP addresses and ports. Attackers could use this capability to identify accessible internal systems and send crafted requests to internal services. N-able

N-able disclosed the vulnerability while investigating a cyberattack against its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environments. The company confirmed that attackers had accessed a web server and said its investigation had found no evidence of exploitation beyond a single N-able-hosted server. However, it has not confirmed whether CVE-2026-134624 was the vulnerability exploited to gain initial access. No threat actor has been publicly identified. The flaw was fixed in version 20261121.1943, and N-able restored access to the affected services on November 21, 2026.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 26.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA)

articles.title: ShinyHunters-linked crew resurfaces on new leak site
articles.context: The ShinyHunters leak site went dark in September, but a crew that supplied it with victims seems to have found a new home under the “Inception” name, Okta’s threat intelligence...
articles.full_text:
The ShinyHunters leak site went dark in September, but a crew that supplied it with victims seems to have found a new home under the “Inception” name, Okta’s threat intelligence team has discovered.

Okta tracks the crew as O-UNC-053, a cluster that has been running social engineering and credential-harvesting campaigns since March 2026. Its targets include companies in technology, healthcare, biotech, financial services, insurance, entertainment, gaming, retail, transportation, hospitality and the legal sector.

“While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels wrote.

Between March and September, O-UNC-053’s victims turned up on the ShinyHunters leak site one to 28 days after the gang registered phishing domains to target them. Okta reads that as a sign of a significant relationship, possibly an agreement, though the leak site almost certainly took victims from other intrusion crews as well.

Then came two arrests of alleged ShinyHunters affiliates, on September 15 and 29, and the leak site went offline.

O-UNC-053 kept registering phishing domains through October and early November, with nowhere obvious to post its victims. A legal-themed campaign started in late October, and on November 16 Inception appeared, listing organizations the gang had registered domains for six to 19 days earlier.

O-UNC-053 key events from September through November 2026 (Source: Okta)

“This gap in publishing on any leak site followed by publishing on a new data leak site with a new brand is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors. Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the pair added.

The FBI describes The Com as a largely English-speaking, international network of mostly young cybercriminals with thousands of members and a hacking branch it calls Hacker Com.

“Members of Hacker Com typically have a shared interest, ideology, or goal and work together, adding others to the group and splintering when necessary, to achieve their mission,” the bureau said.

Okta stops short of saying O-UNC-053 runs Inception, and allows that the crew may simply be working with another extortion outfit.

ReversingLabs on the same trail

ReversingLabs published separate research linking Inception’s extortion claims to a vishing operation targeting single sign-on accounts. Within five days of its launch, the site claimed AMD, Cigna Healthcare, Henry Schein, Paychex, PepsiCo, AutoZone and Lucid Motors as victims, though ReversingLabs stresses that none of these claims have been verified.

“Rather than relying on traditional email lures, this operation is using voice phishing (vishing) to compromise single sign-on (SSO) credentials. Technical analysis of the adversary’s domain infrastructure directly corroborates this out-of-band delivery model. None of the legal-themed lure domains tied to the campaign possess MX records, DKIM, DMARC, or any other email-related DNS configurations,” explained Robert Simmons, principal malware researcher at ReversingLabs.

Most of the kits mimic the target’s Okta sign-in page, though the one built for Lucid Motors copies a NetIQ/OpenText Access Manager login, which tells you the crew checks each target’s SSO setup before dialing.

“The core of this campaign relies on tailoring the landing page to the specific identity provider of the target. All the domains in the confirmed cluster are configured to filter unwanted visitors and forward them to the victim’s legitimate authentication infrastructure,” Simmons noted.

The company has also spotted lure domains for dozens of businesses that haven’t appeared on the leak site so far, among them Activision Blizzard, Riot Games, Starbucks, Nintendo and Paramount.

“Because this adversary targets the identity layer rather than endpoints, defenders must prioritize phishing-resistant authentication across all identity providers, enforcing FIDO2 security keys, passkeys, or origin-bound authenticators alongside managed device restrictions and alerts for unexpected MFA changes,” Simmons advised.

articles.title: Hackers Found a Way Around GitHub SHA Pinning. This Webinar Explains How to Close the Gap
articles.context: Attackers have already found a way around it
articles.full_text:
Pinning GitHub Actions to an exact version of their code, known as SHA pinning, has become the go-to defense against software supply chain attacks. Attackers have already found a way around it.

In March 2026, the hackers who hijacked Trivy, a widely used open-source security scanner, planted malicious code that looked like it came from GitHub's official checkout tool. They even labeled it a security fix. Teams pinned to it would have passed every check.

The trick works because GitHub lets copies of a project, called forks, share code with the original. In May, the same technique hit the popular actions-cool/issues-helper tool, stealing credentials from the pipelines that ran it.

The lesson: pinning guarantees the code won't change, but not who wrote it.

That gap is the focus of an upcoming webinar, GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning. If your team treats pinning as the finish line, save your seat to learn what it actually protects you from, and what it doesn't.

Immutability Is Not Provenance

Pinning earned its reputation. When the tj-actions/changed-files compromise repointed tags to a malicious commit across more than 23,000 repositories in March 2025, teams that had pinned to SHAs were unaffected.

GitHub now lets administrators enforce pinning as an organization-wide policy, and few security teams argue against it.

📅 Save Your Spot: Learn Why “Best Practice” Won’t Stop the Next GitHub Actions Attack

But a pinned SHA leaves three questions unanswered:

Authorship: A SHA doesn't tell you who wrote the commit. Any fork commit can be pinned.

Project membership: Org-level enforcement checks that a reference is a 40-character SHA, not that the commit actually lives in the upstream project.

Runtime: A Docker-based action pinned to a SHA can still build its image at runtime, pulling in dependencies that were never frozen.

With agentic development pushing more code through CI than ever, each of those gaps gets exercised more often and reviewed less closely.

GitHub's Lockfiles Help. They Don't Finish the Job.

GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap, published March 26, put deterministic dependency locking front and center. Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14 and became generally available on October 28, 2026. They tie every run to recorded commits for actions and their transitive dependencies, even if a tag moves later.

That's real progress. Locked commits must exist on a branch of the source repository, which blunts fork-only impostors. But GitHub's own changelog is clear that locking "does not determine whether the dependency itself is safe." Commit authorship and runtime builds remain open; immutable releases only help when maintainers opt in, and lockfiles aren't currently supported on GitHub Enterprise Server.

Not sure where your pipelines fall in that gap? Register for the webinar for a clear-eyed breakdown of what GitHub's roadmap fixes and what it still leaves to you.

What You'll Learn

Led by Erika Heidi, Staff Developer Relations Engineer at Chainguard, the session draws a hard line between immutability and provenance, and covers:

What org-level pin enforcement actually verifies, and the false confidence it can create

How impostor commits work, and why GitHub's repository network makes them possible

What GitHub's Actions roadmap addresses, and what it doesn't

Other ways to close the trust gap, including a curated catalog of vetted actions

Who Should Attend

Platform and DevOps engineers who own CI/CD, AppSec and DevSecOps teams writing pipeline policy, and security leaders who signed off on SHA pinning as "done." If your workflows pull in third-party actions, this session is for you.

Attackers have already shown they can disguise a malicious commit as a hardening fix. The next one won't announce itself either.

Register now for GitHub Actions Security Beyond SHA Pinning, pick the session time that works for you, and find out what your pins aren't telling you.

articles.title: Bedrock Data enhances AI agent governance with intent-aware DLP
articles.context: Bedrock Data has announced that Agent DLP, its runtime data loss prevention for AI agents, now infers a user’s intent (the business purpose behind the task) and evaluates the...
articles.full_text:
Bedrock Data has announced that Agent DLP, its runtime data loss prevention for AI agents, now infers a user’s intent (the business purpose behind the task) and evaluates the agent’s behavior (the sum of its actions across every tool and LLM call) against that intent and the organization’s policy.

By weighing both intent and behavior, Agent DLP lets employees keep working with AI agents while sensitive data stays protected. Agent DLP adds support for off-the-shelf AI tools employees and developers use, including AI assistants such as Claude, Claude Cowork and ChatGPT; coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Snowflake Cortex Code; data platform agents such as Snowflake Cortex; and AI gateways such as Bifrost.

According to Forrester, “Governing AI agents starts with controlling intent and authority, not models or tools. Agentic systems interpret goals, make decisions, and act across systems. Governance must therefore define and monitor whom an agent is allowed to act for, under what authority, and within which bounds.”

Enterprises are putting agents to work across development, customer support and business processes. In EY’s 2026 survey of senior AI executives at U.S. companies with at least $1 billion in revenue, 85% of executives whose organizations use agentic AI said some of their systems execute actions without real-time human involvement.

Agents are goal-oriented and take whatever actions reach the outcome a user asks for, even risky ones, such as changing security settings to get around a block, saving sensitive files to unsecured locations or sending data to unapproved MCP servers. Identity and access controls decide what an agent can access, not what it does with that access.

“Most enterprises have more agents than they think, and like most new technology, developers got there first,” said Bruno Kurtic, CEO of Bedrock Data.

“Tools like Claude Code Enterprise put agents in the hands of developers who already have broad access to production systems, credentials and customer data. In our early deployments, the riskiest activity often matched no existing policy at all. Seeing what those agents do tells a security team which policies to write first and which data to clean up, so they can enforce where the risk is real and let the rest of the work run.”

Intent, behavior and policy define how Agent DLP governs AI agents

Agent DLP looks at what an agent does: the actions it takes, the data it touches, and the MCP servers and tools it calls. It evaluates this behavior alongside the inferred intent, the business purpose the user set out to accomplish. Authorized work continues uninterrupted. When that behavior puts sensitive data at risk, Agent DLP responds according to policy by alerting the security team, masking the sensitive data or blocking the action.

“CISOs don’t want a tool that blocks authorized work, but they also don’t want policies that miss exposure,” said Sanjay Srivastava, VP of Product at Bedrock Data. “Agent DLP reads why the user asked, sees what the agent does with the data and applies the organization’s policy to both, so authorized work proceeds and exposure is stopped.”

Agent DLP judges each action in light of the user’s intent and the actions that came before it, then reviews the session as a whole, so it catches individually allowed actions that add up to exposure, with minimal latency at runtime. It plugs in wherever agents act: as a hook in tools such as Claude Code and Codex, at gateways such as LiteLLM and Bifrost, and in agent runtimes such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and NVIDIA OpenShell.

Agent DLP also inventories the agents in use and the tools, MCP servers and identities each relies on, and keeps a full audit trail of every action for regulatory review.

Security teams write policies in natural language to describe what agents may do. Agent DLP enforces them against the same classifications Bedrock Data uses for data security posture management (DSPM), covering structured and unstructured sensitive data across on-premises, SaaS and infrastructure platforms, so a policy means the same thing for stored data and for data an agent is using.

Sensitive data includes regulated and business-critical categories such as PII, PHI, payment card data, credentials and secrets, financial records, material nonpublic information (MNPI) and proprietary source code or IP, plus any category a customer defines.

“Home service pros trust us to run their businesses, and that trust extends to the homeowners they serve,” said Nate Burford, Housecall Pro SVP and CIO. “As we put AI to work across our teams, Bedrock Data’s Agent DLP gives us visibility into how our agents handle customer data, so we can move fast and keep it governed.”

For example, Agent DLP can block an agent from downloading regulated PII or sending it to Slack, email or another MCP server. It can also detect a toxic data combination, such as a name, a date of birth and a medical diagnosis, whether it appears in one action or builds up across a session, and mask one element so the full combination never appears in plain view.

A global investor in enterprise technology and a leading advocate for agentic AI uses Agent DLP to govern how agents work with sensitive data across its own teams. According to the CISO at this global private equity firm, “We put agentic AI to work in our own business, not just in what we invest in, and our people use agents every day on sensitive information. Agent DLP understands what each agent is doing with our data and why, so our teams can move fast while meeting the regulatory and contractual obligations we hold ourselves to.”

articles.title: Elastic puts AI agents to work on the SOC alert backlog
articles.context: Rules and models target AI threats The 143 AI security SIEM detection rules cover coding agents hijacked to execute attacker commands, malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP)...
articles.full_text:
Elastic announced Elastic Security 9.6, which introduces AlertZero, a set of AI agents that triage alerts, hunt threats and tune detection rules in the background. The release also adds ransomware protection for Linux, expanded entity resolution and an expanded set of 143 detection rules covering AI agents and large language model platforms.

AlertZero takes on the alert queue

AlertZero organizes its agents, called Workers, into four teams known as Watches: triage, threat hunting, detection engineering and forensics. The technical preview includes six Workers. Each Worker runs on a schedule or in response to events such as new alerts, then submits a proposed action, such as closing a false positive or isolating a host, along with supporting evidence.

Alertzero Workers (Source: Elastic)

Depending on the Worker, teams can choose from three autonomy levels: Manual, Assisted and Supervised. In Manual mode, proposed actions require analyst approval. Assisted mode allows Workers to investigate detection rules and coverage gaps independently, but changes still require approval. Supervised mode permits selected actions without prior approval, with analysts reviewing the results afterward. Actions approved by analysts run with their privileges and are recorded as their decisions.

Analysts spend more time gathering context around an alert than deciding what to do with it, according to Elastic. “We built AlertZero to do that digging for you,” the company wrote.

Customers choose the models used by Workers across three tiers: Efficient, Balanced and Frontier. Options include open-weight and self-hosted models. AlertZero is available in technical preview in Elastic Cloud Serverless. It is expected to become available in Elastic Cloud Hosted and Elastic Self-Managed deployments in early December with an Enterprise subscription or a trial license.

Entity Analytics adds a daily starting point

The Entity Analytics updates are generally available with an Enterprise subscription. A refreshed overview features six tiles highlighting users, hosts and services with changes in risk, alerts or behavior. An AI brief summarizes entity risk and identifies up to three entities to investigate first.

Entity Analytics (Source: Elastic)

Entity resolution links accounts belonging to the same person across endpoint, identity and cloud data to provide a single view of risk. Version 9.6 adds matching rules for Windows and CrowdStrike security identifiers, Microsoft Entra globally unique identifiers (GUIDs) and Microsoft 365 user principal names, along with case-insensitive email matching.

Elastic Defend adds Linux ransomware protection and custom YARA scanning

Elastic Defend extends its behavior-based ransomware protection, already available on Windows and macOS, to Linux hosts. In Prevent mode, it blocks attacks as they occur.

Security teams can also load custom YARA signatures to scan process memory. A match generates a Memory Threat – Detected alert that displays the matched signature name and memory strings. Both capabilities reach general availability with version 9.6.

Migration tools gain AI-assisted editing

Automatic Migration now lets analysts edit translated detection rules through chat and confirm the changes in the same interface. The feature supports rules from Splunk, QRadar and Microsoft Sentinel.

Rules and models target AI threats

The 143 AI security SIEM detection rules cover coding agents hijacked to execute attacker commands, malicious Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, credentials pasted into prompts, jailbreaks and stolen API keys. Coverage spans endpoint telemetry, Amazon Bedrock, OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise, Anthropic, Google Cloud Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI. The rules map to the MITRE ATLAS and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks.

Elastic cited two real-world incidents that illustrate the threats covered by the rules. In August 2025, malicious versions of the Nx build tool invoked installed AI coding tools to find sensitive files. In another incident, an npm package impersonating a Postmark MCP server copied every outgoing email to an attacker.

On developer machines running macOS or Windows, Elastic Defend can terminate a process if it was launched by a coding agent and attempts to establish persistence.

A Security for AI integration package, available in technical preview with a Platinum or trial subscription, adds four small models that score prompts and responses as they are indexed. The models run within the customer’s own cluster. Eight prebuilt detection rules act on the results.

Availability

Most Elastic Security 9.6 capabilities are available now in Elastic Cloud Serverless, except for the new Elastic Defend features. Elastic expects version 9.6, including those features, to become available in Elastic Cloud Hosted and Elastic Self-Managed deployments in early December.
