In this article

Microsoft plans to bring eight Windows security checks together in 2027

Windows baseline protection will flag missing safeguards and let you turn some on with one click

Apps could use the result to warn you, limit features, or block access

Microsoft announced plans to introduce Windows baseline protection, a feature that brings eight existing safeguards together into a single, verifiable security status.

With the feature expected to become generally available in 2027, Microsoft wants to make a familiar Windows security problem less confusing. Your PC has a collection of built-in protections, but working out which ones are enabled and what to do when they aren’t can take some digging.

Windows baseline protection will show you what’s missing and help you fix it. It will also give software developers a simpler way to check whether your computer meets their requirements and decide whether to let an app run at all.

On the positive side, that could make security easier to manage. But it could also mean more encounters with software that says your PC isn’t secure enough to use it.

The protections already exist in Windows. What’s new is the way Windows evaluates them together and shares the result. For people using personal or unmanaged PCs, the most immediately useful change may be the explanation that comes with the result.

Microsoft says the new baseline protection page in Windows Settings will show which protections are missing.

Preview of Windows baseline protection in Settings (image courtesy of Microsoft)

Where possible, a single button will enable the missing protections and restart the computer. If you need to change your PC’s firmware settings, for example to enable Secure Boot or the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), Windows will provide guidance.

The first version checks these eight requirements:

Security processor: Dedicated hardware, such as a TPM, that helps protect sensitive information.

Secure Boot: Protection against malicious software loading during startup.

Virtualization-based security: Hardware-assisted isolation that helps protect critical processes.

Memory integrity: Protection against malicious code running in protected parts of Windows.

Signed drivers only: A requirement that drivers have digital signatures.

Windows-certified drivers: A requirement that drivers meet Windows hardware signing requirements.

Kernel debugger protection: Restrictions that help prevent debugging tools from bypassing Windows security protections.

Vulnerable driver protection: Protection against known vulnerable drivers that could weaken the system’s security.

An application that wants to check a computer’s security configuration can use Windows’ baseline protection signal instead of maintaining its own collection of checks.

The intended uses are straightforward. An exam service might want to verify a student’s device before a test. A game might check protections relevant to anti-cheat measures. An organization might require a device to meet its security requirements before granting access.

Main takeaways

Windows baseline protection brings existing safeguards together into a common, hardware-backed security assessment and helps users enable any missing protections. That could make Windows security less confusing, but it also gives software vendors a simpler way to warn users, restrict features, or deny access when a computer falls short.

The developer decides what happens next. Will they require the entire baseline, or only the protections their application actually needs?

Windows baseline protection and security software such as Malwarebytes address different parts of the problem. Microsoft’s checks establish whether a set of underlying Windows safeguards is enabled. Malwarebytes Premium Plus adds protection against threats such as malware, ransomware, exploits, and malicious websites, along with browser protection and a VPN. Neither replaces the other: Installing security software does not switch on a missing Windows safeguard, and passing Microsoft’s checklist is not a guarantee that your PC is free of malware.

The feature is still in preview, and Microsoft says feedback will shape it before general availability.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: OpenAI, Cisco Unveil Open Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems
articles.context: Shirudo is designed to help defenders address the challenges introduced by AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, which is increasing pressure on organizations...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI and Cisco on Monday unveiled Shirudo, an open source security platform that uses AI agents to prevent the exploitation of vulnerabilities in Linux systems and applications.

The project is an AI-focused rewrite of Cisco-owned Isovalent’s Tetragon runtime security platform. Tetragon was open-sourced in 2022, and it also powers Cisco’s Live Protect vulnerability mitigation technology.

Shirudo is designed to help defenders address the challenges introduced by AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and exploitation, which is increasing pressure on organizations to deploy patches quickly.

The tool leverages eBPF technology to modify Linux kernel behavior without restarting the OS.

According to Cisco and OpenAI, agents can analyze vulnerability information, generate so-called ‘shields’ to prevent exploitation, and test their effectiveness without disrupting important services. Security teams still retain control over which shields are deployed.

Protections are digitally signed and verified before deployment, with mechanisms designed to prevent even attackers with root privileges from disabling kernel-level enforcement.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

In a controlled test targeting the recent Java4Shell vulnerability, a shield generated using OpenAI’s Codex blocked an exploitation attempt targeting an Elasticsearch instance without requiring a restart.

Shirudo is currently in pre-release development and not ready for production use. The tool requires specific Linux kernel capabilities, additional kernel patches, and TPM 2.0.

OpenAI and Cisco hope that down the line Shirudo shields can be distributed alongside vulnerability disclosures to give organizations temporary protection until they can install permanent patches.

Amiram Shachar, CEO and co-founder of cloud security firm Upwind, commented, “Writing the most sensitive kernel code on the fly and deploying it straight to runtime is a very risky concept. I love the idea, but doing it with open source is very risky.”

“There are countless Linux versions and distributions this has to work across. It needs to be tested, packaged and automated before anyone should trust it in production,” Shachar added.

articles.title: Azure API Management vulnerability exploited to steal customers’ secrets
articles.context: Attackers have exploited a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) to steal credentials stored in customers’ instances, Microsoft has warned
articles.full_text:
Attackers have exploited a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) to steal credentials stored in customers’ instances, Microsoft has warned.

Among the victims are several Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, and organizations in other sectors and outside Norway, the country’s National Security Authority (NSM) confirmed.

APIM Classic tiers affected

APIM is a gateway that sits in front of an organization’s APIs and handles authentication, routing and rate limiting. To call the backend services behind it, the gateway often needs to hold their credentials.

Microsoft’s advisory, delivered to customers via the Azure Portal, says that, on November 18, Microsoft identified a “security issue” affecting APIM Classic tiers that could allow unauthorized access to certain management functionality, “if the service was not configured according to documented security best practices.”

While Microsoft fixed the flaw and closed the access path the next day, it discovered that credentials or configuration secrets associated with some customers’ API Management resources may have been accessed by an unauthorized party.

Microsoft says Classic-tier instances without its recommended network integration, or with secrets stored in APIM rather than in Azure Key Vault, may have had their named values, identity-provider and OpenID Connect client secrets, subscription keys and direct management API tokens accessed.

“If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM. What they can reach depends on the credential’s permissions and whether it is still valid,” security researcher Anders Kristiansen explained.

The vulnerability does not impact Azure API Management v2 tiers, Microsoft added.

What to do?

Microsoft’s remediation does not invalidate the customer credentials that may have been accessed by the attackers before Microsoft rolled out the fix. It’s on affected organizations to do that and check if the credentials have been misused to access their resources.

The Norwegian National Security Authority advised everyone using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and named values have been compromised, and to rotate all tokens and secrets. They should also check whether their APIM instance has been updated to (fixed) runtime versions 0.52.31936 or higher, or 0.53.31938 or higher.

NSM advises organizations whose instance hasn’t been updated to contact Microsoft directly, and asked organizations that have been compromised to contact them.

“It is also important that organizations identify what information sits behind their APIM instance, so they can determine the potential scope if evidence of compromise is found,” the NSM added.

Kristiansen published (and is keeping updated) helpful what-to-do instructions for affected organizations and advice on what to search for in which logs.

articles.title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity
articles.context: NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James...
articles.full_text:
A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked as CVE-2026-108398.

Oracle fixed the VirtualBox flaw in September, and Microsoft fixed the Windows one on October 13, both before the write-up appeared.

VirtualBox on Windows monitors the system calls that load program files into its virtual machine processes, so a less-trusted user on the same computer cannot push code into them. Forshaw got past that watch through the .NET Framework.

The framework can run a .NET program file from a plain copy in memory when the normal way of loading it, as an executable image, fails. Version 4 of the framework takes that fallback on one specific error, and the memory copy skips the image checks a loaded program would face.

The VirtualBox check returned that error for any .NET file compiled as AnyCPU, a form meant to run on any processor, so an unchanged file loaded through the path the hardening never inspects.

To get the file loaded while a virtual machine was started, he registered a COM object in the current user's settings that a protected VirtualBox process would pull in, a method known as COM hijacking. He set out the mechanism in his technical analysis.

Oracle rates the flaw, CVE-2026-87268, as a local problem that needs low privileges and no user interaction, scores it 7.8, and lists VirtualBox 7.2.16 on Windows hosts as affected. Its security advisory says a successful attack can result in the "takeover of Oracle VM VirtualBox."

The code runs inside the protected VirtualBox process. It is not a break out of a guest virtual machine onto the host, and the attacker begins as an ordinary user on that host.

The same idea worked against Windows' own code-integrity checks, which decide what user-mode code is allowed to run. There is no VirtualBox hook here, only the system call that maps a file as an image.

The researcher found that clearing a single bit in a .NET file's header, the IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE flag, made that call reject the file while .NET still loaded and ran it.

"This single bit change is all you need to load an untrusted .NET assembly," he wrote. He tried it on Windows 11 S Mode, which enables User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), the policy that limits which user-mode programs can run. A logic error in .NET's own policy check let the file load even with UMCI enforced.

The flaw, CVE-2026-108398, works through the .NET Framework version 4 loading path and needs a program willing to load the assembly. It is not a way to seize any Windows machine over the internet.

Microsoft rates it a local, low-privilege security-feature bypass, scores it 8.8, and fixed it on October 13. The company lists it as publicly disclosed but not used in attacks.

The same file reached a more sensitive target as well. Protected Process Light, or PPL, is a kind of Windows process that ordinary programs, even ones with administrator rights, are not meant to enter. By hijacking a COM object that WerSecureFault.exe loads, he ran his test code inside a PPL process at the highest protection level without administrator rights.

The older Protected Process type resisted the technique because the .NET runtime files lack the page hashes it requires. The October fix corrects the policy check for UMCI but does not change loading for protected processes, so that PPL route should still work, according to the researcher. It carries no separate CVE.

What to patch

On Windows hosts, update VirtualBox to a build that carries the September fixes. The affected versions are 7.2.16 and 7.2.18, and 7.2.18 shipped on September 15 with that set. An upstream code fix is not the same as a released binary, so check the running version rather than assume an older build already has it.

.NET systems need the October 13 update that matches the exact Windows and .NET Framework version in use, not one shared package. The update release notes list the right KB for each. On Windows 11 version 26H2, for example, it is KB5127694.

Flaw

Affected

Fixed in

CVE-2026-87268 (VirtualBox)

VirtualBox 7.2.16, Windows hosts

Oracle's September update, build 7.2.18

CVE-2026-108398 (.NET Framework)

.NET Framework 4 on Windows, UMCI case tested on Windows 11 S Mode

October 13 update, per-version KB

Forshaw first presented the Windows code-integrity bypass at the 44Con conference in September, having judged it fell outside Microsoft's rules for what gets fixed. After .NET developers told him the behavior he had counted on was accidental, he reported it in late September. The fix arrived in October's Patch Tuesday, less than a month later.

articles.title: Introducing CORNERSTONE: delivering external services for the NCSC
articles.context: We want to create an operating model that enables NCSC services to achieve greater impact, reach more organisations, respond more quickly to changing threats and technology, and...
articles.full_text:
The NCSC's existing services have developed strong standards, trusted market relationships and significant reach. But as demand grows, we need to consider how these services can be delivered in ways that are scalable, sustainable, and responsive to the UK’s changing needs.

As a result, the NCSC is exploring how it can modernise the way its external services are designed, delivered and developed. We want to create an operating model that enables NCSC services to achieve greater impact, reach more organisations, respond more quickly to changing threats and technology, and make better use of the capabilities that exist across the cyber security industry.

CORNERSTONE is a multi-year project to develop a more scalable relationship between the NCSC and industry, with each focusing on where it can add most value. Our ambition for CORNERSTONE is not simply to outsource services currently run by the NCSC; we want to make our services more impactful, accessible and adaptable. This will allow the NCSC to focus on those areas where it brings unique insight as the national technical authority for cyber security.

articles.title: Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster: defending against agentic cyber attacks
articles.context: We recently blogged about unlocking the potential of agentic cyber defence across a range of areas including enhanced threat detection and automated incident response
articles.full_text:
The NCSC believes the adoption of AI-enabled cyber can close the gap between attackers and defenders. We recently blogged about unlocking the potential of agentic cyber defence across a range of areas including enhanced threat detection and automated incident response. However, it will take time for defensive AI-driven programmes to mature, so organisations can’t sit back and wait for agentic defence to protect them. AI-enabled cyber defence is not the sole answer to agentic attacks; the foundations of cyber security and basic cyber hygiene remain the priority.

As we stated in the NCSC’s 2026 ‘The State of the Cyber Nation’ Annual Review, AI does not make established cyber security controls obsolete. In fact building strong foundations has never mattered more. AI is making weaknesses easier to find and faster to exploit; a forgotten key or an unprotected API which might once have gone unnoticed for years can be found in minutes.

Nearly everything the NCSC has seen can be prevented by implementing cyber security best practice, the application of modern cyber security approaches like zero trust, and by the diligent application of technical controls in line with your organisation's technologies and processes. For organisations seeking a structured approach:

zero trust principles can help protect against agentic attacks; explicitly verify identity, ensure least privilege everywhere, and deploy controls as if attackers are already inside your network

the Cyber Assessment Framework helps organisations responsible for essential services or critical functions assess and improve their cyber resilience

the NCSC’s Cyber Essentials sets out the minimum technical controls for organisations, as recommended by the government

Although they may not always be applied in the right place, the controls that mitigate the threat from agentic offensive frameworks will already be familiar to many organisations. Today's frameworks may be replaced by quieter, more capable ones, and tools will change. But the cyber security fundamentals won't.

This is your chance to get ahead of the threat. Consider how your organisation would answer the questions above, and make sure your answers hold up against an attacker that never needs a break and never gets tired of asking.

Kris B, Incident Handler, Incident Management

Ellen T, Lead Data Scientist, Vulnerability Management Team

David Chismon, CTO for Architecture

articles.title: OpenAI and Cisco Release Open-Source Tool to Shield Unpatched Linux Systems
articles.context: OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux security tool designed to temporarily block exploitation of known vulnerabilities until organizations can install...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo, an open-source Linux security tool designed to temporarily block exploitation of known vulnerabilities until organizations can install permanent patches.

In a November 23 announcement, OpenAI said that Shirudo could guard live systems without forcing a restart.

Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, commented, "Finding a bug today doesn't mean you can patch every system tomorrow."

How the Shields Work

Shirudo is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which allows vetted mini-programs run inside the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system.

Each shield was designed to target only the one operation an exploit needed, leaving normal requests untouched, and operators could trial a proposed protection before approving it. OpenAI said shutting off a risky function entirely could cause an outage, because the same function could serve both attackers and legitimate users.

Shields carried a cryptographic signature that was verified before it could load. A Trusted Platform Module (TPM), a hardware security chip, kept a log of every protection added or removed, giving teams evidence of what had been active on a system.

Isovalent, a Cisco-owned company, described Shirudo as a rewrite of Tetragon, the open-source eBPF security platform it released in 2022. It said Tetragon already powered Live Protect, which Cisco uses to mitigate flaws in its own products.

Read more on Linux flaws: Linux Flaws Exposed Before Fixes as Root Exploit Goes Public

Java4Shell Test and Early Limits

In a single controlled test, a shield written by OpenAI's Codex inserted validation into Java's Base64 decoding routine.

Attached to an Elasticsearch instance that was already running, it stopped a Java4Shell exploit attempt while the application stayed online. Isovalent said the mitigation "appears to be effective" and would protect affected applications until OpenJDK was patched.

The result came from a test designed and run by the project builders rather than an independent evaluation.

Isovalent engineer John Fastabend said at a Linux kernel summit in 2026 that his team often came across vulnerabilities with no suitable point in the kernel where a shield could attach, LWN reported.

Shirudo's GitHub repository described the project as pre-release, with production use requiring a Linux kernel carrying Shirudo's kernel patches and a TPM 2.0 chip.

OpenAI said it hoped eventually to release shields that had already been tested at the same time flaws were disclosed. It added that the two companies were designing Shirudo so AI agents could investigate flaws, write shields and check that they worked and called automatically generated least-privilege policies a longer-term aim.

articles.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: 1.5 Million Impacted by Data Breach at South Korean Electric Company KEPCO
articles.context: KEPCO attributed the incident to an external attacker and noted the growing sophistication of AI-driven cyberattacks
articles.full_text:
South Korean state-owned electric company Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO, KRX: 015760, NYSE: KEP) has disclosed a data breach impacting approximately 1.5 million people.

The incident, the company says, involved KEPCO ON, its integrated customer service portal, and the supplier relationship management (SRM) platform, which handles procurement and service contracts.

KEPCO attributed the incident to an external attacker and noted the growing sophistication of AI-driven cyberattacks. It did not disclose how the attacker gained access or confirm that AI was used in this breach.

According to KEPCO, it suspended the affected services immediately after discovering the incident, blocked external access, conducted a thorough review of the relevant systems, and took remediation actions.

On November 20, the company confirmed that data was exfiltrated from its systems, including electricity customer and SRM user information.

From KEPCO ON, the hackers stole the personal information of 650,487 people, including names, addresses, phone numbers, unique ID numbers, customer numbers, card numbers and details, bank names, bank account numbers, account-holder names, card issuers, cardholder names, and billing/payment details.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Additionally, the information of 869,761 individuals was stolen from the SRM systems: the names, unique ID numbers, email addresses, and company addresses of 426,827; and the names, affiliation, employee IDs, email addresses, phone numbers, and company phone numbers of 442,934 (including KEPCO staff and partners’ employees).

The company has notified the affected individuals directly and reported the incident to the relevant authorities. It is also strengthening its security against AI-assisted attacks, and will share details on the exposure of financial information with government and financial institutions.

KEPCO’s disclosure followed a November 19 post on a dark web forum by a user operating under the handle Noiem, who reportedly claimed to have stolen KEPCO user and supplier data, as well as bidding and contract documents.

South Korea’s Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) has launched an investigation into the incident, noting that KEPCO received an email from the hacker, verified sample data received from the sender, and confirmed a dark web posting. PIPC has not attributed the data breach to Noiem.

articles.title: Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
articles.context: Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised.

Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer.

The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.”

The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added.

Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. The advisory said only the Classic tiers of the service are affected, not Azure API Management v2, the report added.

The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment.

Norway tells customers to assume exposure

In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management.

“Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian.

It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway.

“Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.”

In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors.

Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20, the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised.

NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation.

“When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment.

Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw.

Urgent need to rotate credentials

Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added.

In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog, Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management.

The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies.

Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM.

“Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report.

NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets.

The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said.

Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said.

Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough.

“If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post.

His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

articles.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
articles.context: " The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22
articles.full_text: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

articles.context: In the first, attackers compromised the hosting provider that was running the AI service
