articles.title: Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection
articles.context: So a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree, and at least one is something your own traffic never does
articles.full_text:
APIs have run digital businesses for more than a decade. For a while, there seemed to be nothing new left to say about them. That changed in 2026, when AI endpoints joined them. Teams now run large language model (LLM) inference endpoints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and Agent2Agent (A2A) servers beside their REST APIs, on services such as Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and more companies sell their API as the product itself. On the other end, AI agents read API descriptions, pick the tools they need, and chain calls with no person clicking through an app.

APIs have always had two kinds of callers: other services and people who use an app. Now there’s a third: AI agents that act on a person’s behalf. It feels like everyone has a personal AI agent that can call APIs for them. Who knew curl would be important again?

Today, we’re launching capabilities across AWS WAF, Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon API Gateway that help you discover and protect the APIs and AI endpoints that services, apps, and AI agents call:

API Portal, a new feature in Amazon API Gateway, discovers your APIs and AI endpoints.

API Security, a new managed rule group in AWS WAF, protects your APIs.

AI Security, a new managed rule group in AWS WAF, protects your AI endpoints.

All three are generally available today. You can enable discovery in API Portal for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations. The two rule groups protect the resources that you associate with your protection pack (web ACL). They work together: API Portal shows which discovered endpoints AWS WAF protects, and the security events that AWS WAF detects appear on each managed API’s detail page.

Same APIs, new callers, new attack surface

Your APIs are the same APIs they always were. What changed is how you expose them, who calls them, and what threatens them.

How you expose them. A new MCP server or LLM endpoint takes minutes to stand up. It can be placed behind a load balancer or a CloudFront distribution without ever passing through your API gateway, so it’s missing from the API registry and the security review. An agent that can reach it doesn’t need your documentation, either, because the endpoint describes itself: an MCP client asks the server for its tools with tools/list, and an A2A client reads the agent card that the server publishes.

Who calls them. The following table compares the three kinds of callers that reach your APIs today.

Caller

What normal looks like

What abuse looks like

What it means for protection

Service to service

Predictable, authenticated calls that repeat the same pattern

A stolen API key, or a partner that scrapes beyond its contract

Track rate and behavior for each API key and endpoint

Person to service, through an app

Sessions and UI-driven calls at a human pace

Account takeover and scripted checkouts

Browser-based signals, such as CAPTCHA and browser fingerprints, apply here

AI agent to service, for a person

Human intent with machine behavior, from an HTTP client or an automated browser

An agent with stolen credentials, or a bot that poses as an agent

Browser signals only go so far, so you need visibility into the API itself

What threatens them. The APIs behind your web and mobile apps were built for one client: your own app. Your app calls them in the right order, at a human pace, with input it already validated. Legitimate agents now call those same APIs directly, and so do attackers and fraudsters. None of them have to follow the rules that your app follows.

What we’re launching

Here’s how we respond to those changes, as shown in Figure 1. In the figure, services, people, and AI agents call your APIs through their entry points. There, API Portal maps your endpoints, and AWS WAF runs API Security and AI Security on the same traffic to stop threats.

Figure 1: API Portal inventories the APIs and AI endpoints that services, people, and AI agents call. AWS WAF protects the entry points in front of them

API Portal builds an inventory of your APIs from their configuration and live traffic, identifies which of them are AI endpoints (LLM inference, MCP, and A2A), and shows you what to protect. It does this by analyzing configuration and traffic across your API entry points: CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway.

API Security covers three kinds of API abuse: broken object level authorization, authentication attacks such as tampered tokens and credential stuffing, and reconnaissance such as probing for undocumented routes. It does this with rules that work from a single request and with behavioral detections that learn your traffic.

AI Security identifies your AI traffic (LLM inference, MCP, and A2A), validates MCP and A2A requests against their protocol, and checks prompts and responses through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for prompt attacks, harmful content, and sensitive information.

All three work with Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancer. For the current list of supported resources, protocols, and endpoint types, see AWS WAF API Security and AWS WAF AI Security rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

The three capabilities live in two places. API Portal is in the Amazon API Gateway console. That’s where it can be found, not what it covers: it discovers APIs behind CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway alike. API Security and AI Security are in the AWS WAF console.

Discover: You can’t secure an invisible API

Ask a platform team how many APIs they run, and you’ll get a number from a registry. Ask what’s answering requests on the internet right now, and the number changes. The MCP server that a team set up for a hackathon isn’t in the registry. Neither is the v1 endpoint that nobody turned off. Both still answer requests.

API Portal builds the inventory from both live traffic and API configuration. You enable discovery in API Portal for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations, and you can exclude resources that you don’t want in the inventory. It reads the service logs and configuration records of your API entry points. There’s nothing to attach, no logs to forward, and no traffic to reroute. It lists the endpoints that receive traffic, by host, path, and HTTP method. Every endpoint starts as a shadow API: deployed and reachable, but not yet governed. When you promote it, it becomes a managed API. For APIs you manage, API Portal also flags zombie APIs, which have no traffic and no configuration change for a set period, and orphaned APIs, whose owning account was closed or removed from your organization. Retire a zombie API that nothing needs, and resolve the ownership of an orphaned one. For the classification rules, see the API Portal Developer Guide.

API Portal also discovers your AI endpoints. It reports each endpoint’s type, such as an LLM inference endpoint, an MCP server, or an A2A server. It finds them in the traffic at the same entry points (CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway) and lists them in the same inventory as your other APIs, so you don’t build a separate view for them. Combined, one row can show a shadow MCP server that nobody manages yet. Figure 2 shows the inventory.

Figure 2: The API inventory in API Portal lists the endpoints discovered behind API Gateway and Application Load Balancer, with each endpoint’s AWS WAF status, classification, and AI workload type

“We can manage our API environment more effectively when we have a clear picture of what’s running across AWS. API Portal gives us that visibility without requiring teams to change how they deploy APIs or route traffic, helping us create a more complete view across the enterprise.” — Mike Hasani, Senior Software Engineer, Principal Financial Group

Some abuse shows in one request. Some appears only over time.

Two requests show why protecting an API takes two kinds of detection. Here’s the first one:

GET /v1/orders/48213 HTTP/1.1 Host: orders.example.com Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhZG1pbiIsInJvbGUiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.

This JSON Web Token (JWT) declares alg: none. It asks your API to skip signature verification, and a correctly built client doesn’t send that. The API Security managed rule group blocks the request before it reaches your origin, from the first request and with no learning period. The same rules catch other token tampering, such as pointing the token at a signing key that the attacker controls. These rules check the structure of a token in the Authorization header. They don’t verify its signature, so your application still has to validate the token. For the full list of rules and what each one does by default, see API Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Here’s the second one:

GET /accounts/1337 HTTP/1.1

Nothing is wrong with this request, and the caller’s token is valid. It’s abuse only if the caller doesn’t own account 1337, and no single request can tell you that. This is broken object level authorization (BOLA), the first entry in the OWASP API Security Top 10.

So, the managed rule group also learns. It builds a baseline from your own traffic and looks for callers who don’t fit it. There’s nothing to set up for this. You don’t turn on logging or mirror traffic.

The hard part is to avoid flagging your own scripts. For example, a nightly export job reads thousands of records on a steady machine schedule. On those two signs alone, it looks like an attacker. So a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree, and at least one is something your own traffic never does. For example, the caller reaches records through a sequence of calls that your app never makes, or your API keeps denying it access. High confidence also needs a caller that AWS WAF can identify from a credential on the request, such as a token. A caller that AWS WAF knows only by IP address stays at medium confidence. Figure 3 compares a nightly export job with an attacker on these signs.

Figure 3: Volume and timing alone don’t reach high confidence. A sign that your own traffic never shows has to agree with them

The behavioral detections cover more than object access. They also flag credential stuffing, where one source presents an unusual number of different credentials in the Authorization header, and probing, where a caller keeps requesting routes or parameters that your traffic never uses.

The same thinking applies to the response, what your APIs send back. The behavioral detections take account of the status codes that your application returns, such as a caller’s rate of denied or failed requests. A caller stands out when, for example, its successful calls turn into a run of authorization failures. API Security doesn’t inspect the content of responses. Figure 4 shows the APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard in the AWS WAF console.

Figure 4: The APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows API Security detections over time, the detections that matched the most requests, and how AWS WAF handled the labeled requests.

Every detection is a label under awswaf:managed:aws:api-security:. A label starts with a stage (attack, recon, or warning) and names the finding. Behavioral detections also end with a confidence (high, medium, or low). Each rule has its own default action. The single-request rules that identify token tampering and unsafe methods block, and the posture and schema discovery rules count. Behavioral detections block at high confidence and count at medium and low confidence, at either stage. Detections that work from a single request have no confidence. For example, attack:alg_none:jwt_header and attack:object_level:high block, and recon:path_schema counts. AWS WAF also repeats a caller’s finding as an actor_identity label on that caller’s later requests across the whole protection pack (web ACL), for about five minutes after the last detection. At high confidence, the rule group blocks those requests by default. At medium and low confidence it counts them, and your own rules can act on the label.

AI Security understands the protocols that agents speak

LLM inference endpoints, MCP servers, and A2A servers are APIs, too. API Portal shows you which of your endpoints they are, and the API Security managed rule group already inspects their requests like any other API path.

The AI Security managed rule group adds checks made for agent traffic. It first recognizes the traffic and labels each request as LLM, MCP, A2A, or not recognized, so the checks that follow fit each endpoint type. It runs in the same AWS WAF protection pack (web ACL) as your other rules, with no new service to deploy.

Its first layer checks each MCP and A2A request against the protocol version that the request declares in its MCP-Protocol-Version or A2A-Version header. It supports MCP versions 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, and 2026-07-28, and A2A version 1.0. For the current list, see AI Security managed rule group. These protocol compliance checks are deterministic and run entirely in AWS WAF. They come in two levels. Baseline covers the violations that let a request slip past routing or inspection, as the example that follows shows, and blocks by default. Strict adds malformed requests that are worth flagging but are usually an outdated client, and counts by default. Each failed check also adds its own label, so you can see exactly which check failed. Here’s the kind of trick that Baseline catches. The header tells every component in front of the MCP server that the request only lists tools. The body calls a tool that reads a file:

POST /mcp HTTP/1.1 Host: tools.example.com Content-Type: application/json MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28 Mcp-Method: tools/list Mcp-Name: read_file { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "read_file", "arguments": { "path": "/etc/passwd" } } }

A gateway or authorizer that trusts the header treats the request as read-only, and the server runs the tool. AWS WAF blocks the request at the API entry point, because the header and the body disagree about the method.

Its second layer checks content through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. You don’t create or configure a guardrail for this. You turn on the option in the rule group and choose a service role, and AWS WAF assumes that role to call Bedrock Guardrails with your account’s identity. Bedrock Guardrails returns a score for each check. AWS WAF groups the scores into three levels (high, medium, and low), and the rule group has one rule for each check at each level, so you choose the action for each one. AWS WAF picks the checks for each endpoint type and each direction, as the following table shows. Response checks run only when you turn on response inspection. They cover the response body up to the body size that AWS WAF inspects for that resource, and content beyond that size isn’t checked.

Bedrock Guardrails check

What it looks for

On requests

On responses

Prompt attack

Jailbreaks, prompt injection, and attempts to extract the system prompt

Yes

MCP and A2A only

Content filter

Hate, insults, sexual content, violence, and misconduct

LLM and A2A only

No

Sensitive information

Personal data such as card numbers, US Social Security numbers, email addresses, and bank account numbers, plus credentials such as passwords and AWS access keys

No

Yes

By default, AWS WAF blocks a high-severity prompt attack, on the request or the response. Everything else counts and adds a label that names what matched, such as a prompt injection or a card number. You can change the action for any rule. If Bedrock Guardrails can’t check a request, AWS WAF adds a label that says why and lets the request through. The label is guardrails:not_assessed when the content can’t be assessed, such as an empty prompt. It’s guardrails:call_failed when the call to Bedrock Guardrails fails, plus a second label with the reason, such as guardrails:call_failed:throttling. Like every label, these appear in your AWS WAF logs and CloudWatch metrics. For how labels work, see Web request labeling in AWS WAF. To fail closed when the call to Bedrock Guardrails fails, set the Guardrails_CallFailed rule to block. Throttling then blocks requests, too. Content checks run in the supported Regions listed in AWS WAF AI Security rule group. Figure 5 follows one request through these checks.

Figure 5: AWS WAF recognizes agent traffic and checks its protocol itself, and calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to check the prompt on the way in and the answer on the way out

The AI Security labels follow the same steps, under awswaf:managed:aws:ai-security:. For example, traffic:recognized_mcp says what the traffic is, protocol_compliance_level:baseline:mcp is the level you act on, protocol_compliance_check:mcp_method_mismatch names the check that failed, and request:guardrails:prompt_attack:severity:high carries the Bedrock Guardrails result. For the full label list, supported protocols, and configuration, see AI Security managed rule group. Figure 6 shows the AI endpoints view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard.

Figure 6: The AI endpoints view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows AI Security detections over time, the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails findings that matched the most requests, and how AWS WAF handled AI traffic

Every detection is a label, and labels work with the rest of AWS WAF

Every detection from the API Security and AI Security rule groups is also a label on the request. Any rule that runs later in your protection pack can match those labels and combine them with labels from other managed rule groups. Examples are AWS WAF Bot Control, AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention, and the Amazon IP reputation list. That list draws on MadPot, the threat intelligence tool that Amazon uses to protect customers from cybercrime. Use request labels in your own rules. Labels from response checks, such as sensitive information in a response, drive the AI Security rule group’s own actions and appear in your CloudWatch metrics.

Here are four examples of what that makes possible:

Rate limits keyed on labels. One probe for your API schema can be noise. Fifty from the same caller in 5 minutes is reconnaissance. A rate-based rule scoped to the reconnaissance labels counts only those requests.

No unsigned agents on your MCP server. If your MCP server is only for agents you work with, block requests without an access token or a verified Web Bot Auth signature. Then match the Bot Control bot name label for the operators you trust. Application Load Balancer JWT verification, CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge, or your MCP server still validates the token itself.

Two weak signals that add up. A low-confidence API Security label or a Bot Control signal by itself isn’t enough to block. Block only the requests that carry both.

Tighter limits on sensitive paths. Bot Control targeted protection labels callers by confidence. Use those labels to set a lower rate limit on /checkout than on the rest of your API.

The following rule shows the first example. For each IP address, it counts the requests that carry an API Security reconnaissance label. When an address sends more than 50 requests in 5 minutes, the rule blocks them. Place it after the API Security managed rule group so that its labels are available.

{ "Name": "RateLimitAPISecurityRecon", "Priority": 40, "Statement": { "RateBasedStatement": { "Limit": 50, "EvaluationWindowSec": 300, "AggregateKeyType": "IP", "ScopeDownStatement": { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "NAMESPACE", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:api-security:recon:" } } } }, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "RateLimitAPISecurityRecon" } }

Labels don’t have to stop at AWS WAF. With custom request headers and dynamic label interpolation, AWS WAF can forward the matched labels to your origin. Your application then sees what AWS WAF saw and can show less data, require step-up authentication, or log the request for review. For how it works, see Do more with AWS WAF labels using dynamic label interpolation.

We keep adding labels, so the documentation holds the current lists. See API Security labels, AI Security labels, and AWS WAF Bot Control rule group.

See what the rule groups found, and act on it

Every label is also an Amazon CloudWatch metric, with no extra setup, and appears in your AWS WAF logs. The protection pack (web ACL) dashboard in the AWS WAF console shows them as traffic arrives. In API Portal, each managed API’s detail page shows the security events that AWS WAF detected on it, as shown in Figure 7.

Figure 7: Each managed API’s detail page in API Portal shows the events that AWS WAF detected on it

The managed rule groups enforce their own detections at your API entry points. To write a rule of your own, start from a label. Scope a rate-based rule to the paths it appears on, key it on the IP address or TLS fingerprint, and start in count mode.

When a detection type spikes, your existing alerting can act on it. That can be a CloudWatch alarm, or the observability or security platform that already reads your metrics and logs. For log destinations, see Logging AWS WAF protection pack (web ACL) traffic.

How we test API Security

No single test shows whether a detection works, so we combine several for API Security:

Automated red teaming – LLM-powered agents run continuously against deliberately vulnerable test APIs that we maintain. They probe, adapt, and chain steps the way an attacker does.

A growing attack suite – Each working exploit that the agents find becomes a repeatable test case. We replay the suite against the managed rule group when it changes.

Realistic legitimate traffic – We replay traffic such as batch jobs, seasonal spikes, and power users next to the attacks, so we measure false positives together with detections.

Results from our test environment don’t transfer directly to yours, because your APIs and the attacks against them differ. The numbers that matter come from your own traffic, and the next section shows how to get them. API Security is designed to detect and block callers who walk object IDs to harvest other users’ records, and tokens whose structure shows tampering. It also flags credential stuffing against the Authorization header and callers who probe for routes that your API doesn’t serve. Efficacy and expansion work for API Security, like AWS WAF security in general, is a continuous effort. For the current list of detections, see API Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Check what gets blocked on your own traffic

The managed rule groups apply their default actions from the moment you add them. To see what a rule group finds before it blocks anything, first add it with all rule actions overridden to count, review the results, and then remove the override. Later, to review one rule, override only that rule to count. AWS WAF still evaluates an overridden rule and adds its label, so you see what it would have blocked on your own production traffic.

Behavioral detections need time to learn your traffic. For the learning period, see Testing and deploying AWS WAF API Security. For a step-by-step evaluation, see Testing and tuning your AWS WAF protections.

Availability

API Portal, API Security, and AI Security are generally available today. Detection of data exfiltration and sensitive data exposure in responses for API Security is coming soon.

Pricing

Each capability is priced by the service it runs in. For API Portal, see Amazon API Gateway pricing. For the API Security and AI Security managed rule groups, see AWS WAF pricing. For the content checks that AI Security runs through Bedrock Guardrails, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Get started

To get started, complete the following steps:

In API Portal, enable discovery for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations, and exclude any resources that you don’t want in the inventory. This step doesn’t need AWS WAF. As the inventory builds, look for endpoints you didn’t expect, such as shadow APIs and AI endpoints, and add them to your managed APIs.

In the AWS WAF console, add the API Security managed rule group to the protection pack in front of your APIs. Start with all rule actions overridden to count, review what it finds on your own traffic, and then remove the override.

If you run AI endpoints, add the AI Security managed rule group to the same protection pack. To turn on the Bedrock Guardrails checks, choose a service role that AWS WAF can assume to call Bedrock Guardrails, and turn on response inspection if you want responses checked and your protection pack (web ACL) protects CloudFront or an Application Load Balancer. Start with the four rules that block by default overridden to count, review what they find on your own traffic, and then remove the overrides one rule at a time.

After the first baseline is available, the behavioral detections label abuse and block it at high confidence. Watch the labels in your CloudWatch metrics, and in your AWS WAF logs if you turn on logging.

Use those labels in your own rules, such as a lower rate limit on your most sensitive paths.

For step-by-step instructions, see Adding the API Security managed rule group and Adding the AI Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Best practice: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of your APIs

Put Amazon CloudFront in front of your API Gateway APIs, your Application Load Balancers, and any other endpoint that is public on port 80 or 443, and associate your protection pack (web ACL) with the CloudFront distribution. That includes APIs that run outside AWS, with another cloud provider or on premises: CloudFront works with any HTTP or HTTPS origin, so those APIs get the same delivery, acceleration, and protection. The same applies to your MCP servers, A2A servers, and LLM endpoints, whether you host them on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, on Amazon EKS, or elsewhere. With this setup:

AWS WAF inspects requests at the edge, before they reach your origin.

AWS WAF sees the caller’s own IP address.

AWS WAF mitigates attacks close to their source.

For origins in AWS, CloudFront VPC origins mean your Application Load Balancer or private API Gateway REST API isn’t exposed directly to the public internet and is reached through CloudFront.

For more information, see Use AWS WAF protections and Restrict access with VPC origins in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide, and the posts Introducing Amazon CloudFront VPC origins and Accessing private Amazon API Gateway endpoints through custom Amazon CloudFront distribution using VPC Origins.

Conclusion

Your APIs are the same APIs they always were. The callers changed, and so did the attack surface. With API Portal, you can see the APIs and AI endpoints that the internet is calling. With API Security and AI Security in AWS WAF, you can protect them at their entry points, without changes to your backend code.

AWS built the building blocks for what comes next: an inventory from traffic, labels that you can act on, and protection where requests first arrive. As agents and the protocols they speak change, those building blocks are where new protection shows up. For the most up-to-date information, see AWS WAF API Security and AWS WAF AI Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

To get started, enable discovery in API Portal, and add the API Security and AI Security managed rule groups in the AWS WAF console.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Gopinath Durairaj

Gopinath is a product leader who built enterprise technology businesses across cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure, AI / ML and networking. He currently leads web application security product strategy at AWS, a portfolio that includes AWS WAF, API security, and security for AI-powered applications.

Eitav is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS and a technology leader with over 15 years of experience in the tech industry. He specializes in edge computing, serverless, and platform engineering, and works with engineering teams to design secure, globally scalable architectures on CloudFront and AWS WAF. His current focus is on internet-scale systems—from global content delivery to edge security.

Gabe Sin

Gabe is a Senior Product Manager at AWS on the Amazon API Gateway team, focused on API management. Before AWS, he led product and strategy at a cryptocurrency exchange, where he built the company’s end-to-end analytics infrastructure on AWS, bringing the same visibility and governance to data that he now brings to APIs.

Aykut Tuzunkan

Aykut is a Senior Technical Program Manager at AWS, based in Seattle, with more than 15 years of experience across edge security, distributed networks, and infrastructure capacity. He owns AWS WAF’s cross-org programs, which cover protection for web applications, APIs, bots, and AI traffic. He focuses on adding new protections to AWS WAF and strengthening the ones customers rely on.

articles.title: US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise
OpenRouter drops AI providers over leaked prompts and secrets
articles.context: " Dragos discovered that, in some cases, those credentials were leaked to outsiders and used in the wild, indicating that the test prompts had escaped
articles.full_text:
OpenRouter removed three AI providers from its platform after discovering that they had violated their stated data-handling policies and exposed sensitive data.

The company also revoked Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution and notified all potentially affected customers.

OpenRouter is an AI model broker that lets developers access AI models from different companies using a single API key.

When an app sends a request, OpenRouter forwards it to a provider that runs the selected model and passes the answer back.

Operational technology security company Dragos alerted OpenRouter after sending two million test prompts through the platform, each containing a unique tracking link or decoy credential, and detecting "activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed."

Dragos discovered that, in some cases, those credentials were leaked to outsiders and used in the wild, indicating that the test prompts had escaped.

“We observed activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed. Our seeded test prompts were used in attempts to access our controlled test systems and canary AWS accounts,” Dragos says.

OpenRouter says there was no breach on its own systems, making the leak point at the provider level and leading to the decision to remove the three leaking inference providers: Together AI, Phala, and Novita.

Another provider, Atlas Cloud, said it would voluntarily withdraw its models from OpenRouter pending security testing, following a third-party security incident.

The other three published separate announcements responding to Dragos’ findings and explaining how the leaks occurred.

Together AI said an AI coding agent exposed a repository credential on GitHub, allowing an unauthorized party to download stored prompt samples from June and July involving MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6.

Phala said an attacker compromised a server processing DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests routed through OpenRouter between October 21 and 22, and possibly up to November 8, and obtained application credentials from affected virtual machines.

Novita said a routing misconfiguration forwarded some MiniMax requests, including those sent through OpenRouter, to MiniMax’s official API between May 28 and November 11.

All four providers are tightening security controls, strengthening their zero data retention or data deletion policies, and advising potentially impacted users to rotate any secrets that may have been exposed in the leaked requests.

OpenRouter is also adapting Dragos’ tests for ongoing use to check whether AI providers forward or leak user requests/responses to third parties, and will require validation before restoring ZDR eligibility.

articles.title: Microsoft Azure flaw exploited to steal customers' API credentials
articles.context: Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is warning customers that a security vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) Classic tiers was exploited to steal stored API credentials, with Norwegian authorities linking the flaw to cyberattacks against energy companies.

Azure API Management is a cloud service that lets organizations publish, secure, monitor, and manage APIs that connect applications, services, and data.

In an Azure Service Health security advisory (Tracking ID: MZK9-GH0) sent to customers and shared with BleepingComputer, Microsoft said it identified the vulnerability on November 18, 2026, and deployed a mitigation the following day.

"Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue," Microsoft said in the advisory.

According to Microsoft, the vulnerability allowed unauthorized access to certain management functionality when APIM Classic instances were not configured according to recommended security best practices.

This access could have allowed attackers to perform administrative operations, including accessing secrets stored in the service.

Microsoft said the following information may have been exposed:

Secrets stored in Named Values

Client secrets associated with identity providers

Client secrets associated with OpenID Connect providers

Subscription keys

Tokens used to call direct management APIs

These credentials could potentially allow attackers to access additional applications, services, or backend systems, depending on their permissions.

Microsoft said it closed the unauthorized access path on November 19 and rotated Microsoft-controlled keys and credentials where appropriate.

However, the company warned that its remediation would not invalidate customer credentials that may have been compromised before the fix was deployed.

"This remediation blocks the unauthorized management-plane access path that could allow an actor to perform administrative operations, including secrets management, against Azure API Management services," Microsoft warned.

"However, it does not automatically invalidate credentials that may have been accessed before the fix was deployed."

The vulnerability affects Azure API Management Classic tiers, while Microsoft said APIM v2 tiers are not impacted.

Microsoft urged affected customers to immediately rotate potentially exposed credentials, investigate suspicious activity in systems accessible through those credentials, and review available logs for signs of unauthorized access.

In a Reddit post, an administrator claimed their organization discovered the vulnerability after detecting unauthorized access to Azure Key Vault using a valid administrator token.

"Our company has been fighting this for days, after discovering that someone logged into our keyvaults using a valid administrator token and not following the normal access pattern," the administrator claimed.

The administrator alleged that attackers exploited a zero-day authentication bypass in a deprecated legacy API to gain access to a privileged system account on APIM instances.

According to the administrator, the legacy API did not generate logs that customers could use to detect the unauthorized access. They also alleged that Microsoft initially attributed the suspicious activity to leaked customer credentials before deploying a global fix.

BleepingComputer has not independently verified these allegations.

The vulnerability has also been linked to attacks affecting Norwegian organizations, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi.

In a security advisory, Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) said an unknown threat actor targeted access tokens, secrets, and named values stored in Azure API Management.

The agency said Norway's energy sector first discovered the vulnerability and that organizations in other countries and industries were also affected.

Equinor disclosed an ongoing cyberattack on November 17, a day before Microsoft says it identified the APIM vulnerability. The company later announced that it had stopped the attack and found no indication that data had been stolen or altered.

Skagerak Energi also reported an attempted cyberattack but said it had no impact on its operations and no evidence that information was compromised.

While Microsoft says it deployed a remediation on November 19 that required no customer action, NSM's advisory warns organizations to verify that their APIM instances have received the security update.

The agency warns that instances running below specific runtime versions remain vulnerable and advises customers to contact their "service provider" if they have not received the update.

It is unclear whether the runtime updates are separate from Microsoft's initial mitigation.

Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen shared threat-hunting queries to help organizations investigate potential exploitation and identify credentials stored in their APIM instances.

BleepingComputer contacted Microsoft with questions about the attacks but has not received a reply yet.

This Azure API Management incident comes just days after Microsoft confirmed another security breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, where attackers exploited a vulnerability to steal tenant configuration information and administrator email addresses.

articles.title: Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
articles.context: Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it
articles.full_text: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote. That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked. “The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.” Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle. To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6. “The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy said. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added. “This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.” Luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the update. Unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers. ®

articles.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Attackers Copied Payment Card Data From Its Platform
articles.context: Cleverbridge confirms attackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes, warning customers to watch for fraudulent transactions
articles.full_text:
Cleverbridge confirms attackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes, warning customers to watch for fraudulent transactions.

Cleverbridge, which runs checkouts, payments and subscriptions for other companies, has confirmed that attackers copied payment card data from its platform. The company says it found the problem on 4 November and started notifying affected people on 20 November. That’s a gap of 16 days.

“On 4 November 2026, Cleverbridge detected unauthorised activity in our platform and took immediate steps to contain the incident.” reads the incident update published by the company. “Whilst our investigation remains ongoing, regretfully, we have been able to determine that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform.”

Affected systems went offline for a short time and were back online the same day. Only later did the investigation show that a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform, and the company says that the investigation is still running.

The company’s website lists customers such as SUSE, Red Hat and Parallels, but the company has not said which businesses were affected.

If you bought a product or service from a company that uses Cleverbridge, it may have handled your payment and stored your card details. Cleverbridge provides payment and subscription services to software and SaaS companies.

Cleverbridge has not clearly explained what information was stolen on its public incident page. It says the exposed data may include payment card details and directs affected customers to check their individual notifications. However, a notification reviewed by BleepingComputer provides more details: the stolen information may include card numbers, expiration dates and CVV or CVC security codes.

That last item is the one that matters. The card industry’s own rules generally bar companies from keeping the security code once a payment is authorised, so BleepingComputer asked Cleverbridge why the codes were accessible at all.

The company did not disclose technical details about the attack, however, its answer excluded a ransomware attack.

“None of our systems were encrypted.” continues the update.

Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion/Cyberscout, a third-party vendor, to support the notifications, and that a notice sent on its behalf is legitimate. It has offered credit or identity monitoring where available, with sign-up details in the notice. Asked why people weren’t told sooner, it says it moved fast and notified them without undue delay.

Cleverbridge advises users to watch for phishing attempts and warns that it will never request card details, passwords or security codes by email, phone or text.

“As always, we recommend that our users follow general best online security practices, remain vigilant, and be aware of phishing attempts.” the company states. “Out of an abundance of caution, please be cautious of unexpected emails, calls, or messages about this incident. Cleverbridge will never ask you for your card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text message. ”

Call your card issuer sooner rather than later. Cleverbridge says the issuer may decide to replace your card after you report the incident.

We recommend that you check your card statements carefully and tell your card issuer right away about any transaction that you do not recognise.” concludes the report. “You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card. ”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, payment card data)

articles.title: Spanish LaLiga confirms hackers stole soccer fans’ personal data
articles.context: According to the organization, the incident occurred between November 14 and 16, and the attacker extracted data from compromised systems
articles.full_text:
LaLiga, Spain's top men's professional football league, disclosed a data breach that exposed personal information belonging to users of its services and those of some affiliated clubs.

According to the organization, the incident occurred between November 14 and 16, and the attacker extracted data from compromised systems.

LaLiga organizes Spain’s top two men’s professional football divisions.

The top league is one of the world’s most prominent football leagues, where clubs with a global audience, such as Real Madrid, FC Barcelona, and Atlético Madrid, play.

On November 16, the organization’s security team identified the source of the unauthorized access and implemented measures to block the attack and stop the data extraction.

“LALIGA was the target of a cyberattack on one of its technology platforms for fan services,” reads the announcement.

“Between November 14 and 16, a cybercriminal gained unauthorized access to the platform and extracted personal data belonging to users registered for digital services offered by LALIGA and some clubs.”

LaLiga underlined that the incident was confined to a specific platform and did not extend to other systems that support the running of the competitions.

After implementing containment measures, LaLiga launched an investigation to determine the scope of the incident and introduced more thorough monitoring to detect future attempts to breach its systems.

The football organizer also reported the incident to the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and filed a complaint with the National Police’s Central Cybercrime Unit.

Impacted clubs were also directly notified, and actions to inform impacted fans are being coordinated.

At the time of writing, no ransomware group has claimed responsibility for the attack on LaLiga.

BleepingComputer has contacted the organization to learn more about the attack and which clubs were impacted, but we have not received a response as of publication.

articles.title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
articles.context: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any...
articles.full_text: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers. CVE-2026-76466, which carries a 9.8 CVSS rating, affects Cisco Expressway-C and Cisco Expressway-E gateways configured in clusters, both virtual and physical appliances running vulnerable software. These provide firewall traversal, VPN-less remote access, and call routing for remote users connecting to voice, video, and messaging collaboration services. The bug involves hard-coded authentication credentials and insufficient certificate validation in clustered Expressway deployments. “An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands,” Cisco said in October, when it disclosed the bug and issued a software update that fixed the flaw. “A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device.” At the time, the networking vendor said it wasn’t aware of any abuse of the vulnerability. That all changed late last week, however, when Russian security firm F6 said it was investigating “the first observed case” of miscreants exploiting CVE-2026-76466, shortly after a public proof-of-concept exploit became available. “The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices,” F6’s Cyber Defense Center said on Thursday. “Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization’s internal network. After obtaining root access, the attackers began preparing tooling for further lateral movement across the infrastructure.” Specifically, the criminals prepared custom Python code to scan the victim’s network and identify files and folders shared over the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. The scripts were also designed to interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials and other sensitive information. The Python scripts used in the attack indicated that the operator used an AI assistant, according to F6. The security shop also noted that one of the key indicators of compromise is a nodeup “wombat@127.0.0.1” entry in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices. A day later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76466 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and told federal agencies to patch by Monday. Cisco updated its advisory on Monday to acknowledge CISA’s addition, while noting that it has no direct evidence of active exploitation. The Register reached out to the networking and security vendor for additional details about the scope of the attacks, but did not receive any response. We will update this story as we learn more. ®

articles.title: Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors
Webworm Suspected of Modifying SoftEther VPN to Evade Detection and Hide Remote Access
articles.context: One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-...
articles.full_text:
The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks.

The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence.

First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations.

One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026.

"The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions."

The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN."

One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity.

It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response.

The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark.

Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below -

Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB.

Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII.

What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth.

"It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools.

"We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

articles.title: Bulgaria evicts cyber snoops who lurked inside government networks for 5 years
articles.context: Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government...
articles.full_text: The Ancient Thracian heartland of Bulgaria says it has shut down a cyberespionage operation that gave intruders access to government networks for five years – the longest-running known campaign against its administration. Bulgaria's Ministry of Innovation and Digital Transformation said the unauthorized and officially unattributed attackers first gained access to infrastructure used by government institutions to exchange information in 2021. It explained that the intrusion went unnoticed for so long because "the previous means of protection did not work as a single, integrated system," and that without a new, recently installed product, it may have gone undetected for much longer. "The incident was discovered thanks to the new national cybersecurity system, which for the first time provides a single picture of what is happening in state networks," the ministry added. "Without it, this activity would most likely have remained hidden for an indefinite period of time." Bulgaria acknowledged that "sensitive information related to the work of the state" was accessed, but did not specify the scale of the compromise. Innovation and Digital Transformation Minister Ivan Vasilev said attackers had downloaded more than 130 GB of data over five years. He also put the volume at 62 million pages. The Register contacted the Bulgarian government for confirmation of these numbers. The ministry said that it has not yet found any evidence that citizens' personal data was compromised, and that the affected infrastructure "will be under increased surveillance for 90 days" in case the attackers try to regain access. Vasilev said multiple international hacking groups had accessed government systems since 2021. He did not specify the names of these groups, however, nor did he name any specific countries that may have been involved. In a follow-up interview with bTV, Vasilev blamed political instability and frequent changes of ministerial leadership for leaving government systems inadequately protected. A representative of the Progressive Bulgaria party, which back in May won Bulgaria's eighth general election in five years, Vasilev said the "constant change of leadership" means "important things for the state do not actually happen." Vasilev said the intrusion was discovered over the summer as the national cybersecurity system was upgraded, and that teams had spent the past three to four months removing the attackers. ®

articles.title: Protect identity data with point-in-time recovery in Amazon Cognito
articles.context: The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed
articles.full_text:
Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, microservices, and AI agents in minutes. Many of you rely on it for some of the most critical data you operate: the identities and attributes your applications use to authenticate and authorize every request. Recently, we launched point-in-time recovery (PITR) for Amazon Cognito user pools, which lets you restore a user pool to an earlier point in time if an accidental deletion, a faulty migration, or an erroneous bulk operation changes data you need. It’s turned on automatically for user pools on the eligible feature plans.

Before this launch, protecting user pool data meant building your own solution, such as exporting user attributes and group data on a schedule. That approach was time-consuming to build and operate, versioning the exports to find a clean point in time was another challenge, and reconstructing a pool from them was complicated. Users also got new sub identifiers as part of the restore process, which might break any downstream reference to the originals. Passwords, multi-factor authentication (MFA) settings, and passkeys might not be recovered, so every affected user had to reset.

In this post, we show you how to recover a user pool after an erroneous bulk operation, using the preview to review changes before you approve them.

How PITR works

On eligible user pools (see Prerequisites), Amazon Cognito now tracks changes so you can recover the pool to any point within the recovery window. The length of that window depends on your user pool feature plan. The window accrues from the time the pool is on an eligible feature plan, and you can only recover to a point at which PITR coverage already existed.

One behavior to understand is what happens to passwords during a recovery. A recovery restores passwords for users it recreates. A user who still exists and changed their password after the target time keeps the same password. The recovery doesn’t revert password changes, so users who legitimately changed their credentials don’t lose them.

A recovery is preview-based and has three steps:

Initiate a recovery to a target point in time (InitiatePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito pauses write operations to the user pool and generates a preview for your review before any changes are applied. Read operations and sign-in continue to work normally. The call returns a RestoreId.

Review the recovery preview (DescribePointInTimeRecovery). Amazon Cognito reports how many users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys the recovery would create, update, or delete to return the pool to its state at the target time.

Approve or cancel. If the preview looks right, you approve the recovery with StartPointInTimeRecovery, and Amazon Cognito restores the pool to its state at the target time. If it doesn’t look right, you cancel it with CancelPointInTimeRecovery; no changes are applied, and write operations resume.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

An AWS account with an Amazon Cognito user pool on the Essentials or Plus feature plan. The recovery window is up to 1 day on Essentials and up to 14 days on Plus. The examples use a pool named anycompany-prod-user-pool in the US East (N. Virginia) AWS Region (us-east-1).

The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with permissions for the Amazon Cognito user pools PITR operations.

Before you run a recovery, keep these limits in mind:

You can run one recovery at a time per user pool, and one successful recovery per 24 hours per pool.

The target time must be at least 15 minutes in the past and no earlier than the pool’s creation time.

Recovery is initiated from the pool’s primary Region and can’t start while a multi-Region replication (MRR) operation, such as replica creation or deletion, is in progress on the pool.

Recovering a user pool after an unintentional change

AnyCompany runs its user sign-in on an Amazon Cognito user pool, anycompany-prod-user-pool.

At 15:45 PDT, an operator runs a bulk change that’s supposed to set an attribute on a subset of users. A defect in the script instead deletes and modifies users. By 15:54 PDT, support receives cases of failed sign-ins and the operator halts the script. The team needs the pool as it was at 15:39 PDT. They decide to use PITR and preview the recovery before approving it.

Step 1: Start the recovery

The team initiates a recovery with a target time of 15:39 PDT by running the command in the preceding example. Figure 1 shows the same step in the console, where the team enters the target time and starts the recovery. The response includes a RestoreId that identifies this recovery throughout the workflow, along with a RestoreStatus and the RestoreTimestamp that you targeted.

aws cognito-idp initiate-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-timestamp 2026-10-28T22:39:00Z

Figure 1: Initiating a recovery to a target point in time

Step 2: Review the recovery preview

DescribePointInTimeRecovery returns the Restoration for this RestoreId, including a RestorePreview that summarizes how many entities will be affected if the pool is returned to the target time. The team reviews the preview and confirms the number of affected users matches the scope.

aws cognito-idp describe-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a69b8c1e-9866-441d-EXAMPLE11111

In this case, the preview reports 16 users to create and 5 users to update, as the following sample response shows. Figure 2 shows the same preview in the console, with the create, update, and delete counts for users, groups, MFA settings, and passkeys. These numbers match the scope of the bulk operation, so the team continues. If the preview had shown unexpected changes, the team could cancel the recovery with no changes applied.

{ "Restoration": { "RestoreId": "a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111", "RestorePreview": [ { "Entity": "Users", "CreateCount": 16, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 5 }, { "Entity": "Groups", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "User MFAs", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 }, { "Entity": "Passkeys", "CreateCount": 0, "DeleteCount": 0, "UpdateCount": 0 } ], "RestoreStatus": "PREVIEW_GENERATED", "RestoreTimestamp": 1793227140, "TriggerTimestamp": 1793228700 } }

Figure 2: Reviewing the recovery preview before applying

Step 3: Approve the recovery

If the preview is correct, the team approves the recovery with the command in the following example, and Amazon Cognito restores anycompany-prod-user-pool to its 15:39 PDT state. Figure 3 shows the approval step in the console, and Figure 4 shows the confirmation that appears after the recovery starts. Writes to the user pool resume automatically after the recovery completes or is canceled.

aws cognito-idp start-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Figure 3: Approving the recovery

Figure 4: Recovery confirmation

aws cognito-idp cancel-point-in-time-recovery \ --user-pool-id us-east-1_EXAMPLE \ --restore-id a7c41e92-0d3b-4f6a-EXAMPLE11111

Your application integration doesn’t change

Because PITR rolls back the data in your existing user pool rather than creating a new one, your application integration doesn’t need any changes. A recovery restores user data and leaves your user pool configuration in place, so configuration changes you made after the recovery point are preserved. For example, a custom attribute you added to the schema, an AWS Lambda trigger you updated, or a password policy you tightened stays as it is. The user pool ID also stays the same, and so do your app client IDs and secrets, managed login and domain, identity provider and SAML/OIDC configurations, and the provider Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) that services such as Amazon API Gateway and Application Load Balancer use to validate tokens. Recreated users keep the same sub identifiers, so downstream references to them keep working.

How PITR complements multi-Region replication

Multi-Region replication and PITR address different failure modes. Multi-Region replication keeps a synchronized replica of your user pool in another Region, so if the primary Region is impaired, you can fail over traffic to a replica Region with minimal downtime. PITR helps with data problems, such as erroneous bulk operations that corrupt your user pool’s state. You roll back to any point within your recovery window without changing your application integration.

Security considerations

A recovery changes the identity data that every sign-in and authorization decision depends on, so treat recovery permissions like any other high-impact administrative access.

Separate who initiates a recovery from who approves it. Because initiating and approving are separate API actions, you can assign them to different AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Give an operator the permission InitiatePointInTimeRecovery, and give an approver the permission StartPointInTimeRecovery. Both permissions need DescribePointInTimeRecovery and ListPointInTimeRecoveries to review the preview, and CancelPointInTimeRecovery to stop a recovery. IAM keeps the two permissions on separate roles, but it doesn’t stop one person from assuming both. Assign the roles to different people or teams, and grant the approver role only for the duration of an approved change.

Treat initiating a recovery as sensitive. Initiating a recovery pauses write operations on the user pool until the recovery is approved or canceled. If no action is taken within 24 hours, the preview automatically cancels and write operations are resumed. While writes are paused, users can’t sign up, reset their passwords, or update their profiles. A user pool also allows only one successful recovery per 24 hours, so an unauthorized recovery uses up a recovery you might need for a real incident.

Review restored users after a recovery. A recovery recreates users who were deleted after the target time, including users you removed on purpose, such as employees who have left or compromised accounts. After a recovery completes, check the recreated users against your incident timeline. Disable any that should stay removed and revoke their sessions with AdminUserGlobalSignOut.

Monitor recovery activity. Amazon Cognito records PITR API calls in AWS CloudTrail. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that notifies your security team whenever InitiatePointInTimeRecovery or StartPointInTimeRecovery is called, so that no recovery goes unnoticed.

Pricing

PITR is included at no additional charge in eligible feature plans with a recovery window of up to 1 day on the Essentials feature plan and up to 14 days on the Plus feature plan.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how to recover an Amazon Cognito user pool after an erroneous bulk operation with PITR, from reviewing the changes in a preview to approving the recovery. PITR provides protection for your users’ identities, with no custom export-and-restore pipeline to build or operate. Because the recovery happens in place on the same user pool, your application integration keeps working unchanged. PITR is already enabled for eligible user pools. Before you need it, separate the initiate and approve permissions, add an alert on recovery calls, and practice the preview workflow on a test pool.

To get started:

Related post: Improve your application resilience with Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication

Related post: Amazon Cognito unlocks advanced capabilities with next-generation infrastructure

See PITR in the Amazon Cognito console.

Learn more on the Amazon Cognito page.

Read the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide for feature details.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Howie is a Product Manager at Amazon Web Services, where he strives to make auth easy by default. Outside of work, Howie enjoys exploring cultures and food through travels and making new ice cream flavors inspired by them.
