articles.full_text:
Of the visits that claimed to come from Perplexity agents, 63% were probing for secrets. Cequence cautioned that agent names were self-reported and open to any bot, so the figure did not show Perplexity itself was behind the probing.

Dana Simberkoff, chief risk, privacy and information security officer at AvePoint, noted that organizations needed least-privilege access, identity controls, monitoring, audit trails and human approval for high-risk actions.

Aviv Nahum, co-founder and CEO at Above Security, added that organizations "must treat AI agents as first-class identities and a new class of insiders."

Read more on AI-driven bot traffic: AI Drives Surge in Bot and API Threats

AI Agents Shift From Reading to Buying

Among established AI agents tracked throughout the study, 13% of visits involved taking action in November, up from 1.4% in May. Taking action meant signing in, booking, buying, managing an account or paying. Action-taking visits grew 240%, while read-only visits fell 73%.

articles.title: Azure Flaw Exploited to Target Secrets at Norwegian Energy Firms
articles.context: The vulnerability may have allowed threat actors to gain access to secrets stored in some APIM instances
articles.full_text:
A security issue discovered in Microsoft’s Azure API Management (APIM) service appears to have been responsible for the security incidents reported last week by two Norwegian energy firms, with impact extending beyond Norway.

Microsoft is notifying customers about the issue in Azure APIM, which is designed for publishing, securing and managing APIs. The vulnerability may have allowed threat actors to gain access to secrets stored in some APIM instances.

According to a private notification shared on Reddit by one customer, the tech giant discovered the issue on November 18 and closed the access path the next day.

“Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue,” Microsoft said.

Exposed data can include secrets stored as named values, client secrets for identity providers, subscription keys, and tokens for APIM’s direct management APIs.

Microsoft noted that APIM Classic tiers that don’t follow its documented security guidance are affected. Instances on v2 tiers are not impacted.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said on November 20 that the vulnerability had affected several organizations in the country, including energy companies Equinor and Skagerak Energi, which independently disclosed cybersecurity incidents last week.

Equinor reported the attack on November 17, one day before Microsoft identified the APIM flaw. The company said it found no evidence that data was stolen or altered. Skagerak Energi disclosed the incident on November 18, saying it did not impact operations or production, and it found no evidence of information compromise.

NSM said an unknown threat actor targeted tokens, secrets and named values stored in APIM. It’s unclear how widely the weakness has been exploited, but the organization noted that several sectors in Norway and abroad are impacted.

APIM users have been advised by NSM to treat their secrets and named values as compromised and replace them. They should also verify that their instances have been updated and identify the data accessible through the service.

Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that credentials lifted from APIM could be used against outside services. The extent of the exposure depends on each credential’s permissions.

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: VMware 0-Day, Java4Shell, NGINX2Root, Ruby2Shell, and a Whole Lot of Shell Trouble
articles.context: ⚡ Threat of the Week Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been...
articles.full_text:
A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open.

This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need.

The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week.

⚡ Threat of the Week

Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines.

Is Your Workforce Secured from AI Threats?

Attackers now weaponize AI to launch personalized phishing attacks faster than employees can react. Fight AI with AI, using realistic simulations to train employees to spot and stop threats. Stop phishing before it becomes a breach.

Book a Demo ➝

🔔 Top News

Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks.

Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue.

New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.

GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks.

‎️‍🔥 Trending CVEs

Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser).

🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers.

8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts.

Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them.

📰 Around the Cyber World

Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers.

A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India.

The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs.

Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries.

Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.

Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism.

Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed.

Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027.

Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days."

Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both."

Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025.

Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences."

At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service."

Conclusion

The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done.

That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

articles.title: Signal Moves to Block  iOS and Android AI Agents From Reading Chats
articles.context: Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, outlined the measures in a November 20 blog post, calling AI agents woven into operating systems, such as Google Gemini...
articles.full_text:
Signal has moved to stop AI agents built into iOS and Android from capturing users' chats, warning that it could not control anything they collected.

Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, outlined the measures in a November 20 blog post, calling AI agents woven into operating systems, such as Google Gemini on Android and Apple's Siri AI, "an existential threat to Signal."

Protections Vary by Platform

On Android, it said Screen security, an existing setting, would switch on automatically when Signal spotted an AI assistant trying to read the screen. Signal explained that because there are multiple versions of Android beyond Google, for many vendors, there is no reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Signal said it chose detection over blocking all screenshots, which would have impacted the user experiance.

Users could turn the protection off, though Signal warned this could leave their messages, and their contacts', open to AI agents. Blocking screenshots also does not stop agents from reading data already stored on a device, Signal said.

On iOS 27, Signal said it was preventing screenshots and showed a setting called "Block Siri AI."

However, on macOS 27, Signal said it had no dependable way to stop screenshots and that Apple's screen-protection options covered only streaming and copy-protected media. It advised users to add Signal to the Siri Excluded Apps list.

In 2025, Signal began blocking screenshots by default on Windows 11 to keep out Microsoft Recall, which takes screenshots every few seconds and stores their text in a searchable database that Signal said could keep even disappearing messages indefinitely.

Read more on AI agent security: 65% of Enterprises Have Seen AI Agents Act Out of Scope

Signal Presses Platform Makers for an Opt-Out

Signal also pointed to third-party agents such as Meta Muse, which it said were using accessibility settings to reach app data. Those settings let apps read and control the screen and are designed for assistive tools.

It asked Apple, Google and Microsoft for a documented way for apps to opt out of AI access to their screens, files, notifications and other system features without breaking how they work, plus clearer documentation of how agents handle data.

Signal said confidential computing, which protects data while it is processed, fell short because AI providers would still decide how much privacy users got. Google and Apple were engaging with Signal, which said it was "cautiously optimistic" about some major operating system providers.

Whittaker said Signal's developers had put significant effort into forensic analysis of Android and iOS to learn how AI systems reached app data, and that the lack of documentation made strong privacy harder to build.

articles.title: Everything going down at once wasn't evidence of a conspiracy – but the truth may be scarier
articles.context: This went offline and when something at a secretive government agency like the NSA goes offline, immediately the first thought is, "Who's attacking us
articles.full_text: Have you or someone you love been affected by a tech outage this week? Yeah, us too. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube. Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live In a week of big stories the biggest one seems to be the fact that everyone from Microsoft to the NSA was dealing with outages, and here's what might be the worst part: It doesn't seem to be AI, nor hostile countries intent on destroying our infrastructure. Unfortunately for all of us, what the past week of outages reveal is that – as we discussed on The Kettle less than a month ago – all of our essential tech infrastructure is basically held together with duct tape and twine. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons, and open source reporter Liam Proven to discuss what comes next, and whether we can fix any of this without tearing all of it out and starting from scratch. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:04) Hi everyone and welcome to the latest episode of the Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and if you're hearing this, then that means there isn't an outage right now, which seems like that might be a lot to ask of our technology in the past week. It's been a busy week. We had Anthropic's IPO, Nvidia drama continuing, and other stuff going on. But the one thing that everyone seems to be talking about is what's become known in the zeitgeist as Outagepalooza, as it seems like everything was offline at some point in the past few days. With me to discuss the chaos and the conspiracy theories they're giving rise to is Reg cybersecurity editor Jessica Lyons and our open source reporter Liam Proven. Guys, what's happening? Jessica Lyons (00:45) I've got my tinfoil hat on right now, so I'm ready. Brandon (00:48) Yes, I've had family calling me being like, my god, what's happening? Who's ending the world right now? Is it AI? Jessica Lyons (00:55) Ha ha ha. Brandon (00:56) We'll get to that part. Liam Proven (00:57) Wonderful. My mum's wardrobe door stuck this week and we found a company on the little rock in the middle of the Irish Sea that fixes sliding doors and he didn't get my emails because he's one hundred percent Microsoft and he uses Hotmail and it's Hotmail. Liam Proven (01:18) And when I got it through, you'd be amazed at the ramifications. I SMS'd him in the end and he got that and then was really angry because I said, "Dude, I've been trying to get you for three days. Can you at least reply and say Friday?" And he's like, "No, I've got no email, I've got no internet, I've got nothing." Brandon (01:32) My god. Yes, it's been an interesting week. So Jess, catch us up on everything that's fallen apart in the past few days. We've got quite a list growing here. Jessica Lyons (01:40) Yes. Well, we'll start with Outlook. I'm sorry, Microsoft. It was larger than just Outlook, but similar to Liam, I got this message from my dad. We were at dinner with some friends and he said, "What is going on? I haven't been able to access Outlook all day. What is happening?" So this happened last week and there was this massive Microsoft outage and ultimately, people assumed it was maybe a cyber attack. Is somebody DDoSing Microsoft? What's going on? And then a few days later, Microsoft said, "No, this was a faulty software update that we pushed back in July, and it's affecting all of our 365 services now." So that was last Thursday. Then a day later, the FAA grounded all planes. Brandon (02:29) Right. Jessica Lyons (02:29) And again, in light of Microsoft, people were still having problems with Microsoft. All the planes are grounded. At the time, we just knew it was some type of communication error. And that sounds like something that a lot of nation states would really like to hit and attack. And this one, we ultimately learned that it was due to a network upgrade. Their provider, L3Harris, was switching out the copper wiring with fiber. And this has been an ongoing project. Also, kind of seems like maybe Friday the 13th isn't the best day to undertake this. Brandon (03:03) I hadn't even thought about the fact that it was Friday the 13th that all that happened. Jessica Lyons (03:09) So we see that right after Microsoft. And there was kind of a lull over the weekend, which was nice. But then Monday first thing, customers at Chase and US Bank and other major American banks couldn't withdraw any money from their accounts. And this we find out is also due to a massive outage. Chase later said it was a software bug in an on-premises hardware system, and they said it wasn't a cyber attack. Then the next day, the classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for their internal communications went offline. This is really classified stuff that they are communicating about internally. This went offline and when something at a secretive government agency like the NSA goes offline, immediately the first thought is, "Who's attacking us?" The agency later said this was due to scheduled routine maintenance. And actually I almost forgot: Tuesday, Apple had a bunch of issues. It was affecting different services like Apple Support, iCloud, Apple Pay, and their retail stores. There were people waiting in lines because they had some tech issue that they wanted to get help with, and they're not able to get any help because Apple's offline as well. So we have all these outages at these major agencies and companies over the last week. So everybody automatically goes to, "Who's attacking us? Who is responsible for this?" What people assume to be a massive coordinated cyber attack And that wasn't the case. Brandon (04:50) Right. In pretty much every instance. Liam, Canonical was having an outage too, right? Liam Proven (04:53) Yes. I was going to say, we didn't notice the FAA very much in Europe, but Canonical got hit by a distributed denial of service attack. I probably don't need to spell that out. At the end of last week, just before their now semi-annual Ubuntu Summit, which is when they have a bunch of talks about what's coming up and what's new. They've been hit by a number of attacks before. It was very bad timing. Some of their services stayed up. Brandon (05:29) So this was actually attributable to an attack though. Liam Proven (05:32) I believe in this case it looks like it was another DDoS, but it's not the first time. It's not obvious in the open source world that sometimes big, very visible projects are actually from tiny companies. And sometimes things that don't look so important actually have huge companies behind them. But Canonical is not a very big company. And they're a hundred percent remote company. They don't really have headquarters. There's this lovely office which is part of a floor of one building in London, but not that many people work there. It's all hot desks. It's relatively easy to take such a distributed company offline. And so it's becoming hard to say whether some of these things really are due to attacks or due to general vulnerabilities that are being maybe not even exploited, just massive scale attempts to exploit them. And it's not sometimes targeting anybody in particular. There's just a million bots trying to take down PHP and loads of things run on PHP. So you've got PHP in your infrastructure and that means you're not taken down, but your servers are struggling under the load. The number of bots that are trying to crawl all kinds of websites and things constitutes effectively a DDoS at the moment, although it's not really a true DDoS. Brandon (07:16) Right. It's not intentional. It just becomes one by volume. Liam Proven (07:22) So it's actually becoming a little bit moot what exactly constitutes a denial of service attack versus merely being under extremely heavy load. I'm sure that the jokes are international about phoning your bank or some other institution and getting a recorded message saying, "We're sorry, we're experiencing an unusual volume of calls at the moment. You are number forty-two in the queue." You've always got that volume of calls. It's not unusual. That's your normal volume of calls. Hire more people. That's web service now, isn't it? Brandon (07:57) Yes, gosh. But there's that. Aside from maybe the Canonical thing being a bit of an outlier in this broader discussion, it seems like there's not necessarily a single thing to blame here, right? It's very easy to immediately jump to the conclusion that this is AI. Right? They're lying to us. Jessica Lyons (08:14) Well, I think we can establish the cause under the larger umbrella of deferred maintenance because we have this aging, underfunded infrastructure. That was the case with the FAA outage, and we have all of these really old bugs in software that are just now coming to light because AI has gotten so good at finding them in a lot of either commercial projects or open source code that wasn't really built with security top of mind. And so all of these things are now happening right at once. There's this massive need to upgrade infrastructure. There's this need to patch all of these vulnerabilities really quickly before attackers reverse engineer them with AI and then exploit them. And it's creating this perfect storm that looks like it could be an attack, but it's software vulnerabilities, it's deferred maintenance, and that's at least the primary cause of all the outages. Brandon (09:24) Yes.You don't think... I mean, I'm just going to put my tinfoil hat on and say, "Well, are these people lying to us?" Are they trying to cover up another big wave of OpenAI agents crashing networks due to stupidly miscoded exercises that are escaping sandboxes? Liam Proven (09:39) Can I propose a rephrasing of the question? Brandon (09:43) Yes. Liam Proven (09:44) Yes, they're lying to us, but are they lying about this? Jessica Lyons (09:48) Yes, right. And and that's the thing. I mean, it's always the that's that's always a question at the back of everybody's minds. Like over the weekend I had someone who a friend of mine, she's not involved in cybersecurity, she's not involved in government, and trying to convince me that no, this this was all part of a coordinated cyber attack. And very convinced. Um some people, there's there's a few people in the security industry who are saying, "Well, it seems that they were really quick to rush and say, 'no this was just scheduled downtime or an upgrade that we had planned.'" But the consensus from all of the security folks who are a lot smarter than I am is that no, this doesn't appear to be a coordinated cyber attack. This really does look like it has to do with a bunch of bugs being discovered in all of our interconnected systems.And this has a cascading effect across so many critical systems and services that we all use. Brandon (10:47) Right. I know you covered this in the story you wrote about the greater impact of all this. Can we expect more of this going forward? I think we probably all know the answer to that. Liam Proven (10:58) Yes. Jessica Lyons (11:00) Yes. It's a definite yes on that one. Brandon (11:02) Yes. Liam Proven (11:03) Yes, concur. Brandon (11:04) That raises the big question of this. I've been telling my family and my friends all along that there's not an indication that this is connected. But it was less than a month ago that the three of us were on here talking about PHP2Shell and how that basically opened the box to us realizing the entire digital sphere that we exist in is held together with duct tape and twine. Yes. Jessica Lyons (11:33) Right. And we see some real attacks too, with the refrigeration attacks and the water system attacks in America over the summer. So there are real attacks that are happening and affecting critical systems too. So it's not like these outages are occurring in a vacuum with nothing being perpetrated by criminals, or spies, or nation-state attackers. Brandon (11:57) Yes. You think about it like the modern internet that we have... Liam, you lived on the continent for a while. So, in history, Europe was a whole bunch of very small, very isolated communities. They developed their own languages, their own culture, everything. And then they grew and they became one connected mass. But in some ways they still can't talk to each other. And I feel like that's the kind of technology that we have now. We have all these disparate systems that existed as separate entities. The FAA's 50-year-old systems didn't need to be connected to the internet and talking to X, Y, and Z. And now they do. But all those other systems are talking a different language too. So we have a massive technical debt. Every week, with PHP2Shell, the refrigerator attacks, everything. . Every week we turn around and we learn one more way in which there's a huge technical debt that wewe're now in the point where we're like, "oh oops, you know, uh..." Liam Proven (12:59) Yes, this is a growing problem. I want to start to wave my arms around and talk about synergistic network effects. I have interviewed some of the people behind the original ARM operating system on The Register and I still attend the meetings of the London Acorn User Group. Over the years they've had some pretty big names in the industry. We had Sophie Wilson, the inventor of the ARM chip, there a couple of times. One time somebody asked a question: "Do you feel happy and proud that there's an ARM chip inside every iPhone and every Android phone?" She laughed at the question, and when the person looked surprised, she said, "There isn't an ARM chip inside every iPhone. There are six or eight ARM chips inside every iPhone." Bear in mind this was more than a decade ago. She said there's a central ARM chip with several cores powering it, but there's an ARM chip in the GSM mobile signaling stack, there's an ARM chip in its USB controller, there's an ARM chip in its memory controller, there's an ARM chip in its Bluetooth controller, because it's cheaper to embed an ARM chip and run a bit of software on it than design dedicated silicon to manage all the different wireless networks. It's all ARM chips all the way down. Your iPhone isn't an ARM device; it's a loose cluster of multiple different ARM devices of different generations. And nobody is entirely sure anymore if they're all running the same stack. A very visible example of this was in Intel chips until about the early Core 2 Duo era: they had an embedded management processor that was derived from the accelerator in a Nintendo Famicom game from the nineties called Quark. Then Intel replaced it with a cut-down x86 core running Minix, the experimental operating system that inspired Linux. They never gave back any of the code, and the Minix project faltered and is dormant because Dr. Andy Tanenbaum, the guy who founded it, retired. Nowadays in any modern internet-connected server there'll be Linux in its instrumented lights-out monitoring chip. There'll probably be Linux in its network interfaces. There'll be Linux running on the main CPU cluster. I wrote recently about a Linux-powered RISC-V graphics card which runs Ubuntu on loads of RISC-V cores in the GPU. Are they all on the same Linux version? Have they all been patched against vulnerabilities? No. Brandon (16:24) Right. So basically the problem goes down to the individual device level. Liam Proven (16:28) Yes. There's legions of distributed systems inside your pocket right now, and inside every server. They're running loads of copies of Linux, probably some BSDs, Wind River, ThreadX, QNX, and other embedded operating systems. And some of the same vulnerabilities are in all of them. The Microsoft stack is held together with Linux. Brandon (16:59) Yes. That's not to say that distributed systems are bad, obviously. Liam Proven (17:05) No. Brandon (17:05) If we had more distributed systems, many of the outages we experienced in the past week wouldn't have been such a problem. But it makes me wonder if there's anything we can do... Can we stop the castle from sinking into the swamp without completely tearing it down and rebuilding it from new foundations? Are we stuck with what we've got? Liam Proven (17:27) We can do what they have done in Rome and Istanbul:build a new layer on top. Brandon (17:33) Right. Jessica Lyons (17:34) I think it's going to get worse before it gets better because AI is going to continue to unearth all of these vulnerabilities. Last week we surpassed a hundred thousand CVEs, and that's more than double 2025's total and we're there in mid-November. Liam Proven (17:49) Wow. Jessica Lyons (17:49) That comes on the heels of two Microsoft Patch Tuesdays with more than a thousand CVEs that they patched and disclosed. Brandon (18:06) And that's not slowing down. Jessica Lyons (18:07) No, it's not. As vendors, security researchers, and attackers are all using AI to find all these long-hidden vulnerabilities, that creates a massive backlog of software that needs to be patched. Eventually we're going to get to the other side of this where it will make for more secure code and more secure digital infrastructure. Until then, we're going to see more outages. We're going to see more of the same, and it's not going to be very fun for anybody. Liam Proven (18:42) Maybe. Brandon (18:42) Liam, you seem to express some doubt there as to whether it would come out on the other side. Liam Proven (18:46) I'm not convinced that this problem is fixable. We have to allow the possibility that maybe they're going to keep finding more holes in this. There's a famous talk by Ken Thompson called "Reflections on Trusting Trust" [PDF]. He embedded a remote access hole intentionally into the original C compiler, and the compiler inserts it into anything it compiles without the code being in the source code of the compiler. You have a compiler which is a binary that runs source code to generate a new binary. The binary can contain the hole, which is never in the source code, as long as it knows to put it in the next one. He did it as an exercise and revealed it at his Turing Award lecture. Stuff as fundamental as that exists because virtually every one of those controller chips has code written in C. And we don't really know what's in all that C, but virtually all of it came from the same early 1970s root of the development of C. There could be nasties lurking in there that are in all of them. They're in all the BSDs, in Linux, and Windows NT is built in C and inherited code from DEC VMS. There could be stuff in there for decades that we have no idea about that's going to crop up, and it's in everything. Some of these devices have no way of being updated; the software's burned in ROMs that are not visible to the operating system that's running. This could keep crumbling away. I once was a big fan of a website called LoperOS.org by Stanislav Datskovskiy. He was a Lisp evangelist. He's gone very quiet in recent years, but he compared building software out of C to building a model of a bridge or the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks or matchsticks. The end structure is not very strong because it's mostly weak wood and glue. You build it out of this poor structural material because loads of people can work together on it. And C and tools like C are good at this; you can farm out development to whole teams of people. They're working with tweezers and toothpicks instead of bricks and cement because it's easier to do this over a team. Somebody said, "If we built houses the way that we build software, then the first termite colony to come along would destroy civilization," because we built it out of bad materials. I'm not personally Christian, but I read the Bible and there's that line about building your house on sand. It doesn't matter how tough you make the house: if you built it on sand and the sand shifts, you've got a big problem. This problem goes all the way down. This might be a good time to invest in companies developing software in languages like Ada that aren't built on C and don't contain any C whatsoever. When Ada was introduced – Ada is a French language originally from INRIA – it was criticized as being too big and heavy compared to C. But now, compared to C++, it's quite small and quick, and there's a good GNU toolchain and tools like SPARK and AdaCore that have open source development and distribution systems for it. Maybe we're going to have to replace the whole thing. Brandon (23:18) God, I hope not. One of the things I think about happening is how in past generations of software we slapped new things on top of old things to protect the old things from the new things. Liam Proven (23:31) Yes. Brandon (23:33) And it makes me wonder if the next version of slapping something on top of our entire infrastructure is AI. We put AI on top of it. We make AI handle bug hunting, vulnerability remediation, and security. It creates a situation where the stuff is safe for now, but software always abstracts layers as you get further up the stack. I wonder if AI is going to be the next level of abstraction to the point where we don't really understand what the code's doing anymore at all. We just rely on the agents that are running it to handle protecting us. What do you think? Is that a potential next generation that we see here, Jess? Jessica Lyons (24:24) I think it definitely could be. There's a lot of push in the security industry to use AI for both finding and fixing bugs.On the code-writing side of things, it's not there yet. But it's appealing when there's a shortage of human workers who can do this and AI is cheaper. You don't need to pay AI. Brandon (24:52) And faster. Jessica Lyons (24:53) Right. Over time. So I think it's likely that is going to be one of the ways we try to solve this problem. Brandon (25:06) I don't see another way out of it because of the sheer volume of flaws that are being found. Like Liam said, there's low-level stuff getting discovered now that no human would have found, but the fact that an AI found it means someone's going to exploit it at some point. Liam Proven (25:23) I think for management this is going to look like a very tempting option, but it will accelerate the problem. We're in an iterative race at the moment – the Red Queen's race. You have to run as fast as you can to stay where you are. We've got new tools that are finding problems faster than ever, so it's tempting to try and use similar tools to fix them faster than ever, but that means nobody understands the fix. Then if another hole is found deeper down, the whole layer of fixes collapses. One of the predominant development tools on the PC platform used to be Turbo Pascal. DOS wasn't written in C. Way back when, people accused Microsoft of plagiarizing CP/M. Microsoft didn't write DOS; Tim Paterson of Seattle Computer Products wrote the original. CP/M was written in a high-level language, PL/M, whereas DOS was hand-coded in Assembler. It wasn't plagiarism because they went a level down. In the early days people wrote this stuff in Pascal. I remember Unix catching on and C becoming trendy because it was so fast. For a little while a company called TopSpeed sold a Modula-2 compiler because not only was the code faster than C, but it compiled faster than C compilers back then. Ultimately the sheer inertia of C and C-related languages caught on and all that stuff got sidelined. Borland went through various transitions and Turbo Pascal became Delphi, which went to Embarcadero and is still around, though I'm not sure anybody cares anymore. I worked through one industry shift where Assembler and Pascal-related languages were replaced by C. It could happen again. It wasn't all that bad last time. I know it seems unimaginable now, but I'm not that old. Working in this field for less than four decades, I've watched an entire software industry get swept away and replaced. And we all kept our jobs, and we all kept working on pretty much the same hardware. Maybe that's going to happen again. I know it sounds unimaginable, but it honestly wasn't that bad. Brandon (28:04) Speaking of hardware, given these outages, connected services going offline are causing chaos. Setting aside the FAA – that's a public service that stranded travelers – banks, Apple, and Microsoft are business problems. We're seeing with AI where everyone is weighing the cost-benefit between hosted services where you pay for tokens versus turning the server closet back into a server closet. Is it time to come back on-premises with a lot of these things? Is it time to run your own Exchange server again or host your own file shares on your own network? It makes me wonder if the solution to some of these outage concerns going forward is going to be a return to on-premises. Liam Proven (29:09) Personally I think that's an excellent idea. Jessica Lyons (29:11) I agree, but so many of these companies are entrenched in every other company – Microsoft, for example. It's going to be pretty hard to completely swing to the opposite end of the spectrum here. Brandon (29:32) Sure. Maybe they need to start offering more self-hosted services again. If you're a business concerned about outages that will probably keep happening,the safest thing to do would be to bring it back on-premises. But if everything you do is in Google or Microsoft 365, it's going to be hard to get yourself out of that, and probably very expensive, at least at first. Especially with the cost of hardware right now not going down given the AI push. So maybe we're all just trapped. Liam Proven (30:01) This is part of the digital sovereignty push in Europe at the moment. And it's interesting that on either side of the border between Denmark and northern Germany, there have been two very different stories in the last couple of years. In the last year or so, Schleswig-Holstein has successfully migrated from Microsoft 365 over to Open-Xchange, which is a standards-based email server that can look like and support Outlook. Across the border, Denmark weighed up going all open source. They did a pilot program that failed. They reverted to their Microsoft-based solution just in time to have a massive outage. Have fun. Jessica Lyons (30:58) Yes. Liam Proven (30:59) But you know what, I bet some of this came down to senior government officials saying, "I don't understand this new email client you're showing me. Give me Outlook back, or I'm going to fire the lot of you."" Maybe somebody needs to go in there and say, "We will send somebody around to teach you to use it, or if you're not able to use it, maybe it is time that you give way to somebody who can, because you've just cost us 300 million dollars because you won't change email clients." Brandon (31:31) Right. Liam Proven (31:31) We do have standards-based solutions. HTML, SMTP, and IMAP give us standards for moving around email, messages, and documents. We can replace Microsoft-based software iteratively: first the applications, and when people get used to the applications, the operating system. When Ubuntu launched twenty-two years ago, it only filled about half a CD – it took about 300 megabytes – and they wondered what to put on the rest of the CD because in those days they mailed CDs rather than making you download it. So they put Windows installers for all the apps on the CD. You could put it in your Windows box and install LibreOffice, Thunderbird, Firefox, and VLC to get used to the apps. When you were comfortable with the apps, you installed Ubuntu and got the same apps with the new desktop. Brandon (32:42) Yes. Liam Proven (32:42) Sweet, happy times. You can do this. Brandon (32:43) Yes. Liam Proven (32:44) You can do this with a government department. Brandon (32:47) Yes. Jessica Lyons (32:47) It requires political will, and in America I don't think we have that. So that's a Brandon (32:50) Sure. No. Liam Proven (32:51) It's a problem stateside. But the argument that some EU states are making is: why don't we spend hundreds of millions of (insert local currency symbol here) with local companies? We're not claiming we'll save you any money, but we'll keep the money in the country or with an EU partner instead of sending it across the ocean, and we free ourselves of a dependency. That works with senior political types and bureaucrats. This is fixable, but the price may look unacceptable right now to a lot of people. The outages I fear are going to come closer and closer together. Brandon (33:41) Right. That's going to be the determining factor. It's going to be interesting to watch over the next few months to see what new outages we experience: whether the pace keeps up or increases. We'll see. The US government is overhauling a lot of old systems in aerospace and other sectors, so the push to move to more independent systems or back on-premises is going to be driven by the acceptability of outages. Liam Proven (34:12) Yes. "I'm sorry guys, we can't afford to fix it." Jessica Lyons (34:14) Right. What's the pain tolerance? When is it too much, or do people get used to these outages as a part of life? "Today we won't be able to do any work because Microsoft is out again." Brandon (34:26) Yes. The economic movers and shakers are not going to accept that if it keeps happening. There's going to be a point where the pain tolerance is reached and people say, "No, we can't keep doing this." Liam Proven (34:39) You know what? I actually disagree there because, to take a different example: I used to be a motorcyclist. Early in my career I switched from tech support to IT manager to designing and building networks, and I turned up to work on a motorbike. Then I had a really bad crash, switched to three-wheelers, and discovered how bad London traffic had gotten. My injuries prevented me from going back on a solo bike most of the time, but years later I switched to bicycling. You can still cut through traffic very well on a bicycle in a lot of Europe. Car drivers got used to the delays; it gets ten minutes longer to get to work every year, but you don't notice ten minutes over a year, so you put up with it. My next-door neighbor didn't know what underground line he lived on because he drove everywhere. People got used to it taking two or three hours to drive to work and just put up with it. I've seen photos of massive West Coast freeways with eight lanes of stationary traffic. People will put up with amazing levels of delay and non-functionality if it happens gradually enough. Brandon (36:12) Yes. We will see what comes of everything. You could be right; it could be a slow enough roll that everyone just accepts that we're going to lose some money, but you can't disrupt the tech. Liam Proven (36:29) Yes, right. Brandon (36:29) Right. No matter what happens, if there are more outages, we will be here to talk about them on The Kettle. If there are fewer, we probably won't, but one can hope. Thanks for coming on today, guys, and thank you for listening in. We will talk to you soon. Liam Proven (36:44) Thank you for having me. Goodbye. ®

articles.title: US Lawmakers Propose CISA Board to Review Major Cyber Incidents
articles.context: It would also set out criteria for selecting incidents for review, require a majority vote to launch investigations and provide for regular congressional oversight
articles.full_text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) could soon be empowered with new authority to investigate and review major cyber incidents affecting national security.

Representatives Morgan Luttrell (R-TX) and Ritchie Torres (D-NY) introduced a new bill on November 18 that seeks to establish a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board (NCAI Board) within CISA.

This new board would examine significant cyber incidents affecting US organizations, identify root causes and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future.

The proposed bill, provisionally called the Reviewing Origins, Outcomes, and Threats from Cyber and Artificial Intelligence to Understand Security Events Act (ROOT CAUSE Act), specifies that the NCAI Board would have no regulatory or enforcement authority, and its reviews would not assign civil or criminal liability.

The legislation would establish governance rules covering board membership, conflicts of interest, access to information and the protection of sensitive material. It would also set out criteria for selecting incidents for review, require a majority vote to launch investigations and provide for regular congressional oversight.

Commenting on the legislation introduced through House Homeland Security Republicans, Rep. Luttrell described cyber as “the next phase in the evolution of warfare.”

“As our adversaries become increasingly sophisticated in this space, it is more critical than ever that we take action,” he added.

Read more: New UK Cyber Monitoring Centre Introduces 'Richter Scale' for Cyber-Attacks

Republican Congressmen Introduce Three Additional AI and Cybersecurity Bills

The proposed ROOT CAUSE Act was among four new bills proposed by Republican representatives of the US Committee on Homeland Security on November 18.

The Improving Nonhuman-Agent Security, Identification, Governance, Handling and Traceability Act (AI INSIGHT Act) would establish a framework for securing AI agents operating on US federal networks, requiring agencies to identify, monitor and control their access to systems and data.

Meanwhile, the Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act (BRIDGE AI Act) would create a CISA pilot program to recruit AI and emerging technology specialists from the private sector, academia and research institutions to strengthen the agency's technical capabilities.

Finally, the Sector Engagement for Cybersecurity through Unified Responsibility and Expertise in Information Technology Act (SECURE IT Act) would formally designate the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as the Sector Risk Management Agency for the Information Technology Sector, reinforcing its role in coordinating efforts with industry to protect critical technology infrastructure.

Read now: UK Cyber Monitoring Centre Sets Its Sights on US Expansion One Year After Launch

articles.title: Critical binary-parser Flaw Enables JavaScript Injection via Malicious Parser Definitions
articles.context: A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code
articles.full_text:
A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1.

"Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

"Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled."

According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation.

The parser options include -

length

lengthInBytes

key

tag

offset, and

the alias passed to namely()

"Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead."

CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters.

"[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

In this article

Hackers reportedly breached the FBI’s national crime database

The database held more than 19.3 million records in 2025. How many, if any, were exposed is unknown

If someone calls demanding payment over a warrant, hang up and call the agency directly

The FBI is investigating a reported breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a database police use to check for outstanding warrants, identify stolen vehicles, and look up missing-person records.

CNN first reported the breach on November 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation. It is unclear when it happened or how the attackers got in. A law enforcement source confirmed the hack to ABC News. The FBI hasn’t publicly confirmed the incident.

NCIC is a computerized database that local, state, and federal agencies can all use. It holds records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. Police officers use it during traffic stops, investigations, and background checks.

The system held more than 19.3 million records in fiscal year 2025. It’s still unclear whether anyone stole data. The database includes the following types of records:

Wanted-person and warrant records

Missing-person records

Criminal history data

Protection orders

Records of stolen vehicles, firearms, and other property

NCIC is one of the databases the FBI checks during firearm background checks. The reports do not say that attackers breached the background-check system itself or that gun buyers’ information was exposed.

If someone stole NCIC data, people who could be affected include those with past arrests, people with protection orders, missing people and their families, and victims of crime. Possible risks include the following:

Exposure of sensitive records. Criminals could use criminal history or details from protection orders for harassment, extortion, or doxxing.

Targeted scams. Scammers could pose as police officers and use details from a real warrant to make a demand for payment sound convincing.

Data enrichment. Records from other sources could be linked to the data in this database, providing attackers with more details to make their messaging believable.

This is the second reported intrusion involving FBI systems in about two months. FBI employees whose information was exposed in the September breach face risks including phishing and identity theft. CNN reported that some felt left in the dark about whether they were affected.

How to stay safe

If you feel your data might be involved, here are some steps you can take while we learn more about the breach:

Be wary of unsolicited calls, emails, or messages from police or the FBI. Law enforcement won’t demand gift cards, crypto, or wire transfers.

Be wary of breach notification emails and texts. Don’t click links. Go to official sites directly.

Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication on your accounts. Passkeys are even better where they’re offered as an option.

Check your own online exposure with a tool like Malwarebytes’ Digital Footprint scan, and keep your devices updated.

Once more information or an official confirmation becomes available, we’ll keep you posted.

If your data was involved in a breach, read our guide for more advice: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

What do cybercriminals know about you?

Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online.
