articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning
articles.context: Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are exploiting a now-patched security flaw in ConnectWise ScreenConnect to target managed service provider (MSP) servers.

The activity revolves around CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9), a critical ScreenConnect client flaw that allows a guest to transfer and execute a malicious payload on a connecting technician's host.

"On November 12, 2026, we observed one managed service provider's (MSP) technician's workstation exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file, which then reported to a Telegram bot, downloaded an installer from masterdarky[.]com, and started a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing at the attacker's own relay, all in about 9 seconds," Huntress security researcher John Hammond said.

The batch script, "update_224ac089.bat," is designed to decode a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID, and register the new infection. Subsequently, it downloads an MSI installer that masquerades as a Windows update ("WindowsUpdate.msi") to launch a ScreenConnect client, enabling the attacker to gain remote access to the technician's machine.

The activity, observed between October 20 and November 16, 2026, is said to have sprayed servers blindly, with Huntress observing at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat hitting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses. The guests have been found to make repeated requests that have blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames.

In another instance, a guest machine at 91.224.92[.]167 pushed a seemingly harmless text file ("marker.txt") two seconds after a technician joined a session, effectively acting as a canary to alert the operator that the exploit works against the target before sending the actual payload.

What's more, a targeted attack aimed at an MSP server in October 2026 had the attacker joining as a guest across three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to run a file designed to drop a batch script ("Sync.bat") into the technician's computer's Windows Startup folder.

It's worth noting that this activity is distinct from a recently disclosed attack wave in which unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to partner ScreenConnect environments by leveraging an authentication flaw in a third-party extension to deploy a malware toolkit called SCKit, which then exploits the flaw to propagate the malware to a technician's workstation.

The attacks also coincide with another cluster in which thousands of unauthorized ScreenConnect guest sessions have originated from machines with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names like BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, and LAPTOP-BINANCE to trick technicians into connecting to them. No following malicious activity such as file transfers or command execution has been observed.

Specifically, the threat actors have been found to obtain access to publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract the relay address needed to register a guest client with the corresponding ScreenConnect server, and then create fake guest sessions and make those sessions appear online.

"Someone is registering unauthorized guest computers on MSPs' servers, where they sit in these session lists. They come from a scripted emulator that impersonates a Windows ScreenConnect client, and nearly all of them had connected from a single IONOS-hosted IP, 74.208.158[.]106," Huntress said.

"As of November 13, we've seen related activity across at least 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers belonging to 109 Huntress-protected organizations. In total, we found 2,408 unauthorized sessions enrolled since November 3, 2026."

Organizations are advised to ensure that technicians' ScreenConnect host clients are updated to 26.6.5 or later, hunt for signs of exposure, isolate affected workstations, and rotate all credentials reachable from that workstation. If immediate patching is not feasible, it's recommended to remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups.

"An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target," Huntress said. "When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs."

"A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

articles.title: Norway links energy firm cyberattacks to critical Azure API Management flaw
articles.context: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations
articles.full_text: Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations. According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft said the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2. It said of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue." Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault. Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration. The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs. Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM. "If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid." Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets. The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise. NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations. The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation. "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said. "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation. "When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses." Customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear. Microsoft said it identified the security issue on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day. The Windows giant said customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied. NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched. Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

articles.title: N-able Discloses Critical Mail Assure Vulnerability Found During Breach Investigation
articles.context: N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for...
articles.full_text:
N-able yesterday disclosed a critical flaw it found while investigating the breach of its Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud, an email filtering service it runs for managed service providers.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-134624, is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw. It allowed a user with high-level API access to open connections to internal systems of the user's choosing on the platform's servers.

The company fixed the flaw and restored access to the dashboard and APIs late on Saturday, closing an outage that began last Monday. Email delivery and spam filtering kept working throughout, according to the company. It has not said whether the flaw was the attackers' way in.

The bug sat in a connection check that Mail Assure runs for LDAP synchronization when a relay is configured. Before the fixed build, nothing restricted that check's destination, so the server could be pointed at any internal host and port to see which ones answered.

"An authenticated API user can cause the server to connect to arbitrary internal hosts and ports, determine which are reachable, and send crafted data to internal services.," the vendor's security advisory says.

The advisory gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.3, and lists builds earlier than 20261121.1943 as affected, with that same build as the fix. It does not claim code execution.

N-able informed customers of a service disruption last Monday and initially traced it to platform configuration and service dependencies, according to its incident timeline.

Last Wednesday, the company said the outage was, in fact, a security incident: an unauthorized party had accessed one of the Hosted Cloud servers. The dashboard and APIs were kept offline as a precaution while it investigated.

It responded by taking the affected server offline, rotating internal platform credentials, revoking customers' existing API tokens, invalidating OAuth tokens, and resetting local users' passwords.

The company says it has found no evidence that customer data was compromised, including tenants' mailboxes, and no sign of exploitation beyond that one server since the fix was implemented.

The investigation is still open, and the breach is unrelated to the N-central incident, according to the company. In that earlier incident, it took its hosted remote-monitoring platform offline on November 9 after a researcher published 33 unpatched flaws.

For hosted customers, the work now is reconnecting. Scripts and integrations that used the revoked API tokens or OAuth tokens will need new credentials. The exact steps differ by setup: each partner has been emailed guidance specific to its environment, and anyone who has not received it is asked to contact support.

The hosted platform itself is already patched, according to yesterday's incident update, so there is nothing for Hosted Cloud users to install.

SpamExperts Local Cloud runs on customer hardware, with software updates applied on a weekly schedule, according to the product's update documentation. The incident statements describe the Hosted Cloud only, so Local Cloud operators should confirm their servers are on build 20261121.1943.

What the account so far does not say is how the attackers first got in, or whether any of the credentials they may have reached were actually taken. An outside digital forensics and incident response team has been brought in, and the company says a formal root cause analysis is due within two weeks of yesterday's update. Separate restoration times for quarantine, logging, and mailbox synchronization, which were being brought back in phases, have not been given.

articles.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
articles.context: One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive
articles.full_text:
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.

Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.

Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.

When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.

Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.

The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.

The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.

The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.

The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability

CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Cleverbridge admits attackers stole customers' credit card and CVV numbers. Yep, you read that right
articles.context: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data...
articles.full_text: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization. The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems. The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather important blanks. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers. Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach. More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach. Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk. That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems. In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion. Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase. Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®

articles.title: OXLoader abuses DLL hijacking to distribute different malware families
articles.context: Elastic first documented it in June 2026, when attackers used Google Ads to distribute CASTLESTEALER through OXLoader
articles.full_text:

In this article

OXLoader can lead to malware that steals browser passwords and data or gives criminals remote access to a Windows PC

Fake copyright complaints and cracked software activators are among the lures used to spread it

What to watch for in suspicious downloads and how to reduce the risk

We’ve seen an increase in activity involving OXLoader, a loader that installs other malware on a computer. Elastic first documented it in June 2026, when attackers used Google Ads to distribute CASTLESTEALER through OXLoader.

The malware installed varies by campaign. We found OXLoader distributing Remcos, OverLord, PureRAT, Lunex Stealer, LOLD, and Hermes. Depending on the payload, attackers could steal saved browser passwords and other data, remotely control the computer, or download more malware.

We found OXLoader in malicious ZIP files disguised as complaint or copyright-infringement notices, as well as fake software activators. One campaign we analyzed used fake activators downloaded from GitLab.

Below, we take a technical deep dive into how that campaign works, including how OXLoader uses DLL hijacking to unpack and run malware.

How to stay safe

Here are a few simple ways to stay safe:

Be wary of emails or links that tell you to run software in connection with copyright infringement or complaints.

Watch for executables with very long names or double extensions, such as .docx.exe or .pdf.exe.

Pay attention when you extract an archive. If some of the files it contains don’t appear, be cautious.

Downloading activators or cracks can compromise your device.

Install Malwarebytes Browser Guard, our free browser extension, to block malicious websites and suspicious downloads.

Use Malwarebytes Premium to block malware in real time, including malicious files.

Overview of the detected campaigns

In this section, we analyze several detected campaigns. In the cases we examined, OXLoader was decrypted either by malicious code embedded in legitimate executables, as in Elastic’s analysis, or through DLL hijacking. DLL hijacking is one of the key new features we observed in these campaigns. The rest of the infection chain is similar to the one Elastic identified.

We identified several DLLs used to decrypt and execute OXLoader, including:

Qt5Widgets.dll

Qt6Core.dll

SDL3.dll

UnityPlayer.dll

ANCUtility.dll

dbghelp.dll

msvcr100.dll

In some cases, we found other DLLs that had been tampered with to launch the malicious DLL. The executables involved were associated with Microsoft applications, Steam, OBS Studio, and PDF or Word readers.

Across different campaigns, OXLoader was distributed using themes related to complaints and copyright infringement. Malicious ZIP files were distributed in several ways. For example, a user might receive an email with an attached PDF prompting them to download and run a ZIP file, claiming there had been “unauthorized copying of brand intellectual property.”

Example of a PDF attached to an email that downloads a malicious ZIP file

When the user runs the executable, the infection chain begins through DLL hijacking, and a fake PDF opens. In this case, WindowsCodecs.dll is the trojanized DLL used to decrypt OXLoader.

The contents of the malicious ZIP file The fake PDF that opens

In some cases, a batch file is present instead of the executable and DLLs. It downloads a ZIP file containing the malicious DLL from different websites or hosting providers. The batch file’s content is similar to the one analyzed by Elastic. These files have long names, for example:

Photo_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Product_Review_Order_Front_Back_PDF.bat Form_Video_{ RANDOM NUMBERS }_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat Case_Form_Video_{RANDOM NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back_{RANDOM_NUMBERS}_Review_Front_Back.bat

In other cases, OXLoader was distributed through ZIP archives named Evidence_of_Violation.zip, downloaded from Google Sites. These websites used different titles and graphics.

Google Site used to distribute the malicious archive

In this case, WinWord.exe is renamed with a double extension, such as Travel_Point_Conditions.docx.exe or evidence_of_violation.docx.exe. OXLoader is then executed through DLL hijacking using the malicious DLL msvcr100.dll.

Example of one of the malicious archives

Finally, in the campaigns analyzed in this post, OXLoader was distributed through fake activators and cracks for popular software, downloaded from GitLab.

Malicious activators hosted on GitLab that distribute OXLoader

Technical analysis of OXLoader

In this campaign, users download software activators from GitLab, triggering the infection chain.

Stage 1: DLL hijacking

The archive downloaded by the user contains several legitimate DLLs, along with a legitimate executable from Take-Two Interactive Software, which is used to perform DLL hijacking using the UnityPlayer DLL. The manifest.json contains encrypted shellcode, which is decrypted and injected into another legitimate DLL.

The extracted archive with the malicious DLL

The DLL at address 0x18054485b contains a jmp instruction that calls the code responsible for decrypting the remaining code at 0x1807a3372. This decryption code differs across the cases we analyzed.

The call to the decryption function The self-decryption function

The code is heavily obfuscated using opaque predicates, control flow flattening (CFF), and mixed Boolean arithmetic (MBA). We therefore used the Sogen emulator to trace the main functions that execute and identify the malware code that called them.

Partial Sogen execution with some functions related to anti-analysis and language checks Termination of the malware if a virtualized environment is detected (Sogen output)

The values ​​used by the remaining functions are decoded using two functions:

The function at the address 0x1807a2282 decrypts the data ​​using the following formula: input1 ^ (input2 + 0x33fda).

The function at the address 0x1807a2624 is responsible for decrypting an 8-byte chunk; this function is called multiple times by other wrappers to decrypt the complete strings.

The decrypted strings

The anti-analysis and language checks we observed are similar to those identified by Elastic, with the minor addition of a check using WNetGetResourceParentW to detect virtualized environments.

Description

Value

Invalid values to detect virtualized environments

Pass invalid values ​​using the functions WNetAddConnection2W and WNetGetResourceParentW and check if the LastErrorValue is ERROR_BAD_NET_NAME (67) and ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS (487)

CPU-count

NumberOfProcessors greater than or equal to 3

Display Refresh rate

Executes a PowerShell command and it checks if the result is equal to or greater than 20 Hz

Geographical location

GetUserGeoID compared with 5 (Azerbaijan), 7 (Armenia), 29 (Belarus), 137 (Kazakhstan), 130 (Kyrgyzstan), 152 (Moldova), 203 (Russia), 228 (Tajikistan), 247 (Uzbekistan), 238 (Turkmenistan)

UI-Language

GetUserDefaultUILanguage compared with 0x419 (Russia)

The refresh rate is obtained using this PowerShell command:

powershell "Get-WmiObject Win32_VideoController | Select-Object -ExpandProperty CurrentRefreshRate"

It’s possible to bypass the anti-analysis checks by patching the function 0x1807999c2. Otherwise, if an analysis environment is detected, the system is shut down via a cmd command, or jumps to an invalid address.

The necessary files are then copied to a randomly named folder in ProgramData. In this case, the files were:

C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\ fl studio pro.exe C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\unityplayer.dll C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\manifest.json C:\ProgramData\{Random 7 characters}\awindows.storage.dll

A cmd command is executed to add a RunOnce registry value and executes the extracted main executable.

cmd /c cmd /C"set XG=n\&&set N8C=\Software\Mic&&set N5bM=r&&set 7Xg4=RunOnce /t REG_SZ /f&&set hjaB=re&&set wj= add&&set G7E=rentVersio&&set 3uc=rosoft\Windows\Cu&&set NF= HKCU&&set fD6k=g&&call set ku8m=%hjaB%%fD6k%%wj%%NF%%N8C%%3uc%%N5bM%%G7E%%XG%%7Xg4%&&call %ku8m% /v "NAAHjWuOj" /d "C:\ProgramData\fjwgyNK\ fl studio pro.exe""

Stages 2 and 3: Shellcode decryption and Donut Loader

awindows.storage.dll is a legitimate DLL used to inject the next stage. It has an additional .text section that contains the original digital signature while the DLL is on disk. After the DLL is loaded into memory with LoadLibraryA, the contents of the new section are replaced with the shellcode decrypted from manifest.json. This differs slightly from Elastic’s analysis, in which the shellcode was located in the .reloc section.

The loaded DLL from the ProgramData folder

The shellcode is decrypted and executed using call r12. It performs several XOR self-decryptions of the code, in a manner similar to the DLL previously analyzed.

The decryption of shellcode present in manifest.json

In addition to the windows.storage.dll, we identified other DLLs used by OXLoader for injection, including:

windows.StateRepository.dll

wmp.dll

mshtml.dll

ieframe.dll

The encrypted shellcode on disk can also have different names, such as Dependencies.manifest or titles.png.

After the code is decrypted, Donut Loader executes a DLL compressed with APLib.

Stages 4 and 5: A PE loader and LOLD downloader

The next stage executed by Donut Loader is another obfuscated PE with control-flow flattening, MBA, with a custom section .text0 and just four imports. Despite the complex obfuscation, the next stage is saved in cleartext at address 0x140001000 and loaded into the memory of the process itself.

This stage is a downloader which has some internal references marked as LOLD (for example, the mutex “LOLD_”). We won’t analyze it in detail in this post because it is outside the scope of this investigation.

The strings and the configuration are decrypted using a custom SplitMix64 XOR algorithm; the configuration is stored in a custom section called .mscfg.

The decrypted config

The decrypted strings include references to the malware’s injection phases:

payload launch: GhostedHollowing backend

Self-donor direct module target selected

ElevatedGhostedHollowing

GhostedHollowingSelfDonor

GhostedHollowingLaunchPayloadElevatedSelfDonor returned failure

At the time of our analysis, the C2 servers associated with LOLD were offline. Based on our analysis of other activity related to OXLoader and LOLD, we observed several HTTP requests to port different ports, including 8093, 8080, and 8700.:

/chunks/p_{RANDOM}/{different numbers}.bin

/ws/publisher?deviceId=

/files?prefix=inbox/

/api/client/report

/api/modules/pins

/api/modules/client-recovery/1.1.8

These HTTP requests and the artifacts analyzed are attributed to the Hermes malware family.
