Now, we're opening up EFS in public beta. In this post, we explain how EFS works in more detail, how it stays compatible with ZDR, and how businesses can join the beta program.

How EFS provides automated safety monitoring with ZDR

Customers who rely on legacy ZDR are protected by Claude's classifiers: our real-time safeguards that screen individual requests to assess whether they might cause harm. But sophisticated attacks generally occur across multiple queries—and any single request might, in isolation, look harmless.

For example, our September threat intelligence report describes an operation against roughly fifty organizations in which an AI agent divided the work of an attack among many other agents running in parallel. It saved the credentials it had harvested between sessions, so that the attackers could easily resume their campaign. Viewed one request at a time, this attack would have appeared as separate, more benign tasks.

To catch attacks like these, we use a second defensive layer, known as automated safety monitoring. This layer looks for patterns of misuse across many requests. Through EFS, Anthropic can provide automated safety monitoring without storing any customer data. Instead, our automated safety monitoring system analyzes data stored entirely on infrastructure controlled by our customers.

When automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for you to review. These cases can be read from your cloud storage or through an API, and can be integrated with security information and event management systems. They do not include inputs and outputs.

Once it's set up, automated safety monitoring can help your team detect intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm (like offensive cyber operations). It can also help detect agents that take actions beyond a user's intentions, such as—in extreme cases—using a software exploit to access an internal database or external system.

Zero data retention and EFS

With EFS, you bring your own storage for storing inputs and outputs. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider keeps a copy of your data once it is delivered to storage you control. This provides you the following guarantees:

Zero data retention. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider retains your data. You bring your own storage and store your own data. Inputs and outputs are deleted promptly after they're written to your own storage. You configure your own access policies and audit logging, and encrypt safety data with your own keys.

No operator human review. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider personnel access your inputs and outputs. Only automated safety monitoring can access this data.

We never train on your data. Inputs and outputs are used only for automated safety monitoring, never for model or classifier training.

You can use EFS through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, or Claude on Google Cloud. When you use EFS through Amazon Bedrock or Claude on Google Cloud (Google Managed), it's operated by your cloud provider, and the end-to-end data flow stays within that cloud's boundary.

You can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage in your own account for your storage, depending on where you use Claude. Your cloud provider bills you for that storage as usual, including reads, writes, and key operations (plus any applicable network transfer).

Get started

EFS is available on the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude on Google Cloud. Support for EFS in Microsoft Foundry is coming soon.

Eligible customers will be notified with instructions on how to get started. Read our developer docs to learn how to set it up, and our security whitepaper (opens in new tab) for how the architecture works, or deploy it through consulting partners like Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC.

articles.title: The enterprise guide to securing coding agents
articles.context: Unlike traditional malware, it can try multiple routes the attacker doesn’t have to proactively define
articles.full_text:
Shipping fast and secure

Coding agents likely write code and open pull requests at your organization already. For many leading enterprises, they are reviewing, testing, and merging it too.

For example, after standardizing on Claude Code across its engineering organization, Salesforce¹ reported:

79%

more pull requests merged per developer at Salesforce

5%

fewer total incidents at Salesforce

As agents do more, technical and security leaders must mitigate risks like prompt injection and privilege abuse with layered controls such as checked permissions and bounded environments.

The first two chapters focus on scoping the risk. We discuss the requirements every AI provider should meet and four agentic risks to mitigate.

The next three chapters focus on bounding the risk. We highlight the defensive layers you can deploy with Claude Code as well as how to centrally manage and enforce those controls.

This guide aims to provide a helpful agent security framework that can give organizations the confidence and trust to run agents effectively at scale.

This guide is written for organizations on Claude Team and Enterprise plans. If you reach Claude through a cloud provider such as AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure, the same principles and local controls apply.

01 Setting the bar for agent security

Six questions for every coding agent · Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider

“A CISO's responsibility in the age of agentic AI is not to achieve zero risk. Instead, our jobs are to make agentic risk legible and bounded. This way, we can deliberately accept what we can manage, so the business moves on our terms instead of around us.”

Six questions for every coding agent

Here are six questions leaders can ask when evaluating coding agents to verify they are enterprise ready.

Question to ask

Why you should care

Good answer

Weak answer

Does the model refuse when it should?

The model is the first check on a harmful request, making a bad action less likely.

Refusal trained into weights, with published rates.

"Our system prompt instructs the model to decline."

Are actions automatically inspected outside the model before they run?

External checks can catch when the model is tricked or using bad judgment.

Static analysis of commands and a separate evaluator model. Prompt injection probes.

"The model is very capable."

Is blast radius bounded by the environment?

This bounds the severity, and therefore risk, of an incident.

Kernel-level sandboxing that admins can require and set to fail closed, or an isolated VM for each session. Egress allowlisting at the network layer.

"The agent is instructed not to leave the working directory."

Can policy be locked centrally?

Sets minimum standards that can’t be undone by individuals.

Managed settings with hard-deny rules a local user can't override.

“Per-developer config files, and an honor system policy doc.”

Is the code the agent writes secure?

Code volume is scaling and vulnerabilities can ship unless checks scale with the volume.

Automated security review with a person approving high-risk changes.

“The model is trained to write secure code.”

Can you reconstruct an incident?

Compliance. Improving security over time.

Session telemetry export, audit API (Enterprise), and named known gaps.

"Logs are available on request."

Applying SaaS requirements to your AI provider

You already have a SaaS provider checklist with controls such as single sign-on, role-based access, data handling terms, and audit logs. Hold AI providers to a similar checklist. For example, Claude Code supports these security expectations through:

Single sign-on and role-based access control (Enterprise), managed the way you manage your other enterprise tools.

We don’t train generative models on code or prompts under our commercial terms, unless your organization has chosen to share that data with us.

Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (rolling out in phases) combines the privacy of zero data retention with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse across highly capable models. Data can be encrypted with your own keys and kept in storage you control for a limited time. Learn more.

On Enterprise, BAA coverage for the Claude Code CLI and the desktop app’s Code tab in local mode, once the HIPAA configuration is applied.

Encryption options on cloud platforms: customer-managed keys in AWS KMS on Amazon Bedrock, CMEK on Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry’s Hosted on Azure option.

A SOC 2 Type 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate in the Anthropic Trust Center.

02 Identifying AI-specific risks

Leaked credentials and privilege abuse · Unvetted dependencies and extensions · Data exfiltration · Prompt injection

Security and technical leaders are familiar with risks like leaked credentials, abused privileges, compromised dependencies, and insider threats. However the attack surfaces, velocity, and scale all change when it comes to agents. Let’s look at some of the risks.

Risk

How you handle it today

What changes with an agent

Leaked credentials and privilege abuse

Least privilege, short-lived tokens, keyless auth through workload identity or OIDC. Regular review of over-privileged accounts.Named accounts for people, per-workload identity for software.

Credentials should be short-lived and scoped to the task or job, not the developer’s full access.The agent acts inside a developer’s session and most logs outside Claude Code only show the developer’s name.

Unvetted dependencies and extensions

Pinned versions, review gates, two reviewers on manifest changes. Version controlled configuration.

Agents add both vetted and unvetted dependencies faster than manual processes. Extensions instruct the agent the moment they connect.

Data exfiltration

Egress allowlisting at the network layer.

A compromised agent can send data out through services you already allow. Unlike traditional malware, it can try multiple routes the attacker doesn’t have to proactively define.

Insider risk

Social engineering awareness training, verification, reporting paths.

Prompt injection: The check moves to the tool call and the network boundary.

Risk 1: Leaked credentials and privilege abuse

Anything an agent can read, it can leak. That includes credentials like a long-lived AWS access key or GitHub token.

Anything the agent can do, a compromised or overeager agent can misuse. By default, an agent in Claude Code runs under the identity of the developer who oversees it. In the event of an incident, you may need to distinguish between agent and developer actions so you can appropriately respond.

Risk 2: Unvetted dependencies and extensions

Agentic coding accelerates the rate at which code is generated and reviewed, which includes the speed at which dependencies are added and configuration changes are made.

When you ask an agent to add JSON schema validation, it will find a package, add the latest version, and have working code in minutes. That speed can be a risk if agents aren’t pointed in the right direction.

MCP servers, plugins, skills, subagent definitions, and a repository’s CLAUDE.md file are dependencies too, and they deserve the review you give a package. Unlike a compromised library, which waits to be called, they reach the agent as soon as they load. Their descriptions and instructions enter the context window before the agent has done any work.

On Enterprise plans, skill and plugin scanning checks third-party skills and plugins for malicious content when someone uploads or edits them in your organization.

Risk 3: Data exfiltration

Every leak needs a route out. The challenge is a domain allowlist can't tell your account from an attacker's account. For example, if you allow github.com, then the agent can push to a repository the attacker owns.

DNS is a second possible exfiltration route that HTTP allowlists miss as data can be encoded into the names an agent looks up.

And of course once a token has leaked, an attacker doesn't need the agent's network at all. They can use the credential from anywhere, so egress filtering never sees the request.

Risk 4: Prompt injection

OWASP has ranked prompt injection as the top risk in every edition of its Top 10 for LLM Applications since the list began in 2023.

Social engineering and prompt injection work the same way. Social engineering gets past technical controls because the deceived person takes the action and the system sees an authorized request. An injected agent also acts with its own permissions with every log showing a legitimate request.

For a coding agent, that prompt injection can happen multiple ways including via:

Issue trackers and pull request comments;

Dependency READMEs and changelogs;

Web pages the agent fetches;

Responses from MCP tool calls;

Comments in source files; and more.

03 The judgment layer

Defending in layers · Understanding alignment training · Prompt injection probes · The auto mode classifier

Defending in layers

In Claude Code, a compromised or misaligned agent has to get past multiple controls and two layers of defense before it can do damage.

The first layer is judgment-based. These controls decide whether something looks wrong.

Alignment training teaches Claude to refuse malicious requests and favor cautious actions.

Prompt injection probes scan incoming tool results in auto mode before Claude acts on them and flag content that looks like an injected instruction.

The auto mode classifier checks most proposed tool calls against the intent the user stated.

The second layer enforces fixed boundaries by limiting what any command can do:

Permission rules, command analysis, and hooks check each action against the rules you set before it runs.

Sandboxing and egress allowlisting limit what a permitted command can touch and where data can go.

This chapter covers the judgment layer and the next will examine the fixed boundary layer.

Understanding alignment training

Claude is trained toward good judgment backed by a list of firm rules like don't write malicious code that can cause significant damage.

In Claude Code testing without production safeguards, current Claude models refused 81% to 85% of malicious requests while completing 98% to 100% of dual-use and benign ones, such as running reconnaissance tools or testing a site for vulnerabilities.

Claude is also trained to prefer cautious actions over irreversible ones, and to raise concerns or ask for guidance rather than improvise. Claude is trained not to act on instructions inside fetched content as if they came from the user.

Keep in mind, model alignment training makes a bad outcome less likely, but it doesn’t limit how bad that outcome can be.

Prompt injection probes

Claude’s prompt injection probe is designed to flag any suspected injected instructions in tool results.

The probe adds a warning beside the injected instruction to tell Claude the content is suspect and that the user’s original request is still the task. Warning and anchoring lets Claude use the content while treating the instructions in it as data rather than commands.

The auto mode classifier

A model that’s been convinced that deleting a directory is a legitimate task will delete it with the same thoroughness and competence it brings to everything else.

This sort of destructive, overeager action is exactly what the auto mode classifier was built to catch. For actions your rules and built-in approvals don’t already decide, the auto mode classifier judges whether the proposed action matches the intent of the developer’s instructions.

For example, a command that makes sense for "fix the failing test in auth_test.py" looks different from one for "exfiltrate the contents of .env.”

Tool results are stripped from the classifier requests Claude Code sends, so injected text can’t manipulate the classifier directly. If the action fits what the user asked for, it runs. If not, it's blocked or Claude goes back to ask the developer for permission.

Auto mode is now the default starting mode for interactive sessions on every plan. Headless claude -p, Agent SDK, and HIPAA configuration default to manual.

Auto mode is the default because multiple tests showed it catches more dangerous actions than human approval does. For example, in a controlled study Anthropic published in August 2026, 1,053 paid testers caught 13.6% of dangerous commands, and auto mode blocked 89% of the same commands.

Configuring auto mode covers tuning the classifier and overriding its block and allow rules.

Approving high-stakes actions

Auto mode relies on classification systems and does not eliminate all risk.

Before rollout, identify high-stakes actions by asking, is this action irreversible, and would a single mistake cost more than having a person review every instance? When the answer is yes to both, require human approval.

For most organizations the list looks like this:

Production database migrations

Changes to IAM policy, and credential rotation

Edits to infrastructure definitions

04 Enforcing fixed boundaries

Setting permission rules · Bash command analysis · Gating actions with hooks · Containing agent actions with sandboxing

The judgment layer is good at catching novel attacks, but its controls are probabilistic, so each one has the chance of being beaten.

The fixed boundary layer can be made deterministic and sets an agent’s blast radius. Permission rules, command analysis, and hooks decide whether an action runs and the sandbox along with egress allowlists limit what can be reached and where data can go.

Their limitation is that they only block what you tell them to block, so they need to be set up with your environment in mind.

Setting permission rules

Permission rules come in three kinds:

Allow rules let an action run,

Ask rules prompt a person before an action runs, and

Deny rules block the action.

Claude Code first checks deny rules, then ask rules, and finally allow rules. This prevents an allow rule from creating an exception to a deny rule. A deny rule defined in managed settings can’t be overridden by any user or project setting. You want to avoid allow rules for any command broad enough to run arbitrary code, such as Bash(python:*).

Subagents inherit the parent session's permission rules and permission mode, so a broad rule written for the top-level session applies to every agent it delegates to.

Bash command analysis

Claude Code parses every Bash command before it runs. Without parsing, a permission rule allowing git status would also approve git status && curl attacker.example, and wrapping a denied command in a subshell would get it past the rule.

Parsing is deterministic, so the same command gets the same answer every time. Deny and ask rules apply to each part of a command in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions.

Gating actions with hooks

A hook is a script, HTTP endpoint, or MCP tool that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point in a session. Two that are particularly important for security are:

PreToolUse runs before a tool call and can block it, approve it, ask a developer, or (in headless runs) defer it for approval later. For example, you may want to block a commit that contains a secret.

ConfigChange runs when a settings file changes mid-session and can reject the change. This is how you identify when a repository or developer is trying to loosen a control locally.

Hooks sit inside the fixed boundaries rather than above them. A PreToolUse hook can block a tool call, but a hook returning "allow" can’t approve past a deny rule, an ask rule, or a critical-path deletion.

Hooks defined in managed settings run on every machine and individual developers can’t remove them. allowManagedHooksOnly goes further and prevents user, project, and plugin hooks from running at all, so a hook that reaches the agent is one your platform team put there.

Containing agent actions with sandboxing

Sandboxing is one of the most important ways to contain the severity of an incident because it limits the agent’s scope. But containing agents is easier said than done, as constraint and capability are often inversely correlated.

There are three main Claude Code environments: local, local with sandbox, and cloud.

We’ll discuss the default settings and how to consider which is appropriate for each of the use cases within your organization. The defaults can be modified and locked centrally, which is covered in the next chapter.

Local

Most Claude Code sessions happen locally via the terminal, IDE, or desktop app. By default, the agent can access anything on your computer that you can. In auto mode, the classifier reviews actions your rules and built-in approvals don’t already decide.

This is the least contained environment and appropriate for low-stakes, self-contained work. For most enterprise organizations, we recommend enforcing the sandbox for local sessions.

Local sandbox

The Claude Code sandbox isolates each shell command at the operating system level, so commands can only change files in the project folder and connect to sites on the allowlist unless an exception is approved.

By default, the developer or the auto mode classifier can approve agents to operate outside the sandbox or reach sites that aren’t on the allowlist if they deem it safe.

Using managed settings (more on this in the next chapter), admins can make local sandbox use mandatory, contain agent commands to that sandbox, and allow agents to only visit centrally approved sites.

Once you’ve contained an agent to the sandbox, you don’t want it to escape by accessing credentials by reading files outside the project. To combat credential leaks, admins can add Read deny rules for the organization’s credential paths and also set credential masking, which lets a command sign in without ever holding the real value.

Cloud sessions

Claude Code cloud sessions run on an Anthropic managed environment with each task getting its own VM. Not only does this contain where Claude can execute, it also keeps GitHub credentials outside the VM.

Cloud sessions suit work that reads untrusted content or runs unattended. That’s because they are isolated from the developer’s machine and internal networks by default, and VMs can be discarded at any time.

When a developer creates a new cloud environment, Claude starts with a limited set of pre-installed tools and allowed domains, although developers can add exceptions. Developers must select what repos will be cloned over every session.

Organization owners can set a default environment and publish shared environments with settings individual developers can’t change.

Developers can still create new environments and modify those environment settings. Organizations that need to lock this down host their own sessions, running Claude Code on infrastructure they launch and run, so they control the policy for those sessions.

Keep in mind, cloud sessions aren’t available to organizations that use zero data retention, the HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.

05 Enforcing policy

Central settings at a glance · Which settings apply

We covered the default settings in previous chapters. The table below covers two additional configurations.

We’ve labeled one baseline, which you should choose when you want to create alternative defaults–or a starting point that individual developers can add to.

We’ve labeled the other locked, which is how admins can lock in a set of rules that can’t be changed at the developer level. Locking a setting is what turns a written policy into an enforced security control.

This is not an exhaustive list of settings, but rather those that focus on the key dimensions for bounding agent risk.

Central settings at a glance

Local sessionsset in managed settings

Cloud sessionsset in claude.ai admin settings

Is it allowed?

Can be turned off in the desktop app (disableDesktopLocalSessions), not in the terminal

Cloud sessions toggle for the organization

How contained is it?

Baseline: sandbox on for all local sessions (sandbox.enabled)Locked: no running without it and no unsandboxed retries (failIfUnavailable, allowUnsandboxedCommands: false)

Baseline: Owners create shared environments with settings members can't change on the Cloud environments page, and pick one as the organization's default environmentLocked: run Claude Code on infrastructure you operate. On Anthropic-hosted environments, developers can still create personal ones with their own settings

Where can it connect?

Baseline: a managed list of approved sites that developers can add to (sandbox.network.allowedDomains)Locked: only your list counts (allowManagedDomainsOnly). The list covers shell commands, so limit the WebFetch tool with its own permission rules

Baseline: Anthropic's trusted list by default (package registries, GitHub, cloud SDKs), or the network access Owners set on each shared environment (connector, GitHub, and Anthropic API traffic isn’t limited by this setting)Locked: use self-hosted environments (public beta), where your own network boundary limits connections. Anthropic-hosted environments have no organization-wide allowlist

What can it read?

Baseline: Read deny rules for sensitive paths (permissions.deny)Locked: restrict file-tool reads to the project and block listed paths (permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories, sandbox.filesystem.denyRead)

Baseline: the same Read deny rulesLocked: no full lock. Limit the Claude GitHub App to approved repositories to control what sessions can clone and push. Developers can still upload a local repository from the terminal.

What credentials can it use?

Block credential files with Read deny rules and set credential masking (sandbox.credentials)

Owners store keys as Network secrets on shared environments, never as environment variables.

Which connectors can it use?

Baseline: an approved list that developers can add to (allowedMcpServers).Locked: only your list counts (allowManagedMcpServersOnly)Connectors the desktop app delivers skip this list and are limited in organization connector settings.

What can it do without asking?

Baseline: managed deny and ask rules, with developers adding their own allow rules.Locked: only your rules and hooks apply, and bypass mode is off (allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, allowManagedHooksOnly, permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode).

Which settings apply

Managed settings can reach a session three ways: server-managed settings from the Claude admin console, an MDM or OS-level policy, and a managed settings file. Only server-managed settings reach Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions.

By default, Claude Code applies only the highest-ranked source and ignores the others, in that order, with no warning. If your MDM profile turns on the sandbox and a managed settings file holds the egress allowlist, the allowlist never applies.

06 Getting started

The controls in this guide work as layers, each covering what the others miss. A pilot on one repository shows how the layers hold up in your environment before you widen the rollout.

Pilot checklist

Tier your repositories and run the vendor review. Rank the repositories the agent will touch by sensitivity, then check your provider against the requirements in Chapter 1.

Pick a repository from your lowest tier, such as an internal tool under active development. It should be busy enough to generate real sessions and low-stakes enough that a miss costs little.

Deploy a central policy baseline. Set sandboxing on in strict mode, deny rules on credential paths, credential masking, an egress allowlist, and auto mode. Set and configure a default cloud environment. Add the security-guidance plugin and whatever hooks enforce your non-negotiable rules.

Turn on the record. Enable OpenTelemetry export with tool content (beta), and make sure sandbox and egress logs are being kept.

Run for two weeks without changing the policy, so every result traces back to one configuration.

Review what the layers did. Look at classifier denials, sandbox blocks, unsandboxed retry attempts, and refused egress. Each one is either a control doing its job or a legitimate need the baseline didn’t anticipate. Add the allowlist entries the work needed rather than relaxing deny rules.

Score the pilot against Chapter 1’s five questions before you widen to a second team.

Done right, this secure framework will accelerate rather than slow your team’s ability to run at full speed with coding agents.

¹ Salesforce Ventures is an investor in Anthropic.

articles.title: Building security review into your SDLC with Codex Security
articles.context: Threat models, repository security policies, and architecture documents make that knowledge available
articles.full_text:
As AI accelerates the SDLC, it’s putting pressure on security workflows. Security teams need to prevent insecure code from being committed in the first place, but manual security reviews for PRs can’t scale at the same pace that agents are producing and revising code.

Application security programs have followed the pace of human development: a design review before implementation, a manual pass on the riskiest pull requests, and periodic work to triage vulnerability backlogs. To keep up, we must now deploy agentic security workflows that match the speed of agentic SDLC.

This post presents four principles for agentic security workflows, then shares how to build and run those workflows through Codex Security and our CLI.

Four principles for agentic security workflows

Expanding security review capacity requires a clear basis for evaluating changes and a clear way for teams to assess the results. We recommend four principles for integrating security agents into development:

Give agents system-specific context

Agents need to understand the application’s assets, trust boundaries, and security requirements to evaluate a change. Threat models, repository security policies, and architecture documents make that knowledge available. Regularly reviewing these artifacts and keeping them current gives agents a reliable foundation for their investigations.

Integrate review into development

Security feedback should reach developers while changes are still in progress. Connect reviews to local work, pull requests, and CI workflows, with clear triggers for when they should run. This makes security review a consistent part of the development process.

Set review scope and reporting thresholds deliberately

Review scope should reflect the change and the components it could affect. A diff scan, a component assessment, and a full repository scan serve different purposes. Reporting thresholds should also reflect risk, giving sensitive areas such as authentication and billing appropriate attention.

Make findings inspectable

Reviewers need enough information to evaluate a finding and determine what action to take. Reports should explain the relevant code locations, reasoning, severity, confidence, and remediation guidance. They should also identify what was reviewed, excluded, or deferred so teams can understand the investigation’s limits.

Seeding context for security reviews

Differences among threat models, AGENTS.md, SECURITY.md, and knowledge bases

AGENTS.md keeps shared engineering instructions that establish consistent expectations. SECURITY.md tells Codex how your organization wants that reality evaluated and reported. A threat model describes the security reality of the system. They overlap, but the threat model is usually one part of the broader policy.

For example, a threat model would include details about assets, entry points, attacker-controlled inputs, trust boundaries, authentication assumptions, privileged operations, and risky components. Commit it as a separate file, docs/security/threat-model.md, so Codex Security can reference it during pull request reviews and security scans.

<!-- docs/security/threat-model.md --> # Threat Model The public API accepts untrusted JSON and file uploads. Requests cross from the internet-facing API into internal billing and identity services. Attackers are unauthenticated users or compromised tenant accounts. Protect tenant data, billing mutations, and service credentials.

The SECURITY.md file tells Codex how your organization wants that reality evaluated and reported.

<!-- SECURITY.md --> # Security Policy ## Security Invariants - Every billing mutation must be authorized for the active tenant. - Uploaded content must be parsed within explicit size and resource limits. - Service credentials must never be returned to clients. ## Reportable Findings Report realistic violations of tenant isolation, authentication bypass, unsafe parsing, secret exposure, or unauthorized billing mutations. ## Severity Context Cross-tenant access is Critical. Single-tenant unauthorized mutation is High. ## Out of Scope Development-only tools that cannot be included in production builds.

Finally, a knowledge base supplies supporting documents to particular scans. This can include architecture documents, policies, additional threat models, or operational context that the CLI scanner should consider. Here’s an example of a Markdown architecture document you can pass to the CLI when running a security scan against a codebase.

<!-- docs/security/payment-service-context.md --> # Payment Service Security Context ## Purpose The payment service creates charges, issues refunds, and stores references to payment-provider customers. It does not store full card numbers or CVVs. ## Deployment and Exposure - `POST /api/payments` is internet-facing through the API gateway. - `POST /internal/refunds` is reachable only from the support service. - Background workers consume messages from the `payment-events` queue. - The service runs with access to the payment-provider API and billing database. ## Authentication and Authorization - Public endpoints use JWTs issued by the identity service. - The API gateway validates signatures, issuer, and expiration. - This service remains responsible for tenant authorization. - Internal requests use workload identity; network location alone is not trusted. - Refunds above £1,000 require a previously recorded approval. ## Trust Boundaries 1. Internet client → API gateway 2. API gateway → payment service 3. Payment service → payment provider 4. Payment service → billing database 5. Message producers → `payment-events` consumer Inputs crossing any of these boundaries must be treated as untrusted unless the receiving component performs the documented validation. ## Sensitive Assets and Operations - Payment-provider API credentials - Customer-to-provider identifier mappings - Charge creation - Refund issuance - Webhook signature secrets - Tenant billing history ## Important Data Flows ### Creating a charge 1. The API receives an authenticated request containing an order identifier. 2. The service retrieves the order using both tenant ID and order ID. 3. The service calculates the amount from server-side order data. 4. The service creates the provider charge with an idempotency key. 5. The resulting provider identifier is stored in the billing database. Client-supplied amounts must never be passed directly to the provider. ### Processing a webhook 1. The raw request body is retained. 2. The provider signature is verified over the raw bytes. 3. The event timestamp must be within five minutes. 4. Duplicate event IDs are ignored. 5. State changes occur only after all validation succeeds. ## Relevant Code - `src/http/payments.ts`: public payment endpoints - `src/http/refunds.ts`: refund endpoints - `src/webhooks/provider.ts`: webhook validation - `src/workers/payment-events.ts`: asynchronous event processing - `src/auth/tenant.ts`: tenant authorization - `src/provider/client.ts`: provider API wrapper ## Security Assumptions - The identity service is trusted to authenticate users, but not to authorize access to payment records. - Queue publishers may be compromised; consumers must validate message content. - API-gateway authentication does not replace service-level tenant checks. - Provider webhook payloads are attacker-controlled until signature validation completes. ## Known Limitations - Legacy refunds created before 2025 do not have idempotency keys. - Webhook replay protection is local to one region. - The development payment-provider emulator does not validate signatures.

It can be supplied to the scan using the following command:

npx @openai/codex-security scan . \ --knowledge-base docs/security/payment-service-context.md

Putting it all together, a useful arrangement could look like the following:

SECURITY.md docs/security/ ├── threat-model.md ├── architecture.md ├── payment-service-context.md ├── authentication.md └── deployment-boundaries.md

Seeding a threat model

Committing a threat model is a core component of informing how Codex should conduct security reviews. You can initialize a threat model by invoking the threat model skill within Codex and committing it.

Generate a Threat Model of this repository that covers entry points and untrusted inputs, sensitive data paths, and privileged actions.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

You can invoke the threat model skill through Codex by simply typing $threat-model. Once a threat model has been created, commit it to the repository under /docs/security and then link to the threat model within the Codex Cloud settings for the selected repo. If a threat model is not specified, Codex will regenerate the threat model for every security review.

When generating a threat model, pay particular attention to assumptions that the code alone can’t establish, such as compensating controls and responsibilities shared with other services.

Want an even better example? Look at the trust model for Backstage, an open-source framework for building an internal developer portal. A generated model might treat its authentication and catalog plugins as isolated because they run on separate hosts. However, Backstage’s threat model explains that this separation does not establish a security boundary if the catalog plugin can still access the authentication plugin’s database.

Correcting the model allows a review to inspect deployment configuration and access grants to determine whether another plugin can read or modify authentication data. This turns an architectural assumption into a requirement. Changes to database access, shared caches, or plugin placement should trigger another review of that boundary.

Lastly, don’t forget to revisit the threat model when entry points, trust boundaries, or privileged operations change. Those are useful triggers for keeping the review context aligned with the application.

Seeding a SECURITY.md

You can use the $define-security-policy skill to generate a seeded security policy within the repository.

Define Security Policy for the Northstar Bank API. Here are key policies that should be included: Authentication and Authorization: - Every non-public endpoint must authenticate the caller. - Sessions and tokens must be validated for issuer, audience, signature, expiry, revocation, and intended authentication context. - Authentication failures must fail closed. - Sensitive operations must require recent or stronger authentication where appropriate. - Password-reset, account-recovery, MFA, and identity-linking flows must not permit account takeover.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

A strong security policy should include thorough details about how the application operates. Here’s an example of what to ask Codex to include in SECURITY.md:

<!-- SECURITY.md --> ### Authentication and Authorization - Every non-public endpoint must authenticate the caller. - Sessions and tokens must be validated for issuer, audience, signature, expiry, revocation, and intended authentication context. - Authentication failures must fail closed. - Sensitive operations must require recent or stronger authentication where appropriate. - Password-reset, account-recovery, MFA, and identity-linking flows must not permit account takeover. - Authentication secrets and tokens must never appear in logs, URLs, analytics, or error responses. - Authorization must occur before every read, mutation, transaction, export, or administrative action. - Possession of a valid account or resource identifier never proves authorization. - Customer, account, and tenant isolation must hold across list, detail, search, bulk, export, and indirect-reference endpoints. - Server-side authorization must not rely on client-supplied roles, ownership fields, prices, balances, or approval state. - Administrative and service-to-service permissions must use least privilege. - Failures allowing cross-customer access are reportable even when only one endpoint is affected. ### Transaction and ledger integrity - Transactions must be authorized against the authenticated customer and eligible source account. - Amounts, currencies, destinations, fees, limits, and approval state must be validated server-side. - Transaction requests must be protected against replay, duplication, race conditions, and idempotency-key confusion. - Balance checks and ledger updates must be atomic. - Posted ledger entries must be immutable or corrected through auditable compensating entries. - High-risk transactions must enforce applicable limits, step-up authentication, approval, or fraud controls. - No failure path may produce an ambiguous transaction state without reconciliation. ### Data protection - Sensitive data must be encrypted in transit and at rest using approved controls. - Secret material must come from an approved secret-management system rather than source code or ordinary configuration files. - Logs, traces, metrics, support tooling, and security artifacts must exclude credentials and minimize personal and financial data. - Data exports and backups must receive equivalent authorization and protection to primary data. - Error responses must not expose internals, sensitive records, credentials, or authorization details. - Retention and deletion behavior must follow the system’s approved data-governance requirements. ### Input and output handling - Treat headers, paths, query parameters, bodies, uploaded files, webhook payloads, third-party responses, and stored customer content as untrusted. - Apply schema, type, range, length, and format validation before security-sensitive use. - Database access must use parameterized queries. - Outbound requests must restrict destinations, protocols, redirects, DNS behavior, and response sizes. - Parsers, uploads, decompression, and serialization must be bounded against resource exhaustion. - Customer-controlled content must be safely encoded for its output context.

Let’s take a look at Apache Superset, an open-source business intelligence web application, as an example. The application connects to databases and lets users explore data, run SQL in SQL Lab, and build and share charts and dashboards. The security policy within their open-source repo establishes detailed context concerning roles and capabilities, as well as how async execution and realtime notifications operate. For example, the policy defines:

Asynchronous execution paths do not create a separate data-access capability. A background task is a continuation of an already-authorized action, such as reading chart data or executing SQL through SQL Lab. The initiating route, command, or scheduler must enforce the same route-level and object-level checks the synchronous path would enforce before it creates the task, and the worker must execute under the initiating principal’s effective identity when row-level security, impersonation, embedded guest-token scope, or similar controls affect the result.

This makes vulnerability reporting more precise because it defines what must remain true as execution moves from a request into a background worker. A reviewer can trace the initiating user, the requested resource, the authorization checks before task creation, and the identity used during execution. As a result, reports from both security researchers and agents can test the policy requirement, the code paths that could violate it, the attacker’s starting permissions, and the resulting unauthorized capability.

Codex Security

Once context is established, you should choose a review workflow that works with your team’s existing development process. Local review gives a developer feedback before a PR is opened. Automatic PR review provides a consistent team checkpoint. The CLI supports workflows that need explicit targets, saved artifacts, or custom CI integration.

You can also use multiple workflows. However, you should start with one workflow, inspect its results on a change the team understands, and then expand once the review is producing evidence people can use.

Codex Security Review in GitHub Cloud

The fastest way to automate security reviews in GitHub Cloud is through the Security Review feature within ChatGPT. This is available through the same product surface as Codex Code Reviews available within your organization at https://chatgpt.com/codex/cloud/settings/code-review.

Codex Security Review goes deeper than Code Review on security-specific risks by analyzing the pull request diff, supporting repository context, and configured threat models or security guidance.

Difference between Code Review and Security Review

Code Review is a broad engineering review that assesses code quality. For example, Code Review asks: “Could this change break the product or introduce a serious engineering problem?” It reviews issues such as incorrect control flow, data corruption or loss, compatibility regressions, or incorrect API behavior. The intended users for Code Review are software developers within the organization.

Codex Security is a specialized, deeper assessment of security risks in the same PR changes. Security Review is for both software developers responsible for remediating vulnerabilities, as well as application security engineers responsible for securing CI/CD pipelines and source code. It assesses issues such as authentication and authorization bypasses, cross-tenant access, injection and unsafe parsing, or sensitive data exposure.

Configuring security reviews

There are two options for configuring security reviews. The auto-review reporting determines which findings Codex posts to the PR when Security Review runs automatically. It is defaulted to High, so only High and Critical findings are posted.

The option for manual review controls which findings Codex posts after someone explicitly requests a Security Review. It is defaulted to Medium, so Medium, High, and Critical findings are posted.

When configured, posted vulnerabilities will surface within the PR.

It’s best to choose automatic reporting thresholds around what the team is prepared to investigate consistently. For a targeted investigation, use the manual review settings to surface the additional detail relevant to that question.

Setting path overrides

Path-based reporting overrides the minimum severity published to the GitHub PR. Given that a repository’s risk is rarely uniform, this feature can tailor the risk threshold for more critical paths, such as:

Lowering the threshold for authentication, authorization, payments, cryptography, CI workflows, or infrastructure.

Keeping a higher threshold for lower-risk or especially noisy areas.

You can modify the path overrides within the Codex Cloud settings for the selected repo. In this example below, we have established that src/** should have auto reviews for low vulnerabilities or higher. Changes to GitHub workflows or dependencies will enforce reporting for medium vulnerabilities.

A practical starting point is to identify the application’s sensitive operations and map them to paths with their owners. For the payment service example at the beginning of this post, that includes tenant authorization and billing mutations. I would review those paths with the team that owns them and choose a reporting threshold that reflects the consequence of a missed issue.

Going back to our Apache Superset example, I would keep a High repository-wide reporting threshold, but lower it for these paths:

Repository-relative path prefix

Minimum severity to report

Why it deserves additional attention

superset/security/

Low

Path contains code for central authorization, guest tokens, password recovery, and session invalidation

superset/row_level_security/

Low

Path controls the policies determining which data rows users can access

superset/sqllab/ and superset/commands/sql_lab/

Medium

Path focuses on SQL execution, query authorization, result retrieval, and exports

superset/embedded/

Medium

Path focuses on boundaries for dashboards embedded in other applications

If these settings were applied, then Codex Security Review would only report High vulnerabilities for all paths except those stated above. In those paths, Low and Medium would be reported given the additional sensitivity of the code.

Codex Security Review in Codex Desktop

For a more interactive experience reviewing PRs or uncommitted changes, you can also execute reviews through the security tab within Codex.

Alternatively, you can prompt Codex within the repository project of Codex by invoking the skill.

Please run a Security Diff Scan on the changes in the current branch.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

This workflow is most useful when the implementation is still fresh in your mind and you can investigate a finding immediately. If the review points to an authorization assumption, you can inspect the caller and the affected operation before the change moves into a separate review queue.

Codex Security Review in the CLI

Reviewing uncommitted local work

You can use the CLI to review uncommitted local work with seeded context about the repository and security policies.

Run the examples in the same shell from your Git checkout. They assume your security policy is in SECURITY.md and your supporting documents are in docs/security/. The setup creates a temporary directory for scan results.

northstar_repo="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" northstar_kb="$northstar_repo/docs/security" northstar_results="$(mktemp -d)"

npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --working-tree \ --base HEAD \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/working-tree"

This reviews staged and unstaged changes relative to HEAD.

Before starting, be sure to confirm that the working tree contains the change you intend to assess. Unrelated edits broaden the investigation and can make it harder to connect the findings to the question that prompted the review.

Reviewing PRs or branch commits

Another option is to review a PR or branch for security issues. Check out the branch to review and fetch its target branch. This example uses origin/main.

northstar_pr_base="$(git -C "$northstar_repo" merge-base origin/main HEAD)" npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --diff "$northstar_pr_base" \ --head HEAD \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/branch"

Note that a diff scan evaluates the proposed changes and does not scan the entire repository. Once complete, the output directory will contain the following files:

report.md: readable review

scan-manifest.json: confirms the exact base, head, target, and artifacts

findings.json: presents the severity, confidence, locations, and remediation

coverage.json: identifies the reviewed surfaces, exclusions, deferred work, and completeness

Scanning monorepos

In a monorepo, a change to a shared library can affect multiple services. Codex should receive enough context to review those interactions, while CI determines which components and checks are required.

Repository context

Keep shared engineering instructions in AGENTS.md and security expectations in SECURITY.md. A typical repository could look like this:

monorepo/ ├── AGENTS.md ├── SECURITY.md ├── docs/security/ │ ├── architecture.md │ └── threat-model.md ├── packages/auth/ └── services/ ├── billing/ └── reporting/

Use existing ownership and build metadata to connect each component to its dependencies, consumers, and tests. For example, a change to packages/auth may require reviewing both services even when their files are unchanged. This scope mapping is maintained by your organization; it is not automatically configured by adding Codex.

Component assessment

Large repositories may not always require scanning the entire codebase for each PR. One option is to use a path scan when a monorepo contains separate services or packages. Repeat --path to assess a shared library and its consumers together.

npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --path packages/auth \ --path services/billing \ --path services/reporting \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_repo/SECURITY.md" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/paths"

This scans only the selected paths rather than the entire repository.

PR and diff scanning

For a PR, use its exact base and head commit hashes from authenticated GitHub metadata. Both revisions and their history must be available in the checkout. The following example reuses the variables above and saves the diff results separately:

BASE_SHA="<full PR base commit SHA>" HEAD_SHA="<full PR head commit SHA>" BASE_REVISION="$( git -C "$northstar_repo" merge-base "$BASE_SHA" "$HEAD_SHA" )" || exit npx @openai/codex-security scan "$northstar_repo" \ --diff "$BASE_REVISION" \ --head "$HEAD_SHA" \ --knowledge-base "$northstar_kb" \ --auth chatgpt \ --output-dir "$northstar_results/pr"

A diff scan focuses on the proposed changes. If a shared-library change requires broader consumer review, also run the component assessment against a clean checkout of that PR’s head revision. Keep the results distinct: --diff and --path are separate scan modes and cannot be combined.

Scanning alerts from GitHub

You can also assess code scanning alerts from the default branch using the Codex Security CLI.

northstar_github_repository="example/northstar" northstar_github_alerts="$northstar_results/github-alerts.json" # Import all open alerts as complete JSON. npx @openai/codex-security import github "$northstar_github_repository" \ --format json \ > "$northstar_github_alerts" # Or import a selected subset. npx @openai/codex-security import github "$northstar_github_repository" \ --github-alert 12 \ --github-alert 18 \ --format json \ > "$northstar_github_alerts" # Run from the corresponding local repository; imported contents are data. cd "$northstar_repo" npx @openai/codex-security validate "$northstar_github_alerts"

GitHub Actions workflows

Instead of enforcing security reviews through Codex, it is also possible to create custom workflows that run the Codex Security CLI. We’ve packaged this workflow to easily be used as a GitHub Action.

# .github/workflows/codex-security-repository.yml name: Codex Security review on: workflow_dispatch: schedule: - cron: "23 7 * * 1" # Mondays at 07:23 UTC permissions: contents: read jobs: security: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 steps: - name: Set up the Ubuntu sandbox run: | sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install --yes bubblewrap apparmor-profiles sudo apparmor_parser -r /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 with: persist-credentials: false - uses: openai/codex-security@3f61e5150981a5087c32e4395bbaa8ce5ce0c3e3 # action-v0.3.0 with: model: gpt-5.6-sol effort: high env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY }}

These workflows can also be applied to other source code management tools like GitLab, BitBucket, or Jenkins. Take a look at our documentation page to learn more: Run Codex Security in CI.

Managing supply chain risk in CI/CD

You can also leverage the Codex Security CLI to assess dependencies in the codebase, such as when a new dependency is introduced or a version is bumped.

This is extremely useful in preventing vulnerable packages from presenting supply chain risk – you can achieve this by deploying the Codex Security CLI as commands within custom workflows.

Validating Dependabot alerts

Codex Security provides a skill for validating existing third-party vulnerabilities, including Dependabot, for reachability and exploitability. You can invoke the skill directly in the UI or through the CLI.

Use Triage Finding to import and triage Dependabot vulnerabilities against this repository.

GPT-6.1 SolExtra High

Codex will triage each of the Dependabot alerts and subsequently present a ledger of each presented risk with a reason why the alert was validated or not.

Looking at Apache Superset again, we can take its documentation toolchain to identify a security advisory related to it (such as webpack-dev-server advisory).

Using Codex, we can trace the dependency through Docusaurus, check the resolved version, and follow the development, build, and deployment paths to establish where the affected functionality could run. The reviewed lockfile selected version 5.2.6, which the advisory identifies as patched.

Codex’s analysis therefore supported a specific conclusion: the advisory did not affect the version selected by that documentation revision. Before closing a corresponding Dependabot alert, we would reconcile its reported version and revision with this evidence and verify the installed dependency.

Running scans when package versions change

It is also possible to run security scans against the latest version of a dependency when the version is changed.

# .github/workflows/codex-security-dependency.yml name: Codex Security dependency scan on: pull_request: paths: - package.json - package-lock.json permissions: contents: read jobs: scan: name: Scan dependency changes if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 timeout-minutes: 45 steps: - name: Set up the Ubuntu sandbox run: | sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install --yes bubblewrap apparmor-profiles sudo apparmor_parser -r /usr/share/apparmor/extra-profiles/bwrap-userns-restrict - name: Set up Node.js uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7 with: node-version: "26" - name: Set up Python uses: actions/setup-python@5fda3b95a4ea91299a34e894583c3862153e4b97 # v7 with: python-version: "3.14" - name: Install Codex Security run: | set -euo pipefail npm install \ --prefix "$RUNNER_TEMP/codex-security" \ --ignore-scripts \ --no-audit \ --no-fund \ @openai/codex-security - name: Verify Codex Security env: CODEX_SECURITY_BIN: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security/node_modules/.bin/codex-security run: | set -euo pipefail test -x "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" --version - name: Check out the pull request uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} fetch-depth: 0 persist-credentials: false - name: Install project dependencies run: | set -euo pipefail npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund - name: Run full repository scan env: OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY }} CODEX_SECURITY_BIN: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security/node_modules/.bin/codex-security CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-state SCAN_DIR: ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-results run: | set -euo pipefail "$CODEX_SECURITY_BIN" scan . \ --auth api-key \ --output-dir "$SCAN_DIR" \ --fail-on-severity high \ --json > "$RUNNER_TEMP/codex-security.json" - name: Preserve scan results if: always() uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7 with: name: codex-security-dependency-results path: | ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security-results ${{ runner.temp }}/codex-security.json if-no-files-found: warn retention-days: 7

Wrapping up

As agents contribute more code, security teams must carve the right scaffolding for agentic systems to reason across the codebase for application security reviews and enforce gates when insecure code could be committed.

Start with a few critical repositories, commit your threat models and security policies, then review the pull requests to assess how accurately agents are reasoning against enterprise context and the codebase. When you begin to feel confident in the quality of the results, begin to expand into a broader number of repositories or pipelines as you expand agentic security coverage in the SDLC.

Curious about learning more or wondering what to tackle next? Review our security use cases within our developer docs or explore details about the Daybreak Defense Factory for continuous security reviews.

articles.title: A brief history of syslog timestamps, (Sun, Nov 22nd)
articles.context: Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2...
articles.full_text:
BLUF: Debian and Ubuntu dropped a config directive in the rsyslogd package in early 2023.

As any of my FOR577 students will tell you, I'm a fan of ISO-8601 (ok, RFC 3339, too, see below). They'll probably also tell you I'm a firm believer in UTC||GTFO especially on servers (also true, and I've made stickers to prove it). I was also asked recently why the syslog timestamps in newer Ubuntu and Debian systems changed to ISO-8601 (well, probably actually RFC 3339, but I won't got down that rabbithole in this handler's diary) timestamps from the historical Mmm dd hh:mm:ss format we've known since the 1980s. I had noticed the same, a few years ago, but never really paid attention to it. Given the question from a student, I decided to do a little research on the subject and this diary is the result.

To back up some, the syslog protocol and syslogd were originally the creation of Eric Allman in 1983 because he needed a way to debug sendmail[1]. They became part of BSD 4.2 that same year. BSD 4.2 also happened to be my introduction to Unix in 1983. Syslog then made it into AT&T's System V Unix in about 1989 in SVR4 (System V Release 4) through an effort by AT&T and Sun Microsystems to try to merge the features of the 2 major branches of Unix at the time. System V adopted the protocol and routing interfaces but built the daemon on top of System V internals.

The first effort to develop the protocol into an actual standard was an IETF draft in Oct 2000 that evolved into RFC 3164[2] in 2001, by which time the protocol was actually already 18 years old. This is the syslog message format we've all come to know so well over the years. Meanwhile, around 2005, rsyslogd added the option of outputing RFC 3339 timestamps. In 2009, RFC 3164 was superceded by RFC 5424[3] which defined the timestamp to be of the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss]Z or YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss[.ssssss](+/-)hh:mm. Despite the new RFC, the default setting even for rsyslogd in most Linux distros continued to be to write messages to the log files in the older format (referred to as the BSD format, as specified in the title of RFC 3164), by setting a directive in /etc/rsyslog.conf (the RSYSLOG_TraditionalFileFormat directive).

That brings us to 2023, with the release of Debian 12 (Bookworm) and Ubuntu 23.04 (not a LTS release) both distros stopped installing rsyslogd by default and defaulted to the systemd journal for logging and removed the directive from the default config file for those who did install it.. Many system administrators continue to install rsyslogd because they had infrastructure in place for forwarding syslog to central log servers and/or SIEMs. These are the folks most likely to have noticed the format change. Meanwhile, Fedora and Alma (and presumably the rest of the RedHat family) have left the directive in place when the package is installed.

From a Ubuntu 24.04 system:

From a Fedora 44 system:

Meanwhile you can get either one with journalctl by setting the output format to either short (BSD format) or short-iso-precise (ISO format).

Also, note that rsyslogd is not the only option for a syslog server. I've been using syslog-ng as the syslog server on my home log collector since about 2000. In syslog-ng, the new 'ISO' timestamps can be enabled by setting the following two options in syslog-ng.conf: ts-format(iso) and frac-digits(6). Since I have just been upgrading my central log server for years, I haven't done a fresh install lately, so I'm not sure if that is the default. I had to explicitly add it to my config.

References:

1. The History of Centralized Logging

2. RFC 3164: The BSD Syslog Protocol

3. RFC 5424: The Syslog Protocol

articles.title: Signal Is Blocking AI Agents From Reading Your Screen
articles.context: “We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy...
articles.full_text:
Signal is blocking OS-level AI agents from reading its app on iOS 27 and Android, warning that Gemini and Siri AI threaten its privacy guarantees.

Signal is restricting new AI agents built into iOS 27 and Android from capturing its data, president Meredith Whittaker announced. The company already did something similar on Windows last year, blocking screenshots to stop Microsoft’s Recall from capturing Signal messages by default. Now it’s doing the same wherever it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the Signal screen.

The process is simple, but it raises serious privacy concerns. Operating system-level AI agents, such as Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI, scan the content displayed on your screen so they can answer questions and perform tasks for you.

This means these AI agents can capture your Signal data and use it to answer your questions and carry out your requests.

“In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.” reads the announcement. “The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

Signal’s security model is based on open-source code and encryption that has been formally checked and reviewed by independent researchers for more than a decade. However, this protection can’t help if an AI agent reads your messages directly from the screen before encryption becomes relevant. Once captured, the data may be stored in a local database or sent to a remote server used by the AI agent, completely outside Signal’s control.

Google, Apple, and Microsoft aren’t just three companies among many here.

“these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem.” continues the report. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy.”

When the ocean starts working against the fish swimming in it, the fish can’t simply find a different ocean.

Signal’s fix is narrow: block screenshots on iOS 27, and block AI assistant screen capture attempts on Android. Users can turn the protection off in settings if they want to take screenshots, but doing so exposes their messages, and their contacts’ messages, to the same agents Signal is trying to keep out. The company is upfront that this doesn’t close every door, since an agent could still reach app data through the filesystem rather than the screen.

MacOS gets no protection at all right now, because Apple and Microsoft don’t give developers a clean way to block AI access without wrecking the normal user experience. Signal says it spent real engineering time just doing forensic work across Android and iOS to figure out what these AI systems actually do with app data, because the documentation isn’t there. That’s a strange place for a company Signal’s size to be: reverse-engineering the privacy behavior of the platforms it depends on.

Signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft to take two specific steps. First, they should give app developers a clear way to prevent AI agents from accessing their data, including information on the screen, files, notifications, and APIs. Second, they should explain exactly how these AI agents access, collect, and process user data.

Signal also raises concerns about third-party AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which can use accessibility permissions that users originally granted for other purposes. The company adds that confidential computing doesn’t solve the problem because the platform still controls the privacy decision, not the app developer or the user.

Signal says it’s already talking with Google and Apple about better support for apps that handle sensitive information. The company is cautiously optimistic, but whether these discussions lead to real changes will depend on what the two companies actually do over the coming year.

Signal frames the stakes plainly for anyone tempted to see this as one company’s problem.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data.” the report cocludes. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Signal)

Security Affairs AI-CYBERSECURITY newsletter includes a collection of the best articles and research on AI in the international landscape

Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing cybersecurity, reshaping both the techniques used by attackers and the tools available to defenders. AI agents can automate tasks, analyze large amounts of data, discover vulnerabilities and accelerate offensive operations. At the same time, AI is creating new capabilities for threat detection, incident analysis and response. Security Affairs’ new newsletter follows this evolution, covering every week the latest threats, attacks, vulnerabilities and developments at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.
