In this article

A ransomware group leaks files linked to Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase customers

The data may include emails, phone numbers, and travel or dining bookings; no card numbers have been reported exposed

Scammers could use personal details to make their messages more convincing

Customer information linked by researchers to Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase has appeared after cyberattacks on third-party service providers. The companies report no impact to their payment networks.

On November 19, the companies acknowledged incidents involving third-party providers. JPMorgan told Reuters:

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”

But “no payment data” doesn’t mean “not useful to criminals.” Knowing your name, email address and which financial services you use can give a scammer a convincing opening line.

Visa said it was aware of the claims and that they were associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia-Pacific. Mastercard said an incident at a third-party provider exposed a limited number of email addresses associated with a particular card-benefit program.

Cybernews researchers say similar formatting suggests the data came from the same third-party provider. The provider and its role haven’t been identified, but it may handle card benefits such as dining, reservations, or loyalty programs, rather than payment processing. The leaked records appear to relate to those extra services.

A ransomware group calling itself n0n has claimed responsibility and published data it says it stole.

What information was exposed?

The answer depends on the company and on whether we are talking about company disclosures or researchers’ analysis of the purported stolen files. The leaked data has not been independently verified.

The companies have disclosed the following:

JPMorgan Chase: Marketing data held by vendors, potentially including some customer names and email addresses.

Visa: An incident at an Asia-Pacific service provider. Visa says its systems were not affected and there is no indication that payment data, such as card numbers, was affected.

Mastercard: A limited number of email addresses belonging to a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program. Mastercard described this as non-payment information.

The n0n leak site lists JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard and claims their data was published after the ransom deadline passed on November 16.

Screenshot of n0n leak site, November 20, 2026

Researchers at Cybernews reported additional details from the leaked datasets:

JPMorgan: Roughly 16,000 customer email addresses, some phone numbers, identifiers described as account IDs, and more than 100 employee email addresses.

Visa: A dataset involving more than 6,000 premium customers, with fields including names, email addresses, phone numbers, messaging-app information, and booking details such as dates and addresses.

Mastercard: Data posted by n0n includes marketing information related to customers in North America, the Middle East, and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses, according to Reuters.

How to protect your accounts

If you’re concerned your information may be involved, these steps can help protect your accounts and identity:

Verify messages independently. Open your bank’s official app, use a website address you already know, or call the number on your card or statement. Do not use a link or phone number supplied by someone claiming to be investigating the breach.

Never read out a login or payment-verification code to an unexpected caller. Those codes can be the missing piece that allows a criminal to access your account. Enter them only when completing an action you initiated through the genuine service.

Do not transfer money to “protect” it. A caller who tells you to move your savings into a “safe account” is trying to steal them. Hang up and contact your bank independently.

Verify any offer of breach support before enrolling. JPMorgan says it will contact affected customers where appropriate and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.

Consider a credit freeze as a separate identity-protection measure.

If you’re unsure whether a message is a scam, use Malwarebytes Scam Guard. It’s free and can help you assess the message and decide what to do next.

If your data was involved in a breach, read our guide for more advice: Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know.

What do cybercriminals know about you?

Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online.

articles.title: Linux KVM Flaw CVE-2026-99312 Lets Guest VMs Access Host Memory on AMD Hosts
articles.context: The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2
articles.full_text:
A flaw in KVM, the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, let researchers read about 127 GB of a cloud server's memory from inside a virtual machine of their own on DigitalOcean.

On a shared server, that memory can include other customers' virtual machines. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-99312, affects only hosts with AMD processors and nested virtualization enabled.

Fixed kernels shipped upstream on Tuesday, the day before the research went public. The provider patched its own fleet with a live patch, telling Droplet customers: "No action needed on your part." Operators who run their own KVM hosts on AMD hardware need to update the host kernel or turn nested virtualization off.

Oren Yomtov, a researcher at the security firm Terra Security, found the flaw and reported it through the provider's bug bounty program. The provider confirmed the exploit worked on its own hosts and treated it as critical, and the Linux KVM maintainers, told on October 21, merged a fix on November 2.

In the test on one of its Droplets, the first thing to come back was the host's kernel version banner, followed by about 127 GB of the host's RAM, mapped read-only, the provider said in a disclosure post yesterday.

The write test ran on the researchers' own bare-metal AMD server, with no other customers attached. There, the guest wrote 32 chosen bytes into a live page of the host kernel's memory, and a witness module loaded into that kernel confirmed the change.

Both tests started with root access inside a VM controlled by the researchers. An attacker would need the same position: control of a guest on a vulnerable host, not just network access to it.

Intel-based KVM hosts are not affected, because the vulnerable code exists only in KVM's support for nested virtualization on AMD. Many cloud providers the researchers surveyed were not vulnerable because they had not enabled nested virtualization on AMD.

There are no reports of the flaw being used outside research, according to VirtFusion, a virtualization platform vendor that is tracking the issue for its operators. No exploit code has been published either, and no guidance exists for detecting a past attempt.

Severity ratings disagree. The Linux kernel's CVE team scores the flaw 8.8 out of 10, with high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability, while Red Hat's preliminary security assessment rates it as Moderate at 5.6 and treats the impact as denial-of-service only. The provider treated it as critical for its own shared cloud.

Terra's technical analysis, published on Wednesday, describes a pointer left pointing at freed memory. KVM confines each VM with a table, the nested page table, that translates the VM's memory addresses into the host's real memory, and the processor finds that table through a pointer kept for each virtual CPU.

Some hosts let a VM run a VM of its own, a nested VM. When a reset signal called INIT stops the nested VM, KVM skips restoring the outer VM's pointer, leaving it pointing to a page of memory the kernel has already freed.

Once the kernel reused that freed page, the guest could fill it with entries of its own choosing, and the processor followed them as if they were the real table. The forged entries could name any physical page on the host, which is how about 127 GB of the server's RAM came into reach of a guest that was never given it.

The fix makes KVM reset that memory-management state on every INIT.

The flaw was created by a security fix. A 2022 patch for a different nested-virtualization bug, CVE-2022-3344, switched a reset path back to the outer VM's control block but missed the page-table pointer, the researchers say, and the error then sat in the kernel for just under four years.

In earlier work called PatchSlop, the team found that the fix for another one introduced 3.2% of kernel vulnerabilities.

What to Do

The fix lives in the host kernel. Updating the operating systems inside the VMs changes nothing, and a host keeps running its old kernel until it is rebooted.

Upstream, the fix shipped on Tuesday in stable kernel 7.3.5 and in the long-term kernels 6.18.64 and 6.12.118, the kernel team's CVE announcement shows. The affected code goes back years: it entered the 6.1 kernel in 2022 and was carried into the 5.15.81 and 6.0.11 releases, so older kernel lines and the distribution kernels built on them are in range.

Distribution kernels mostly do not have the fix yet. As of publication, Debian's security tracker lists the kernels in all of its releases as vulnerable, with a fix only in unstable, and Ubuntu's CVE tracker rates the flaw High and lists its kernels as vulnerable with no fixed package released. Red Hat lists the Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 kernels as affected with the fix deferred, and the Enterprise Linux 8 kernel as not affected.

Until a fixed host kernel is installed and the host rebooted, the only available protection is to turn nested virtualization off. That closes this path completely, but VMs can then no longer run VMs of their own, so warn tenants who depend on that before making the change.

Nested virtualization is on by default in the kernel's kvm_amd module, according to VirtFusion's operator guide, so an unpatched host is exposed unless the setting was deliberately changed. To check and change it:

Check the setting with cat /sys/module/kvm_amd/parameters/nested. A value of 1 or Y means nested virtualization is on.

If the host cannot be updated yet, add options kvm_amd nested=0 to the host's module configuration.

Reboot the host. The setting cannot change while VMs are running, and a newly installed kernel does not protect the host until the reboot either. Confirm with uname -r and by reading the nested setting again.

The flaw is the latest in a series of KVM isolation failures disclosed this year, after a 16-year-old flaw in KVM's shadow memory management that affected both Intel and AMD systems, and the PwnEscape flaw in Linux's networking code, which let a guest read host memory in Vercel's live sandboxes in October.

articles.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
articles.context: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument...
articles.full_text: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest. "We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed. "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now." The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026. The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users. The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals. A government spokesperson said: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public. "A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data. "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so. "Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies." Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

articles.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2025-42884 SAP NetWeaver Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic Vulnerability

CVE-2026-76466 Cisco Expressway Series Use of Hard-coded Credentials Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123890 VMWare vCenter Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-129448 Apache Roller Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: The Path to AI Autonomy in the SOC
articles.context: In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents
articles.full_text:
Security leaders are about to hand AI agents a lot more authority. In a recent a16z survey of CISOs at organizations with more than 1,000 employees, 36% said they are comfortable today letting AI agents act autonomously on low-risk security actions. In 12 months from now, 60% expect to be comfortable at that level. Overall, AI SOC was the highest ranking initiative for 2027.

The pressure behind the shift is easy to see. In the same survey, the most common worry was AI-accelerated attacks outpacing the team's ability to respond, selected by 55% of respondents. Analyst time is the scarcest resource in the SOC, and every alert still means pulling evidence from several systems, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether it matters.

The same respondents are cautious at the top end. Only 1% are comfortable with agents acting autonomously on most actions today, and only 7% expect to be a year from now. Most teams want more autonomy, just not all of it.

Discussions today frame autonomy as a single slider that runs from "AI suggests" to "AI acts," and that exact framing is why so many programs stall. Autonomy is a set of decisions made per stage of the workflow and per action, and the teams that get it right treat it as something an agent earns with evidence.

Autonomy is not “all or nothing”, but rather a spectrum

The question "how much do we trust the AI" is too broad to answer. Researchers worked this out decades ago, in a framework later applied widely in aviation and air traffic control, long before anyone was building SOC agents.

In a widely cited 2000 paper, Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens proposed that automation applies to four broad functions. Those are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Each function can sit at a different level of automation, from fully manual to fully automatic, within the same system.

Mapped onto security operations, the four stages look like this.

Evidence collection. Querying the SIEM and EDR, pulling process trees, enriching indicators, gathering identity and cloud context.

Analysis and verdict. Correlating what was collected, reconstructing what happened and deciding whether the alert is a real threat.

Response recommendation. Proposing what should happen next, such as containing a host, resetting credentials or closing the case.

Response execution. Actually changing something in the environment.

This split gives security leaders a cleaner set of choices. A team can automate the first two stages heavily, since that is where analyst hours go and where mistakes are cheapest to catch. The same team can stay conservative on the fourth stage, where a wrong move disrupts the business. As the a16z report itself puts it, gathering logs is different from changing a production system.

Human IN the loop vs. Human ON the loop

Once autonomy is split by stage, teams need a shared way to describe how much of it each stage gets. A useful vocabulary comes from researchers at the University of Washington, who define five levels of agent autonomy by the role the human plays.

Level

Human role

What it means in practice

L1

Operator

The human directs and decides, and the agent carries out instructions

L2

Collaborator

Human and agent plan and execute together

L3

Consultant

The agent leads and checks in for expertise or preferences

L4

Approver

The agent works independently and asks for approval only in risky or predefined cases

L5

Observer

The agent acts on its own while the human monitors and can hit the stop button

The authors make a point every SOC leader should take to heart. Autonomy is a deliberate design choice, separate from how capable the agent is. A highly capable agent can still run at L2 if the stakes call for it.

Read through this lens, the a16z data describes a market moving from roughly L2 today toward L4 for low-risk actions within a year. Gartner offers a complementary distinction between a human in the loop, who approves each action, and a human on the loop, whose oversight is strategic.

Enterprises evaluating AI SOC vendors should make sure that both models can be applied as appropriate, across their entire operations.

How to decide where and how much autonomy to grant an AI SOC

The levels mentioned above tell you what the options are. Deciding where each SOC action belongs takes a rubric, and three questions do most of the work.

Reversibility. If the agent gets this wrong, how quickly and completely can it be undone?

Blast radius. How many users, systems or business processes does the action touch?

Receipts. How strong and verifiable is the evidence behind the decision? An action backed by forensic proof of what was executed deserves more latitude than one backed by an LLM hunch about what looks suspicious.

Scoring real actions against those questions produces a map that most security teams will recognize.

Example action

Reversibility

Blast radius

Suggested starting level

Query SIEM, EDR or identity logs

Nothing to reverse

None

L5, fully autonomous

Enrich indicators and pull process trees

Nothing to reverse

None

L5, fully autonomous

Close a false positive with a full evidence trail

Easy, the case can be reopened

Low

L4, autonomous with sampling review

Open and route a ticket to an owner

Easy

Low

L4, autonomous with sampling review

Block a known malicious hash or domain

Easy

Low to medium

L4, autonomous within defined policy

Isolate a standard employee laptop

Moderate

One user

L3 or L4, approval for sensitive groups

Disable an account or revoke sessions

Moderate

One user, possibly many if a service account

L3, approval required

Isolate a production server or domain controller

Hard

Business-wide

L2, human decides and agent executes

The exact placement will differ by organization, and that is the point. The rubric forces an explicit decision for each action, instead of a single policy that is either too loose for the dangerous actions or too tight for the safe ones.

When human approval becomes a rubber stamp

According to the a16z survey, 52% of CISOs want agents to act only with human approval. It sounds like the safe choice, and in many cases it is. It also hides a failure mode that rarely gets discussed.

Human approval is only as good as the context the reviewer receives. When an approval step arrives without clear evidence or criteria, reviewers start clicking through requests to keep the queue moving, and oversight quietly disappears.

If the AI shapes how every investigation is framed, the human approving the final action is approving a conclusion they never saw being reached.

Only when the reviewer can actually check the AI’s logic and work along with hard, forensic evidence that conclusively points in one direction or another, is the approval actually worth anything.

In practice that means every approval request should show three things.

The evidence the agent collected and where it came from.

The reasoning that connects that evidence to the verdict.

What the agent checked and ruled out along the way.

A useful test if this is working, is time spent. If a reviewer cannot verify a verdict in a minute or two, the approval step is ceremonial and the team is paying for a human-in-the-loop without getting it.

Autonomy you earn, autonomy you lose

The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications gives this approach a name. It extends least privilege into least agency, granting agents only the minimum autonomy needed for safe, bounded tasks and letting that autonomy grow as it is earned.

Earning it requires criteria that are set before the pilot starts. Otherwise autonomy expands on vendor promises and gut feel. A practical set of graduation criteria for moving an action class up one level looks like this.

Measured agreement. Track how often the agent's verdicts match analyst review over a defined period and alert volume, and set the threshold in advance.

Dry runs first. Run new actions in a test mode that executes the logic but mocks every write, so the team sees what the agent would have done before it does anything.

A complete evidence trail. Every decision at the new level must be auditable after the fact, including what the agent looked at and why it concluded what it did.

A rollback path. Define how the action is undone and who owns that before expanding scope.

Autonomy should also move down. A drop in agreement rates, a major change in the environment such as a new EDR or cloud migration, or a single serious miss should trigger a demotion until the criteria are met again. Teams that only ever ratchet upward are building risk they cannot see.

Your SOC agent is an agent too

Every level of autonomy granted to a SOC agent has a second effect. It raises the damage that agent can do if it is wrong, manipulated or compromised.

Security leaders already feel this risk across the enterprise. In the a16z survey, 46% of CISOs listed AI agents acting outside their intended permissions, or compromised agents, among their five biggest worries, and 29% cited prompt injection or data leakage through AI applications. Meanwhile 55% already run MCP servers or other agent-to-application integrations in production, and 34% run autonomous agents with tool access or write permissions.

The lesson for the SOC is that autonomy itself is a risk factor, scored alongside the vulnerability. Treat the AI SOC agent the way you would treat a new privileged identity.

Give it its own identity, never shared credentials.

Scope its permissions to the actions it is approved for at its current level.

Log every tool call, query and action in a form a human can review.

Watch it with the same detections you would apply to a new admin account.

A playbook for the next 12 months

The move from 36% to 60% will happen with or without a plan. Security leaders who want the capacity gains without the incident that sets their AI program back a year can start with five steps.

Inventory every action. List everything your AI SOC agent can do today, from read-only queries to response actions, and place each one on the reversibility, blast radius and receipts rubric.

Automate investigation aggressively. Evidence gathering and analysis consume most analyst hours and carry the least risk. This is where full autonomy pays off first.

Gate disruptive response with real evidence. Keep approval on high-impact actions, and make sure every approval request carries proof a reviewer can verify quickly.

Write graduation and demotion criteria now. Agree on the accuracy thresholds, test periods and rollback paths before the pilot starts, so autonomy expands on data.

Govern the agent like a privileged identity. Scope it, log it and monitor it, because its autonomy is also its blast radius.

Crossing the trust threshold

Every SOC that adopts AI agents will eventually face the same question for each action. Is the agent's work trustworthy enough to act on without a human checking it first?

A helpful way to think about it is a trust threshold. Below it, AI assists analysts, and humans still validate every conclusion. Above it, teams can safely hand off execution and supervise outcomes instead of steps. What moves an action across that line is depth and proof. An agent that can show what actually executed, where it came from and what it did, gives a human something real to verify, and gives the organization a defensible reason to extend its autonomy. Forensic-level investigation, the approach Intezer’s AI SOC is built on, is what moves an action across that line.

That is what earned autonomy means in practice. The agent gets more authority one action class at a time, each step backed by evidence the team can inspect, and each step reversible if the evidence stops holding up.

Note: This article has been written and contributed by Zev Schonberg, PMM at Intezer.

articles.title: Mail Bombing Attacks Fuel IT Helpdesk Impersonation Scams
articles.context: FIRE said that there are some indications that these attacks are likely an AI Agent setup, where the agent is instructed to crawl every webpage available for newsletter...
articles.full_text:
Cybercriminals are conducting large-scale “mail bombing attacks”, followed by IT helpdesk impersonation in order to compromise user accounts.

Fortra Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) are tracking the campaign, which involves inboxes being deliberately flooded with emails.

In an update on the campaign, published by FIRE on November 19, the researchers noted that mail bombing does not require access to a target mailbox. Rather a target’s inbox is flooded with subscriptions after an attacker has submitted a target email address to newsletter, registration and other signup forms across unrelated websites.

This email flood can interrupt activities like customer service and routine correspondence, as well as obscuring account alerts, payment notifications and other messages that may require attention.

FIRE said that there are some indications that these attacks are likely an AI Agent setup, where the agent is instructed to crawl every webpage available for newsletter subscription boxes.

Mailchimp and its transactional service, Mandrill, were the most frequently observed delivery services, followed by Amazon SES and SendGrid.

“In the attacks observed so far by the FIRE team, the average email delivery of a mail bombing attack is at a peak of 10k messages per active campaign, around 1k emails per day,” Fortra said.

FIRE said it has also detected phishing attempts during these mail-bombing waves, which are harder to detect among the wave of otherwise legitimate emails.

The mail bombing campaign has been followed by vishing calls in which contact is made by the threat actor through Teams.

“In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality, attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both,” the researchers explained.

Fortra said that these mail bombing campaigns can be difficult to detect because individual subscription emails can appear entirely normal and may not contain malicious links.

Meanwhile, allowlist exceptions can make containment harder when they cover delivery platforms carrying the flood.

Security Teams Advised to Monitor Email Volumes

Fortra recommended that security teams monitor email volume per recipient against the normal baseline. Investigate bursts involving many unrelated senders, subscription wording and mailing-list headers.

Security teams should also confirm the scope and duration directly with the email delivery provider.

During FIRE’s investigation, Mailchimp advised that senders could request temporary subscription blocking for a specified recipient. Mailchimp also documents a separate automatic control that restricts an address from joining additional audiences for 24 hours after rapid repeated signups.

Fortra did not attribute the campaign to a particular group.

articles.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in
articles.context: Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2
articles.full_text: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2. The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again." Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored." Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID. Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected. An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets. Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

articles.title: Hackers Exploit Critical Cisco Expressway Flaw, Breach Four Devices and Reach Internal Network
articles.context: Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors have been observed exploiting a recently disclosed critical security flaw in Cisco Expressway to breach a Russian organization shortly after the public release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit.

The activity involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8), a vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root.

"This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies," Cisco said in an advisory released late last month. "Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated."

"An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device."

Patches for the flaw were released in the following versions on October 21, 2026 -

Cisco Expressway Series Release X14 and earlier - Migrate to a fixed release

Cisco Expressway Series Release X15.5.3 and earlier - X15.5.20

In a report published Thursday, Russian cybersecurity company F6 said it observed what appears to be the first case of in-the-wild exploitation of the flaw to gain remote command execution on compromised Cisco Expressway X15.5.3 devices with root privileges after a PoC exploit became publicly available.

"The attackers initially compromised two Cisco Expressway internet-facing devices," F6 said. "Through one of them, they gained access to two additional cluster nodes located on the organization's internal network."

Following root access, the attackers are said to have undertaken efforts to move laterally across the network and use custom Python scripts to scan the network, discover accessible SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and access GitLab repositories in order to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive data.

Analysis of the scripts indicates that they were possibly developed with assistance from artificial intelligence (AI) tools, given the presence of comments and descriptions of fixes.

The company has shared the following indicators of compromise (IoCs) associated with the activity -

IP addresses geolocated: 66.179.31[.]32 and 18.130.47[.]116

Presence of "wombat@127.0.0.1" in the Erlang system log (erlang.log) on affected Cisco Expressway devices

Python scripts staged in "/mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py"

The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Users are advised to update to the latest supported version of Cisco Expressway, audit environments for signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, determine the scope of the attack, and block potential lateral movement vectors.

"This incident demonstrates that compromise of a perimeter device can open a path for an attacker to an organization's critical systems," F6 said. "That means protection should therefore include not only timely vulnerability remediation but also properly configured segmentation and infrastructure monitoring."

articles.title: Combatting adversarial distillation
articles.context: Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests
articles.full_text:
Protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

articles.title: Catching Ransomware: Introducing encrypts-files and Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486
articles.context: Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the...
articles.full_text:
When we search for ransomware samples during an investigation or detection test, we usually want to answer a direct question: Did this file actually encrypt user documents when executed?

Modern ransomware families implement file encryption in many different ways. While commodity builders may call standard operating system cryptographic APIs, contemporary Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) payloads written in Rust, Go, C++, or .NET frequently embed statically linked AES, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA, or custom intermittent encryption routines that never touch OS crypto libraries. At the same time, benign installers, browsers, and updaters legitimately use cryptography and write thousands of temporary files during normal execution.

This week, we rolled out three updates across VirusTotal and Google Threat Intelligence to identify malware that encrypts user files:

New encrypts-files Tag Across Windows and macOS Sandboxes: A cipher-agnostic behavioral trait (behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) and file-level search tag (tag:encrypts-files) emitted across CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only when dynamic analysis confirms real encryption of user documents.

Stricter MITRE ATT&CK T1486 Gating in CAPE Sandbox: Previously, generic CAPE file-churn signatures mapped high-volume file deletes, overwrites, or moves directly to T1486. Newly scanned CAPE reports now require verified user-file encryption before emitting those T1486 mappings, cutting CAPE-only daily T1486 hits from 1,039/day (78.5% with 0 AV detections) to 0 on benign files and reducing false positives across platform-wide T1486 volume by 97.6% (from 7,238 to 171 files per day).

Real-Time VirusTotal Livehunt Support: Real-time YARA-X matching on sandbox reports via vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES.

Figure 1: High-level overview of how CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage verify user-document encryption before emitting tag:encrypts-files and gating CAPE T1486.

How Cipher-Agnostic File-Encryption Verification Works

Across CAPE Sandbox (Windows), Zenbox (Windows), and macOS Mirage (Apple Silicon), each sandbox environment contains realistic user documents across standard user profile directories.

During and after detonation, our sandboxes apply three verification gates before emitting encrypts-files (and before CAPE emits generic T1486 mappings):

Content Destruction and Entropy Verification (Cipher-Agnostic): Rather than hooking OS cryptographic APIs, each sandbox inspects modified user-file content on disk using format-aware verification tailored to its platform. Depending on the file type and sandbox, checks evaluate destroyed file structures, elevated entropy, or non-text byte patterns alongside corroborating ransomware behaviors without relying on a single fixed entropy threshold. Because verification evaluates the resulting files on disk, it catches AES, ChaCha20, intermittent encryption, and XOR ciphers alike.

Coordinated Ransomware Extension Renames: Many ransomware families read original user documents, write encrypted copies under a uniform new extension (for example, .k404, .lkd, .INC, .BLWZ, or .heartbreaker), and delete the originals. Our sandboxes correlate reads, writes, moves, and unlinks across user directories to confirm coordinated encryption renames across user documents.

Benign File-Churn Exclusion Guards: Self-extracting archives, software installers, compilers, browser caches, and logs are explicitly excluded when they only generate routine temporary or application files rather than encrypting user documents. Similarly, dropping a README.txt file or calling crypto APIs alone never triggers encrypts-files without corroborated document encryption.

Real-World Ransomware Caught in Action

Across 328,257 newly submitted unique files (405,469 total files including rescans) analyzed in CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage since November 17, tag:encrypts-files matched 55 files and surfaced in-the-wild and validation payloads across Windows executables, Python scripts, DLLs, compressed archives (ZIP and RAR), and a rescanned Apple Silicon macOS binary with zero benign software false positives across all 55 manually reviewed matches (alongside 0 benign false positives across 9,976 random CAPE reports and 400 macOS Mirage runs in pre-rollout backtesting). Below are three examples you can inspect on VirusTotal.

1. Catching Zero- and Low-Detection In-the-Wild Lockers: The .k404 Campaign and lkd.exe

Static signatures often lag behind script-based or freshly compiled lockers. In an active .k404 extortion campaign submitted on November 17-18, Python locker fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354 (system_update.pyw) was flagged by 0 out of 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis, while companion PE binary 3dd45ab8e2f9c1af773a75221d792fb78870764419170e9c9c5941160364c700 (K404T_Fidye.exe) had 10 / 75 detections and separate Windows locker a8c2402ef3ae115300f5428712ccb0b5461f4a2f14b5bfdfbe08d5ad86bd3087 (lkd.exe) had 3 / 75 at the time of analysis.

Figure 2: VirusTotal Behavior report for undetected Python locker system_update.pyw (fb0982bb9f5d5700685dcf4e99ff695f4593fbc3e3d0359d4c2baf23c545f354, 0 / 59 AV on GUI at capture), showing encrypts-files, T1486, and Desktop user files encrypted with the .k404 extension.

When detonated in Zenbox, system_update.pyw runs under pythonw.exe from AppData\Roaming\WindowsSystemUpdate\, self-deletes, and rewrites Desktop user files into .k404 ciphertext, while K404T_Fidye.exe and lkd.exe encrypt user documents in CAPE Sandbox using .k404 and .lkd extensions alongside k404t.txt and read_me_restore.txt ransom notes. In CAPE Sandbox, verified encryption sets both tag:encrypts-files and T1486. Note that Zenbox, macOS Mirage, and third-party sandboxes (such as Dr.Web vxCube or VMRay) keep their own rule-level T1486 mappings, so a file can carry T1486 from another sandbox rule without tag:encrypts-files.

2. Enterprise RaaS & High-Speed Windows Encryptors: INC Ransom and BlackWizardLock

Modern Windows ransomware families optimize encryption speed using asynchronous I/O and multi-threaded directory queues. In sample d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645 (INC Ransom), CAPE Sandbox captures the payload binding user files to Windows I/O Completion Ports (IOCP), rewriting user documents into .INC files, and dropping INC-README.txt across directories.

Figure 3: INC Ransom (d243031985f7fa82a741e5677a227c65b2e2f1b07e0e10f00fe575dcc0eb4645) Behavior report showing T1486 user-file encryption and user documents rewritten with the .INC extension.

Similarly, sample 98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e (BlackWizardLock) executes unpacked payload code from dynamically allocated memory, stages temporary .~BLWZ.tmp files, overwrites user documents with .BLWZ extensions (such as bitaddress.pdf.BLWZ and cover-letter-uidev.docx.BLWZ), and presents a full-screen Russian extortion lock screen that directs victims to @seedware on Telegram and threatens to destroy the Master Boot Record (MBR) after five wrong key attempts.

Figure 4: BlackWizardLock (98110dedcca5803bc211f2d8dd640de79a2ba2a69d1def2f4970fa7799313f3e) Behavior report showing encrypts-files, T1486 impact, and user documents encrypted into .BLWZ files.

3. Native Apple Silicon macOS Ransomware: Heartbreaker (Historical macOS Sample Rescanned in macOS Mirage, 16 / 75 AV at Analysis)

While native macOS ransomware is rare in the wild compared to Windows, re-analyzing historical macOS samples validates Apple Silicon coverage. Sample 6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18 (first submitted in May 2025 and rescanned in macOS Mirage) is a self-signed 64-bit ARM64 Mach-O binary detected by 16 out of 75 antivirus engines at the time of analysis.

Figure 5: Native macOS Heartbreaker ransomware (6bdf42a575d2daee3de2530161cb5b1fef6ca78b4abfa74f329d6b6c72890d18) Behavior report in macOS Mirage showing encrypts-files, T1486, and user files in Downloads encrypted to .heartbreaker.

When detonated on bare-metal Apple Silicon in macOS Mirage, the binary installs a persistent LaunchAgent (/Users/admin/Library/LaunchAgents/com.network.startup.plist), drops /Users/admin/Desktop/README.txt, and encrypts user documents in /Users/admin/Downloads/ into Invoice_INV-2026-0842.pdf.heartbreaker and Vendor_Payment_Schedule.xlsx.heartbreaker. This triggers both ENCRYPTS_FILES and T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact).

Summary of Verified Public Samples

Every sample below is publicly available on VirusTotal and carries verified file-encryption behavioral telemetry across diverse file formats and ransomware families:

Sample SHA-256 (Behavior Link)

Format
