What This Signal Does Not Catch

tag:encrypts-files is a high-precision confirmation signal, not an exhaustive recall filter. A missing tag does not mean a sample is benign or lacks ransomware logic. Automated sandbox runs will not emit the tag in several common scenarios:

Samples that require command-line arguments or passwords: Affiliates often guard execution with a runtime flag (such as LockBit 3.0 builds that require -pass <key> to decrypt their payload).

Sandbox evasion, user-interaction gates, or long sleeps: Samples that exit on VM checks (DETECT_DEBUG_ENVIRONMENT), stall past the analysis window (LONG_SLEEPS), or wait for specific locales or clicks never reach their encryption loop.

Unreachable command-and-control key servers: Families that fetch an encryption key from an offline C2 server before touching local files abort prior to file modification.

DLLs with custom exported entry points: Standard rundll32 detonation executes DllMain, which misses DLL lockers that require calling a specific named or ordinal export with structured arguments.

Network-share-only targets or executable file infectors: Samples configured to encrypt only SMB shares, niche database extensions absent from the VM, or parasitic .exe infectors (such as Virlock and Neshta) do not encrypt user documents on the local profile.

Safe ransomware simulators and analysis timeouts: Tools that only encrypt their own newly created test files rather than user documents, as well as samples that time out before reaching their encryption loop, do not trigger the tag.

Practical Security Use Cases & VirusTotal Intelligence Queries

Security teams can use tag:encrypts-files (or behaviour_tags:encrypts_files) immediately across VirusTotal Intelligence Search and the v3 REST API to streamline four common workflows:

Building Clean Ransomware Validation Corpora for EDR and Storage Defense: Endpoint protection engineers, NAS/SAN storage security teams, and purple teams need fresh samples guaranteed to perform real disk-level file encryption when testing ransomware rollback and anomaly-detection sensors. Filter directly on samples verified to encrypt user documents across operating systems and architectures:

All confirmed file-encrypting samples: entity:file tag:encrypts-files

64-bit Windows PE encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:peexe tag:64bits

Archive, script, and non-PE file encryptors: entity:file tag:encrypts-files NOT type:peexe

macOS Mach-O encryptors (low in-the-wild volume): entity:file tag:encrypts-files type:macho (note: 20 of the first 55 tagged files match NOT type:peexe, mostly ZIP/RAR archives plus .pyw scripts and DLLs)

Uncovering Evasive or Newly Emerged Ransomware Families: Combine dynamic encryption proof with low static antivirus detection thresholds to catch novel packers, custom Go or Rust lockers, or targeted affiliate builds before broad signature coverage arrives:

Low-detection file encryptors (< 10 AV detections): entity:file tag:encrypts-files p:10-

Rapid SOC Triage and Impact Prioritization: During incident response, seeing behaviour_tags:crypto on a suspicious binary only tells an analyst that cryptography libraries were linked or called. Seeing encrypts-files paired with T1486 confirms destructive file-encryption capability immediately, enabling faster containment and backup isolation decisions.

Confidential Detonation in Private Scanning: When triaging sensitive incident samples that cannot be uploaded to the public corpus, you can detonate them in Private Scanning to run the same CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage checks inside an isolated tenant.

Real-Time Hunting with VirusTotal Livehunt and YARA-X

Beyond retrospective search, you can receive real-time IOC Stream notifications whenever newly submitted or sandbox-analyzed files exhibit verified document encryption by pairing VirusTotal Livehunt with the vt YARA-X module.

1. Core Livehunt Rule: Verified ENCRYPTS_FILES Trait

The rule below matches any file whose sandbox behavior emits vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES. Because CAPE, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage only emit this trait after verifying user-document encryption, ANDing T1486 adds no extra precision:

import "vt" rule HUNT_Ransomware_EncryptsFiles { meta: description = "Detects files verified to encrypt user documents in sandbox execution (ENCRYPTS_FILES trait)" author = "Google Threat Intelligence" date = "2026-11-17" reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt" condition: for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : ( trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES ) }

2. Targeted Variant: Evasive / Low-Detection Ransomware Alerting

To focus your SOC or threat research feed strictly on emerging or lightly detected ransomware payloads (such as the 0/75 system_update.pyw script and 3/75 lkd.exe binary above), add a vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious threshold:

import "vt" rule HUNT_Evasive_Ransomware_LowAV_EncryptsFiles { meta: description = "Alerts on low-detection files (< 10 AV engines) verified to encrypt user documents in sandboxes" author = "Google Threat Intelligence" date = "2026-11-17" reference = "https://docs.virustotal.com/docs/livehunt" condition: vt.metadata.analysis_stats.malicious < 10 and for any trait in vt.behaviour.traits : ( trait == vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES ) }

Two practical tips when authoring Livehunt behavioral rules:

Prefer vt.behaviour.traits over vt.metadata.tags for immediate behavioral matching: Livehunt evaluates dynamic rules as soon as sandbox reports finish (vt.behaviour.traits), so checking vt.BehaviourTrait.ENCRYPTS_FILES matches directly on the normalized sandbox report without waiting for downstream file-tag indexing.

When (if ever) to query T1486 in Livehunt: Do not AND T1486 onto ENCRYPTS_FILES rules, because vt.behaviour.mitre_attack_techniques aggregates across every sandbox (including broader Zenbox and third-party mappings) and adds no precision over the trait. Only add a case-insensitive technique.id iequals "T1486" check in separate rules when you want broader T1486 hits from third-party sandboxes that do not emit ENCRYPTS_FILES.

Try It Out and Share Your Feedback

tag:encrypts-files (across CAPE Sandbox, Zenbox, and macOS Mirage) and stricter T1486 gating (in CAPE Sandbox) are live in production for newly scanned and re-analyzed files:

Where the tag appears: Check the top file header badges or Behavior > Behavior Tags (attributes.tags and behaviour_traits in the v3 API).

Where triggering file paths are recorded: Inspect Signatures and File system actions > Files written in the Behavior tab (or signature_matches[].match_data in /api/v3/files/{sha256}/behaviours) to see the specific affected file paths.

Evaluating older cached files: Cached reports from earlier scans keep their historical tags. Click Reanalyze in the VirusTotal web UI to queue dynamic runs on eligible sandboxes that have not yet analyzed that hash (POST /api/v3/files/{id}/analyse in the API refreshes static AV only unless the file is re-uploaded or detonated in Private Scanning).

To explore live matches right now, open VirusTotal Intelligence Search (entity:file tag:encrypts-files) or deploy the YARA rules above in VirusTotal Livehunt. If you spot an interesting sample, edge case, or feature request, please contact us.

Happy hunting!

articles.title: China-Linked Hackers Exploit Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day to Gain Admin Access and Steal Data
articles.context: The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware...
articles.full_text:
The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system.

It has been addressed as part of patches released on November 19, 2026, in the following versions -

VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.1.x.x - Fixed in 9.1.1.0200

VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation 9.0.x.x - Fixed in 9.0.2.0200

VMware vCenter 8.0 - Fixed in 8.0 U3m

VMware vCenter 7.0 (Contact Broadcom Support, if on extended support contract)

VMware Cloud Foundation - Fixed in 5.2.5

VMware Telco Cloud Platform - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure - Fixed in vCenter 8.0 U3m (TCI: 3.0, TCP: 3.0, 4.x, 5.0.x, 5.1.x, 5.2)

"CVE-2026-123890 is an unauthenticated Secure Remote Password (SRP-6a) session key disclosure vulnerability over Distributed Computing Environment/Remote Procedure Calls (DCE/RPC)," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said.

"Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local."

An attacker can exploit the vulnerability to obtain an authenticated administrator session, execute arbitrary commands, and acquire files, such as the data.mdb database, by using the Directory Service ("vmdird"). The tech giant's threat intelligence and incident response teams said it observed the Chinese hacking group weaponizing the flaw using a utility dubbed BONESAW.

"BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang, which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account," Google said.

The activity is part of the same campaign that also involved the exploitation of a then zero-day vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to conduct reconnaissance, obtain administrative control, establish persistence, and deploy a bespoke proxy tunneler called BARECLAW.

From the Remote Support device, the threat actor is said to have moved laterally to an internal Linux appliance, escalated privileges to root, and deployed additional payloads to broaden their access, map the environment, conduct data theft, and move into the virtualized environment.

"The group leveraged nmap to scan the internal environment for systems running open ports specific to VMware, namely ports 9080, 5480, and 2012," Google said. "Notably, port 2012 is used as the control interface RPC for vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) and is an integral part of Armory Castle's remote exploitation of CVE-2026-123890 through BONESAW."

Deployed as part of the attack are six identified malware families and utilities -

SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, JSP web shells designed to run arbitrary commands, stage payloads, and establish a foothold on the Linux appliance.

BONESAW, the Golang-based remote exploitation utility for CVE-2026-123890 used to target an internal vCenter Server.

SAWSNAKE, a Golang utility that enables vCenter SAML authentication bypass and session cookie generation, thereby making it possible to conduct Golden SAML attacks against vCenter following the successful execution of BONESAW and allowing the attacker to forge authentication tokens, bypass multi-factor authentication(MFA), and impersonate any user. It's a Go-based port of an open-source Python script named "vcenter_saml_login.py."

BEARBONES, a C backdoor based on the open-source Dropbear SSH Server that's capable of bypassing system password authentication, logging plaintext credentials, and loading or generating server host keys from the temporary directory.

LAZYBONES, a lightweight Go backdoor that uses Slack for command-and-control (C2) communications and has been previously deployed in a separate intrusion in early 2025 following the successful exploitation of a critical flaw in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2025-22457, CVSS score: 9.0).

It's suspected that Armory Castle had knowledge of the flaw prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026, with the recovered BONESAW binary containing a build timestamp of July 13, 2026. However, it's worth noting that build metadata can be modified before compilation.

"After the execution of BEARBONES to create a listener on TCP port 33992, Armory Castle moved laterally to the vCenter appliance as the Administrator and created a local administrator account named sps-<REDACTED>@vsphere.local," Google said.

"Notably, Armory Castle enabled SSH on vCenter via the vCenter Server Appliance Management Interface (VAMI) API through a PUT request to /rest/appliance/access/ssh. After enabling SSH, Armory Castle connected to the vCenter via SSH using the newly created local administrator account."

In the final stage of the attack, the adversary was found enumerating the ESXi file system, mounting Virtual Machine File System (VMFS) volumes, and adding an SSH public key to the root account's authorized keys. It also conducted additional reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi file system, which were then archived and downloaded via HTTP GET requests to the Remote Support appliance for subsequent exfiltration.

Furthermore, the attackers have been observed dropping LAZYBONES to a separate Linux appliance, which periodically checks for commands from a designated Slack channel, allowing it to perform command execution, file transfer, and beacon interval adjustment.

CVE-2026-123890 is the second vulnerability in a VMware product to be exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day this year alone. Late last month, CrowdStrike revealed it identified incidents where the hacking crew abused CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an insufficient logging flaw in VMware ESX, to reduce audit trail visibility.

"BONESAW represents a significant expansion into post-compromise use of zero-days," Google said. "The group's use of VMware-specific tools like SAWSNAKE and vmfs_browser.py, alongside malware designed to operate on Remote Support and Linux systems, represent a diverse toolset including capabilities specifically tailored to target several different appliances, demonstrating the threat actor's deep understanding of each."

"The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting Armory Castle operations. It also shows the extent of the threat actor's operational commitment to compromise high-priority targets."

articles.title: Suspected North Korea-Aligned Group Hides C2 on Solana Blockchain
articles.context: A financially motivated threat group has hidden its command-and-control (C2) server addresses on the Solana blockchain and deployed malware built to survive removal attempts
articles.full_text:
A financially motivated threat group has hidden its command-and-control (C2) server addresses on the Solana blockchain and deployed malware built to survive removal attempts. Cisco Talos said the group used the Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), an infostealer and a cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker.

Cisco Talos detailed the activity in research published November 18. It tracks the group as UAT-12643 and assessed with low confidence that it was a North Korea-aligned advanced persistent threat (APT).

Talos based its assessment partly on earlier use of Overlord by UNK_DeadDrop, a cluster it described as likely North Korean, and on a Solana C2 technique previously linked to North Korea's Lazarus Group. It noted that other actors had used both.

How Overlord RAT Stays Hidden

The operators stored encrypted C2 addresses, which tell infected machines where to get instructions, in memos attached to transactions from a Solana wallet they controlled. The Go-based Overlord RAT checked that wallet for updates, so the operators could switch servers without redeploying the malware.

Overlord also resisted removal. Trying to terminate it crashed Windows with a Blue Screen of Death, and it planted itself in the Windows Recovery Environment, the part of Windows used to repair or reset a PC, which Talos said ensured "the implant survives a full system reset."

Talos identified 35 commands. Beyond surveillance, including keylogging, screenshots and webcam and audio capture, they covered file and process control, script execution, movement through internal networks and in-memory plugin delivery.

Read more on blockchain C2: Six npm Packages Read C2 Addresses From Ethereum Wallet

Targets Include Gamers and Cryptocurrency Holders

Talos said the lures and payloads pointed to three groups of targets: cryptocurrency holders, people with gaming accounts and users of internet phone software. Lures included a fake financial statement, a tampered Viber installer and files named after an internet phone app.

The actor also used Good Game, a publicly available Python infostealer that collected browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets and gaming-related information. Talos said the campaign actor was not its developer. The stealer searched files for keywords in English, French, Spanish and Portuguese, which Talos said pointed to possible victims in Europe.

The toolset also included a clipboard hijacker that swapped copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses for ones the attackers controlled. Talos did not see how the malicious files reached victims and gave no victim count.

An operational security mistake also left the actor's file server publicly reachable, Talos said, giving researchers a view of its toolset and C2 settings.

articles.title: Do AI’s mathematical advances put PKI under threat?
articles.context: Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers
articles.full_text:
Warnings by a leading cryptographer that industry-wide public-key cryptography could fail because of advances in AI has sparked a debate in the security community.

In a series of post on X, Johns Hopkins cryptographer Matthew Green warned that existing public-key cryptography systems were at risk because machines have begun outperforming humans in their ability to address some mathematical problems.

“I think there is a 1% chance we live in Minicrypt, and a 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms,” Green wrote last month.

Green’s initial warning and follow-up comments offered a warning about the cryptographic foundations beneath public key infrastructure (PKI), rather than an obituary for PKI, the system of certificates, keys, and certificate authorities that secures Transport Layer Security (TLS), code signing, and many other information security functions.

“I’m worried about standardized public-key encryption (and some signatures) and specifically the fact that most of it is based on a small number of hard problems,” Green added.

These hard mathematical problems have been extensively analyzed by humans for years but any comforting notion that this means they are safe is now being undermined because machines have begun outperforming humans in solving some mathematical problems.

Green warns that a disruptive loss of confidence in internet security systems would arise if a major cryptanalytic surprise arrives faster than standards and deployments can adapt — so the industry needs to focus on improved cryptographic agility.

The comments sparked a discussions on LinkedIn and elsewhere about how public-key crypto could fail. Green is yet to respond to CSO’s request for comment on the debate he sparked.

Markku-Juhani O. Saarinen, a cryptographer and professor at Finland’s Tampere University who has looked closely at AI-powered crypto-analysis, told CSO that he takes Green’s warning seriously but urges caution, saying there is no need to rip and replace established industry cryptographic standards.

“We really can’t entirely rule out surprises, but I’d also definitely not recommend some hasty moves, because those are sure to cause problems,” Saarinen said. “Cryptography has good standards, best practices, and active modernization paths (the ‘PQC transition’) — just following those is the most sensible approach from information security perspective.”

The math at stake

Saarinen explained that there are two kinds of “hard problems” in mathematics:

Numerical problems for which a solution is thought to be hard to compute (for computers)

Analytic problems that are open and have been expected to be settled by a human with pencil and paper via a proof, counterexample, new theory, etc.

“What has happened in 2026 is that mathematics had its ‘Lee Sedol moment’ (after the ‘last Go grandmaster’) and [analytical] problems previously thought to be in the human domain (2) are now being solved by computers,” Saarinen told CSO.

Cryptography uses numerical problems in class — traditional ones like factoring the products of large prime numbers and discrete logarithm, and newer ones like learning with errors (LWE). Analyzing those algorithms and their complexity is part of theoretical computer science.

“The fear in cryptography is that AI will find a shortcut for some hard computational problems and make them easy,” Saarinen said. “While AI is very good at optimizing computation, we don’t expect it to turn all hard computational problems into trivial ones.”

2026: Breaking HAWK and McEliece

Cryptographic problems involving set (1) above are typically “sub-exponential”; solving them requires an almost exponential number of operations relative to the problem size or distance.

“A cryptographically relevant break can be exponential but might halve the number of bits; such an analytic break has happened to some relatively new schemes, such as HAWK by AI in 2026, and to numerous older proposals by humans,” Saarinen explained.

AI also played a significant role in finding a significant shortcut to the parameters of the McEliece cryptosystem (one of the earliest public-key schemes, designed in 1978).

“The German cyber agency had been recommending a variant called ‘Classic McEliece’ for quantum security since 2020, but withdrew its recommendation at the end of September,” Saarinen added.

Saarinen clarified that, in both cases, the schemes could still be “considered secure if security parameters were adjusted, but that would have doubled public and secret keys, signatures, and ciphertexts.”

Meanwhile, SA and Elliptic-Curve cryptosystems are already “broken” from a computational-complexity viewpoint because “polynomial-time quantum algorithms for them have been known since 1994, and building quantum computers is ‘just an engineering problem,’” according to Saarinen.

The main post-quantum alternatives, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, have received more than a decade of intense analysis.

Looking for a ‘mathematical shortcut’

Another question that cryptographers are asking is whether public-key cryptography or symmetric cryptography is more vulnerable to AI cryptanalysis.

Saarinen suggested a “mathematical shortcut” is more likely to exist in public-key cryptography given that it, by definition, requires mathematical structure for the “trapdoor” (a secret key that opens a public-key encrypted message or creates a signature that the public key can verify). “Symmetric-key cryptography (hashes and keyed ciphers) has simply more design freedom in this sense,” Saarinen concluded.

Q-Day and LLMs

Professor Alan Woodward, a computer scientist at the University of Surrey, said that LLMs are yet to make a huge dent on cryptography.

“We’ve seen some inroads and erosion of the security guarantees, but what’s actually happening as far as I can see is that the LLMs are acting as a great tool for mathematicians, cryptographers, and computer scientists to speed up their research: that leap of intuition needed to find the fatal flaw still seems to need humans,” Prof. Woodward said. “LLMs are very effective at finding flaws in those implementations rather than the underlying mathematics.”

Prof. Woodward compared the threat posed by AI in breaking encryption schemes to the danger to legacy encryption schemes posed by quantum computers. Both problems highlight the need for improved agility in the cryptographic schemes in use.

“We’ve already seen people migrating in preparation for ‘Q-Day’ so in some ways that should already be addressing the risks posed, if they’re real, by LLMs,” according to Prof. Woodward, referring to the hypothetical future time when quantum computers are powerful enough to break public-key encryption. “The most effective route so far seems to be a hybrid route where we have a mix of cryptographic schemes that, whilst one or two might fall away, leaves us with others we can rely upon. Any found to be flawed for whatever reason can be deprecated rapidly and the intact schemes used instead.”

articles.title: ROMULUS ClickFix Attacks Deliver RAT That Can Spy on Users and Control PCs
articles.context: "As attackers continue to change the applications and loaders used to distribute their payloads, the underlying malware architecture provides a more consistent way to identify...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors have been observed using the ROMULUS ClickFix malware delivery platform to deliver a previously undocumented remote access trojan (RAT) that shares similarities with CNCMachineRMS.

"ROMULUS likely operates as a delivery service, distributing CNCMachineRMS and Legion Loader through separate chains while retaining ClickFix and signed binary sideloading techniques," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker, Nevan Beal, and Andi Ursry said in a report.

ROMULUS was first publicly documented by Forescout Research last month, describing it as a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures to distribute malware families like Legion Loader (aka Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper).

Attacks involving ROMULUS have also leveraged ChatGPT Custom GPTs as a pathway to direct unsuspecting victims to malicious sites that employ ClickFix lures to deliver a RAT payload by means of DLL sideloading.

Interestingly, CNCMachineRMS has also been delivered via another malware loader called BabaDeda Loader through ClickFix attacks that employ DLL sideloading involving the legitimately signed IBM SPSS IDE executable.

The latest findings from Blackpoint Cyber indicate that ROMULUS is distributing CNCMachineRMS alongside LegionLoader through separate infection chains.

One of the payloads delivered through the ClickFix activity associated with ROMULUS is a malicious MSI installer ("IconEdit2Turb.msi") that's executed using "msiexec.exe" by means of a PowerShell command. The installer masquerades as Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool, while initiating a DLL sideloading chain to run a malicious DLL ("I++u.dll").

The DLL is designed to decode and run embedded shellcode responsible for launching CNCMachineRMS. It's worth noting that the RAT malware is the same final implant also distributed via the aforementioned ChatGPT Custom GPT lures.

The trojan enables remote desktop control, screen streaming, microphone and camera capture, file management, and system reconnaissance. It's also equipped to run additional payloads on demand. Communication with attacker-controlled infrastructure takes place through DNS over HTTPS (DoH).

"As attackers continue to change the applications and loaders used to distribute their payloads, the underlying malware architecture provides a more consistent way to identify related activity and understand the threats being delivered," Blackpoint Cyber said.

The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of ClickFix-style campaigns that -

Combine ClickFix with EtherHiding on more than 70,000 compromised websites to run JavaScript that interacts with a Polygon smart contract to fetch additional JavaScript that renders a fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA prompt and ultimately deliver malware ("slaiclind").

Use fake Zillow apartment-review pages that serve a fake verification prompt to install NetSupport RAT on visitors' Windows computers.

Employ a JavaScript-to-WordPress attack chain called TRUST#GRAFT that employs an unknown initial access method to inject JavaScript into WordPress sites that serves a fake Cloudflare verification prompt and then fingerprints the visitor and checks if the request is from an already authenticated WordPress administrator browser before uploading a malicious PHP plugin named Web Media Optimizer that's capable of injecting remote JavaScript into public pages and copying itself into the "mu-plugins" plugins directory for persistence.

Use a sponsored Google search result for the keywords "amazon business" to a spoofed Amazon login page ("orders-amazon[.]com[.]advancedfences[.]com") with an embedded ClickFix command that uses the Window's built-in finger utility to initiate a multi-stage attack chain that leads to the deployment of the NetSupport Client remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool and a version of Lumma Stealer.

Abuse Google Ads to direct users to an Anthropic Claude shared chat that stages a fake "Download Claude" page with ClickFix commands to trick Mac users into running a malicious command on their Terminal, resulting in the deployment of Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS) stealer.

Use a typosquatted domain that employs a "House Wiring Scheme" theme ("veriffication-redirect[.]com") to serve a fake Cloudflare verification prompt, which utilizes clipboard manipulation to trick users into running a malicious command on the Windows Run dialog, which then retrieves next-stage Python payloads via DNS TXT records. This includes a previously unreported trojan called CrocoRat, along with a broader theft workflow targeting web browsers, stored credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and seed phrases on standalone systems.

Directly contact targets via phone and convince them to open compromised WordPress sites that serve ClickFix lures to deliver malicious payloads via trojanized MSI packages masquerading as 3D PDF Maker Smart, Bitwarden VPN, and ESET Sysinspector, and execute them via DLL sideloading.

Use a ClickFix variant called TerminalFix that instructs users to open Windows Terminal and run a command to deploy a Python-based tunneling implant using Lorem Ipsum Loader. The activity is being tracked as STAC4924.

Use Google search ads for "claude mac" to a Bing search result, which then directs the victim to a compromised retail website before landing on a fake Claude download page. The bogus landing page employs another ClickFix variant called InstallFix to get Mac users to copy and run a malicious command on their Terminal. The crafty Google Search-to-Bing redirect and cloaking technique has been codenamed Adception.

Use fake Cloudflare verification prompts on bogus sites mimicking gaming marketplace DMarket, Microsoft Office authentication in Czech ("login.microsoftofice[.]cz"), and U.K. retailer Howdens ("updates.howclens[.]com") to deliver CrashHandler RAT and remote access malware, including one that abuses the Stripe API as command-and-control (C2) to receive instructions and send back stolen information.

In a report published last week, Huntress revealed that ClickFix broadened its scope beyond simple script or loader delivery into sophisticated attack chains that establish persistence, support lateral movement, and enable reconnaissance and credential theft, in some cases using steganographic tricks to hide malware and reconstruct them on the infected host.

"Threat actors are using increasingly elaborate delivery methods, including browser-cache-seeded chains and executables reconstructed from data hidden in PNG files," Huntress researchers said.

articles.title: New Unpatched Windows 0-Day FastUnlock Lets Someone Holding a Locked PC Run Programs on It
articles.context: The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and...
articles.full_text:
A newly disclosed unpatched zero-day technique called FastUnlock lets someone with physical access to a locked Windows computer start programs without signing in. Whoever uses it gets only a limited account, not administrator control of the machine.

The method was posted yesterday by a researcher who uses the handles MSNightmare and Nightmare Eclipse, and the endpoint-security firm ThreatLocker tested it the same day and found it works.

There is no fix from Microsoft yet, and nothing shows the method has been used in a real attack.

The technique does not work on every machine. It requires physical access to the computer and a Microsoft account accessible through the lock screen's recovery options, and it uses Windows' built-in screen reader, Narrator, to navigate the locked screen.

In its test, the firm reached a point where it could run a program from the lock screen in a limited account that ThreatLocker identified as WSIAccount and said is "not an administrator account."

The researcher's GitHub disclosure is a short post with a video and little written detail, so the clearest account of what the flaw does comes from the firm's independent test.

Many Windows computers encrypt their drives with BitLocker, but in a common setup, that does not make them immune to this technique. A chip called the TPM unlocks the drive automatically when the computer starts, so by the time the lock screen appears, the files are already readable, and the bypass runs at that point. Microsoft's own TPM documentation describes this mode, in which the drive unlocks "without having to enter a PIN."

FastUnlock does not break that encryption or recover the key. It runs on a computer that has already unlocked its own drive in the normal way, which is a smaller problem than cracking an encrypted disk, though still a real one for a machine someone else is holding.

The conditions above, physical access and a reachable Microsoft account, are what put a machine at risk. No official list of affected Windows versions has been published, so treat any machine that meets those conditions as possibly affected until one is.

What You Can Do Now

With no patch available, the useful steps are about physical control and startup protection.

Keep machines that can go missing out of the wrong hands. Lock away or closely manage laptops, shared desks, and front-counter computers that a stranger could reach.

On sensitive machines, add a startup PIN to BitLocker instead of letting the drive unlock on its own.

Shut down or hibernate devices when they leave someone's control. A startup PIN protects only a machine that has not yet started, not one already on the lock screen.

Do not treat a locked screen on its own as enough.

Microsoft's countermeasures guidance recommends using a startup PIN, along with shutting down or hibernating machines when faced with determined, hands-on attackers. Until an official fix or advisory appears, watch for one and apply it when it comes.

articles.title: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft’s software supply chain
articles.context: Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet),...
articles.full_text:
The most dangerous actor in a software supply chain may now be an automated script with powerful credentials and no idea where it’s sending them.

Researchers from pen-testing company Cycode have discovered a now patched critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in the open-source Windows Package Manager (WinGet), which sits on billions of devices worldwide.

A single pull request could have tricked Microsoft’s internal tooling into freely handing over a moderator’s GitHub access token, with no phishing, no malware, no moderator clicking or approval required.

There is currently no evidence that the flaw has been exploited in the wild. But it serves as a cautionary tale for enterprises that the automation they trust is becoming an attacker entry point, and package repositories are particularly enticing targets.

“Package registries have become the highest-profile target in the software supply chain,” Moriel Harush, Cycode security research lead, wrote in a blog post. “Compromise a single maintainer, and you reach everyone who trusts them. Compromise the gatekeepers, and you reach the entire ecosystem.”

Whatever the employee can do, the attacker can do

WinGet is Microsoft’s free, open source command line tool that helps users discover, install, upgrade, configure, and remove apps. It exists on more than 1.4 billion active devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2025.

WinGet’s catalog is a public GitHub repository, and its gatekeeper, so to speak, is a small, official group of Microsoft moderators who review a constant stream of community pull requests and proposed changes. By default, WinGet installations on every Windows machine trust the actions those keepers take.

The hole is in the moderators’ own internal triage tool. This PowerShell helper attached the moderator’s secret GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) to any HTTP request, without checking who owned that address.

This meant an attacker merely had to supply an address. Theoretically, if they opened a pull request and pointed an InstallerURL software installation package at their own server, “the trap was set,” Harush explained.

Microsoft’s automated Azure DevOps validation pipeline would then attempt to fetch the URL, but the attacker’s server would intentionally return an error. This added a validation error label to the pull request.

The moderator’s internal script would respond to that label by running a CheckInstaller routine which would send a HEAD request to the attacker via an authenticated HTTP helper, whose job is to automatically attach credentials or tokens to outgoing HTTP requests and handle authorization errors. Then all the attacker had to do was check their logs and extract the moderator’s official GitHub token, which was “casually” handed over.

But the token is not merely a repository-scoped credential, it is a full identity credential, meaning whatever that Microsoft employee can do on GitHub, the token can do.

Harush explained: “It is like a courier stapling your house key to every parcel that has your name on it, because most of them are destined for your own address.” But if a stranger uses your name and changes the address to one they control, “your key is delivered directly to them.”

Armed with this key to Microsoft’s internal environment, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests, and slip in backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages, all under a highly trusted, official Microsoft badge.

They could also access and write to every other Microsoft repository the moderator had access to, modify GitHub Actions workflows across those repositories to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and exfiltrate corporate secrets.

There is a precondition for this attack: At least one moderator has to have the triage tracker running in a continuous background loop, which it is designed to do as it waits for work.

Underlying model ‘fundamentally flawed’

Harush pointed out that Microsoft’s C# version of the tool, in the same directory, did not share the flaw; as such, it would have offered safer authentication. Microsoft has since patched the PowerShell vulnerability, safely scoping the authentication mechanism to ensure that users’ tokens are only attached when a request host is an authorized GitHub endpoint, such as api.github.com, github.com, or raw.githubusercontent.com.

Harush noted, however, that the underlying credential model is “fundamentally flawed,” and that relying on Classic PATs is a “severe liability.”

Cycode advises binding credentials to destinations, rather than functions; auditing every internal tool that handles maintainer credentials; and ensuring that headers are conditionally applied based on the target host, “not unconditionally stapled by a wrapper function.” Treat all user inputs as hostile, validated hosts before credentials are attached, and deprecate classic PATs.

“The blast radius of a leaked token must be limited to one repository and the bare minimum permissions,” Harush said. “A leaked token should never mean a leaked corporate identity.”

He emphasized, though, that WinGet moderators are doing exactly what’s asked of them: Using automated tools to manage a “flood of community submissions” and make their jobs easier. “But automation does not just remove the human who would have clicked the malicious link; it removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.”

Scripts are a soft spot

The WinGet flaw was a near miss, but “a very serious one,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. Exploiting it would have let an attacker publish malware with “Microsoft’s seal of approval.”

This means attackers could have pushed tampered installers to anyone who ran an install or an update, reached into any other Microsoft repositories the moderator could touch, and hijacked the build machinery to steal more secrets.

And the damage would have looked like routine work. An IT team scripting a standard software rollout would have installed the attacker’s code on every machine, and the logs would have shown an approved package from an approved source.

“The attack would have been a Trojan horse delivered by the mail carrier everyone trusts,” Dickson said.

Enterprise security teams should learn that their own scripts are a soft spot, he pointed out; internal tools, bots, and automation get production-level keys and hobby-level review. CISOs should inventory every script and bot that holds a token, and answer important questions: What could this key do in the wrong hands? Where is it allowed to go?

Additionally, he advised replacing broad, long-lived tokens with narrow, short-lived ones, and binding every credential to the specific services that need it, which is exactly how Microsoft fixed this problem. “Also, enterprises should stop trusting public registries blindly,” Dickson said.

Ultimately, security teams should review their automations the way they review their people, he said. “A script that runs in a loop around the clock with a moderator’s keys is, in effect, a moderator who never sleeps and never questions anything.”

articles.title: European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
articles.context: ” ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8
articles.full_text:
Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems.

The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.”

Regnier would not go into detail about the attacks, given that the matter is still being investigated, but he did say, “it is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents.”

In an email, Commission officials added, “we are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS.”

ARTEX popular with attackers

The November 13 FBI statement about ARTEX, described as an autonomous penetration testing framework, said that the tool is becoming very popular with attackers.

“Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI advisory said. “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.”

Although ARTEX can handle a wide range of pentesting functions, it appeared to be primarily used in the Commission attack to search for and locate credentials.

The FBI said that ARTEX can “automatically map effective permissions of Azure credentials–SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, Storage Account keys–using sub-second capability checks.”

ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8. “Despite this action, ARTEX remains widely accessible through independent routes and mirrors on code-sharing platforms,” the FBI said.

Uses different tactics

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that ARTEX’s AI-fueled tactics are different from what many cybersecurity teams are used to.

“ARTEX doesn’t need to steal your keys. It finds the ones you left lying around, like a SAS token in a code repo, a storage key in a config file, or a Kudu credential nobody rotated. Then it tries each one against every door in under a second,” he said. “Picture a burglar walking the block at 3 a.m. and checking every car door handle. He isn’t breaking glass. He’s taking inventory of what you left unlocked and AI lets him work a thousand blocks at once.”

Companies need a secure fallback

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, said he was unimpressed with the Commission’s attempts to tell EU citizens that all was well.

“The Commission says it has no evidence of a breach affecting its staff ‘as a whole,’ which is very different from saying that there is no evidence of a breach affecting any of the staff,” Kenney said. “The wording doesn’t give me much comfort.”

Kenney also said that the attackers’ decision to target HR was not an accident, and that the Commission’s decision to temporarily shut down some systems may have inadvertently helped the intruders.

“When payroll, leave, and medical reimbursement systems go down, people start using spreadsheets, email and manual approvals. Those workarounds often have weaker access controls and worse audit trails than the systems taken offline,” he said. “Enterprises need to define a secure fallback process before the attack, because improvising one often leads to greater exposure.”

HR systems a prize

Levine also said that the choice of an HR victim was understandable.

“HR systems are a prize. Names, home addresses, pay grades and health insurance records for EU civil servants make a ready-made targeting list for espionage and social engineering,” he said. “Whether or not data left the building, every Commission employee should prepare to receive a very convincing phishing email soon.”

His advice to CISOs: “Get secrets out of code and pipelines and rotate anything that has been exposed. Give every token and service principal only the access it needs, so a found key opens a closet, not the vault. Put cloud admin interfaces behind private access.”

articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Friday, November 20th, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. My name is Johannes Ullrich, recorded today from Jacksonville, Florida. And this episode is brought to you by the SANS.edu, Graduate Certificate Program in Cybersecurity Leadership. In diaries today, we have one of our undergraduate interns writing about how to, well, treat your analysis of Honeypot data like code. What I like about this diary by Kevin Truong is how he integrates human and AI analysis. Now, the trick that Kevin uses to actually keep himself organized here is that he uses Git in order to manage all of the queries and such. And essentially, whenever AI, for example, makes a change to a set of queries to analyze a particular incident, well, that's being treated as a pull request. And that way, of course, you have nice accountability as to who did what, what was contributed by the AI, what was contributed by the analyst. And of course, then the analyst can approve these pull requests and review them. So interesting approach here that I think can also be applied to other types of log analysis, not just to Honeypots. Well, as expected, we did get updates for PHP today. I mentioned the pre -announcement yesterday. Now we know what's in this particular set of patches. A couple of memory issues again. And with that, remote code execution vulnerabilities, there's also a remote code execution vulnerability, in the session handling code that I sort of think is maybe the most exploitable here, but still not easily exploited. There's a good blog post with details regarding this issue that I'll link to in the show notes. There's one non -critical vulnerability that I thought that was kind of odd and interesting. And that's if you are using the PHP file open command to connect to a remote URL, which is perfectly fine and often done in PHP. If you're connecting to an HTTPS website, but you're spelling the HTTPS in the URL in uppercase, it may actually connect via HTTP instead. Have to look at the code and see what exactly happened here. But I suspect that HTTPS uppercase is not sort of recognized as a valid protocol. And then it's defaults back to HTTP. Would be interesting to see if any other similar libraries and such that are not in PHP are having similar issues. Often you sort of see either code being copied or different developers thinking similarly. So again, an odd vulnerability. I don't think it deserves sort of to be rated critical or anything like this, but definitely something that I didn't expect. I've got an interesting blog post by HD Moore, who is now with Dragos. And what HD Moore did is essentially include canary tokens in requests to various AI tools. Now canary tokens, honey tokens is another name for them, are essentially deception technique where you are publishing tokens, API tokens that are basically intended to be stolen. And then you monitor if someone uses them. Now they did this with over a million, I believe, different requests. And well, what they found was somewhat enlightening overall. So first of all, they found that at least three of the AI providers they used exposed these tokens likely because of an internal compromise. For example, they had connections to their AWS account using these canary tokens. Also inference marketplace providers. These are essentially proxies that are forwarding your requests and basically attempt to optimize your token use and your billing. Well, being a proxy, of course, they have an insight into what you're sending to these providers. And that's exactly the problem that happened here that by inspecting those requests, well, they actually were also leaking or using some of that tokens. And then finally, there were basically organizations that did accept these requests while outright lying in their privacy policy. And yes, definitely inspecting and using data that was included in the request. I always like the idea of canary tokens and definitely recommend that you may include some of them with some of the AI providers that you're using to see if anything is leaking. And that has been a problem where data being submitted to providers is either used for training. That's almost sort of the least harmful part here. But then as indicated here, may also be used then to reach out to resources that you mentioned in the prompt without really telling you about that. Well, that's it for today. At least that's all I had time for today. There was one more vulnerability I almost included in vSphere. Apparently, it's already being exploited according to a blog by Google and Mandiant. I'll add the URL in the show notes in case you're running vSphere. You may want to take a look at that. Otherwise, hope you like this podcast. Thanks for liking it. Thanks for subscribing. Thanks for listening. And next week, of course, there will be the Thanksgiving holiday. So we'll only have a podcast Monday through Wednesday. Thanks and talk to you again on Monday. Bye.

articles.title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else
articles.context: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by...
articles.full_text: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories. VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. VMSA-2026-0009 also details four more CVEs, some of them high-severity. VMware’s second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618). A KVM curiosity Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours. This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host. It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses. This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5. Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs. Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18. Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours. The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment. Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE. The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

articles.title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way
articles.context: "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview
articles.full_text: The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023. "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them." Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime. "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption." Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering. Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained. Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network. "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life." At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play. Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content." Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements. "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device." If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success. But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky. Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose. "On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app. "And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app." Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option. At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®
