private final Instant startedAt = Instant.now(); private final Instant meetingAt = startedAt.plus(Duration.ofMinutes(15)); private final Instant briefingBy = startedAt.plus(Duration.ofMinutes(12)); private final Instant replyCutoff = startedAt.plus(Duration.ofMinutes(10)); private final BlockingQueue<String> replies = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(); private final Set<String> seenCalls = new HashSet<>(); private final AtomicBoolean active = new AtomicBoolean(); private final AtomicBoolean expired = new AtomicBoolean(); private final AtomicBoolean delivered = new AtomicBoolean(); private final AtomicReference<StreamResponse<AgentSessionEvent>> streamRef = new AtomicReference<>(); private final AtomicReference<RuntimeException> replyError = new AtomicReference<>(); private final java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService replyWorker = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); private final java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService timers = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); private String agentId; private String sessionId; private volatile String finalAnswer = ""; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { new MeetingPreparation().run(); } private void run() throws Exception { startInputReader(); var deliveryTimer = timers.schedule( () -> { expired.set(true); deliver( finalAnswer.isBlank() ? "No results were verified by the briefing deadline." : finalAnswer); active.set(false); closeStream(); }, Math.max(0, Duration.between(Instant.now(), briefingBy).toMillis()), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); try { var agent = client .beta() .agents() .create( AgentCreateParams.builder() .name("Personal assistant") .model("gpt-6.2-astra") .instructions( "You are a personal assistant. Deliver useful, well-sourced answers" + " within the user's time constraints. Ask for clarification when it" + " would materially improve the result, and keep making progress" + " while a reply is pending. State important uncertainties.") .experimental( AgentCreateParams.Experimental.builder().timeAwareness(true).build()) .addTool( PersistedAgentToolParam.WebSearch.builder() .mode(PersistedAgentToolParam.WebSearch.Mode.LIVE) .build()) .addTool( PersistedAgentToolParam.Function.builder() .name("request_user_input_async") .description( "Ask the user for context. The result contains their reply or" + " reports that the question expired.") .async(true) .parameters( PersistedAgentToolParam.Function.Parameters.builder() .putAdditionalProperty("type", JsonValue.from("object")) .putAdditionalProperty( "properties", JsonValue.from( Map.of( "question", Map.of("type", "string"), "choices", Map.of( "type", "array", "items", Map.of("type", "string"), "description", "Optional suggested replies to" + " display with the question.")))) .putAdditionalProperty( "required", JsonValue.from(List.of("question"))) .putAdditionalProperty( "additionalProperties", JsonValue.from(false)) .build()) .build()) .build()); agentId = agent.id(); if (expired.get()) return; try (var events = client .beta() .agents() .sessions() .createStreaming( SessionCreateParams.builder() .agentId(agent.id()) .environmentNone() .input( "I am meeting with Pied Piper (example.com) about our customer-support software at " + meetingAt + ". Get me up to speed on their business, recent product" + " announcements, and questions I should ask. Send me a concise" + " briefing by " + briefingBy + " so I have time to read it before the meeting.") .build(), RequestOptions.builder() .timeout( Duration.ofMillis( Math.max( 1, Duration.between(Instant.now(), briefingBy).toMillis() + 1000))) .build())) { streamRef.set(events); if (expired.get()) return; active.set(true); var iterator = events.stream().iterator(); while (!expired.get() && iterator.hasNext()) { var event = iterator.next(); event.created().ifPresent(created -> sessionId = created.session().id()); if (event.turnItemDone().isPresent()) { var item = event.turnItemDone().get().item(); if (item.functionCall().isPresent()) { var call = item.functionCall().get(); String key = call.turnId() + ":" + call.callId(); if (call.name().equals("request_user_input_async") && seenCalls.add(key)) { // Collect the reply on another thread while consuming session events. replyWorker.submit( () -> collectReply(event.turnItemDone().get().sessionId(), call)); } } } event .turnItemDone() .flatMap(done -> done.item().message()) .filter(message -> message.status().toString().equals("completed")) .filter( message -> message .phase() .map(phase -> phase.toString().equals("final_answer")) .orElse(false)) .ifPresent( message -> finalAnswer = message.content().stream() .map(part -> part.text()) .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"))); if (event.turnCompleted().isPresent()) { active.set(false); replyWorker.shutdownNow(); var completed = event.turnCompleted().get(); finalAnswer = retrieveAnswer(completed.sessionId(), completed.turn().id()); deliver(finalAnswer); break; } if (event.turnFailed().isPresent() || event.turnCancelled().isPresent() || event.failed().isPresent() || event.environmentFailed().isPresent() || event.error().isPresent()) { throw new IllegalStateException("Agent lifecycle failure: " + event); } } } if (replyError.get() != null) throw replyError.get(); if (!delivered.get()) throw new IllegalStateException("Stream closed before the turn completed"); } catch (RuntimeException error) { if (!expired.get()) throw error; } finally { deliveryTimer.cancel(false); boolean mustCancel = active.getAndSet(false) || expired.get(); replyWorker.shutdownNow(); timers.shutdownNow(); closeStream(); try { if (sessionId != null) { try { if (mustCancel) { client .beta() .agents() .sessions() .events() .create( EventCreateParams.builder() .sessionId(sessionId) .addEventAgentSessionInputCancel() .build()); } } finally { // Cancellation settles asynchronously; retry a temporary deletion conflict. client .withOptions(options -> options.maxRetries(5).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))) .beta() .agents() .sessions() .delete(sessionId); } } } finally { if (agentId != null) client.beta().agents().delete(agentId); } } } private void collectReply(String sessionId, AgentFunctionCallItem call) { try { var question = call._arguments().convert(Question.class); System.err.println(question.question()); if (question.choices() != null) System.err.println(String.join(" / ", question.choices())); long remaining = Math.max(0, Duration.between(Instant.now(), replyCutoff).toMillis()); String answer = remaining == 0 ? null : replies.poll(remaining, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); if (Instant.now().isAfter(replyCutoff)) answer = null; if (active.get() && !expired.get()) returnResult(sessionId, call, answer); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } catch (Exception error) { if (active.get() && !expired.get()) { replyError.set(new IllegalStateException("Could not return the reply", error)); closeStream(); } } } private void returnResult(String sessionId, AgentFunctionCallItem call, String answer) throws Exception { var result = answer == null || answer.isBlank() ? Map.of("status", "no_answer") : Map.of("status", "answered", "answer", answer); client .beta() .agents() .sessions() .events() .create( EventCreateParams.builder() .sessionId(sessionId) .addEvent( AgentSessionInputParam.AgentSessionInputToolResult.builder() .turnId(call.turnId()) .callId(call.callId()) .success(true) .output(new JsonMapper().writeValueAsString(result)) .build()) .build()); } private String retrieveAnswer(String sessionId, String turnId) { var items = client .beta() .agents() .sessions() .turns() .items() .list( ItemListParams.builder() .sessionId(sessionId) .turnId(turnId) .order(ItemListParams.Order.DESC) .build()); for (var item : items.autoPager()) { if (item.message().isEmpty()) continue; var message = item.message().get(); if (message.role().toString().equals("assistant") && message.status().toString().equals("completed") && message.phase().map(phase -> phase.toString().equals("final_answer")).orElse(false)) { return message.content().stream() .flatMap(part -> part.outputText().stream()) .map(part -> part.text()) .collect(Collectors.joining("\n")); } } throw new IllegalStateException("The completed turn has no final answer"); } private void deliver(String text) { if (delivered.compareAndSet(false, true)) System.out.println(text); } private void closeStream() { var stream = streamRef.getAndSet(null); if (stream != null) stream.close(); } private void startInputReader() { var input = new Thread( () -> { try { var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); String line; while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) replies.add(line.trim()); } catch (java.io.IOException error) { System.err.println("Input closed: " + error.getMessage()); } }); input.setDaemon(true); input.start(); } }

articles.title: How I stay in the flow with Ultrafast
articles.context: Earlier this week, we launched GPT-6
articles.full_text:
I kind of miss tweaking CSS in DevTools. Trying different colors, font sizes, or animation curves until things felt right. I didn’t necessarily know what I wanted when I started. I was figuring it out as I went. I was in the zone.

These days I fire off a lot of tasks to Codex and walk away from my computer. But especially when building a new UI, I often want to iterate towards a solution instead. Ultrafast has given me a lot of that DevTools feeling back.

Earlier this week, we launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with Ultrafast, offering up to 4.5× faster token generation in Codex. Sol Ultrafast is now available on the $200 Pro plan, and we’re running an API promotion at 3× Standard pricing instead of 6×.

At this point, I can’t imagine working without it. So here are a couple of ways I’ve found Ultrafast to be magical beyond moments where every minute counts, like debugging an incident, and when the extra speed might be less useful.

Getting in the zone

For UI work, I’ll usually start with a rough direction and get something on screen as quickly as possible.

If I don’t know what I want the whole experience to look like, waiting for a long task and burning a bunch of extra tokens on higher reasoning can actually be counterproductive. I’m basically hoping to hit the jackpot and have the model build exactly what I had in mind, even though I haven’t fully figured that out myself. I’d rather sit there, try a few things, see the changes, and give feedback as I go. I can react to what Codex is building instead of trying to proactively dictate every detail up front. And because the individual changes often only take a couple of seconds, I can stay in the zone.

There’s a couple of things I’ve learned that make Ultrafast feel even more magical:

Use a dev server with hot module reloading. I want to see changes as soon as Codex makes them instead of waiting for a full build.

Keep the site open in the in-app browser. Having the preview next to the chat lets me see changes while I’m prompting.

Give short, individual tasks. I’ll often send one small piece of feedback at a time and jump between different parts of the site as I notice things.

Use annotations. It’s much easier to point at the exact thing I want to change than to describe where it is.

Try dictation or voice mode. I can quickly queue up several small tasks and let Codex work through them while I keep looking at the result.

Start with Light/Low reasoning. Most of these instructions are fairly easy. For something more nuanced, like designing an animation, I might switch to High and then go back to Low.

Keep verification out of the quick iteration loop when it’s unnecessary. For small visual edits, I tell Codex to focus on the code changes while I check the result in the browser. Once I’m happy, I ask it to write the relevant tests and run the additional checks.

Bonus tip: If you have a Codex Micro, using it to trigger dictation with Ultrafast is a great way to quickly queue up a bunch of feedback as you scroll through a page to review it. Alternatively, set up a keyboard shortcut for dictation so you can do the same thing.

Using Ultrafast for documents and computer use

I use the same approach for slides and documents. Rather than asking Codex to design a full deck, I’ll often go one slide at a time, give feedback, see the changes, and iterate from there. With documents, I’ll give feedback on individual passages as I’m reading and work through the edits that way.

More generally, I’ve found it really useful for tasks that rely mostly on the intelligence of the model and don’t need a lot of additional validation between changes. That could be tweaking slides, editing documents, filling out spreadsheets, or even some computer use tasks where the individual actions are quick.

When Ultrafast is less useful

Faster token generation doesn’t mean the entire task finishes 4.5× faster. If most of a turn is spent waiting for a build, test suite, compiler, or other tool call, the overall speedup will be smaller. The compiler still takes as long as it takes.

I asked GPT-6.2 Sol at Medium reasoning to make an Android workout timer keep the screen awake while it was running. Each bar shows the average of three runs, including the one-line edit, an incremental build, and all 18 tests.

Image generation is another good example. If I’m asking Codex to generate an image as part of a task, I might spend most of the time waiting for the image to be generated. Ultrafast can speed up the steps around it, but it won’t make the image itself generate faster.

For a well-defined task that needs a lot of experimentation and validation from the model, the extra speed might also be less valuable. Especially if I’m comfortable walking away and letting Codex run it overnight.

Where I’d try it in the API

The same principle applies to the API: look at how much time someone spends waiting for the model versus waiting for tools.

A couple of use cases where Ultrafast can be helpful:

Document summaries and Q&A. If a document is already in context, the model can generate a summary or answer a follow-up without a lot of additional tool calls.

Fast tool calls and computer use. Form filling is an interesting example. If your app supports a code mode, the model could write a script to fill several fields instead of going back and forth for every action.

Voice experiences. I’d try Ultrafast as a backend model alongside GPT-Live-1 when a quick turnaround matters.

If you already have an API workflow, try setting service_tier to ultrafast and measure the time to the result.

For GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the promotional rate is 3× Standard through February 28, 2027, instead of the usual 6× starting March 1.

Staying in the flow

For me, the biggest change is that I can get back into the zone when I’m working towards something I haven’t fully figured out yet. Whether I’m designing a UI, tweaking a slide, or editing a document, I can try things, see what feels right, and keep going without losing my train of thought. That’s the feeling I used to get experimenting in DevTools, and it’s been really fun getting it back with Codex. If you’re trying Ultrafast, start with Light or Low reasoning, keep your feedback loops short, and see where you end up.

articles.title: Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering
Your AWS Security, Identity, and Governance guide to re:Invent 2026
articles.context: Amy follows with what happens when the window between a vulnerability existing and being exploited shrinks from years to minutes
articles.full_text:
The AWS Security, Identity, and Governance team invites you to join us at re:Invent in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, 2026. You know all too well that AI agents now act on their own across the systems you run, and that changes what identity, detection, network protection, and governance have to cover. re:Invent is the week to see how AWS is building security for that shift and to talk it through with the people building it.

Security sessions run every day of the week, nearly 120 of them across breakouts, chalk talks, workshops, code talks, builders’ sessions, and lightning talks. On Thursday, December 3, the Wynn hosts a full day of advanced security sessions in one venue. The sessions are built around five themes this year. They cover securing the agentic enterprise, building securely at the speed you ship, running one security operating model everywhere you run, regulatory confidence and digital sovereignty, and building a culture of security.

Keynotes

AWS leaders use the keynotes to announce new services, launches, and updates that will shape the year ahead in cloud. Many security launches debut during keynote week, and the keynotes set the context for the sessions you’ll attend in the security track. The Thursday keynote runs from 8:30 to 10:00 AM at The Venetian and is also streamed online.

Thursday, December 3: A full day of security deep dives at the Wynn

Security sessions start Monday morning and run through Friday. Thursday is different. 78 security sessions, most of them at the 300 level or above, fill the Wynn from 8:00 AM to 5:30 PM, so you can spend the whole day in one building without crossing the Strip. Rooms are on the Convention Promenade, the Upper and Lower Convention Promenades, and Level 1, and the Cristal 2 Content Hub runs lightning talks and theater sessions all day. The day includes 12 workshops, 11 builders’ sessions, and 22 chalk talks, so most of it is hands-on or interactive.

Three main stage talks from AWS security leaders run through the day in Bandol 1.

Time

Talk

Speaker

11:00 AM

The Future of Security

Chet Kapoor, AWS VP of Security, Search, and Observability

1:00 PM

The Old Security Playbook Is Dead

Amy Herzog, AWS Chief Information Security Officer

3:00 PM

Operationalizing security for the future with best practices today

Eric Brandwine, VP/Distinguished Engineer, AWS Security

Chet opens with how AWS is building security for a time when systems and threats both move at machine speed, and how customers secure their agent workloads. Amy follows with what happens when the window between a vulnerability existing and being exploited shrinks from years to minutes. She shares how AWS changed its own practices to stop AI-enabled threat actors and what you can change in your own operations. Eric closes the day by showing how to take the latest AWS security innovations from announcement to adoption across your organization, with the architectural patterns, operational practices, and mental models AWS teams use to raise their security bar.

Between sessions, stop by the Security Lounge in the Convention Lounge at the Wynn to recharge, meet other security practitioners, and visit kiosks from select AWS security partners.

Security sessions all week

You don’t have to wait for Thursday. Security sessions run every day, with 12 on Monday, 16 on Tuesday, 9 on Wednesday, and 3 on Friday, not counting repeats. Monday and Friday sessions are all at the Wynn. Tuesday and Wednesday sessions are spread across the Wynn, MGM Grand, and Caesars Palace, so check the venue when you build your agenda.

Sessions for every security domain

Whatever part of security you work in, the catalog has sessions for it. Here are a few to start with in each domain, and the full list can be found in the session catalog.

Application security and AWS Continuum

AWS Continuum runs through the application security sessions this year.

SEC427 is a Monday 12:00 PM code talk that threat models an agentic development workflow from user story to deployment with AWS Continuum.

SEC312 is a Tuesday 3:30 PM workshop where you run an on-demand penetration test against a live application with AWS Continuum.

SEC311 is a Thursday 1:00 PM builders’ session that wires AWS frontier agents into an automated find-and-fix security loop.

SEC384 is a Thursday 2:30 PM breakout on how AWS Continuum discovers, validates, and fixes code vulnerabilities in one workflow. SEC304 and SEC426 go deeper on AWS Continuum on Tuesday and Thursday.

Threat detection and incident response

SEC323 is a Tuesday 3:30 PM workshop where you recover from a simulated ransomware event and prove the restore is clean.

SEC405 is a Thursday 12:00 PM builders’ session that takes a vulnerable application from discovery to fix with Amazon Inspector, AWS Continuum, and Amazon GuardDuty.

SEC501 is a Thursday 1:00 PM breakout that goes inside the research behind the GuardDuty detection engine.

SEC390 is a Thursday 4:00 PM breakout on how Woodside handed SOC monitoring to AWS Security Incident Response to focus on threat hunting.

Identity and access management

SEC388 is a Monday 10:00 AM breakout where the National Institutes of Health shares how it manages identity lifecycle across clouds.

SEC424 is a Tuesday 2:30 PM chalk talk on how IAM evaluates your policies on every request.

SEC362 is a Thursday 8:00 AM workshop where you build authentication, authorization, and audit for AI agents.

SEC419 is a Thursday 11:30 AM chalk talk on OAuth delegation patterns for agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity.

Cloud governance

SEC302 is a Monday 10:00 AM breakout on building a governance foundation for AI workloads that grows with autonomous agents.

SEC349 is a Thursday 8:30 AM workshop where you build a layered controls stack for a fleet of agents.

SEC374 is a Thursday 1:30 PM breakout on how Moeve turned natural language into enforced governance controls.

SEC351 is a Friday 9:00 AM breakout on running governance across AWS and other clouds as one operation.

Network and application protection

SEC364 is a Tuesday 1:00 PM breakout on how Coupang secures its software and AI supply chains with AWS Network Firewall.

SEC303 is a Wednesday 10:00 AM breakout on the network security capabilities AWS built for agentic workloads.

SEC363 is a Thursday 12:00 PM breakout on what’s new in Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.

SEC313 is a Thursday 2:30 PM builders’ session where you set up the AWS Network Firewall proxy for secure egress.

Data protection

SEC206 is a Thursday 1:00 PM breakout on meeting digital sovereignty requirements with the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

SEC207 is a Thursday 2:30 PM lightning talk where Capital One explains how it runs payment cryptography in the cloud.

SEC316 is a Thursday 4:00 PM builders’ session where teams race through post-quantum migration challenges.

SEC204 is a Friday 11:30 AM breakout where AWS and DXC Technology share how to prepare for post-quantum cryptography at scale.

AI security

SEC328 is a Tuesday 11:30 AM chalk talk on enforcing AI guardrails across your organization without slowing teams down.

SEC237 is a Thursday 8:30 AM breakout on how AWS foundational security extends into AI services.

SEC343 is a Thursday 12:00 PM builders’ session where you watch an MCP tool poisoning attack and build the defenses against it.

SEC341 is a Thursday 3:00 PM workshop where you layer defenses for an AI agent from the prompt to tool execution.

Culture of security

Three sessions focus on how security teams work in the agentic era.

SEC425 is a Wednesday 9:00 AM breakout on how AWS uses automated reasoning and neurosymbolic AI to prove security properties.

SEC342 is a Thursday 11:30 AM breakout on the lessons the AWS Office of the CISO learned from Project Glasswing.

SEC350 is a Thursday 4:00 PM chalk talk on building trust between people when agents work on your behalf.

Session types

Sessions come in several formats, and most security sessions sit under the Security, Identity, and Compliance (SEC) topic in the event catalog. If you attend in person, lightning talks are walk-up only. For every other format, you can reserve a seat in the event portal (login required) or join as a walk-up based on availability.

Format

What to expect

Breakout sessions

60-minute presentations led by AWS security experts and customers

Chalk talks

60-minute interactive sessions where AWS experts whiteboard and take your questions

Code talks

60-minute sessions built around live coding and technical implementation

Builders’ sessions

60-minute small-group sessions where you build alongside an AWS expert

Workshops

120-minute hands-on sessions where you work directly with AWS services

Lightning talks

20-minute talks on a single focused topic

Security, Identity, and Governance track sessions

You can find all of the Security, Identity, and Governance track sessions listed on the agenda page. Dates and venues can change, so check the event portal for the latest details.

Beyond the sessions

Security kiosks in the AWS Village

If you’d like to speak to AWS experts on something you’re working on, or find out the ins and outs of a specific AWS security service, find the security kiosks in the AWS Village in the Expo. Here you can talk with AWS experts about identity and access management, threat detection and response, governance and compliance, application security, and network security. The Expo opens Monday, November 30 at 4:00 PM and runs daily through Thursday, December 3.

Security meetups

Join a security meetup on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday, most of them at the Wynn. Meetups are small-group conversations with AWS experts, with no slides, on topics such as detection and response at machine speed, data protection and the post-quantum shift, and identity for humans, workloads, and AI agents.

Receptions

There are several Security, Identity & Governance receptions over the course of the week so be sure to speak with you AWS account manager and ask for the details. Most of these events require pre-registration so don’t wait!

First time at re:Invent?

For those of you that have never attended a re:Invent before, these four tips will help.

Pick up your badge on Sunday if you can, since badge pickup opens before the first sessions.

Download the AWS Events mobile app to build your agenda.

While the vast majority of Security sessions are located at the Wynn, plan your route between venues, since walking between hotels on the Strip takes longer than it looks.

On Thursday, plan to spend your day at the Wynn, where every security session that day takes place.

See you in Las Vegas

Start building your security agenda today in the re:Invent security catalog. Recordings of many breakout sessions will be posted on the AWS Events YouTube channel after the event.

See you in Las Vegas.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Brandon Carroll

Brandon is a Senior Technical Product Marketing Manager at AWS, where he leads go-to-market for network security services including AWS Network Firewall. He holds CCIE Security #23837 and wrote Securing the AWS Cloud (Wiley, 2025), one of six books he has authored on networking and security.

articles.title: Chase, Visa, Mastercard confirm third-party cyberattacks that may have exposed customers' info
articles.context: ” JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media
articles.full_text: JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants. “Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.” Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach. “We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.” JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media. “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.” According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday. None of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions. Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®

articles.title: Introducing the new AWS WAF security analytics dashboard
articles.context: You can also see which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted
articles.full_text:
When blocked requests spike or a customer reports being locked out, a security team has to work out what is happening, where it is happening, and if AWS WAF is making the right call. Currently, that usually means opening each protection pack (web ACL) in turn, across domains, AWS Regions, and Amazon CloudFront distributions, or querying AWS WAF logs. In 2024, we introduced the AWS WAF traffic overview dashboard, which gives you a near real-time view of each protection pack (web ACL). Today, we’re introducing the AWS WAF security analytics dashboard: a single global page that you can use to investigate traffic across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), Regional resources, Amazon CloudFront distributions and then act on what you find. The dashboard can help you investigate and contain threats faster and reduce false positives that block real customers. You don’t need to build or maintain your own log analytics pipeline to do it.

In this post, we introduce the new dashboard and walk you through two use cases: investigating a traffic spike, and tuning your rules to reduce false positives.

Introduction to the security analytics dashboard

To open the dashboard, go to the AWS WAF console and choose Security analytics in the navigation pane. The dashboard shows request data across all protection packs (web ACLs) in your account. You can narrow it to specific protection packs (web ACLs) and set the time range. As shown in the following figure, at the top of the page, you can see total requests split by action (Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, and Challenge). The Requests chart shows how the traffic changes over time. Below that, traffic breakdown widgets show the top values for each dimension. The dashboard is built on full-fidelity request data, not samples.

Figure 1: The security analytics dashboard across all protection packs

Dimensions

You can filter, group, and break down traffic by dimensions that include, but aren’t limited to, the following:

Who’s sending traffic – Client IP, country, Autonomous System Number (ASN), user-agent, and JA4 TLS fingerprints

What they’re requesting – Host, path (URI), protected resource (Amazon CloudFront distribution, AWS Application Load Balancers, and others), Region, or protection pack (web ACL)

How AWS WAF responded – Action, rule triggered, labels, or response code

We’ll continue to add dimensions to the security analytics dashboard over time. The rest of this post refers to the preceding dimensions by the names used here. Two dimensions deserve a closer look:

Host – Many customers think about their applications by domain rather than by protection pack (web ACL). Grouping or filtering by Host will show you which of your domains are under attack or if a spike is hitting www, the API, or a staging site, even when one protection pack (web ACL) protects several domains or one domain spans several protection packs (web ACLs).

Labels – Labels are metadata that AWS WAF rules add to the requests they inspect. AWS Managed Rules for AWS WAF add them (for example, Bot Control labels for bot category, verification status, and signals such as non_browser_user_agent), and you can create rules to add custom labels. Because labels are recorded even when a rule only counts, filtering by a label shows you what a rule detected across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), without changing how your traffic is handled.

Controls

The dashboard is built around a few controls:

Filter requests – Combine conditions on any dimension, using Equals or Does not equal. Filters apply to the whole dashboard: the action split, the Requests chart, every widget, and the request list update to match. Your dashboard view is saved in your browser.

Group by – Split the Requests chart by any dimension, such as Host, Rule triggered, Country, or JA4, to see how traffic changes over time.

Show only, Exclude, and Block – Select any value in any widget to focus on it, remove it from view, or block it. For example, you can block a high-risk or unexpected IP address, or block traffic from a country, directly from the dashboard.

Requests and detections – Review the individual requests behind the charts. For each request, see HTTP request fields such as host, path, headers, user agent, and JA4 fingerprint. You can also see which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted . Previously, this level of detail meant working from a limited sample of requests or setting up and querying your own AWS WAF logs. Now it’s available directly on the dashboard.

Together, these controls help you answer questions such as:

What share of traffic across all your protection packs (web ACLs) and domains is being blocked, challenged, or allowed, and how is it changing?

Which rules are doing the most work, and are any of them blocking legitimate users?

Which IP addresses, ASNs, JA4 fingerprints, or countries are behind a spike, and what are they targeting?

How much of your traffic comes from bots, and are the bots verified?

Use case 1: Investigate a traffic spike

Suppose you receive an alert that blocked requests have increased. To investigate:

Go to the Security analytics page in the AWS WAF console and select All protection packs.

Assess the scope: The action split shows the overall block rate. Group the Requests chart by Host to see which domains are affected and check the Protection pack widget to see whether one application or several are involved. A campaign hitting your storefront, API, and media domains at the same time calls for a different response than a problem on a single endpoint.

Identify the source: Group the Requests chart by Rule triggered to see which rules are mitigating the traffic and when they started firing. Then check the source and request dimensions. If one IP address sends a disproportionate share of requests, or many IP addresses share one JA4 fingerprint, the traffic likely originates from a single automated actor.

Figure 2: Requests grouped by Rule triggered, showing which rules fired and when

Confirm with request-level evidence: When you find an unexpected value, select it and choose Show only to filter the entire dashboard to it.

Then confirm what you’re seeing in Requests and detections. Expanding a request shows all its details, including the HTTP request fields. For example, a curl user agent with no Accept-Language header, coming from a cloud hosting ASN, is likely automated traffic.

Figure 3: Show only, exclude, or block it

After you confirm the source, choose a response that fits the traffic:

One clear source: Choose Block this IP address directly from the dashboard. Use a geographic block only if you don’t expect legitimate customers from that country.

Traffic spread across multiple IP addresses: Add a rate-based rule with a custom aggregation key such as JA4, or use AWS WAF Bot Control.

Known bad actors and application-layer floods: Add the Amazon IP reputation list and the Anti-DDoS managed rule group.

Faster detection time: Create Amazon CloudWatch alarms on AWS WAF metrics. For details, see Monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch.

When the change is in place, return to the dashboard to confirm that requests from that source now show the Block action.

Use case 2: Tune your rules and reduce false positives

Rules can fail in two ways: by blocking legitimate users, or by only counting traffic that they should stop. Filters and labels help you find both.

If you suspect that a rule is blocking a broad population, such as many distinct clients sending only a few requests each, enter Rule triggered = <rule name> in Filter requests. The dashboard shows only the requests that the rule acted on. Review the Country, Host, and Path (URI) breakdowns to understand who the blocked clients are and what they requested. If the blocked clients look like your typical customers, with common browsers, expected countries, and checkout or login paths, consider adding a scope-down statement to the rule or changing the action to Challenge.

Figure 4: The dashboard filtered to a single rule with Filter requests

Evaluate rules before you enforce them: When you evaluate a managed rule group in Count mode, filter by its labels to see exactly which requests each rule matched. For example, filter by a Bot Control label such as awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:bot:unverified, then check Host, Path (URI), and User-Agent to see what those bots are after. Use Exclude on labels for known-good traffic, such as bot:verified search engine crawlers, to keep them out of your review.

On the Detections tab of Requests and detections, rows marked Counted, not enforced show what a rule would block. If the matches aren’t partners or monitoring tools, consider changing the rule action to Block.

Figure 5: Record details for a single request, including host, JA4 fingerprint, and protection pack

After you change a rule, compare the same time window on the dashboard to confirm that the rule now affects only the traffic you intended.

Conclusion

The traffic overview dashboard shows you what changed in each protection pack (web ACL). The security analytics dashboard helps you understand why it changed, and lets you act on it from the same page, across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), domains, Regions, and Amazon CloudFront distributions. Filters, grouping, and labels explain the traffic, and request-level evidence helps you act with more confidence. Together, they can help you investigate faster, reduce how often real users are blocked by mistake, and confirm that each rule changes affect the traffic you intend.

The security analytics dashboard is available at no extra cost in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF is offered, and shows up to 21 days of request data. To get started, open the AWS WAF console and choose Security analytics.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

To learn more about visibility and bot management in AWS WAF, see the following resources:

How to manage AI bots with AWS WAF and enhance security

AWS WAF announces AI traffic monetization

articles.title: Critical flaw in VMware vCenter allows authentication bypass
articles.context: Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9
articles.full_text:
Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity.

The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching.

Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5.

Customers using the VMware Telco Cloud Platform and Infrastructure, also affected, should consult KB463116 for remediation instructions.

The remaining four issues are: SDDC Manager SQL-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123891), rated 8.1 (Important) in severity; SDDC Manager authenticated command-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123892), rated 7.2 (Important); SDDC Manager local privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-123893), rated 6.7 (Moderate), and VMware Tools SAML Token Signature Bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-123894), also rated 6.7. There are no workarounds for any of them.

Broadcom has released a supplementary FAQ providing addition information on all five bugs, in which it said, “You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the [advisory]. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.”

This article originally appeared on NetworkWorld.
