articles.title: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
articles.context: On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces...
articles.full_text:
One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day.

The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected.

Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them.

Why Appliances Are the Softer Target

On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled.

Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere.

HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume

HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit.

Defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option.

That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide.

Risk Was the Hardest Call

The clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big issue for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle.

The scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the issue 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs said little about whether a given server was at risk. And PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that one early workaround, turning off session upload progress, was not enough on its own.

We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets.

Defending What Runs on HTTP

I will be teaching SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026, December 14-18 in Washington, D.C., and Live Online. The course starts with how HTTP works, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and covers file upload handling, API security, and AI endpoints across 17 hands-on labs and a Defend the Flag capstone. It is built for the people who defend web applications, whether or not they wrote them.

Register for SEC522 at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026.

Note: This article has been written and contributed by Dr. Johannes Ullrich, Dean of Research at SANS Technology Institute.

articles.title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
articles.context: Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4
articles.full_text: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations. Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time. "What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said. Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday. The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

articles.title: TfL Warns 265,000 Photocard Customers May Have Had Personal Data Exposed
articles.context: Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or...
articles.full_text:
Transport for London (TfL) has been impacted by a cyber incident, which may have exposed the personal data of around 265,000 photocard customers.

On November 16, unauthorized actors sent emails to Oyster Photocard customers from TfL’s system. TfL said these emails were “generated as a result of the compromise.”

The emails asked customers to create an account, despite them already having a photocard account.

In a statement shared with Infosecurity, Shashi Verma, TfL’s director of technology strategy & revenue, said the organization immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated.

"While we acted swiftly, we now believe that around 265,000 photocard customers may have had their account details compromised as part of this incident,” he warned.

Oyster photocards are personalized smartcards which can be used by eligible customers for free or discounted travel across public transport in London.

Customers whose account details were potentially compromised include children with Zip Oyster cards, whose ages range from 5-18. However, Verma said he does not believe the names or date of births of any children with a Zip Oyster card have been compromised.

Other customer accounts that may have been affected are those who have 18+ Student Oyster cards, 18-25 Care Leaver Oyster photocards, 60+ London Oyster photocards, Apprentice Oyster photocards and Veterans Oyster photocard.

TfL’s current assessment is that no passwords, bank or payment card details or customer journey information were accessed in the breach.

Verma added that TfL, which manages most of London’s public transport network, has now contained the incident.

“Due to the speed with which this incident was identified and addressed, we believe that the number of customers who could have been affected was significantly reduced,” he said.

“We are continuing to investigate what has happened but have already contacted affected customers to make them aware of this,” Verma continued.

The body has informed the UK’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), of the incident.

TfL Customers Urged to Change Passwords

While there is currently no evidence that the affected data has been misused, TfL said it will be asking all photocard customers to change their password, security question and answer. It also advises customers to change their password on any other online service using the same information.

Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or text messages impersonating TfL.

“Account holders should be particularly cautious of unexpected communications, avoid clicking suspicious links and always verify messages through TfL's official website or customer service channels,” Akhtar said.

The TfL photocard website remains offline at the time of writing and displays the following message: “We are currently investigating an issue where photocard customers have received emails asking them to create an account, when they already have a Photocard account. We have temporarily taken the TfL Photocard portal down while this is being investigated and apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.”

Current Oyster photocard customers can continue to travel as normal, while any customer who need to renew their photocard or query any journey history can still do so by contacting TfL’s Customer Services.

Verma said TfL hopes to restore the affected website services “as quickly as possible.”

TfL was previously impacted by a cyber-attack in September 2024, resulting in customer data being breached. This included Oyster refund data, encompassing bank account numbers and sort codes for around 5000 customers.

Two individuals, Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, were each sentenced to five years and six months in prison after being convicted of offenses relating to the attack in July 2026, which the judge said was motivated in part by “selfish bravado” rather than purely financial gain.

Image credit: David G40 / Shutterstock.com

articles.title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
articles.context: The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them...
articles.full_text: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related. Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

articles.title: A Fifth of UK Employees Share Passwords with AI
articles.context: It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one...
articles.full_text:
Large numbers of UK employees are sharing sensitive information with unmanaged AI tools and allowing them to take actions on their accounts without considering the security risks, Dashlane has warned.

The credential security specialist polled 1000 UK workers and 250 IT execs as part of a wider survey group of 3800 across the UK, US and France to create its latest report, Misplaced Trust: Inside the Workplace’s New AI Security Blind Spot.

It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one activity without seeking permission first, including accessing emails, company files and customer information.

Read more on AI risks: NCSC Publishes Guidance on Securing Agentic AI Use

Dashlane unearthed a high propensity among UK workers to use shadow AI without thinking about the repercussions for their employer.

It found that:

37% would be willing to lend their login credentials to a new AI tool after one week

15% have granted an AI tool access to a file, system or account they subsequently discovered it should not have accessed, with 45% claiming the access remains active

23% have copied sensitive information into AI that they would not normally share with a colleague, website or other work system

21% have failed to check where information would be stored or sent

Just a quarter (25%) say they always consider security risks when using an AI agent at work

“Our latest data shows an emerging ‘AI Colleague Effect’ where employees are overextending trust to AI systems, sharing credentials and granting access to AI agents, sometimes without fully understanding what those tools can do with the permissions they've been given,” explained Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“That creates significant challenges for security teams trying to detect misuse or investigate incidents.”

Security Leaders Are Over-Confident

Sharing sensitive information with LLMs/agents or allowing agents access to internal corporate systems represent a significant compliance and security risk.

Information may end up on third-party servers which could be compromised, and it may be used to train models and regurgitated in responses to other users. Agents are a possible target for hijacking by threat actors.

In fact, 72% of IT and security executives Dashlane polled said their organization has experienced a security incident involving an AI agent’s credentials or access in the past 12 months.

Yet the vast majority (92%) also claimed they were confident that they know about every AI agent operating within their organization, the report found. That contradicts the claims from a quarter (25%) of employees who said they use AI tools their employer does not know about.

Business demands for adoption are weighing heavily on the minds of security leaders.

More than two-thirds (68%) of UK IT security executives claimed to feel caught between pressure to deploy AI quickly and the need to keep the organization secure.

"The challenge for security leaders is that the pace of change presented by AI and the potential consequences of misuse is unlike any other technology before it,” concluded Frenet.

“The principles that make up the foundation of a good security program for securing human identities – just-in-time provisioning, least privilege, good credential hygiene and authentication – have to be applied to our new AI colleagues as well."

articles.title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
articles.context: "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained
articles.full_text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

In this article

Scattered Spider used phishing texts and SIM swaps to steal $11.6 million in cryptocurrency

Tyler Robert Buchanan’s six-year sentence doesn’t mean the wider group has disappeared

Follow our advice to protect your phone number and accounts from SIM swapping

A US court has sentenced a member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group to six years in prison. Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man, joins four other group members in jail for his part in crimes that netted $11.6 million in proceeds.

Texts, SIM swaps and $11.6 million

Buchanan and his co-conspirators hacked at least a dozen companies in a years-long campaign, according to the Department of Justice. They sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages, also known as smishing, to employees at their target companies. The messages pretended to come from the employer or one of its contractors, such as an IT support provider. They contained links to phishing websites impersonating company websites and designed to steal usernames and passwords. The criminal group used those stolen credentials to access company systems.

The group also used SIM swapping to steal from individuals. In a SIM swap, a criminal tricks a mobile phone carrier into transferring a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. The criminal can then receive calls and text messages intended for the victim, including SMS authentication codes.

SIM swapping allowed Buchanan and his co-conspirators to take over cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing over $11.6 million from victims.

Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and taken into US custody in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He faced a maximum possible sentence of 22 years.

The other four defendants in the US case have also been sentenced. The longest sentence, 10 years, went to 22-year-old Floridian Noah Michael Urban, who pleaded guilty to fraud-related charges.

Joel Martin Evans , aged 27, of North Carolina, is now serving a two-year federal prison sentence for conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both from Texas, each received 45-month sentences for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Does this end the reign of Scattered Spider?

Experts say it’s unlikely, partly because the group is fragmented. Cybersecurity company Group-IB has warned that it contains different subclusters connected by shared tools and techniques. Members sometimes share online chats, too, but the subclusters act separately and rarely include more than five people, the company said.

There is also a significant overlap between Scattered Spider and an online group known as The Com, Group-IB said. The Com has been linked to child sexual abuse material and attacks on companies, including Allianz Life.

Other Scattered Spider members were also sentenced in the UK in July this year. Eighteen-year-old Owen Flowers and 19-year-old Thalha Jubair each received five-and-a-half-year sentences for a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL). The youths live-streamed that attack in August 2024, which stole the personal data of up to 10 million TfL customers.

We also reported last month on the arrest of another person linked to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The name brings together three groups—Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters—that have reportedly worked together on and off since summer 2025.

How to protect your number from SIM swapping

Phishing texts and SIM swaps can put both work systems and personal accounts at risk. These steps can make it harder for someone to take over your number or use it to access your accounts:

Ask your mobile carrier whether it offers an account PIN, port-out lock, or number-transfer protection. These can make it harder for someone to move your number to another SIM.

Where possible, use an authenticator app, passkey, or security key instead of SMS codes. These options aren’t tied to your phone number in the same way.

Never approve a sign-in prompt you didn’t initiate. Attackers may flood you with requests in the hope that you’ll approve one.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

articles.title: Hackers Breach N-able Cloud Server, Disrupting Email Security Management Across 3 Regions
articles.context: N-able on Wednesday disclosed that unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and Spam Experts Hosted Cloud, causing it to disable...
articles.full_text:
N-able on Wednesday disclosed that unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and Spam Experts Hosted Cloud, causing it to disable management interfaces and APIs.

"We have taken steps to mitigate the threat and are continuing to harden our services to reduce the risk of recurrence," N-able said.

"The investigation is ongoing, but at this time we do not have evidence that customer data was compromised, including access to tenants' mailboxes."

The following services remain impacted -

Mail Assure (Americas)

Mail Assure (APAC)

Mail Assure (Europe)

SpamExperts (Americas)

SpamExperts (APAC)

SpamExperts (Europe)

The discovery comes after N-able began an investigation into a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

While it was initially traced to a combination of platform configuration and service dependencies within the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment, it has since been determined that the disruption was actually caused by a security incident.

N-able said it's continuing to work on restoring Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud across all regions, while core mail flow and inbound and outbound mail filtering remain available.

"The management portal (UI), APIs, quarantine, and logging remain offline while our teams work to restore them securely. Access will be restored once validation is complete," it said.

The company also noted that it has directly reached out to Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud partners with "information relevant to their environment and whether action is required or not."

As of November 19, 2026, at 8 a.m. UTC, N-able said the restoration process is still underway, and that it's making steady progress on validating and hardening the management portal and its supporting services.

It's worth noting that the incident is unrelated to the discovery of multiple vulnerabilities impacting N-central referred to as Able2Shell, 4EverAble2Shell, and Agent2Shell.

(This is a developing story. Please check back for more details.)

articles.title: Rakuten Securities Breach Could Impact 15 Million Customers
articles.context: The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its...
articles.full_text:
One of Japan’s leading online brokerages has revealed a major breach of customer account data which could impact nearly 16 million people.

Tokyo-headquartered Rakuten Securities allows retail investors to trade stocks, bonds, foreign exchange and other financial instruments.

The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its systems the day before.

“As a result of our investigation, we confirmed that on Wednesday, November 11 some information managed within our test environment system may have been leaked to an external party,” it said. “We are continuing our investigation into the cause and detailed circumstances of the unauthorized access.”

Read more on Japanese breaches: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs

The securities giant said that branch/customer code, login ID, name, date of birth, address, phone number, email address, employer, withdrawal account details, annual income, asset information, and last login date for around 4.47 million accounts had been compromised.

An even larger group of 11.25 million accounts had just their Rakuten Securities branch/customer code and login IDs taken, it added.

The firm confirmed passwords, PINs and other information have not been taken and there’s no sign of unauthorized access to customer accounts.

Security experts questioned why production data was allowed to be used in a test environment.

“This isn’t some advanced security concept or something that requires sophisticated technology to address. It’s one of the most fundamental rules of protecting sensitive information, and yet we continue to see organizations make these mistakes,” argued Black Hills Information Security owner John Strand.ㅤ

“The proper way to do this is to have separate development, testing, and staging environments, each with clearly defined security controls.”

Rakuten Urges Passkey Adoption

Rakuten Securities warned customers of follow-on phishing attempts, presumably trying to trick individuals into handing over their logins.

It said over 90% of customers currently log in using phishing-resistant passkeys, and urged the remainder to switch to mitigate the risk of account takeover.

Last year, regulator the Financial Services Agency (FSA) warned of a sharp increase in account hijacking at Japanese securities companies, with hackers making illegal trades of over 304 billion yen ($2bn).

It claimed the hackers were attempting to manipulate the market by boosting the value of small-cap stocks that they own, in order to sell them at a bigger profit.

Rakuten Securities’ woes come at the end of a bad year for Japanese companies, which have been hit by a string of data breaches and extortion attacks.

They include Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (8 million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million).

In October, GMO, a virtual desktop company popular with foreign-exchange traders told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by ransomware actors.

articles.title: Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
articles.context: That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms
articles.full_text:
We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work.

For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models.

An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level.

But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach.

The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done.

Most large organizations already know they have significant numbers of vulnerabilities across their technology estates. They have known for years. They have dashboards, reports, inventories, risk ratings and remediation backlogs.

What they frequently lack is the organizational machinery to translate that knowledge into effective, sustained remedial action.

And that is not primarily a technology problem.

The uncomfortable reality behind remediation backlogs

Consider what happens when a large enterprise identifies a critical vulnerability.

The security team assesses its severity and potential impact. It raises a ticket, assigns a priority, identifies an owner and requests remediation.

On paper, the process looks straightforward.

In practice, that is often where the real problems begin.

The infrastructure team may be managing ageing systems with complex dependencies. The development team may have committed to a demanding release schedule. Production operations may be unwilling to accept additional downtime. Business stakeholders may resist disruption to revenue-generating services.

Some systems may have very limited maintenance windows. Others may require extensive regression testing before deploying patches. Legacy applications may depend on components that cannot easily be upgraded.

And ownership itself may be disputed.

Security teams frequently have the responsibility to identify and report vulnerabilities but lack the authority to enforce remediation. Technology teams control the systems but may have competing priorities and insufficient resources.

The result is familiar: escalating tickets, repeated exceptions, missed deadlines, unresolved disputes and growing remediation backlogs.

None of these problems can be solved simply by producing a better vulnerability score.

Prioritization is necessary, but it is not the answer

The industry has increasingly recognized that organizations cannot remediate everything.

That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms.

These capabilities have genuine value: There is an obvious difference between a vulnerability that is actively exploited on an internet-facing critical system and one that exists on an isolated, low-value asset.

But prioritization is only the beginning of a management process. It is not its outcome: A perfectly prioritized remediation backlog remains a backlog.

In many organizations, the difficulty is not deciding which vulnerabilities matter most. It is securing agreement on who will fix them, when the work will take place and who has the authority to resolve conflicts or accept the risk.

These are matters of governance, accountability and business priorities.

The cybersecurity industry remains disproportionately focused on the what, when the real challenge lies in the how and the who.

AI is about to make the problem considerably worse

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics of vulnerability discovery.

AI-assisted tools can analyse code, identify weaknesses and accelerate vulnerability research on a scale and at a speed that would previously have required substantial human effort.

According to Google Threat Intelligence Group, monthly vulnerability disclosures more than doubled between January and August 2026, while observed exploitation also increased significantly. AI is contributing to that acceleration, although changes in disclosure practices also influence the figures.

The consequences for large organizations could be significant.

We are moving towards a world where the identification of vulnerabilities becomes increasingly automated, increasingly inexpensive and potentially continuous.

But what happens when the volume of identified vulnerabilities increases dramatically while the organization’s capacity to remediate them remains essentially unchanged?

The answer is predictable: Larger backlogs. More pressure on technology teams. More exceptions. More disputes over priorities. And potentially greater exposure, despite unprecedented visibility into technical weaknesses.

The Cloud Security Alliance has already highlighted this growing disconnect between accelerated vulnerability discovery and the capacity of organizations to absorb and remediate findings.

AI is industrialising vulnerability discovery while remediation remains trapped in organizational structures designed for another era.

That is the real emerging challenge.

AI cannot negotiate a production maintenance window

Of course, AI can also contribute to remediation.

It can establish proofs of concept, generate and test fixes, propose configuration changes, analyse dependencies and automate certain deployment activities.

These are important developments, and organizations should embrace them where appropriate.

But their practical impact must not be overstated.

AI cannot independently decide that a critical production system should be taken offline during a peak business period. It cannot assume accountability for disrupting customer services or resolve competing priorities between a business unit, an infrastructure team and the security function.

It cannot simply override legacy dependencies, contractual obligations or regulatory constraints.

Even where AI can technically generate a suitable fix, somebody still needs to validate it, approve its deployment, ensure that the fix has not broken something else and verify that remediation has been successful.

Some of those steps can be automated. Others require judgement, authority and organizational coordination.

The more powerful AI becomes, the more visible those remaining management bottlenecks will be.

And this is where the traditional cybersecurity approach is increasingly inadequate.

Vulnerability management needs an operating model, not another dashboard

What large organizations need is not simply better vulnerability management technology.

They need a remediation operating model that establishes clear accountability across security, development, infrastructure, operations and business management.

That model should address several fundamental questions.

Who owns the remediation of vulnerabilities affecting shared platforms or complex applications? Who allocates the necessary resources? Who can authorize emergency changes? Who resolves disagreements when remediation conflicts with business priorities?

How are maintenance windows negotiated and secured? How are persistent exceptions challenged? Who accepts the residual business risk when remediation cannot be completed within the expected timeframe?

And, crucially, who is responsible for ensuring that agreed actions happen?

These responsibilities cannot be left to informal relationships between technical teams or to the persistence of individual security managers.

They need to be embedded in management processes, supported by executive authority and reinforced through meaningful performance measures.

Security should provide risk intelligence, challenge and assurance. Technology teams should own the delivery of remediation within their environments. Business management should participate in decisions where operational disruption or investment trade-offs are unavoidable.

The CISO’s role is to help establish and oversee that machinery, not to become the organization’s chief ticket chaser.

Measuring remediation effectiveness, not just reporting activity

There is also a fundamental problem with how vulnerability management performance is measured.

Too many organizations remain focused on the number of vulnerabilities identified, severity distributions, compliance with remediation deadlines and the volume of outstanding findings.

Those indicators have their place, but they can encourage an administrative approach to vulnerability management: Closing tickets becomes a proxy for reducing risk.

What matters is whether material exposures are being eliminated within acceptable timeframes and whether the organization can demonstrate that remediation has worked.

Management should pay particular attention to recurring remediation failures, ageing high-risk exposures, operational bottlenecks, the effectiveness of exception handling and the time required to implement verified fixes.

The distinction between a vulnerability being reported as resolved and genuinely being remediated is essential.

AI can help generate more accurate and timely evidence. But it cannot substitute for accountability over the results.

Auditability and regulatory obligations add another critical dimension to this challenge.

Regulators increasingly expect organizations not only to identify and assess vulnerabilities, but also to demonstrate that appropriate remedial actions have been taken within reasonable timeframes.

This requires clear ownership, documented decisions, traceable exceptions periodically reviewed and reliable evidence that remediation has been completed.

As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and potentially automates parts of the remediation process, maintaining an auditable chain of accountability becomes even more important.

Ultimately, compliance cannot rest on the ability to identify problems: It needs to rest on the ability to demonstrate that they have been effectively addressed.

The real opportunity for AI is to transform execution

This is where I believe the cybersecurity industry should concentrate its attention.

Rather than simply applying AI to discover more vulnerabilities and refine their prioritization or their treatment, vendors and practitioners should focus on how AI can accelerate the entire remediation lifecycle.

That means understanding dependencies, identifying suitable deployment opportunities, preparing changes, automating testing, coordinating workflows, validating results and providing management with reliable evidence of progress across the whole cycle.

In highly automated environments, AI agents may eventually execute substantial portions of that process under clearly defined controls.

But the objective should not be automation for its own sake: It should be to reduce the friction between identifying a problem and resolving it.

And that requires technology to be designed around a functioning governance model, rather than expecting governance to emerge from the technology.

The technology will change. The management problem will not.

I have argued for years that cybersecurity is fundamentally a leadership and management challenge supported by technology.

Vulnerability management provides perhaps one of the clearest demonstrations of that principle.

The same structural problems that prevented organizations from patching critical systems fifteen years ago remain visible today: fragmented responsibilities, competing priorities, operational constraints, weak governance and insufficient management follow-through.

AI will not make those problems disappear.

On the contrary, by accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the time available to respond, it is exposing them more brutally than ever.

The organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated vulnerability discovery capabilities.

They will be those that have built the governance, accountability and operational discipline required to translate technical intelligence into effective remedial action.

The future of vulnerability management will not be determined by how quickly we can find what is wrong. It will be determined by how effectively organizations can get things fixed.

And that has always been a management problem.

articles.title: Ruby Ships Fixes for 7 Flaws, Including Critical Ruby2Shell, Said to Hit Default Rails Apps Pre-Auth
articles.context: The maintainers say one has proof-of-concept code that corrupts memory under an attacker's control but has not been shown to run code, and the other can only read memory it...
articles.full_text:
Ruby contains seven memory-safety flaws in its regular expression engine and its string case-conversion code. For five of them, its maintainers say, proof-of-concept exploits, or PoCs, have shown that crafted input can run code on the machine.

"We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution," the maintainers said.

The project released fixed versions yesterday: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. Whether an application is at risk depends on whether an attacker can get crafted patterns or strings into the affected code, and the advisories report no attacks so far.

The other two flaws are weaker. The maintainers say one has proof-of-concept code that corrupts memory under an attacker's control but has not been shown to run code, and the other can only read memory it should not or crash the program.

The project set the seven out in a security announcement and a separate advisory for each. The advisories rate three flaws critical, three high, and one moderate, and say which carry the remote-code-execution PoCs. In order of severity:

Critical. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, a one-byte heap overflow when Ruby changes the case of a string in certain single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

Critical. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x, a double free when Ruby compiles a crafted regular expression that uses a character-class intersection (&&). It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

Critical. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w, a heap overflow when the size of a compiled regular expression overflows during compilation. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

High. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a heap overflow when a case change produces a result larger than 4 GiB. It has a remote-code-execution PoC, though the size needed puts it out of reach for most requests. (GitHub advisory)

High. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4, a heap overflow when Ruby turns a crafted compiled regular expression back into text with Regexp#to_s. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

High. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r, an out-of-bounds read during case-insensitive matching. Its PoC shows attacker-controlled memory corruption, and the maintainers say remote code execution is possible but not shown. (GitHub advisory)

Moderate. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h, an out-of-bounds read when Ruby matches a case-insensitive backreference against a crafted subject string. The advisory says it "may disclose memory contents or crash the process." (GitHub advisory)

The project credits Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics and Anthropic with four of the findings, and baba__yaga, aphantom, Hiroya Fujinami and Hiroshi SHIBATA with the other three.

Which Applications Are Exposed

The flaws are in Ruby's own code, so every application on an affected version carries them. Whether an attacker can reach one depends on how the application handles external input.

The regex flaws need an application that builds a regular expression from input an attacker controls and then compiles or runs it. Matching untrusted text against a pattern the developers wrote themselves does not pose the same risk, except in one case below.

The two case-conversion flaws do not involve regular expressions at all. They fire when the application changes the case of a crafted string, so code that runs case conversion over imported or outside text is worth checking.

The one case is the moderate read flaw, which fires when the application matches a crafted subject string against a fixed pattern that uses a case-insensitive backreference. The announcement and advisories do not include the proof-of-concept code.

The fixes are in Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. The affected ranges are:

Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9, fixed in 4.0.10.

Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, fixed in 3.4.13.

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, fixed in 3.3.14.

Ruby 3.2 and earlier, end of life and not fixed.

Those older versions will not get a fix, and the project recommends moving to a supported line. With 3.3.14, the maintainers renamed the Ruby 3.3 phase from security maintenance to legacy maintenance, and support still ends at the end of March 2027.

Because the fixes ship inside Ruby, updating an application's gems or framework does not replace a vulnerable interpreter. The version that matters is the Ruby running on application servers, background workers, and container images, which must be updated and then restarted or rebuilt.

The seven do not have CVE numbers yet. The project says it has requested them, and until they are assigned, the GitHub advisory IDs are the only way to track flaws in scanners and software inventories.

It is the second time in a month that the project has patched its regular expression engine. In the October fixes, released on October 23, it shipped Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to patch compilation bugs GitLab found, which sat behind four critical GitLab flaws.

One of those GitLab flaws drew an attempted attack on Alpine Linux's own GitLab server. CISA later added it to the KEV catalog, its list of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, as actively exploited.

Those are different bugs from this week's seven, and the new advisories do not say that GitLab or any other named product can be attacked through them. What the October case showed is that a regular expression built from user input can become a real way onto a server, not just a theoretical one.

articles.title: Researcher Demonstrates Database RCE Exploits Affecting PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle
articles.context: The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login
articles.full_text:
Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL.

The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login. None has been seen in a real attack.

The work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst. A database account's SQL permissions control which tables and schemas it can access, the researcher argues, not the memory-unsafe C and C++ code the engine runs to read, plan, and execute a query.

Common grants give an account enough room to reach that code. PostgreSQL's default TEMPORARY privilege, or the right to create temporary tables in MySQL and ClickHouse, allows an account to create objects or send input that triggers a memory bug.

Four of the flaws now have vendor CVEs and fixes, but the full attack chains were not reproduced independently, and the research reports no sign that any of them has been used in an attack.

In PostgreSQL, the flaw CVE-2026-116331 allows an account that can create database objects to run code as the operating system user that runs the database.

It was fixed last week in a security advisory, and the CVE record credits the researcher for the report. The researcher's technical analysis shows a plain login role building the objects it needs in its own temporary schema, without touching application data, then turning a type-confusion bug into control of the server.

MySQL has a similar flaw in its query optimizer, CVE-2026-101786, in Server and Cluster versions 26.7.0 to 26.7.1. Oracle's MySQL October advisory rates it as needing high privileges.

The researcher reached code execution on the 26.7.0 image with an account that could only create temporary tables and could not read existing ones, a narrower kind of access than that rating suggests.

Oracle Database is the one case where an attacker needs no account at all, the researcher says. A bug in Oracle Text and a flaw in the GraphQL interface of Oracle REST Data Services, chained against an exposed web endpoint, reach the engine code and run commands before any login.

Oracle patched the Oracle Text bug, CVE-2026-114819, rated 9.9, earlier this week in its November update, and the GraphQL flaw, CVE-2026-91609, in the October update. On their own, the company rates neither as exploitable without a login.

ClickHouse is the fourth target. The researcher reports an integer-overflow write in how it reads a binary row format, reached by a user who sets a single option, format_binary_max_string_size, to zero, and reproduced a shell on version 26.7.5.10.

This one has no CVE and no confirmed fixed version, so operators should check with the vendor for the fix.

Beyond installing the updates, the other move is to review what accounts can do, not only what they can read, and to take away the TEMPORARY privilege and broad temporary-table rights from accounts that do not need them. That step does not close the Oracle path, which starts without any account.

articles.title: CISA Warns of 4 Exploited Flaws Linked to Ransomware, Cryptomining, and LLMjacking Attacks
articles.context: About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code.

CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in REDCap that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An unprotected alternate channel vulnerability in LiteLLM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via bytecode rewriting at the /guardrails/test_custom_code URI.

CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in Synology DSM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via unspecified vectors.

"An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA said about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash."

The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, said it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs.

"To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian said. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for new installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0."

In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are said to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026.

"Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said.

"The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives."

In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting.

Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192.238.253[.]176."

CVE-2026-90436, which affects Axis 1.x versions, remains unpatched as Axis 1 has reached end-of-life (EoL) status. It's recommended to migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively, users can use a build of Axis with the patch from a July 12, 2026, commit applied.

As for CVE-2026-90817, Safe Security said in a report published late last month that it observed an unknown threat abusing the flaw to "stage a transient web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved XMRig disguised as image files, masqueraded the miner as syslog-ng, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key."

The exploitation of CVE-2026-40217 stems from a Google Threat Intelligence Group report this week in which threat actors have leveraged the vulnerability to elevate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials and establish persistence as part of LLMjacking attacks aimed at financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region.

Rounding off the list is CVE-2024-10441, which Synology disclosed earlier this month as being exploited in ransomware attacks targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The attacks have been found to result in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware.

In light of active exploitation, federal agencies have been recommended to apply fixes or necessary mitigations for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, and for the LiteLLM flaw by December 2, 2026.

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Oracle PeopleSoft. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the register method. The issue results from incorrect authorization prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account on any peer.

articles.title: ZDI-26-1038: (0Day) (Pwn2Own) United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP UpdateFirmware Out-Of-Bounds Write Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP UpdateFirmware requests. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in a write past the end of an allocated buffer. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute code in the context of the device.

Additional Details

Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Disclosure Timeline

2026-11-06 - Vulnerability reported to vendor

2026-11-19 - Coordinated public release of advisory

2026-11-19 - Advisory Updated

articles.title: PHP Warns of Critical Security Flaws Affecting All Supported Versions, Fixes Coming November 19
articles.context: The shortcomings have since come under limited active exploitation, targeting publicly-accessible Palo Alto Networks management interfaces and Check Point Security Gateways to...
articles.full_text:
The maintainers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday issued an advisory announcing an upcoming security release that addresses critical flaws.

The release is scheduled for November 19, 2026, between 2 and 2:30 p.m. UTC.

"These releases are part of PHP's regular four-week release cycle and will address security vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions," the maintainers said. "The highest severity is CRITICAL."

However, the project also noted that issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups. It did not disclose any additional specifics.

UPDATE: phpAfterShell Details Emerge — Critical PHP Bug Could Enable RCE

The update is expected to include CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw that succeeds only if the following conditions are met -

An application sets session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, and its code switches the handler to php with ini_set() before calling session_start().

Session upload progress is enabled, which is PHP's default.

As mitigations, users were urged to set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release and restart the PHP worker for the setting to be applied.

The development comes nearly a month after PHP released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively tracked as PHP2Shell that enable unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests.

The shortcomings have since come under limited active exploitation, targeting publicly-accessible Palo Alto Networks management interfaces and Check Point Security Gateways to launch attacks against Active Directory and deliver backdoors.

In a report published on October 30, 2026, Hunt.io said it identified 616 PHP2Shell-related files, spanning shared exploit kits, cloned proof-of-concepts (PoCs), custom heap exploits, scanners, and post-exploitation tooling, across multiple hosts, even as participants in underground forums have sought exploits, discussed prerequisites, and whether circulating PoCs worked.

"Exploit developers are unlikely to create a single universal exploit that works reliably across all affected PHP deployments," CrowdStrike said.

Last month, PHP also released patches to address a critical flaw in Brotli (CVE-2026-111497 aka Node2Shell or Broccoli2Shell), an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the decoder library that could result in arbitrary code execution.

Users are advised to apply the updates as soon as they become available.

Policy & Intelligence

Tom Uren and Amberleigh Jack talk about the Trump administration’s AI task force asking for US federal regulatory agencies to go easy on organisations that fall victim to AI-powered cyber attacks. This makes sense, at least in the short term. But we’d like to see more expansive forward-looking policy that encourages experimentation with AI for defensive purposes.

They also discuss updated regulations on US AI chip exports. They aim to make it harder for China’s AI firms to get access to advanced chips by smuggling or by simply renting access to them in Southeast Asian data centres. France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack

Interesting:

U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “”ow confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected.

The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages.

articles.full_text: Hello and welcome to the Thursday, November 19th, 2026 edition of the SANS Internet Storm Center's Stormcast. I expanded a little bit on the remarks I made at the end of yesterday's podcast and explained why we aren't going to yellow again, even though vulnerabilities like Java4Shell or NGINX2Shell, which we'll talk about next, are certainly sort of the same caliber as the PHP2Shell vulnerability a month ago. But it's really just about the new normal and higher Infocon is supposed to indicate if something that's not normal that requires additional attention is happening. And well, that's as far as the current state of the Internet and security goes, not the case right now. Well, so let's talk about NGINX. It's actually NGINX2ROOT, not to shell, as I mentioned earlier. The reason they call it NGINX2ROOT is that Wiz in their write-up actually demonstrated how you can take this all the way even with address space layout randomization by then also in the end leveraging kernel privilege escalation vulnerability all the way to obtain root access on the system via NGINX. It does not require any specific configuration for NGINX, but it does require quite a bit of traffic, about 256 gigabytes is sort of what's being reported from some of the proof-of-concept exploits that have been released. And yes, Rapid7 has released a proof-of-concept. As many of these memory management vulnerabilities, exploitation is a little bit iffy, so it's not sort of a super reliable exploit even though address space layout randomization can be bypassed using these vulnerabilities. Total of five vulnerabilities being patched here. Not all of them affect the default configuration. Some affect things like proxies and the like set up with NGINX. Now there are two organizations credited with discovering the vulnerability, Wiz and Xint. The real discovery here is modern AI models and that's what we have these days that we often have these multiple organizations finding these vulnerabilities at the same time, which of course means there may be other organizations that didn't report it to a vendor that may also have found these vulnerabilities and have working exploits. The working Rapid7 proof-of-concept exploit only works against NGINX running in containers. So again, a little bit more constrained environment here where some of these exploits tend to work better, tend to be more reliable than sort of your average NGINX install if there is one like that. Well, a quick answer: patch. And I don't like to recommend it, but maybe turn off HTTP/2. I'll leave that up to you. That's something that researchers really have sort of focused in on lately. We also had some Apache vulnerabilities with HTTP/2 and it is a complex protocol. So in particular from a memory management's point of view, there are probably a couple of undiscovered vulnerabilities out there. And then Wiz is also reporting that Microsoft's Agent Framework was compromised on PyPI. This apparently happened yesterday and the root cause, according to Wiz, was a compromised deployment key that was leaked. Now, interestingly, initially the publication of the malicious version actually failed because it came from the wrong IP address. But after using a Microsoft IP address, they were able to publish the malicious version of this Agent Framework.
