articles.full_text:
[This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Introduction When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat.

While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks:

An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [1]

A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [2]

A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [3].

Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them.

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.

Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].

AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with <sensor-ip>, and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].

The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.

A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.

A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.

Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.

Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.

Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings.

References

[1] Honeypot Attack Summary: SSH Brute Force from 77.239.124.204. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-18-ssh-brute-force-mysql-default-creds [2] Honeypot Attack Summary: Telegram Session and SMS Modem Reconnaissance Bot. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-19-telegram-sms-recon-bot [3] Honeypot Attack Summary: PHP Vulnerability Hunt, RedTail and a PHP2Shell-Pattern Request. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-03-php-vulnerability-hunt [4] kevtruo/security repository (README, SECURITY.md, pull request template,homelab/change-control.md). https://github.com/kevtruo/security [5] GitHub Docs, "About rulesets." https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets [6] GitHub Docs, "About push protection." https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection [7] gitleaks. https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks [8] Claude Code GitHub Actions documentation. https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-action [9] https://www.sans.edu/cyber-security-programs/bachelors-degree/

You join a video call, and your contact and a few colleagues are already there, waiting patiently. But they can’t hear you, and a pop-up says you need to install an update to fix your microphone. What could possibly go wrong?

Meanwhile, we explain how changing just a handful of numbers can turn an AI model into a sleeper agent, waiting for the right moment to strike.

Plus, Andrius Buinovskis of NordLayer explains how companies can see which AI tools their staff are really using, and stop sensitive data leaking out, without banning AI altogether.

All this and more in episode 493 of the “Smashing Security” podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Ray Redacted.

And if there is some sensitive data, take some action — whether to block, whether to redact, whether to notify. And then promote tools which are already tested by the security team.

GRAHAM CLULEY

Well, listeners, if you'd like to find out more about NordLayer AI Scout, all you have to do is head over to smashingsecurity.com/nordlayer. That's smashingsecurity.com/nordlayer. And all that remains for me to do is to thank you very much, Andrius, for joining us today for this conversation. Thank you.

Thank you so much.

The best way to find me at any given time is to go to rayredacted.com, but please don't send me a video request with a stolen face. Okay, please don't do that.

Also, of course, big thanks to Joe for helping with the ads and Amanda, who edited like a demon to make me sound intelligent and knowledgeable and edit out all my screams of pain as my sciatica burns away at my upper thigh. articles.title: Prompting GPT-Live for languages and regional accents
articles.context: Start with the right voice First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices
articles.full_text:
Even if a voice agent speaks Spanish, it can still sound off for the audience you’re building for. It might use an accent from a different region, choose wording that feels too formal, or read a price in a way a local speaker wouldn’t expect.

While the default options for GPT-Live can go a long way, there are additional considerations when building voice applications for audiences across languages and regions. Let’s look at voice selection and session instructions to get better results, using regional varieties such as Indian English, Spanish from Spain, and Emirati Arabic.

Start with the right voice

First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices. Some may already have a language or regional influence close to what you need: for example, Bossa and Tempo have a Brazilian Portuguese influence, while Nira is a Hindi voice. Test them with your own conversations before designing something new, as the built-in voices have high naturalness out of the box.

Find a built-in voice Additional GPT-Live voices by language, regional influence, and presentation

Language / regional influence

Feminine

Masculine

English British

—

English Irish

Gleam (natural source)

Meridian (natural source)

English Filipino

—

Beacon (generated source)

English Southern U.S.

Delta (generated source)

Cinder (generated source)

Portuguese Brazilian

Bossa (natural source)

Tempo (natural source)

German

Nuri (natural source) Juni (natural source)

Flitz (natural source)

French

Brise (natural source)

Sillage (natural source)

Hindi

Nira (natural source)

—

Japanese

Harema (natural source)

Shida (natural source)

Korean

Noeul (natural source)

—

Natural source Generated source

Use lowercase API names when selecting a built-in voice (for example, nira). The voice options guide has the complete current catalog.

If you need a more specific regional sound, you can use prompt-to-voice to generate a synthetic voice from a text description. Describe the region as precisely as you can, along with the pitch, pace, and vocal character you want. When generating a voice, you can use the script_hint field to add representative speech in the target language, and for a bilingual voice, include both languages in the sample text and describe the desired sound in each. Use original adult voices, and don’t impersonate real people. See the responsible-use guidance.

Eligible customers can also create a custom voice from a recording of a consenting speaker. Check the supported models and accents before choosing a recording-based voice. Before uploading, obtain the speaker’s express consent and secure the rights needed to use the recordings and the resulting voice in your application. The consent recording and reference sample must come from the same speaker. For any generated voice, make clear to listeners that they are hearing AI-generated speech.

Voice creation is ineligible for Zero Data Retention. See the data controls guide for the settings that apply to GPT-Live sessions.

Example: Hindi-influenced English with Nira

For an English-speaking agent serving users in India, set session.audio.output.voice to "nira" when creating the session, then add this prompt to the session instructions:

You are in a natural, clean English voice conversation. Speak fluent English in your natural Hindi-influenced Indian English accent. Keep that familiar rhythm throughout.

Example: Spanish from central and northern Spain

Suppose you’re building a shopping assistant for customers in Spain. Rather than asking for a generic Spanish accent, open the voice Playground and try this description in its prompt-to-voice workflow:

An original adult feminine voice, clear and lightly bright, with a medium pitch and gentle warmth. Speak Spanish with a natural standard Peninsular Castilian accent of central/northern Spain, with native Spanish vowels, consonants, stress, and sentence melody. Naturally distinguish s from z and c before e or i, without exaggeration. Use a moderately lively conversational pace, natural pauses, and varied intonation.

Pair it with a Spanish script_hint that gives the voice some ordinary connected speech to work with:

Hola, ¿qué tal? Estoy aquí para ayudarte. Podemos revisar las opciones con calma y elegir la que mejor encaje contigo. ¿Prefieres empezar por los colores o por las tallas? Esta chaqueta azul combina bien con unos zapatos cómodos. Acércate a la ventana para ver el color con luz natural.

This targets a particular variety of Spanish; the distinction described in the prompt isn’t universal across Spain or the Spanish-speaking world. With this prompt, you can generate a few candidates, keep the saved voice you prefer, and test it on a fresh sentence that wasn’t in the creation script until you’re satisfied.

Example: Emirati Arabic from Dubai

Arabic is another case where naming the language alone leaves a lot unspecified. For a conversational Dubai voice, an Arabic voice-design description might be:

صوت رجالي خيالي أصلي لرجل بالغ، بلهجة أهل دبي الإماراتية الحضرية المعاصرة. نطق الحروف وحركة الكلام وإيقاعه محليّان ومتناسقان، وتبقى الكلمات واضحة داخل الكلام اليومي المتصل. طبقة متوسطة تميل للانخفاض، ورنين دافي وصافي. يتكلم على مهله، والجملة تمشي كفكرة وحدة بنبر متنوع حسب المعنى.

The description asks for an original adult masculine voice with a contemporary urban Dubai accent, warm resonance, a slightly lower pitch, and connected, relaxed speech. Use a conversational Arabic script_hint as well:

هيه، شفت رسالتك. أنا هني صوب الحديقة، لا، أقصد صوب المواقف عند الباب الثاني. زين؟ المكان أهدى من اللي كنا فيه أمس. خذ راحتك، أنا توني واصل وما عندي شي مستعيل عليه. تبانا نتمشى شوي ولا نقعد؟ عادي، اللي يريحك.

In general, keep the voice design focused on sound. Managing details like whether the agent should answer an Egyptian caller in Emirati Arabic, switch into English, or confirm an order belongs in the session instructions, which we’ll cover later on.

Test the voice on what your application will actually say

But having a solid voice is only the starting point. Once you have a voice, you can build a small listening set with fresh sentences, realistic conversations, and the words or values your application handles most often to stress-test your voice.

A few edge cases are particularly useful to test:

Pronunciation in context: Include names, place names, product names, and specialized vocabulary. For Japanese, for example, give the agent a reading such as 承る（うけたまわる） and test it in a full support sentence. Or if your agent is pronouncing Lakshmi with a “my” ending instead of the intended “mee,” you can include guidance in the session instructions: लक्ष्मी — अंत में ‘क्ष्मी’, ‘क्ष्माई’ नहीं. For tonal languages, listen to important words in several sentence contexts.

Regional number conventions: The Indian system of numeration uses lakh and crore. One lakh is 1,00,000 (100,000), and one crore is 1,00,00,000 (10,000,000). For an English-speaking agent serving India, test whether ₹1,25,000 is spoken as “one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees” when that’s the intended convention.

Identifiers and corrections: Have a caller spell a fictional booking code, pause, and correct one character. Check that the agent waits for the correction and reads back the final code accurately. Test email addresses and other alphanumeric inputs your product accepts.

Mixed-language speech: Try an Arabic sentence containing an English product name and a price, then switch languages for the next turn. Check the spoken amount, currency, and product name separately from the accent.

For dates, amounts, and identifiers, validate what your application actually sends to the backend as well as what the caller hears. In many regions, 04/05 could mean two different dates, so it may be worth asking for clarification and reading the month back by name.

Prompt the agent for the conversation

Once you’ve chosen a voice, select it when creating the GPT-Live session. For a saved generated voice, set session.audio.output.voice.id to the returned voice ID. Put the agent’s role, language policy, delivery, and conversation behavior in instructions, and reinforce the original voice description there.

For a single-language application, write the instructions and examples in the language you want the agent to speak. Here’s a starting point for the Spanish shopping assistant:

Eres un asistente de compras. Habla en español de España, con acento castellano del centro y norte de la península, un ritmo conversacional y una entonación natural. Usa un tono cercano y respetuoso, sin sonar como un anuncio. Responde en español salvo que el cliente pida cambiar de idioma. Haz una pregunta cada vez. Si un nombre o una talla no están claros, pide que los repita. No confirmes precios, disponibilidad ni cambios en un pedido hasta que el sistema los haya verificado.

For a multilingual application, decide what should trigger a language switch and whether the underlying regional speaking style should remain fixed. Those are separate choices. For an Emirati Arabic and English assistant, first extend the earlier voice description with English delivery guidance, such as “In English, speak naturally with a light Emirati influence while keeping the same warmth and lower pitch.” Include representative English speech alongside the Arabic in script_hint, such as “I can check the available sizes for you,” before generating the bilingual voice. Then use a session policy like this:

Answer in the language of the caller's latest clear utterance. Switch between Arabic and English when the caller clearly switches. A short “OK,” number, name, or English product name inside an Arabic sentence does not by itself change the conversation language. When speaking Arabic, use conversational urban Emirati Arabic from Dubai, even when the caller speaks another Arabic variety. Prefer natural local wording where appropriate: شو for “what,” الحين for “now,” وين for “where,” and مب for negation. Keep the dialect coherent without exaggeration. In English, keep the same speaker identity. Use these as phrasing examples, not fixed answers: - Clarification: «تقصد العلبة الصغيرة ولا الكبيرة؟ وكم وحدة تبا؟» - Unclear name: «الاسم مب واضح عندي، ممكن تعيده أو تتهجّاه لي؟» Say amounts in the current conversation language and preserve their exact value and currency. Only confirm a lookup, price, or completed action when the backend supports that statement.

This example deliberately keeps the assistant’s Arabic dialect fixed while allowing English language switches. If your product should accommodate a caller’s requested dialect instead, write and test that policy explicitly. While voice descriptions and session prompts can steer an accent, they don’t guarantee that every reply will retain it, so test switches in both directions, including after a session reconnects.

Give examples of the register you want

Language and accent also leave the level of formality open. In Hindi, a courteous support agent might use आप and respectful verb forms. You can make that preference concrete in the session prompt:

ग्राहक से "आप" कहकर बात करें। सम्मानजनक भाषा और क्रिया रूपों का उपयोग करें। "हाँ, बताओ" की जगह "जी, बताइए" कहें। "तुम कैसे हो?" की जगह "आप कैसे हैं?" कहें।

The examples distinguish a casual “yes, tell me” from a more courteous equivalent. That gives the model a clearer target than simply asking it to sound professional. Use phrases a local support representative would actually say, and test them in context rather than translating an English script word for word.

For more on pronunciation cues, personality, greetings, and interruption behavior, see the GPT-Live prompting guide. The voice agent evaluation guide covers how to turn your listening cases into a repeatable evaluation as you change voices, prompts, or models.

articles.title: Step-up authentication: how to right-size authentication to risk
articles.context: If you request step-up through InitiateAuth on a user pool that isn’t on the Essentials or Plus plan, the API returns a FeatureUnavailableInTierException
articles.full_text:
Not every action a user takes in an application carries the same risk. Viewing an account balance in a banking application isn’t the same as wiring several thousand dollars to a new payee. In practice, though, many applications ask users to prove their identity once at sign-in and then treat every action the same from that point on, whether that sign-in used a password alone or included multi-factor authentication (MFA). That creates a tension: if the sign-in is strict enough for the most sensitive operation, everyday tasks carry unnecessary friction. If it’s easy enough for everyday tasks, the most sensitive operations might not be protected well enough. Even a strong sign-in from hours earlier says little about who is at the keyboard when a high-risk request arrives.

Amazon Cognito now resolves that trade-off by supporting step-up authentication, which records the authentication assurance level and the methods used, and including both in the JSON web tokens (JWTs) it issues. You ask for a target assurance level when a user signs in. Amazon Cognito returns the level the user reached in an acr claim (authentication context class reference) and the methods they completed in an amr claim (authentication methods reference). These claims are part of the OpenID Connect Core specification, so your application can reason about authentication strength in a standard way and match it to the potential risk of what the user is trying to do. In this post, I explain how the claims support step-up authentication and walk through four patterns that put them to use: transaction-level step-up in a banking app, varying risk postures across a portfolio of applications, step-up enforced on API and SDK sign-in, and authentication assurance carried across a federated third-party OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider.

You can request authentication levels through Amazon Cognito managed login using the standard OIDC acr_values and max_age parameters, and through the SDK and API using the USER_AUTH flow with TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE. Requesting step-up authentication requires the Essentials or Plus feature plan. ; For the complete list of features, behaviors, and limitations, see the Authentication levels with ACR and AMR claims.

What ACR and AMR tell your application

Amazon Cognito defines four assurance levels, and the factor combinations that satisfy each one are fixed. You can use the default names as is or rename the level URIs to fit your organization’s own naming scheme. Renaming changes only the label. If you need to relate Amazon Cognito levels to a framework such as NIST SP 800-63 or eIDAS, make that mapping in your application. The following are the default Amazon Cognito defined levels.

Level 1 (urn:cognito:loa:1) is password only.

Level 2 (urn:cognito:loa:2) is a single one-time password (OTP) over SMS or email.

Level 3 (urn:cognito:loa:3) is a passkey on its own, or a password combined with an SMS or email OTP.

Level 4 (urn:cognito:loa:4) is the highest: a password with a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code from an authenticator app.

Amazon Cognito assigns the highest level the user’s completed factors fully satisfy, so a user who signs in with a password and a TOTP code lands at level 4, even though they also met the assurance requirements for every level below it.

Four claims in the token facilitate a step-up decision. The acr claim is the level the sign-in reached and is what your application compares against what the operation requires. The amr claim lists the methods behind that level, so you can confirm a specific factor was used. The auth_time claim records when the user last authenticated interactively and is what max_age is measured against. The iat claim only records when the token was issued, so a refreshed token carries a new iat but keeps its old auth_time. Finally, send a nonce in the request and verify it on the returned ID token, so the result is tied to the request you made.

The following is an example access token for a user completing a level 4 authentication. Notice the four claims I’ve discussed: acr, amr, auth_time, and iat.

{ "sub": "387173a0-60c1-700a-4a02-e84b49bcc7a9", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<region>_123abc", "aud": "123abcn2ci4a99a4ieno123abc", "exp": 1445470140, "iat": 499163700, "auth_time": -446666160, "token_use": "access", "acr": "urn:cognito:loa:4", "amr": ["pwd", "otp", "mfa"], "email": "marty@example.com", "cognito:username": "387173a0-60c1-700a-4a02-e84b49bcc7a9" }

Two important behaviors are worth understanding before you build on this. First, a token refresh preserves the acr and amr values, so a user who reached level 4 keeps level 4 across refreshes and isn’t asked to prove it again on every rotation. Second, a refresh doesn’t reset the auth_time claim. That field records when the user interactively authenticated, not from a non-interactive token refresh. This is what lets you reason about freshness of authentication separately from assurance strength.

At a high level, every step-up interaction in this post follows the same loop: the application checks the token it already holds, redirects for a stronger level only when the operation requires more than the user has, and re-validates the acr claim on the freshly issued token before it proceeds. The following diagram provides a general step-up authentication flow.

Figure 1: General step-up authentication flow to access a sensitive operation

How you request a level, and what stays your responsibility

The request side is deliberately straightforward. On managed login you add acr_values and optionally max_age to the or endpoint. In the SDK and API, you pass TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow of the API. Both acr_values and TARGET_ACR_VALUES accept an ordered list of target levels. The same parameters work whether you’re setting the level for an initial sign-in or raising the level of a user who is already signed in; the patterns later in this post show both. Amazon Cognito acts only on what you send. It doesn’t infer the level you meant, so if you omit the parameter or request the wrong level, the user might not be stepped up the way you intended.

That points to the part your application and API owns: what assurance authentication level is needed. Amazon Cognito issues a token that honestly reports the level the user reached based on what your application requested. For example, deciding that a given operation requires an assurance level 3, checking the token’s acr against that requirement, and refusing the operation when it falls short is enforcement your application and API performs. Amazon Cognito produces the evidence; your code acts on it. In practice, that means checking the token you already hold before you redirect, so you don’t send a user to re-authenticate who already meets the bar, and validating the acr and auth_time claims on the tokens Amazon Cognito returns before you grant access. Amazon Cognito computes these claims itself, so you can’t customize, add to, or suppress them with a pre-token-generation Lambda trigger.

There is one more detail that saves debugging time later. If you rename your acr level URIs after tokens have already been issued, an older token might carry an acr value that no longer matches any configured level. Amazon Cognito treats that as an unrecognized level rather than an error. It still honors the token’s amr values and prompts only for factors not already present, without crediting any particular level. The amr list, in other words, remains meaningful even when a renamed level string goes stale. See Configuring ACR level names to learn how to configure this.

With the claims and the division of responsibility in place, the following four patterns show how they work in practice. Each one applies the same loop from Figure 1 to a different situation: a single application, a portfolio of applications, API-driven sign-in, and federation.

Pattern 1: Transaction-level step-up in a banking app

Consider a retail banking application. Signing in and viewing balances is routine, and the bank is comfortable requiring a moderate assurance level for it. Moving money is considered a privileged action, and a large transfer deserves stronger proof that the person at the keyboard is really the account holder.

The bank sets its baseline at level 2, so a user signs in with a one-time code over SMS or email and can see balances, statements, and pending transactions. When that same user initiates a transfer above $1,000, the application’s own policy says the operation requires level 4. Before it shows the transfer initiation screen, the application inspects the acr claim in the token it already holds. The user authenticated at level 2, level 2 is below the required level 4, so the application redirects the user to managed login with acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:4.

GET https://auth.example-bank.com/oauth2/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=abc123def456 &redirect_uri=https://app.example-bank.com/callback &scope=openid &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:4

Amazon Cognito now requires the user to complete a factor combination that satisfies level 4, for example entering their password and then a TOTP code from their authenticator app. When authentication finishes, Amazon Cognito issues fresh tokens with acr set to urn:cognito:loa:4, amr set to ["pwd", "otp", "mfa"], and a fresh updated auth_time claim. The application validates that the new token meets its requirement and only then lets the transfer proceed. A transfer under the threshold never triggers any of this, so the everyday experience stays light and the friction lands exactly where the risk is.

The application logic reads naturally, here’s a pseudo JavaScript snippet:

// Use your own URIs here, if different than defaults. const ACR_RANK = { "urn:cognito:loa:1": 1, "urn:cognito:loa:2": 2, "urn:cognito:loa:3": 3, "urn:cognito:loa:4": 4, }; const REQUIRED_LEVEL = "urn:cognito:loa:4"; const HIGH_VALUE_THRESHOLD = 1000; function canAuthorizeTransfer(accessTokenClaims, amount) { if (amount < HIGH_VALUE_THRESHOLD) { return true; // baseline session is sufficient } // High-value transfer: require level 4. // An unrecognized acr ranks 0, so it never passes. const achieved = ACR_RANK[accessTokenClaims.acr] ?? 0; return achieved >= ACR_RANK[REQUIRED_LEVEL]; }

You can extend the same idea to freshness. A bank might accept a level 4 session for a high-value transfer only if the user authenticated within the last 5 minutes, which you express by adding max_age=300 to the request. Amazon Cognito compares that window against the auth_time claim in the access token and reauthenticates the user if the window has passed, even if the token was refreshed seconds ago.

Pattern 2: A portfolio of applications with different risk postures

Assurance levels are just as useful across a set of applications as they are within one. Suppose an organization runs five applications from a single Amazon Cognito user pool using managed login, and each one carries a different risk posture.

An internal cafeteria menu is low risk, so it’s fine with level 1, password only. An employee directory and an expense viewer hold personal data but nothing that moves money, so they require level 2: a one-time code over SMS or email on top of the password. A source code portal warrants a passkey or a password plus a one-time code, which is level 3. The production financial console is the crown jewel, so it demands level 4: a password with a TOTP code.

Each application requests its own floor by setting acr_values to the level that matches its risk, and each validates the acr claim on the returned token before granting access. Because the applications share a user pool, managed login keeps a single sign-on (SSO) session across them. A user who has already reached level 4 for the financial console is redirected to managed login when they open another application, finds the existing session, and receives tokens for that application without another prompt, provided the application doesn’t send a max_age that the session has outlived. Each application then compares levels by rank, so a level 4 token satisfies a level 2 floor. Someone who signed in at level 1 for the cafeteria menu, on the other hand, is stepped up the first time they open the expense viewer, because level 1 doesn’t meet the level 2 floor that the application enforces. The user pool stays single and central; the assurance requirement travels with each application’s own policy.

Renaming the level URIs helps here. If the organization already classifies systems against an internal assurance standard, it can set AcrConfiguration on the user pool so that, say, level 3 reports as urn:example-corp:assurance:standard and level 4 as urn:example-corp:assurance:high. The factor combinations behind each level stay fixed; only the names change, so every application validates against strings its developers already recognize.

Pattern 3: Step-up on API and SDK sign-in

Managed login covers browser-based flows, including federation, but plenty of clients authenticate directly against the Amazon Cognito API, and the same assurance model applies there, such as using the USER_AUTH flow with the InitiateAuth API. This matters for a mobile app, a desktop client, or a service that drives sign-in programmatically and needs to raise assurance before a sensitive call.

Take a mobile trading app that signs its users in with the SDK. A user opens the app with a password and reaches level 1, which is enough to browse watchlists and market data. When they place a trade, the app’s policy requires level 4. Because the app authenticates through the API rather than a browser redirect, it starts a new USER_AUTH flow and passes the access token it already holds along with TARGET_ACR_VALUES, requesting the level it needs. Amazon Cognito drives the user through a factor combination that satisfies level 4, then returns tokens whose acr claim the app validates before it submits the order. The InitiateAuth request would look similar to the following API call.

{ "AuthFlow": "USER_AUTH", "ClientId": "abc123def456", "AuthParameters": { "USERNAME": "user@example.com", "ACCESS_TOKEN": "eyJraWQiOi...", "TARGET_ACR_VALUES": "urn:cognito:loa:4", "MAX_AGE": "300" } }

Passing the access token the app already holds lets Amazon Cognito step the user up from the factors in that token; without it, Amazon Cognito authenticates the user from scratch. The MAX_AGE parameter behaves the same way it does on managed login. It ties the requirement to auth_time, so a trade placed after the window elapses forces a fresh authentication even if the app refreshed its tokens in the meantime. One behavior specific to the API path is worth knowing when you test on a lower Cognito feature plan. If you request step-up through InitiateAuth on a user pool that isn’t on the Essentials or Plus plan, the API returns a FeatureUnavailableInTierException. Managed login handles the same situation differently: the authorize endpoint silently ignores acr_values and proceeds with normal authentication rather than raising an error.

Pattern 4: Carrying assurance across a federated OIDC identity provider

The three patterns so far assume Amazon Cognito is where the user authenticates and the authoritative source for the identity. Many organizations federate sign-in to a third-party OIDC provider, so the person proving who they are is doing it against an external identity provider (IdP), while Amazon Cognito brokers the session. The assurance model follows them there.

When your application requests a level, it sends acr_values and optionally max_age to the Amazon Cognito authorize endpoint exactly as before. If that user is configured to federate through an OIDC IdP, Amazon Cognito sends the authorization request to that IdP on the user’s behalf. It translates the level you requested into the acr value the IdP expects, using the mapping you configured, and passes max_age along with it. A standards-compliant OIDC IdP honors acr_values the same way Amazon Cognito does: it drives the user through an authentication that satisfies the requested level, and it returns its own acr value describing what the user reached. max_age carries forward in the same way, so a freshness requirement is enforced at the provider that actually authenticates the user rather than being lost at the broker. Keep in mind that this is only supported with OIDC identity providers.

The request is unchanged from the application’s point of view. It still directs to Amazon Cognito:

GET https://auth.example.com/oauth2/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=abc123def456 &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback &scope=openid &identity_provider=PartnerOIDC &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:3 &max_age=300

The interaction gains a third participant, the downstream IdP, but the assurance requirement is persisted through the entire federated authentication flow as shown in figure 2.

Figure 2: Federation with an OIDC third-party IdP, persisting the acr_values and max_age request parameters

The value that comes back from a partner IdP won’t use Amazon Cognito’s level URIs, so this lets you map the provider’s acr values onto its own levels with the AcrMapping field on the OIDC IdP configuration. A partner IdP that reports, say, https://partner.example/assurance/strong can be mapped to Amazon Cognito level 3 (urn:cognito:loa:3), so that by the time the token reaches your application the acr claim speaks the same vocabulary regardless of whether the user authenticated locally or through a federated provider. Your resource server keeps a single enforcement rule and authorization logic and doesn’t need to have special handling depending on where the user ultimately authenticated. See Step-up authentication for federated users to learn how to map external OIDC IdP acr levels to Cognito.

This is the same pattern that RFC 9470, the OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol, describes: the assurance level is requested at the edge of your application, travels through Amazon Cognito to whatever provider authenticates the user, and returns normalized to a vocabulary your code already understands. A user federating from a corporate IdP and a user signing in against the same user pool directly both arrive at your resource server carrying an acr claim that means the same thing.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed you how the acr and amr claims in Amazon Cognito let you match authentication strength to the risk of what a user is doing, instead of settling for one bar at the front door. Your application requests a target level with acr_values and max_age (or TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow), Amazon Cognito reports the level reached and the methods used, and your application enforces what each operation requires. The four patterns, from a banking transfer to a federated third-party IdP, follow that same loop, and one enforcement rule at your resource server covers every sign-in path.

The larger shift is that assurance is now something Amazon Cognito expresses in a standard way and your application reasons about directly, without building your own step-up tracking. To get started, move your user pool to the Essentials or Plus feature plan, decide the level each operation requires, and add acr_values to your existing authorize requests. For the complete parameter reference and federated behavior, see the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

He loves speaking with customers about how identity and access management can provide secure outcomes that enable both business and technology initiatives. articles.title: AI unearths ‘internet breaker’ flaws in Nginx web server
articles.context: Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can...
articles.full_text:
Nginx, the web server estimated to power a third of the internet, has shipped fixes for multiple vulnerabilities, including a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw that puts millions of websites at risk and has existed in the code for over a decade. Researchers from several security firms independently found some of the same flaws by using AI agents, adding to a string of recent AI-discovered vulnerabilities in widely used internet technologies such as PHP, Node, OpenSSH, and Java.

The most severe flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an attacker manipulate flow-control windows in the HTTP/2 protocol implementation to trigger an out-of-bounds memory copy that researchers from Xint.io turned into command execution with Nginx worker privileges. The vulnerability affects every official Nginx release for more than 10 years since version 1.9.5, which originally added HTTP/2 support in 2015.

A second HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, is a use-after-free vulnerability affecting releases 1.19.7 through 1.31.8. Both are fixed in Nginx 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, which F5 released along with fixes for eight other vulnerabilities.

Xint’s researchers, who used the company’s own autonomous AI harness, found five of the flaws and discovered a separate Linux kernel vulnerability in the SCTP subsystem that can be chained with any of those flaws to gain root privileges on the server. The company has dubbed the collection nginx2root.

In their tests the exploit chain escaped a Docker container running Nginx and obtained root on the underlying host. The kernel flaw has existed since Linux 4.15, released in 2018, and has no CVE or patch so the company is withholding details until distributions can ship a fix.

The exposure of web servers on the internet is vast with the Shodan search engine showing 56.7 million hosts running Nginx, and 98.9% of those that disclose their version report one in the vulnerable range. F5 recommends updating immediately or disabling HTTP/2 on affected ports, which blocks the two most severe flaws but not Xint’s other findings — CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425 — which are in other components.

The CVE-2026-123007 flaw was reported to F5 by researchers from Rapid7, Wiz, Xint, and Ikotas Labs, while CVE-2026-123633, dubbed Drainbreak, was discovered and reported by researchers from Metnir, Wiz, and Xint. Only Rapid7 senior principal security researcher Stephen Fewer doesn’t mention AI in his write-up. The other four teams used AI agents and harnesses, with Xint’s CEO Brian Pak saying that his team’s platform scanned “50,000 lines of code in just 90 minutes” to surface “a critical vulnerability that gave an unauthenticated user a RCE path — essentially an internet breaker.”

Exploitation is likely

No one has exploited either flaw in the wild yet, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s assessment of both CVEs, but every research team built working exploits, and two describe the flaws as readily exploitable.

Xint called CVE-2026-123007 highly exploitable, saying an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port was enough to corrupt the send window, disclose addresses, and execute commands, and validated the attack over public IPs on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent traffic.

Metnir ran its exploit for CVE-2026-123633 with ASLR enabled, taking about 10 minutes, nearly all of it spent on defeating memory layout randomization, and reproduced the use-after-free in OpenResty, crashing the shipped binaries of Kong, Apache APISIX, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and community ingress-nginx, all of which enable HTTP/2 by default.

Rapid7’s Fewer calculated that running his exploit requires transmitting roughly 128GB of HTTP/2 data to the target. That takes about two minutes on a 10Gbit/s network and 17 minutes on 1Gbit/s. The technique also relies on a memory-copy routine in glibc that is used only on CPUs with AVX-512 extensions, but these are common on servers.“Exploitation is by no means a walk in the park, as the vulnerable systems must be directly exposed to the internet with no WAF or CDN terminating HTTP/2,” Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, told CSO. “Memory corruption can also be tricky, as an effective exploit must properly groom and shape the memory heap and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configuration variants. And when the system is internet-facing and under load, exploitation can cause more crashes than successful code execution.”

Patch and check what you’re actually running

Nginx Plus users should also update to 37.3.0.1 on the newer release line or 37.0.8.1 on the 37.0 line. The older R33 through R36 release line will never receive a fix because those versions have reached the end of technical support.

Disabling HTTP/2 comes with costs, as services that depend on it, such as native gRPC, stop working. Xint’s other three flaws require specific configurations. The resolver flaw affects setups that pick their backend per request and use the mirror directive, the HTTP/3 flaw affects QUIC listeners, and the mail proxy flaw affects deployments that use proxy on with auth_http. Xint published per-flaw mitigations in its technical write-up.For the accompanying Linux flaw, until a kernel patch is released, administrators who don’t use SCTP can block the module from loading by adding install sctp /bin/false to a file under /etc/modprobe.d.Administrators should also investigate unexpected Nginx worker crashes or commands launched by Nginx workers, Wiz noted.

“The real risk with this nginx bug isn’t the 11 years it went unnoticed, it’s how many teams will think they’ve patched when they haven’t,” Daniel Shechter, co-founder and CEO of Miggo Security, told CSO. “The version number can be wrong because distros backport fixes without changing it, a reload doesn’t swap out the running code, and the attack happens in HTTP/2 traffic that WAFs and access logs never see. If you can’t prove the fix is actually running, assume you’re still exposed.”

articles.title: Another critical PHP security release has dropped
articles.context: The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical
articles.full_text: Apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.” including at least one rated "critical." These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk. CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.” The earlier informational advisory urged users to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.” These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation said is very unlikely in real-world applications. Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here. The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites. While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26. Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers. The Israeli AI cybersecurity startup said the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®

articles.title: Detecting cross-cloud lateral movement with AWS Security Hub
articles.context: In this blog post, you learn how to configure the Azure integration for Security Hub and use exposure findings to prioritize attack paths across both clouds from one console
articles.full_text:
Most organizations run a multicloud estate, and so do the attackers targeting them. An adversary who compromises an identity in one provider follows that identity wherever it leads, including across a federated trust into a second cloud service provider. The signals enumerating this scenario are rarely missing; the problem is that they live in separate consoles, in different schemas, owned by different teams. No one has visibility into the whole picture, so no one can decide what to fix first.

AWS Security Hub addresses prioritization and triage with exposure findings. Security Hub correlates reachability, blast radius, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and effective permissions, providing a strong correlation layer with an attack-path visualization, providing the context needed to generate risks from findings. That analysis now extends to Microsoft Azure. Security Hub records and analyzes your Azure resources with the same correlation engine used for Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources. The resulting details and meta-data land in the same console, ranked in the same queue, providing holistic, multicloud visibility into your security risks.

In this blog post, you learn how to configure the Azure integration for Security Hub and use exposure findings to prioritize attack paths across both clouds from one console. We follow a realistic scenario: a compromised identity that threatens both an Azure and an AWS environment through a shared, federated identity plane. We show you how the critical exposures along that path are presented as ranked findings that you can triage together, and we map each one to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. We also cover the prerequisites that teams commonly overlook.

Why prioritizing multicloud risk is difficult

Consider an organization whose Microsoft Entra ID tenant is federated into an AWS account, so identities in the tenant can assume an AWS role. This is an ordinary and intentional configuration used to avoid having to manage a second set of credentials. It also means the two clouds share an identity plane: a single compromised Entra identity is both an Azure threat and—through the federation—an AWS threat.

An attacker exploits this, but the defensive signals land in different places:

Where the risk lives

Traditionally visible in

Owned by

Weak Entra identity controls: over-privileged identities, no multi-factor authentication (MFA), vulnerable conditional access policies (CAP)

Entra ID and Microsoft Defender for Cloud

Identity team

Internet-reachable Azure host with admin rights

Defender for Cloud

Azure platform team

Federated trust into AWS

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Cloud security team

Sensitive data and over-exposed resources in AWS

AWS security tooling

Cloud security team

Each team sees one fragment, and in isolation each fragment appears low severity. You see the risk only when you correlate all of it together and discover the same identity plane ties the attack path together. Exposure findings provide that severity within AWS; extending it to Azure closes the multicloud visibility gap.

How the Azure integration works

You create the Azure connector in the AWS Management Console for Security Hub. It authenticates to your Entra ID tenant through an application registration, records and evaluates your Azure resource configurations, and streams Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts and Entra ID audit logs through an Azure Event Hubs namespace. Your Azure resources then flow into the same correlation engine that analyzes signals from AWS Security Hub Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, and Amazon GuardDuty. That engine produces two kinds of findings:

Control findings against standards such as the CIS Microsoft Azure Foundations Benchmark.

Exposure findings, which are ranked, attack-path findings that correlate traits such as reachability, effective permissions, and misconfiguration, with a severity based on how discoverable and exploitable the risk is.

Both use the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and appear in the same console as your AWS findings. However, one filtering detail matters: because Security Hub produces the finding, its top-level cloud.provider is AWS, while the evaluated resource carries resources[].provider = Azure. Filter on resources.provider to scope to a single cloud.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

An AWS account with Security Hub enabled. If you use a delegated administrator account for Security Hub, create the connector there, in the AWS Region where you aggregate findings.

An Entra ID tenant with a Microsoft Azure subscription. You need privileges in Azure to create an application registration, assign roles at the tenant root management group, and create a subscription-level diagnostic setting.

The Azure CLI, authenticated to the target subscription with az login command.

Activity log export. Azure resource recordings are change-driven and depend on activity logs reaching the event hub that the connector reads. The onboarding process assigns an Azure policy to create the required diagnostic setting, but it only remediates existing subscriptions after you create a remediation task. If the connector reports healthy status but resources never appear, run az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription list to confirm the export exists, and create a remediation task if the list is empty.

Configuration

The following steps detail how to connect your Azure environment to Security Hub v2: Registering the Azure application, establishing federated identity credentials, and assigning the roles required for AWS to evaluate your Azure resources.

Step 1: Create the Azure connector in Security Hub

The first step in this configuration is to create the Azure connector in Security Hub. The connector establishes trust with your Azure tenant and defines which subscriptions and regions Security Hub v2 will evaluate.

Open the Security Hub console and choose Integrations.

Choose Create Azure connector.

Enter your Azure Tenant ID and the Application (client) ID of the application registration you created for the integration.

For Subscriptions and Regions, select all. Attack paths cross subscription and Region boundaries, so partial coverage leaves blind spots where a compromised identity can pivot unseen. Scope to specific IDs or Regions only when data-residency rules require it.

Run the generated setup script in your Azure environment, then choose Create connector.

Include the global region scope. Controls that evaluate Entra ID and Microsoft Graph resources require it, and those identity exposures are central to this scenario. If you also create an Amazon Inspector or Security Hub CSPM connector for the same tenant, keep its subscriptions and regions consistent with this one.

Step 2: Verify the connector and its recording activity

Health status alone doesn’t tell you whether recording is flowing. Confirm both.

AWS Command Line interface (AWS CLI) command 1: Verify connector health and recording state

aws securityhub list-connectors-v2 --region <REGION> \ --query "Connectors[?ProviderSummary.ProviderName=='AZURE']" --output json

aws securityhub get-resources-v2 --region <REGION> --max-results 50 \ --filters '{"CompositeFilters":[{"StringFilters":[{"FieldName":"ResourceType", "Filter":{"Value":"microsoft.compute/virtualmachines","Comparison":"EQUALS"}}]}], "CompositeOperator":"AND"}' \ --query "Resources[].{id:ResourceId, captured:ResourceDetailCaptureTimeDt}" --output table

Step 3: Query exposure findings for Azure resources

Scope to Azure by filtering on the resource provider.

AWS CLI command 2: Retrieve exposure findings for Azure resources

​​aws securityhub get-findings-v2 --region <REGION> --max-results 50 \ --filters '{"CompositeFilters":[ {"StringFilters":[{"FieldName":"resources.provider","Filter":{"Value":"Azure","Comparison":"EQUALS"}}]}, {"StringFilters":[{"FieldName":"metadata.product.feature.uid","Filter":{"Value":"security-hub/Exposure","Comparison":"EQUALS"}}]}], "CompositeOperator":"AND"}' \ --query "Findings[].{sev:severity, title:finding_info.title}" --output table​

Step 4 (optional): Add Amazon Inspector for Azure vulnerability scanning

To add vulnerability findings for Azure virtual machines (VMs), function apps, or container registry images, create an Amazon Inspector connector for the same tenant. VM scanning requires each target VM to have a system-assigned managed identity, which you can enforce with an Azure Policy. Figure 1 shows a correctly configured Azure integration inside Security Hub, with vulnerability management and posture management deployed.

Figure 1: Successful configuration of the Azure integration with Security Hub

Step 5: Prerequisites for Microsoft Azure

See the AWS documentation for the prerequisites for Microsoft Azure.

Walk-through: Prioritizing a cross-cloud attack path

In this example, the organization has one identity plane across two clouds, comprising a Microsoft Entra ID tenant with a federated trust into an AWS account. An adversary who compromises the right Entra identity gains an initial foothold in Azure and a path into AWS, because both clouds trust the same identity plane. The following sections trace that path. Each step is a real, high-severity exposure finding that Security Hub ranked on its own. The point of the walk-through is to demonstrate a real-life scenario and examine all findings in one unified security console.

Phase 1: A compromised identity (Azure)

ATT&CK: Phishing (T1566), Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (T1078.004)

The path begins with an Entra identity that is both over-privileged and unprotected. You’ll find this in the Security Hub console under Exposures, where Security Hub raises it as an identity exposure finding and maps the attack path stemming from it:

Potential Unauthorized Access: Azure RBAC user with administrative access has MFA disabled (high). It correlates the user, the role assignment that grants administrative access, and the organization.

The tenant’s authorization policies let an attacker broaden that foothold, and Security Hub CSPM reports each policy as a failed control (high): Microsoft Entra ID authorization policies should prohibit default users from registering applications…should restrict user consent for applications, and Azure authorization policies should restrict guest invitations to admin roles only. Each finding expands what a single compromised, non-privileged identity can do without an administrator.

Phase 2: Foothold and privilege escalation (Azure)

ATT&CK: Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190), Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts (T1078.004)

The tenant contains an internet-reachable VM whose network security group allows inbound from any address, and whose attached identity holds administrative rights over the subscription. Security Hub surfaces this under Exposures, correlating reachability and effective permissions into one finding that shows why it matters: anyone reaching the VM inherits admin control of the subscription.:

Potential Initial Access: Potentially internet reachable Azure virtual machine with open network security group has administrative access (high). It correlates the VM, the role assignment, the network security group, and the public IP address.

The finding’s analysis reads like an attack path. The resource “may be reachable from the public internet,” “overly permissive network security group (NSG) rules allow unintended inbound access,” and “the Owner or Contributor role grants extensive permissions… enabling a threat actor to escalate privileges.” Security Hub evaluates this from configuration and network-path modeling, so it surfaces whether or not the VM is running. Figure 2 shows the correlated attack path for that virtual machine.

Figure 2: An Azure attack-path exposure, analyzed by the same correlation engine as AWS exposures

The cross-cloud bridge: Federation into AWS

The tenant from Phases 1 and 2 is federated into the AWS account through an IAM SAML identity provider. As shown in Figure 2, a role trusts that provider and grants read access to every bucket in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). This trust is what expands the risk across clouds from the same adversary: a compromised Entra identity can assume this role and reach AWS data.

This one hop lives in IAM rather than in Security Hub. Security Hub doesn’t not raise a finding for a role that trusts your own federated identity provider. Confirming it is a normal investigative pivot: the role trusts a SAML identity provider that represents your Entra tenant, the same tenant whose exposures you triaged when you added Amazon Inspector in Step 4.

Figure 3: The federated trust that links the two clouds through a shared identity plane

Phase 3: The impact (AWS)

ATT&CK: Data from Cloud Storage (T1530), Transfer Data to Cloud Account (T1537)

On the AWS side, the correlation engine has already categorized the resources this identity can reach. Under Exposures in the Security Hub console, the sensitive-data objective surfaces this finding because that reachable set includes data at risk; a compromised identity could destroy it:

Potential Sensitive Data Destruction: S3 bucket has sensitive data and versioning disabled and Object Lock disabled and MFA delete disabled (high). A Macie finding, The S3 object contains personal information, is a contributing signal, and the control S3 general purpose buckets should be encrypted at rest with AWS KMS keys fails alongside it.

The same account carries related AWS attack-path exposures. Two examples are Potential Resource Hijacking: Internet reachable EC2 instance with open security group has software vulnerabilities with limited effective permissions and Potential Unauthorized Access: IAM user has weak password policies. In the exposure queue, these sit next to the Azure findings, ranked by the same severity model.

Prioritizing across both clouds in the console

Here is the operational benefit. An analyst is notified of generated exposure findings and opens the dashboard and filters to High severity. In one prioritized list, without switching tools or opening a ticket for another team, they see the Azure admin identity without MFA, the internet-reachable Azure VM with subscription-admin rights, and the AWS sensitive data exposure. Together, these show the full scope of what a single vector, sharing an identity plane, might target. The analyst confirms the connecting federation with one pivot into IAM. The multicloud triage that used to require two products and two teams now occurs in one place. Figure 4 shows that single ranked queue.

Figure 4: Cross-cloud exposure prioritization in a single console

Phase-to-exposure summary

The following table traces each phase of the attack path to its MITRE ATT&CK techniques, the cloud where it plays out, and the ranked Security Hub exposure that surfaces it — following the pivot from Azure into AWS across the shared identity plane.

Phase

ATT&CK

Cloud

Ranked exposure in Security Hub

1. Compromised identity

T1566, T1078.004

Azure

Potential Unauthorized Access: Azure RBAC user with administrative access has MFA disabled (High)

2. Foothold and privilege escalation

T1190, T1078.004

Azure

Potential Initial Access: internet reachable Azure VM with open NSG has administrative access (High)

2.1 Bridge

T1550 (Use Alternate Authentication Material)

Azure to AWS

Federated trust, confirmed in AWS IAM (shared identity plane)

3. Data objective

T1530, T1537

AWS

Potential Sensitive Data Destruction: S3 bucket has sensitive data… (High), plus Macie

Conclusion

A cross-cloud attack is difficult to prioritize because signals are generated across separate consoles, schemas, and teams. In this post, you saw how the Azure integration for AWS Security Hub brings Azure resources into the same exposure engine and the same queue as your AWS resources. One analyst can prioritize an attack path that spans a compromised Microsoft Entra ID identity, across a federated trust, to sensitive data in Amazon S3, without leaving Security Hub.

To recap why this workflow is practical and effective:

Security Hub records and analyzes your Azure security findings and displays them in the same unified console as your AWS resources, and produces ranked, attack-path exposure findings for both clouds.

Findings from both clouds share the OCSF schema, so you filter, group, and prioritize them in one place. Filter on resources.provider to scope an individual cloud.

Security Hub correlates signals into attack paths within each cloud. The analysis creates a cross-cloud narrative, such as a shared federated identity plane, while co-locating ranked correlation findings across both Azure and AWS, creating efficient scoping and remediations.

Confirm your prerequisites. Include the global region scope for Entra ID controls, know that sign-in log signals require an Entra ID P1 or P2 license, and confirm that the subscription diagnostic setting that exports Activity Logs to the connector’s event hub is in place. A connector can report a healthy status while it records nothing.

To get started, see Enabling Microsoft Azure integration in Security Hub and Exposure findings in Security Hub.

His background is in AWS consulting and security architecture and focused on a variety of security domains including edge, threat detection, and compliance. articles.title: Outage or attack? Don’t let social media fill in the gaps
articles.context: AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible
articles.full_text:
Your banking app won’t load. Someone posts that an airline is having computer problems. Then you see a screenshot showing trouble at a cloud provider.

By the time you’ve scrolled through a few more posts, someone is telling you to withdraw cash and prepare for a nationwide blackout.

That is quite a journey from an error message.

Recent technology disruptions have provided plenty of material for this kind of speculation. As CNN describes, real outages have become mixed up with exaggerated reports, unrelated events, and conspiracy theories about what might happen next. A routine emergency alert test was even folded into the narrative.

The outages are real and so is the inconvenience. The problem with reporting on computer failures is how quickly “the system is down” becomes “the system is under attack.”

Non-malicious causes include faulty software updates, configuration mistakes, equipment failures, power interruptions, and damaged cables. Cyberattacks can also disrupt services by overwhelming them with traffic or using ransomware to make systems unusable. From the outside, both can have you staring at much the same unhelpful error message.

There has been a lot of this recently. So much so that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio felt the need to dismiss widespread concerns that the recent tech outages in the past week are connected.

What actually went down

During an outage, users want immediate answers, but investigators need time to establish what’s gone wrong. In that information vacuum, speculation thrives.

Let’s have a look at some recent events:

European refrigeration attacks disrupted cooling systems at some businesses. Separately, monitoring systems at three French blood-storage sites were affected, but staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised.

Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a latent software defect in networking gateways. Several organizations lost a full day of work.

The FAA nationwide ground stop in the US due to a telecommunications failure that disrupted some air traffic control communications. The ground stop led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays are ongoing.

JPMorgan Chase and knock-on banking problems were caused by a software bug in an on-premises hardware system that slowed transaction processing. The issue delayed transactions; no lasting damage has been reported.

Optimizely Web Experimentation supply-chain attack served malicious code on 178 popular websites. The issue was fixed rapidly, but visitors may have been exposed to malicious code that infected their devices.

There is an important distinction between outages caused by bugs and those caused by attacks, but the cause alone doesn’t tell us how disruptive an incident will be.

A technical failure can cause enormous problems without an attacker being involved. And an attack can cause harm without producing a spectacular outage.

We should judge the cause and the consequences separately and not assume that the most visible disruption must be the most sinister.

How social media amplifies the alarm

These things happen all the time, and sometimes the impact is bigger than at other times. That’s not a reason to panic or assume they’re all part of a big conspiracy. The recent claims that the US was about to face a 90-day blackout are a good example.

Combined with social media algorithms, these incidents can quickly pull people who show an interest in these incidents into a vortex of bad news, making it feel as if the end of the world is just around the corner. A feed full of outages is not evidence of an approaching “bugalypse.” Before accepting that explanation, ask what connects the incidents beyond the fact that they appeared in your feed.

The 90-day blackout claim shows how quickly genuine events can be turned into evidence for a much bigger story. Social media users turned a routine US emergency alert test into a prediction of a 90-day blackout. Some posts pointed to the Microsoft outage and FAA ground stop as evidence that the disaster was already unfolding. Others misrepresented military contingency planning as advance knowledge of an imminent crisis.

In reality, the alert was a scheduled test, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) explicitly said there were “no blackouts, no secret emergencies.” The test went ahead without the predicted catastrophe. That is the problem: Genuine disruptions were being used to support a much larger claim for which there was no evidence.

Where AI fits in

AI is helping both software vendors and attackers find more bugs. That can mean larger updates from Microsoft, Google, and others, covering more vulnerabilities at a faster pace. AI can also help attackers find ways to exploit those vulnerabilities, putting pressure on security teams and consumers to install those patches as soon as possible.

Reports of misaligned AI agents can make it harder to see how AI can work both ways. That’s because the balance in cybersecurity isn’t where we want it to be yet. But in other fields, AI is helping scientists and researchers make large strides.

For an example of AI doing something genuinely useful, look at protein research. Determining a protein’s three-dimensional structure experimentally can take years. AlphaFold can often generate a useful prediction in minutes or hours, and its freely accessible database contains predictions for more than 200 million protein structures. Those models still need expert scrutiny and, where necessary, experimental validation. But they give researchers a starting point at a speed and scale that laboratory work alone could not match.

What to do

You can take cybersecurity seriously without treating every error message as a warning of impending disaster.

An outage deserves an explanation. An attack deserves investigation. Neither benefits from speculation presented as fact. Companies need to explain what they know, what they’re still investigating, and what customers should do. Those of us reporting on these incidents have a responsibility to make those distinctions clear and not connect the dots before we know whether there is a connection.

As readers, we can pause before sharing the next alarming prediction. Does it offer evidence, or just a collection of things that happened around the same time? Is there something useful we should do, or is someone simply giving us another reason to keep scrolling?

Keep your software updated. Protect your devices. Have a backup plan for services you depend on. But don’t let someone else’s take on things fill the gaps in what is known.

Scammers know more about you than you think.
