articles.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability Allows Remote Attacks on Major Java Apps
articles.context: Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit
articles.full_text:
Weeks after PHP2Shell, another critical vulnerability has been leaked before its planned disclosure and authorities are now urging organizations to apply patches.

The new vulnerability, known as ‘Java4Shell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory corruption vulnerability in Open Java Development Kit (OpenJDK), an open-source implementation of the Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE) co-maintained by Oracle and a global community of developers and companies, such as Red Hat, Amazon and Microsoft. OpenJDK runs most Java applications.

The vulnerability was found by California-based security firm Calif, which published details on November 17 after some information was leaked before coordinated disclosure.

The flaw affects OpenJDK 17, 21, 25 and 27 and is rated with a high-severity score of 8.1 by Oracle (using CVSS v3.1) and a critical severity score of 9.2 by Calif (using CVSS v4.0).

The exploitation of Java4Shell can allow unauthenticated attackers corrupt memory in Java servers with a single malformed message.

According to a write-up from Calif, the blast radius of a potential exploit could be broad, with many Java-based applications built on OpenJDK also vulnerable.

Services vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) attack which has exploited Java4Shell include Keycloak, Atlassian’s products like Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate as well as many distributions based on OpenJDK:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

Other services can also be vulnerable to a Java4Shell exploit, but only if the attacker is able to authenticate. These include Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Maintainers of OpenJDK have published a fix, but each Java vendor will ship its fixed build on its own schedule.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published an emergency advisory on November 17 urging organizations to apply patches as soon as they are available.

Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit

Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit.

In two separate reports, VulnCheck and Endor Labs highlighted that exploitation of the vulnerability is hardware-specific, depending on the Java version, the underlying server processor and the application running on it.

Both research teams noted that the flaw affects CPUs supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions, while ARM-based servers, including AWS Graviton, are not affected.

VulnCheck said its researchers had successfully reproduced the vulnerability on Ice Lake hardware, adding that processors without AVX-512 VBMI and BW support use an alternative decoding path that does not contain the defect.

Endor Labs noted that the affected processors include recent Intel and AMD server chips, which account for much of current cloud capacity.

As of November 18, no attacks exploiting the vulnerability had been reported in the wild.

CISA Mitigation Recommendations

CISA recommended the following mitigation measures:

Identify affected Java installations: review software inventories for Java Development Kits (JDKs) and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications, container images and appliances, as they may not appear as separate inventory entries

Apply security patches: install relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they become available, prioritizing internet-facing systems

Implement safeguards: where immediate patching is not possible, implement temporary safeguards, such as validating and restricting Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access

Review vendor guidance: consult Oracle’s security advisory for additional patching instructions and recommendations

Monitor for suspicious activity: watch for indicators of potential exploitation, including rogue Java runtimes, unexpected Java Virtual Machine (JVM) crashes and suspicious Java processes

articles.title: New Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years
articles.context: The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack
articles.full_text:
On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.

That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.

Both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days.

AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs.

The TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip.

If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up.

On AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the update and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state.

RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value.

On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart.

For the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes.

Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes.

The BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds.

In both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed.

The researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check.

The researchers have published their attack firmware, board designs, and scripts. They say reproducing the RPMC attacks is not plug-and-play and needs one of their boards. Neither the paper nor the vendor notices published so far describe attacks outside the lab.

Which PCs the Attack Works On and What Vendors Say

Whether the attack works depends on the processor and the flash chip:

AMD-based PCs with RPMC flash: open to the board that blocks counter updates. The chipmaker has confirmed the firmware flaw behind this and plans to fix it.

AMD-based PCs without RPMC flash: on two AMD desktops in the researchers' tests, writing an old copy back with an ordinary flash programmer reset the count, requiring no board. They conclude that AMD processors likely have no other protection against this, though two desktops may not be representative of all AMD systems.

PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the researchers say these are open to the leaked-key method whatever the processor, and that only a new chip design can fix it.

Intel PCs without RPMC-like flash: three Intel systems detected the same write-back in those tests.

The researchers expect the AMD firmware flaw to affect AMD PCs that use the Microsoft Pluton security core as their TPM, but did not show this.

On an AMD PC, the owner can boot Linux, for example from a live USB stick, and run the command grep . /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp/*/rpmc_* from the researchers' exposure check. The output indicates whether RPMC flash is present and enabled, which tells the owner which of the two methods applies. Missing files do not mean the PC lacks RPMC.

For Intel PCs, the researchers know of no such check. Owners would have to open the PC and look for a Winbond chip marked 25R or 74M.

AMD tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-43613 and assigns it a CVSS score of 5.1 in a security bulletin published yesterday.

The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack." The researchers first told it about the flaw in February.

The chipmaker's fix targets run from November to February 2027 across Ryzen, Ryzen AI, Ryzen Threadripper, Athlon and EPYC chips, and one unnamed product has no date yet. These are planned dates for its own firmware, not updates already out for PCs.

The bulletin does not cover AMD PCs without RPMC flash. It also does not say whether the update will prevent an attacker from installing older, unfixed firmware on the PC, which the researchers say a fix must prevent.

Intel, whose processor was in the BitLocker test laptop, said in a security announcement earlier this week that the research "did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component". That matches the tests, in which the attack on the Intel laptop needed the Winbond chip's flaw.

According to the researchers, Intel's security team called the reused value a weakness rather than a vulnerability.

The researchers told Microsoft in April. According to them, the company rated the Windows Hello report as "moderate severity" and below its bar for an immediate fix, issued no CVE or bounty, and committed to raising its recommended minimum Hello PIN length to six digits.

At the company's request, the researchers filed the BitLocker finding as a separate report for a different team. The company declined to give them any further written statement for the paper.

Separately, a Windows 11 test build released late last week makes six digits the minimum for personal-account Hello PINs, with an option to use four. The release notes give no reason, and features in that test channel may never reach regular releases.

According to the researchers, Winbond was first told about its chips' weakness to voltage glitches in January 2025 and received a second report in April showing that a glitch also leaks the key. The flash maker is studying the issue, possibly including a new chip design, but has not committed to a fix or a date.

What Owners and Admins Can Do

Two extra digits make a large difference in the researchers' figures:

Worst-case time to find a numeric PIN

PIN length

With the documented lockout

Hello attack (AMD laptop)

BitLocker attack (Intel laptop)

4 digits

69 days

40 hours

5 hours*

6 digits

19 years

168 days

20 days

8 digits

1,903 years

46 years

6 years

* BitLocker accepts a four-digit PIN only if an admin lowers the six-digit minimum. The times are worst cases calculated from speeds measured on one laptop each.

In May, Microsoft advised moving BitLocker from TPM-only to TPM+PIN to block the YellowKey bypass, as part of its YellowKey mitigation. The same TPM lockout guards that PIN.

Steps for each setup:

Windows Hello for Business: raise the Minimum PIN length policy, under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > PIN Complexity. If it is not set, Windows requires six digits, a worst case of 168 days in the table above, and admins can set it as low as four. The PIN policy settings page lists it on the PIN settings tab.

BitLocker: raise the Configure minimum PIN length for startup policy, which allows 4 to 20 digits and requires six by default. Turning on "Allow enhanced PINs for startup" lets letters and symbols, which the BitLocker PIN guidance recommends for older hardware.

AMD-based PCs: install the firmware update with the chipmaker's fix when one is available for your PC. Until then, the chipmaker advises keeping PCs under physical control and watching for signs of tampering.

PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the flash maker has not committed to a fix, according to the researchers. Intel advises its customers to ask their PC maker about updates.

articles.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability

CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
articles.context: The attacker did not stop after the first release
articles.full_text:
Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.

The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm.

Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack.

Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

How the stealer worked

The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well.

The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps.

Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.

The code was disguised as diagnostics. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The stolen data went to a webhook.site address as compressed, encoded JSON.

The attacker did not stop after the first release. While OX was researching the malware, version 1.26.1 was reverted to the clean 1.26.0. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said.

The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. Both were gone by about 21:20 UTC.

“This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said.

OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened.

The short window may not limit exposure. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. Container images, CI caches, and lockfiles built in the window could still contain it.

AI pipelines in focus

OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access.

It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. No researcher has linked the two attacks.

What security teams should do

Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said.

OX advised teams to check all environments, CI images, and lockfiles for either version and remove it. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido.

If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

articles.title: Java4Shell: A critical flaw with a narrow reach
articles.context: Oracle notes it can only be exploited by supplying data to the affected APIs, such as through a web service
articles.full_text:
.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column490538_289ecd-bb > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}

In this article

Java4Shell can cause memory corruption and, in some applications, remote code execution

Exploitation depends on the Java runtime, processor and application

Most home users are unlikely to be affected, but organizations should patch promptly

A critical-sounding Java flaw is making headlines. Most consumers are unlikely to be affected, but companies running Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and similar tools have work to do.

On November 17, Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in Java’s Base64 decoder. Security firm Calif discovered the flaw and named it Java4Shell. CISA urged organizations to patch immediately.

After a run of high-profile computer problems and security scares, it’s understandable that another vulnerability with a catchy name would set alarm bells ringing. But it’s important to separate the potential damage from the likelihood of being affected. This is a serious issue for organizations running vulnerable applications, not a reason for every home user to assume their computer is at risk.

It doesn’t help that organizations give out different CVSS scores for the same vulnerability.

Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 and describes it as “difficult to exploit.”

Calif rates it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

Meanwhile, there are currently no reports of abuse in the wild. Calif demonstrated remote code execution without logging in on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also demonstrated post-login code execution on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Technical details

Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. It’s used in login protocols, file uploads and network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 CPU instructions.

The bug is in hand-written assembly code for that fast path. A short, malformed input can write 62 bytes past the end of a memory buffer.

For remote code execution, several conditions have to line up:

The right processor. The flaw only affects x86-64 CPUs that support the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. Examples include Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 chips aren’t affected.

A recent OpenJDK-based Java. The flaw affects OpenJDK from 17.0.6 onward, and the distributions built on it.

An exposed Java service. The attacker has to feed crafted data to a Java application that decodes it. Oracle notes it can only be exploited by supplying data to the affected APIs, such as through a web service. It can’t be exploited through untrusted Java Web Start applications or applets.

A target-specific exploit. Calif says there is no universal exploit. Each chain needs a decoder route, a feedback path, a heap layout, and an application-specific action. The attack also works best with low, stable network latency, and Calif rented a VM in the same region as its target.

An ordinary home PC rarely runs a Java server that accepts Base64 input from the internet. Organizations running affected Java applications on vulnerable processors should patch promptly, since attackers may find narrow, application-specific paths to remote code execution.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: Three AI Models Agree on Just One of 121 Potential Code Flaws
articles.context: " If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit
articles.full_text:
Three frontier AI models given the same open source code to audit have produced vulnerability findings that barely overlap, according to new frontier AI research. Of 121 distinct potential issues, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Z.ai's GLM-5.3 all flagged just one, software security firm Echo found.

Echo published the comparison in its November 18 research. Each model worked through two Maven libraries and one npm package with Echo's own hunting framework and the same validation process. Echo reached GPT-5.6 Sol through Daybreak, the program OpenAI runs for vetted security teams.

Of the 121 issues, 83% (100), came from a single model and 20 from the other two.

Read more on AI vulnerability discovery: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

Where the AI Models Disagreed

Claude Mythos logged the most validation passes overall, with 25, against nine for GLM-5.3 and eight for GPT-5.6 Sol. But GPT-5.6 Sol accounted for six of the seven passes on one Maven library, and GLM-5.3 found six validated issues on the other that its rivals missed.

Severity ratings split too. GLM-5.3 rated one flaw in an npm package with more than 350 million monthly downloads as Critical, Claude Mythos put it at High and GPT-5.6 Sol treated it as documented behavior rather than a bug. Automated validation rated it Low.

GPT-5.6 Sol finished its hunts in about 24 minutes, against roughly 198 for Claude Mythos and 174 for GLM-5.3. GLM-5.3 was the cheapest overall, with its three hunts costing about $22, against $303 for Claude Mythos and $30 for GPT-5.6 Sol, though Echo said the costs reflected its own access terms.

How Many AI Findings Held Up

The nine runs produced 446 initial findings, cut to 152 after cleanup. Of those, 74 were rated High or Critical, and 55 went through automated proof-of-concept testing after duplicates were set aside. Forty-two passed.

Echo cautioned that the 42 were not necessarily distinct bugs, since an issue found by more than one model could be credited to each. Findings rated Medium or Low were never tested, so a previously known flaw that Claude Mythos rated Medium never reached validation.

Echo security researcher Yuval Saggie said the race to find the best model was "the wrong question." If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit."

Each model ran only once, and Echo called the exercise "a controlled comparison rather than a comprehensive benchmark." It said automated validation did not amount to confirmation from the projects' maintainers.

Echo said the projects would stay unnamed, and technical details unpublished, until their maintainers had been notified.

articles.title: The Silent Consensus
Watchdog Warns UK Government Is Falling Short on Risk Management
articles.context: The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18
articles.full_text:
The number of chief risk officers (CROs) in UK government has more than doubled over the past decade, but most industry professionals working in Whitehall believe they lack influence, according to a new National Audit Office (NAO) report.

The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18.

It noted that effective risk management is important in helping to manage fast emerging risks, like the recent PHP vulnerabilities, which have the potential to disrupt public services and lead to costly recovery work.

It can also “help public bodies make better decisions, adapt to uncertainty and take well-managed risks to innovate and improve services,” the NAO argued.

However, 58% of risk professionals it polled claimed they are typically brought in too late to shape decisions.

“We found limited evidence of major decisions or organizational direction changing because of input from risk professionals,” the report noted. “In hierarchical organizations, the often low seniority of those leading risk teams can also restrict their access to senior decision-making forums.”

Read more on risk management: 75% CISOs Fear Executives Don’t Understand Cybersecurity Risks Employees Face

In the cyber sphere, a lack of skills and awareness are undermining efforts to embed risk more fully in decision making, the report found.

For example, Audit and Risk Assurance Committees (ARACs) should provide independent advice and challenge the board and accounting officer. But the report noted that “skills gaps among committee members in evolving areas such as cybersecurity” are constraining their effectiveness.

Additionally, leaders don’t always understand the cyber risks outlined in risk registers “or recognize how they relate to their strategic objectives,” the NAO said.

Many government departments are at least defining their risk appetite, but less than half (47%) of those polled said this actually informs decisions. In June 2026, most reported that the majority of their principal risks were outside their stated tolerance.

“Legacy technology and specialist staff shortages may constrain departments’ ability to bring cybersecurity risks within appetite,” the report noted.

In many cases, the result is that known risks aren’t being addressed promptly. The NAO highlighted the case of the British Library, which had already identified risks from growing third-party access to IT systems, but was breached before planned changes were implemented.

Risk Management Critical in Interconnected Environment

Progress is being made, but is uneven across government, with many bodies not making use of performance information, early warning indicators, or assurance mapping to monitor risk management efforts, the report argued.

This is more important than ever given today’s “complex and interconnected” risk environment, it said.

Only a continuous approach to risk monitoring and improvement will do, the NAO argued. This means ensuring risk registers are “robust and ‘living documents’ that reflect significant risks,” it said.

"The past few years have highlighted the scale and complexity of the risks facing government and how quickly they can escalate into crises, with lasting consequences for public services,” said Gareth Davies, head of the NAO.

“Whilst it has made good progress, the government must now put risk management at the heart of how it plans, spends and delivers, making sure that senior leaders are equipped to spot vulnerabilities early and to take well-manged risks to improve public services. This will become ever more important as more decisions and public spending are devolved.”

articles.title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
articles.context: Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne
articles.full_text: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology. "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear." MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases. Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

articles.title: The resilience gap: Why cybersecurity investment alone is not enough
articles.context: If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first
articles.full_text:
Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality.

Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong.

Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing.

Ultimately, the investment didn’t fail; the expectation did. Technology alone can’t deliver an outcome that also depends on people, process, governance and coordination. The lesson is clear: A well-funded cybersecurity program can still be operationally fragile.

The findings in Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study illustrate the problem. Cybersecurity remains the leading strategic investment priority, selected by 48% of CISOs. Yet only 41% report high or very high confidence in their organizations’ ability to protect enterprise value, while just 29% express that level of confidence in responding with agility. Another 54% describe their confidence in their organizations’ ability to respond with agility as moderate.

That gap should concern every CISO. It suggests organizations have built security capabilities without fully developing the enterprise operating model needed during disruption.

The real test begins when prevention ends

Security investment matters. But you aren’t buying away cyber risk. You’re buying it down. Even the most mature organizations will eventually face an event they cannot prevent, often involving a third party, technology failure or circumstance outside their control.

What happens next separates resilient organizations from everyone else. Security works to contain the threat while infrastructure and application teams decide what can safely go offline. Business leaders push to restore critical services, sometimes with competing priorities. Legal weighs disclosure obligations with incomplete information. Communications prepares messages for employees, customers and regulators.

Meanwhile, a cloud, software-as-a-service or other technology provider may control part of the environment the company needs to recover.

That’s where resilience usually breaks down: not within any one team, but in the handoffs and decisions between them. In the exercises we run, the hardest questions are often surprisingly basic:

Who has the authority to shut down a revenue-producing system?

If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first?

If Microsoft 365 or another primary collaboration platform is unavailable, how does the crisis team communicate?

If a critical provider is also down, do its recovery priorities and timelines align with yours?

The useful output of an exercise is not a reassuring score. It is the list of things that didn’t work: unclear authority, gaps in escalation paths, inaccessible backups and dependencies that teams incorrectly assumed had been tested. Consider Quantum Dawn VIII, SIFMA’s sector-wide exercise from November 2025. The polycrisis scenario included an undersea cable cut, and roughly two-thirds of participants said they had either never tested that scenario or weren’t sure they had. That is exactly the kind of blind spot an exercise is designed to expose. Better to uncover it in an exercise than during an actual disruption.

And the event you plan for is seldom the event you get. That’s why resilience cannot depend on following a script. Build a framework that enables collaboration and increases the speed of informed decisions, regardless of what actually happens.

Cyber, AI and third-party risks no longer stay in their lanes

Risks don’t arrive one at a time. A cyberattack can quickly become a privacy issue, a regulatory matter and a business interruption. A third-party outage becomes your outage. And AI can act as a force multiplier, allowing a single issue to move faster and spread across more data, systems and business processes.

The findings support this. Cyber threats remain the highest-rated near-term concern in the Top Risks survey, but privacy, third-party risk, AI, resilience and regulatory uncertainty are now clustered closely behind.

AI doesn’t change the fundamental resilience questions. It raises the stakes. An agent may read customer data, query an ERP system, act through a service account or trigger a workflow without a person clicking the button. So, start with an old question: What can it access? Then ask whose permissions or delegated authority it is using, what actions it can take, where those actions are logged and how quickly you can stop it when something goes wrong.

CISOs appear to recognize that challenge. In our 2027 Top Risks study, 51% identified improving AI governance and accountability as a leading priority, while 45% pointed to workforce readiness. That’s telling. Sustainable adoption requires some basic discipline: maintain an inventory of agents and their owners, map the data and tools each can reach, restrict service accounts and delegated permissions, monitor actions and make sure access can be revoked quickly.

Third parties deserve the same scrutiny. A third-party assessment can tell you a lot about a provider’s controls at a point in time. What it rarely tells you is how that provider will perform on a bad day. Most assessments still rely heavily on documentation, discussion and self-reporting. Those assessments may assure a provider’s security posture, but they do not prove that a critical service will remain available, that the provider’s recovery sequence aligns with yours or that the appropriate people on both sides know how to disconnect, communicate and restore service together.

CISOs should be able to identify the external relationships most critical to business operations, understand the services and data that depend on them, and test what will happen if those relationships are interrupted.

This broader responsibility is increasingly part of the CISO mandate. CSO’s examination of how CISOs can rise to the business resilience challenge describes the role’s evolution from a primarily preventive function toward greater responsibility for response, recovery and business resilience.

Build resilience into the investments already underway

If cyber risk increasingly travels through interconnected systems and infrastructure, resilience has to be part of how those environments are modernized in the first place.

The percentage of CISOs selecting cybersecurity slipped from 53% to 48%, while the percentage selecting infrastructure modernization rose from 21% to 33%. Taken together, those shifts make sense. Security and modernization are increasingly intertwined. A cloud migration, enterprise resource planning (ERP) replacement, identity redesign or data-platform upgrade can retire unsupported systems and standing privileges. It can also create new concentration risk, recovery dependencies and failure points if resilience is not designed in from the start.

CISOs should use these major transformation programs to improve resilience, not complicate it. Questions to ask include:

Are we retiring legacy platforms and connections, or simply putting a new layer on top of them?

Are old accounts, interfaces, backup jobs and vendor dependencies actually being removed?

Can the order-to-cash, payments, customer service or other critical processes be restored faster after the investment?

Are recovery, isolation and alternate-processing requirements in the architecture and acceptance criteria from the start?

Have we tested the new platform’s recovery path, or are we assuming modernization made it more resilient?

Closing the resilience gap

The point isn’t to spend less on cybersecurity. It’s to expect more from the investment. The 2027 Top Risks study shows CISOs balancing cyber threats with AI, third-party risk, resilience and modernization. Those may look like separate priorities on a survey. In practice, they increasingly collide in the same incident.

We aren’t going to prevent every cyber incident. The question is what happens when the next one gets through. Does the organization know what matters most, who makes the hard calls and how to recover? Or does it figure those things out during the crisis?

That gap is the resilience gap. And it is where CISOs should be looking next.

articles.title: How organizations can secure their AI-generated code
articles.context: “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do
articles.full_text:
The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts.

The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure.

“He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit. “We’re EU based.”

When asked whether he had read the AI-generated code or taken any security precautions, the new hire said, “My GitHub repo is private.”

The IT manager took the concern to the CEO, who brushed it aside: “Let it go.”

In many organizations, vibe coders build software without thinking much about security. Their apps may get the job done, but they are ticking bombs.

In SusVibes, a benchmark of 186 real-world feature requests from open-source projects, agents given feature descriptions without security guidance produced working code up to 57% of the time. But only 11.8% of their solutions were secure.

“The failures we saw were not careless errors,” says Danqing Wang of Carnegie Mellon University’s Language Technologies Institute, author of the paper describing SusVibes. “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do.”

What has changed, especially this year, is that AI code-generating tools have gotten so good at producing working code that people are just trusting them, says Dr. Katie Paxton-Fear, staff security advocate at Semgrep. “Developers simply aren’t being as critical now as they were when AI was worse at writing code.”

Whether it’s the vibe-coder in marketing or the seasoned engineering team boosting its productivity, AI-generated code is an increasing security concern for CISOs. Much of that is a function of volume, but even as AI has proved highly capable of finding flaws in code bases, it is not yet adept at contributing code without introducing its own.

Treating AI-generated code as ‘untrusted input’

Leading AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Amazon Q Developer have become developer go-to tools, and CIOs are increasingly enlisting business users to vibe code their own apps.

But as AI-generated code surfaces everywhere, CISOs have only one option: to treat it “as untrusted input that has to earn its way into the codebase,” says Bianca Lankford, VP of engineering at Datadog.

To do so, security leaders are moving security checks closer to where code is written: static analysis, secrets scanning, and dependency checks run on every pull request and, increasingly, in the developer’s editor.

“Companies are also approving specific AI tools, limiting what assistants can access, and training reviewers to spot common AI mistakes like outdated libraries, weak input validation, and overly permissive defaults,” Lankford adds.

At Mimecast, using AI to write code doesn’t remove the developer’s responsibility for it, says Leslie Nielson, CISO at the information security vendor. “A named person owns every AI-assisted change that ships, and that’s recorded in the pull request, not assumed,” he adds. “AI can propose. Only people can approve.”

The volume of code organizations need to review is only growing, and reviewing everything manually can be impossible. That’s why Nielsen recommends security leaders combine automated checks with human judgment.

“We use automation for the known and repetitive, like dependency checks, secrets detection, and standard vulnerability patterns,” he says. “We keep a person accountable for anything involving access, authentication, or sensitive data. Those categories always go to a specialist reviewer, regardless of how clean the scan looks.”

Datadog’s Lankford says the decision to bring in a specialist should depend on what the code could put at risk, not on what entity — human or AI — wrote it. “Anything involving authentication, cryptography, payments, personal data, or infrastructure goes to a specialist, and code owner rules can route those changes automatically,” she says. “Other useful signals include diff size, new dependencies, and changes to permissions or network exposure.”

The goal is to protect the human reviewers’ attention. “A reviewer buried in low-risk changes isn’t reviewing,” Nielsen adds. “They’re approving.”

Another priority should be preserving the knowledge behind the code. “Generative AI may produce software, but it cannot produce understanding,” notes Alex Ștefănescu, security expert and tech activist. “Documentation, a solid test suite, and a written record of every significant architecture decision ever made are going to save developers and organizations countless hours when a security incident hits or when they are debugging complex issues.”

All of this should be created and maintained by people and intended for human use, not externalized to generative algorithms, Ștefănescu adds.

What’s at risk with AI-generated code

The inclusion of third-party libraries or phantom dependencies — dependencies that are not explicitly declared in a manifest file — is a common concern with AI-generated code, as these unreported software packages might not be identified during a scan and can potentially hide vulnerabilities.

One way to address this is to use software composition analysis (SCA) and software supply chain security tools to help identify the libraries in use, as well as the vulnerabilities and potential legal and compliance issues that might bring.

While not unique to AI-generated code, organizations also expose themselves to risks when developers download machine learning (ML) models or datasets from platforms such as Hugging Face.

“In spite of security checks on both ends, it may still happen that the model contains a backdoor that becomes active once the model is integrated,” says Ștefănescu. “This could ultimately lead to data being leaked from the company that used the malicious models.”

When it comes to coding agents and code completion functionality in tools like GitHub Copilot, Ștefănescu worries about hallucinations. “An LLM will always generate the most statistically probable continuation of a given prompt, so there are no real guarantees in place that it will generate a real package from PyPI, for example, after the word ‘import’,” they say. “Some attackers are aware of this and register package names on platforms like npm and PyPI, filling in some functionality that code completion tools suggest in order to make the packages seem legitimate.”

If these packages are imported into real applications, they can do real damage.

Sensitive information inadvertently leaking into codebases because of developers using AI-powered coding tools is another key concern.

To address these risks, CISOs can establish protocols for downloading and integrating ML models or datasets from external platforms such as Hugging Face and ensure those protocols are incorporated in AI code agents’ instruction files where applicable. Such protocols can include implementing automated scanning tools to detect malicious code or backdoors, having a policy that only allows the use of models from verified publishers, or conducting internal testing in isolated environments.

Not all AI-based code comes from teams full of software engineers. “We see a lot of adoption being driven by data analysts, marketing teams, researchers, etc., within organizations,” says Darren Meyer, staff research engineer at Endor Labs.

These teams aren’t traditionally developing their own software but are increasingly writing simple tools that adopt AI libraries and models, so they’re often not aware of the risks involved. “This combination of shadow engineering with lower-than-average application security awareness can be a breeding ground for risk,” he adds.

To make sure these teams are working safely, CISOs must consider forming relationships with these teams early in the process. Cybersecurity leaders might also want to set up training programs tailored to non-traditional development teams to educate data analysts, marketing professionals, and researchers on the potential risks associated with AI-based tools and libraries.

Investing in defense

“Security budgets don’t generally grow at the same pace that software development accelerates, and AI adoption is only widening that gap,” Meyer says. Application security is often underfunded in most organizations, yet allocating sufficient time and resources to it is essential, as AI adoption and AI-assisted coding accelerate the pace of software development.

“A portfolio of high-quality security tools that can help address this gap is no longer optional,” Meyer says. “And while tools are critical to closing the gap, so are AppSec and ProdSec staff that can effectively partner with developers — even non-traditional developers — and understand the technical, compliance, and security implications of AI.”

When it comes to securing enough resources to protect AI systems, some stakeholders might hesitate, viewing it as an optional expense rather than a critical investment. “AI adoption is a divisive topic in many organizations, with some leaders and teams being ‘all-in’ on adoption and some being strongly resistant,” Meyer says. “This tension can present challenges for insightful CISOs and business information security officers (BISOs).”

CISOs that are aware of both the advantages and disadvantages of this might try to set controls to manage risks effectively, but this might create the perception of holding the organization back from innovating if they don’t explain what they do properly. “Organizations need to develop comprehensive strategies that balance the productivity benefits of AI tools with robust security practices,” says Thomas Segura, senior technical writer at GitGuardian.

Cost-effective changes CISOs should implement

But if a security leader has 90 days and no budget to spare, which changes would have the biggest impact?

Datadog’s Lankford says a short, plain-language AI tool policy can make expectations clear. At a minimum, such a policy should spell out which tools employees can use, what code and data they can share, and which changes need specialist review. The aim is to give people answers they can use while they work, with a clear point of contact when they’re unsure.

It’s also important to understand that employees don’t want to circumvent policies. They just want to get their work done without friction and without waiting weeks for approval. Giving them the right tools makes the safer route easier to take.

By contrast, banning tools doesn’t work, because employees will find a way to still use them. A ban can push AI use out of sight, leaving security teams with less visibility into the code being written and the data being shared, Mimecast’s Nielsen says.

CISOs should look across the development process to identify where they can intervene and which risks they can address at each stage. “Understand what layers you can influence and what vulnerabilities you can influence at each layer: in the design phase, in the CLAUDE.md file, as the agent is writing, during a pull request, as part of an AI pentest,” Semgrep’s Paxton-Fead says.

It’s also important to explain to employees who are using AI code-generating tools that security lives in an implicit context: the threat model, the trust boundaries, what the attacker controls. “Agents cannot reliably plan and reason on these, so they optimize for the only signal they have, which is to satisfy the given functionality description,” Carnegie Mellon’s Wang says.

When things go wrong, people in the organization need to feel safe telling security what happened, including which unapproved tools they used and what data they shared. Fear of punishment can delay that conversation, leaving the team trying to contain a problem without the full picture.

“Offer amnesty instead of a crackdown, so people tell you the truth about what they’re using,” Nielsen advises.

Betrayed Expectations: Malware Delivery via Common Brands
articles.context: By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware...
articles.full_text:
By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence observed a 239% rise in phishing campaigns that weaponize brand names to deliver malware onto corporate devices as compared to the first half of 2025. Adobe, the Social Security Administration, Docusign, the IRS, and Zoom are among the most abused. The names are familiar by design: employees who expect a routine document from a recognized sender appear more likely to click, and the borrowed credibility of those brands helps the emails slip past automated security filters. There are two primary ways that brands can be spoofed to deliver malware and abused legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

The first is the initial phishing email. The brand spoofed in the email is what sets the expectation for the context of the campaign. For example, threat actors have used lures such as a refund sent by the IRS (Figure 5) and a benefits-themed document sent by the Social Security Administration (Figure 3). When a victim expects a file but does not realize the sender is malicious, they are likely to click on a phishing link.

The second way a brand can be abused is through the filename. To trick victims, malware may be named “Social_Security_Administration_v02.4_EN_US.msi” (Figure 3) or “setup_Zoom.msi” (Figure 6), depending on the brand used in the phishing email. These malware files are often hosted on cloud services like Google or Amazon, which can bypass the organization’s security controls.

What makes this threat category particularly difficult to manage is that the tools being delivered are not traditional malware. ConnectWise RAT, Datto RMM, SimpleHelp, and similar products are the same software that many IT departments use for legitimate remote support. Threat actors favor them precisely because standard security systems are built to trust them.

Key Points

In the first half of this year, 18% of all malware delivery campaigns impersonated new brands not seen before.

Adobe is the most abused brand when delivering malware in the first half of 2026.

The malware downloaded usually has a filename matching the phishing email branding, like “Adobe software update.msi”.

Threat actors often abuse legitimate cloud services like Google or Amazon to distribute malware and bypass security controls.

94% of campaigns delivering malware abuse legitimate remote access tools (RATs).

Brand Campaign Volume

Malware delivering campaigns increased 239% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025.

The top five brands account for around 24% of all malware delivery campaign volume in the first half of this year.

Figure 1: The relative proportion of brands spoofed in the first half of 2026.

In the first half of 2026, Cofense Intelligence identified brands like Adobe, Social Security Administration, Docusign, IRS, and Zoom being abused in malware delivery campaigns. Docusign and Adobe are part of normal organizational operations. These brands follow the trends first identified in 2021. Social Security Administration-spoofing and IRS-spoofing after April mark the trend of government themed phishing outside of the IRS tax season. Zoom has typically been abused to host documents with links to credential phishing pages—and rarely links to malware pages.

Adobe Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Adobe-spoofing phishing campaigns rank #1 by volume in the first half of 2026.

Adobe-spoofing phishing emails delivering malware experienced an 18-fold increase when compared to the first half of 2025.

Adobe-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (44%), Datto RMM (16%), and GoTo RAT (7%).

These software are technically legitimate remote access tools (RATs) but can be abused by threat actors to gain unauthorized administrative access.

Figure 2: Adobe-spoofing website claiming a software update is necessary (ATR 415874).

In credential phishing, Adobe has been used to host documents with links to malicious websites. Typically, PDFs with shortened links or QR codes obfuscate the credential phishing pages. In Adobe-spoofing campaigns delivering malware, the email usually claims a document is available to view.

After clicking on the phishing link and attempting to download the document, a website opens. The malicious website typically claims that Adobe Reader is out of date, and an update is necessary to see the PDF. Installing the file will deliver a legitimate RAT controlled by the threat actor. In these Adobe software update phishing campaigns, threat actors like to abuse tools such as ConnectWise’s ScreenConnect (ConnectWise RAT) and Datto RMM to take over the victim machine. For example, Figure 2 shows one website that claims Adobe Reader is out of date and downloads malware. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) for Figure 2 are listed in Active Threat Report (ATR) 415874. ATRs contain the context for each threat actor campaign, allowing current and similar campaigns to be blocked.

Social Security Administration Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Social Security Administration-spoofing is the second highest by campaign volume.

Campaign volume in the first half of 2025 is roughly equivalent to volume in the first half of 2026.

SSA-spoofing typically delivers ConnectWise RAT (55%), SimpleHelp (12%), and Faronics Deploy (9%).

Figure 3: Social Security Administration-spoofing email that bypasses email security technology to deliver ConnectWise RAT (ATR 417484).

In the United States, the Social Security Administration (SSA) becomes an important consideration near retirement age (at least age 62). For eligible members of the workforce, this pension information can dictate the lifestyle one lives after employment ends. Previous campaign iterations in Q4 2024 prioritized urgency and consequences when phishing. Current SSA-spoofing emails usually claim to provide information rather than demand it. Figure 3 shows an SSA download statement phishing email, one of the scams the SSA Office of the Inspector General warns about.

If the phishing link is clicked, an SSA-spoofing website typically opens, and a file download starts. The file appears similar to those in the Docusign and Adobe sections. Some files act like benefit letters or document notifications. Others require a download file to be run because “Adobe Reader is out of date”. As usual, running the file will install a threat actor-controlled legitimate RAT. The RATs most commonly installed are ConnectWise RAT and SimpleHelp. The SSA-impersonation campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT has been going on since at least 2024.

Docusign Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Docusign-spoofing emails increased about 250% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Docusign-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (34%), GoTo RAT (11%), Itarian RAT (5%), or some combination of the three.

Figure 4: Docusign-spoofing file is a SuperOps RMM instance abused by the threat actor (ATR 415883).

Docusign is typically used by threat actors to host documents with links to redirect to malicious websites, usually Microsoft-spoofing credential phishing pages. This is because using trusted websites help bypass email security technologies, and abusing legitimate business tools helps malicious content mimic benign content. Docusign-branded emails are also useful for getting recipients to download fake documents. Downloading the fake document will deliver malware instead of the expected file.

Threat actors will typically use the Docusign style for the email, the malware download website, and the filename. As seen in Figure 4, a malicious file is named like a Docusign attachment. Threat actors like to deliver legitimate RATs that they control, like ConnectWise RAT and GoTo RAT.

IRS Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

IRS-spoofing email volume experienced a 10-fold increase when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

IRS-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (50%), Tiflux RAT (13%), Splashtop (13%) or some combination of the three.

Figure 5: IRS-spoofing, tax refund-themed phishing campaign delivering ConnectWise RAT (ATR 415954).

In the first half of 2025, IRS-spoofing campaigns delivering malware were most prevalent before the USA tax filing date on April 15. Now in the first half of 2026, threat actors continue to use the IRS brand in phishing emails past the tax filing deadline but with many themed about late filing deadlines. Well-developed phishing lures used after April 15 include a refund that has been processed or a tax filing extension being made available. As threat actors use current topics like Elon Musk and DOGE offering an IRS tax refund, IRS-spoofing campaigns are expected to increase.

As with the general rise in threat-actor abused legitimate RATs, IRS-spoofing campaigns deliver similar malware in most cases. ConnectWise RAT is once again the most popular RAT to be abused in IRS-spoofing campaigns. There is also a multi-stage campaign where Tiflux RAT is first installed, then Tiflux RAT installs Splashtop and an UltraVNC utility. In earlier group-delivered malware campaigns, the malware was primarily purpose-built for threat actors and entirely malicious. In the case of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop, both are developed by legitimate organizations for IT operations. Unfortunately, the instances of Tiflux RAT and Splashtop delivered in these campaigns are controlled by threat actors.

Zoom Spoofing Campaigns Delivering Malware

Zoom-spoofing emails delivering malware increased over 100% when comparing the first half of 2026 to the first half of 2025.

Zoom-spoofing campaigns typically deliver ConnectWise RAT (29%), TrustConnect (14%), and Atera (7%).

Figure 6: A fake Zoom website that downloads an abused RAT (ATR 416603).

Legitimate Zoom links can prompt users to download the Zoom app to access the meeting. Threat actors frequently spoof Zoom and hijack this expected behavior to trick users into downloading malware instead.

Zoom-spoofing phishing emails match the format of legitimate Zoom meeting emails, but the links will redirect to a malware download page instead of the legitimate Zoom site. The most prominent malware delivered is ConnectWise RAT again. TrustConnect and Atera are similar RATs abused by threat actors and delivered in Zoom-spoofing campaigns. Figure 6 shows a malicious Atera instance being downloaded from a threat actor’s website.

Problems Caused by Legitimate Remote Access Tool Abuse

As legitimate RATs are developed for enterprise use, abuse of these tools by threat actors may hide in plain sight.

ConnectWise RAT is currently the most abused legitimate RAT, instead of NetSupport Manager RAT.

When used for their intended purpose, legitimate remote access tools can reduce costs and improve efficiency. With legitimate RATs, IT professionals can easily maintain and monitor various devices across the organization without needing physical access to it. This elevated privilege becomes problematic when threat actors gain access to it.

Legitimate RATs are just as capable of purpose-built malware in the hands of a threat actor. With PowerShell commands, additional malware payloads can be installed after the initial RAT infection. Threat actors have used ConnectWise RAT to deliver ransomware before.

Organizations can find it hard to identify and contain legitimate RATs used by threat actors. Threat actors may even use the same RATs the organization uses, making context, continuous monitoring, and mitigative controls especially important. If the organization successfully contains one type of RAT, threat actors can easily use a different legitimate RAT for infections. In each of the brands spoofed in this report, threat actors already abuse various legitimate RATs.

Conclusions

This report shows five prominent brands spoofed by threat actors. Some key insights include malicious content nearly indistinguishable from legitimate brands, and the increasing abuse of legitimate remote administrative tools. These tactics by the threat actors can make it harder for both users and security analysts to determine if something is legitimate or not. Especially noteworthy are IRS-spoofing and Social Security Administration-spoofing phishing emails. IRS-spoofing emails will likely continue to increase even outside of tax filing season. Social Security Administration-spoofing emails already are not limited by a specific season.

Page Break

Mitigations

Establish and enforce a software allowlist for remote access tools. Any remote access tool not on that list, including ConnectWise, SimpleHelp, Atera, and GoTo RAT, should be blocked from installing on corporate devices. Organizations that do not have an allowlist should at minimum block the digital certificates associated with remote access tools they do not use.

Update employee security awareness training to reflect current lure themes, specifically Adobe document requests, SSA benefit notices, IRS refund emails, and Zoom meeting invitations. Employees who have been trained on real, current threats are more likely to pause before clicking. Simulation exercises should use these exact scenarios, not outdated generic examples.

Blocking remote access tools and updating training are essential, but threat actors will keep finding new brands, filenames, and legitimate tools to abuse. Organizations need a way to respond quickly when a campaign reaches the inbox or an endpoint. ZDI-26-1037: (0Day) (Pwn2Own) United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP Backend Configuration Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP backend configuration requests. The issue results from the lack of authentication prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device.

Additional Details

Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

articles.title: ZDI-26-1031: (0Day) LiteLLM MCP Command Injection Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LiteLLM
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of LiteLLM. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of MCP stdio configurations. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute a system call. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.

Additional Details

06/17/26 - ZDI reported the vulnerability to the vendor07/03/26 - ZDI asked for updates08/28/26 - ZDI asked for updates09/15/26 - the vendor closed the report as a false positive10/26/26 - ZDI disputed the vendor's closure as the existing fix was incomplete10/29/26 - the vendor reopened the report agreeing the mitigation wasn't enough10/30/26 - ZDI asked for the fix plan11/04/26 - ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish the case as a 0-day advisory on 11/18/2611/13/26 - the vendor stated it planned to ship a fix and issue a GHSA before the 11/18 deadline11/16/26 - ZDI asked the vendor to confirm whether the fix/GHSA had shipped11/17/26 - the vendor clarified no separate patch is coming, and disputed that the report describes a vulnerability11/17/26 - ZDI confirmed the zero-day advisory would publish on 11/18/26

-- Mitigation: The vendor recommends the following mitigation: Stdio MCP servers run admin-chosen host commands; only proxy admins can create or test them. The CVE-2026-42271 allowlist doesn’t limit what admins can run, isn’t a security control, and will be removed. From v1.104.0, stdio servers are disabled unless LITELLM_ENABLE_MCP_STDIO=true is set in env (not via API/config/DB); to stay safe, upgrade to 1.104.0+ and leave unset. Always replace any default/example master key with a strong random value; v1.104.0+ blocks startup if unset, empty, or sk-1234.

Disclosure Timeline

2026-11-18 - Coordinated public release of advisory

articles.title: ZDI-26-1019: (0Day) Open Robotics ROS 2 sros2 load_policy XML External Entity Processing Information Disclosure Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of Open Robotics ROS 2
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows remote attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of Open Robotics ROS 2. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the parsing of policy XML files. Due to the improper restriction of XML External Entity (XXE) references, a crafted document specifying a URI causes the XML parser to access the URI and embed the contents back into the XML document for further processing. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the current user.
