articles.title: Critical Insights on OpenJDK RCE Vulnerability CVE-2026-114938
articles.context: A critical OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can allow an attacker to inject and remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication or user interaction
articles.full_text:
TL;DR

Calif disclosed Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, as an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in OpenJDK.

The flaw is in the Java runtime's Base64 decoding path, not a third-party library. Reachability depends on the runtime build, processor, and whether an application decodes untrusted Base64 data.

Oracle released updated Java builds as part of its November 2026 security update, but its pre-release notice does not map those Java fixes to this CVE by name.

Finding exposure requires checking runtimes on hosts and in container images. Project dependency scans alone will not identify every affected system.

For the current advisory and response guidance, see our Security Event page for the Critical OpenJDK Vulnerability.

A critical OpenJDK vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, can allow an attacker to inject and remotely execute arbitrary code without authentication or user interaction. Calif calls the vulnerability Java4Shell.

The disclosure coincided with Oracle's Java security update on November 17, 2026. That timing has raised questions about which Oracle builds address Java4Shell and what organizations should check.

Teams need to identify vulnerable runtimes across their environments, prioritize network-accessible systems, and apply the patched OpenJDK build through the appropriate vendor.

Java4Shell Is a Runtime Vulnerability, Not a Library Flaw

Java4Shell is a memory corruption vulnerability in the Java runtime itself, not in a third-party library or framework. Because the flaw sits in the runtime, project dependency scans will not identify every affected installation.

Base64 decoding is common in applications that receive data over a network. Our research indicates that a Java 17 application could, in principle, be reachable when it decodes Base64 data from an untrusted source on an affected runtime build and processor.

That does not mean every Java application is exposed in the same way. The runtime build and processor matter, as does whether untrusted input can reach the decoder. The vulnerability is described as pre-authentication, because an attacker may be able to supply that input before logging in or interacting with the application.

Third-party analysis has also reported affected Java versions beyond Java 17. Upwind says it reproduced the memory corruption in tests on Java 17, 21, and 25, and identified Java 27 through code analysis. These are research findings, not a vendor's final affected-version list. Organizations should use vendor guidance to confirm the status of each runtime they operate.

Oracle's November Update Does Not Define the CVE’s Full Scope

Oracle released updated Java builds as part of its November 17 security update. Its November security notice lists 11 Java SE security fixes, all described as remotely exploitable without authentication, with a maximum CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1. Oracle also lists builds for Java SE 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, and 27, along with versions of GraalVM and JavaFX.

The notice is a pre-release announcement and does not identify the 11 issues by CVE. It therefore does not establish which update addresses Java4Shell. The Java versions Oracle lists as affected should not be treated as the confirmed affected-version range for this CVE.

Early coverage reports a 9.2 score for Java4Shell under CVSS 4.0. Oracle reports a maximum score of 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 for its Java SE fixes. Those scores use different CVSS versions and refer to different sets of vulnerabilities. They are not competing scores for the same confirmed issue.

Patch Confirmed Systems and Reduce Exposure

Treat systems confirmed to run a vulnerable OpenJDK build as exposed until the patched runtime is installed. Apply the update supplied by the vendor or distribution responsible for that runtime. Build numbers can vary across distributions, so confirm the fixed version with the supplier rather than assuming a particular version string applies everywhere.

Replacing runtime files on a host does not update a JVM process that is already running. Restart affected services after updating. Rebuild container images using a patched base image, and update products that bundle their own Java runtime. Then verify that the deployed service is running the patched build.

If a product bundles the vulnerable runtime and has no direct upgrade path, contact its maintainers for an update. If no update is available, investigate an alternative component or a mitigating control while tracking the issue to resolution.

Calif’s recommendations describe two possible temporary mitigations: disabling the Base64 intrinsic or limiting AVX use to version 2. The AVX setting applies only to x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and may fail to start. These controls are not replacements for a patched runtime. Test them for compatibility and performance impact, and follow the relevant vendor's guidance.

What Teams Should Do Now

Organizations should:

Inventory runtimes: Check the Java runtime used by each running service, including runtimes on hosts, in container images, and bundled with products. Record the build, vendor, processor, deployment location, and owner. Package inventories can help, but they do not replace checking the runtime a service actually uses.

Assess reachability: Check for the relevant AVX-512 processor support and whether the Java Base64 intrinsic is enabled. Identify which Java services listen for network connections.

Prioritize exposure: Start with internet-facing and other network-accessible systems, then review the rest of the environment.

Confirm and apply the fix: Check Oracle or the relevant OpenJDK supplier for the patched build that applies to each runtime. Restart affected services and rebuild images as needed.

Reduce interim risk: Restrict or monitor network access to confirmed vulnerable systems while updates are being applied. Test any temporary mitigation and follow vendor guidance.

Connect Vulnerability Intelligence to Runtime Inventory

Java4Shell is a reminder that vulnerability response depends on knowing what runs across the environment, including the runtimes beneath applications.

CVE-2026-114938 requires organizations to look beneath project dependencies and account for the runtime installed across their environments. Finding each vulnerable OpenJDK build, assigning an owner, and verifying the patch are essential steps in reducing exposure.

Check Sonatype Guide and the associated Security Event page, which contain current details and response guidance as organizations identify affected OpenJDK deployments and verify remediation.

articles.title: Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks
Optimizely Attack Shows Why Supply Chain Ownership Matters
articles.context: Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and...
articles.full_text:
TL;DR

Malicious JavaScript added to Optimizely projects reached sites across multiple industries, including technology, finance, retail, and media.

The injected JavaScript could swap cryptocurrency addresses, capture payment card information entered into website forms, collect some browser-accessible data, and attempt to deliver iOS exploit chains.

Optimizely said an attacker exploited a vulnerability, added malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and that the company fixed the vulnerability, removed the code, and secured affected accounts.

Organizations using Optimizely should review project code and account access, investigate relevant logs, and assess potential exposure based on how their sites handled payment and session data.

The Optimizely incident shows how a change in one shared service can reach many organizations through software they already trust.

On November 16, 2026, malicious JavaScript was served to visitors of websites using Optimizely Web Experimentation. Report URI identified 188 infected snippets across 178 organizations, including major technology, media, retail, financial services, and travel companies.

A Shared Service Became a Shared Risk

Optimizely lets customers add custom JavaScript to their projects. In this incident, malicious code was placed in a project's custom-code field. The altered snippet was then delivered as part of the site's normal Optimizely integration, so the change did not have to pass through each customer's source repository or software build.

An unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. Optimizely fixed the vulnerability, removed the injected code, secured affected accounts, and added protections against unauthorized code delivery.

This was not a case of attackers changing a customer's application source code or poisoning the CDN cache. The code was added to project settings and delivered as part of a service those websites relied on. An organization can secure its own code and infrastructure while still depending on external services that influence what reaches users.

The Payload Turned Shared Dependence Into Shared Exposure

The injected code used a loader to bring additional JavaScript into the page. Researchers observed multiple loader versions, including one that obscured the external address and another that carried an inline fallback.

That meant blocking one destination alone might not remove every way the code could run.

The payload combined several behaviors:

Cryptocurrency address swapping: The script could replace cryptocurrency addresses in page content and during copy actions, potentially redirecting transfers. Transactions to attacker-controlled wallets were confirmed.

Payment-card skimming: The code looked for card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes submitted through site-controlled forms. It could not access card fields inside cross-origin payment-provider iframes. The available reporting does not establish how many card details were captured.

Browser data collection: The script could send page URLs, screenshots, and cookies available to JavaScript. Cookies marked HttpOnly are not available through document.cookie.

iOS exploit delivery: On Apple mobile devices, the script attempted to load Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. Researchers have not established how many devices, if any, were successfully compromised.

The confirmed cryptocurrency transactions show that at least one part of the operation had financial impact.

These capabilities show why teams need to understand not only what code a service is expected to run, but also what that code can access and how changes to it are controlled.

Integrity and Intelligence Must Cover the Full Path

Component intelligence helps teams identify the software they use, understand its role, and assess its known risks. Artifact integrity addresses a different question: whether the software moving through development and delivery is still the expected artifact. Both matter because organizations need context about their components and confidence in what they build and distribute.

The Optimizely incident exposes a gap between those controls and what happens in production. The malicious code was added through a third-party project setting and delivered to visitors' browsers. It did not need to enter a customer's source repository or change a locally built artifact. A package inventory or artifact check would not, by itself, show whether a vendor-managed script had changed.

That doesn't make component intelligence or artifact integrity less relevant. It means organizations need to understand the scope of each control and account for the code paths it does not cover. Alongside knowing which components enter software and verifying the artifacts teams release, organizations need visibility into the external services that can change code running on their sites.

Software Supply Chain Ownership Is an Operating Model

Organizations using Optimizely Web should consult Optimizely's incident update for current information and use their project and access records to determine whether their sites were affected.

More broadly, this incident shows why responsibility for software inputs and services needs to be shared across development, platform, security, and web teams. Those teams need a common understanding of what their software depends on, how those dependencies reach production, and who is accountable for changes along the way.

Owning the software supply chain means understanding what is being shipped and what external code can become part of the software customers use. Component intelligence, artifact integrity, and runtime visibility each help address a different part of that responsibility. For more on Sonatype's approach, check out our software supply chain security solution.

articles.title: 'TheMailer' Phishing Kit Puts AI in the Driver's Seat
Securely exposing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
articles.context: When you start talking to your agent, the runtime launches a dedicated isolated session that runs in its own dedicated microVM with a completely sandboxed CPU, memory, and...
articles.full_text:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime delivers a secure serverless environment to deploy AI agents and tools at scale. When you start talking to your agent, the runtime launches a dedicated isolated session that runs in its own dedicated microVM with a completely sandboxed CPU, memory, and filesystem allocation. This provides strict data governance, helps to prevent cross-tenant data leakage, and preserves context while isolating stateful reasoning from external sessions.

To govern access control across these environments, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity provisions distinct workload identities to let your agents run. By federating directly with an OpenID Connect identity provider like Amazon Cognito, Okta, or others, the users can only see and interact with agents they’re authorized to use.

But securing the runtime alone doesn’t protect the ingress path perimeter. When you expose your agent to users through a web or mobile application, the AWS Shared Responsibility Model dictates that you should provide a dedicated access layer that enforces tight control over the origin and intent of every request before any traffic reaches the runtime.

The access layer acts as a trusted bridge to authenticate each incoming request, enforce authorization rules, preserve user identity through the request lifecycle, and securely channel all user traffic into the isolated runtime.

This post walks through two architectures for securing access to AgentCore Runtime and provides guidance to help you decide which architecture best fits your organization.

Why propagating identity is important

In an agentic workflow, downstream data access should remain tied to the invoking user’s identity, and each segment in the execution chain is permissioned only for the immediate next hop. Using a single static credential, even one linked to the original requester, grants every immediate component identical, broad access. This directly violates the principle of least privilege, because the ingress gateway, the proxy, and the agent’s tool execution context each require only enough permission to reach the next component.

Recent real-world incidents have demonstrated that agentic workloads can bypass internal prompt guardrails, escape the software sandboxes, and abuse static credentials to move across applications and layers. In a multi-chain agentic architecture, scoping each hop as tightly as possible is key to preventing these exploits.

However, long-running, unattended execution poses a fundamental identity challenge for extended agentic workloads. If an agent runs a complex task that takes hours, the user’s interactive session will expire before the workload ends, making their short-lived OAuth 2.0 access token invalid mid-execution. Refreshing the tokens won’t solve this problem and storing a long-lived, user-scoped credential inside the agent’s runtime environment might reintroduce exactly the broad, standing credential attack surface that the zero-trust architectures are intentionally designed to mitigate.

To mitigate this, identity propagation acts as a critical bridge between authentication at the perimeter and authorization at the data layer. The agent must operate within the invoking user’s authorization scope. Every session receives a short-lived, user-scoped token that provides only the permissions granted to that specific user and authorization is enforced at each hop. If any single segment is compromised, then the exposure is contained in that hop scope. This security model also strengthens a continuous verification process where the tokens are validated at every hop from the ingress endpoint through AgentCore to the downstream resource, so no segment operates with unverified or elevated privileges.

Protecting AgentCore Runtime: What does it need?

We explained in the previous section why identity must follow the user through every hop. However, identity propagation alone isn’t enough to secure the ingress path; it must be integrated within a broader set of ingress controls that together protect the path into the runtime.

AgentCore Runtime provides infrastructure isolation, per session microVMs, per session tool registration, and enforces the application of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. These features and resources protect the execution environment. However, they don’t control who reaches the runtime, how they’re authenticated, or whether their identity is preserved through the chain. That responsibility falls on the ingress control layer that you build. Securing this path requires a defense-in-depth architecture that binds every request to the user’s identity before it ever reaches the agent’s reasoning loop.

To protect and control data access, any architecture exposing AgentCore Runtime to users must satisfy the following requirements:

Authentication: Continuously verify the identity of every requester at the perimeter by validating tokens against the identity provider’s public keys.

Authorization: Determine what the authenticated subject is allowed and authorized to do, which actors they can invoke, which scopes they hold and which operations they can perform.

Per-hop least privilege: Make sure each component in the chain holds only enough permission to call the next hop, eliminating broad-scope credentials. Each hop must exchange the inbound token for a down-scoped, short-lived credential valid only for the immediate downstream call.

Identity propagation: Preserve the user’s identity through the full execution chain, so the agent operates within the user’s authorization scope. For long running or unattended workloads where the user’s session closes mid-flight, the ingress must seamlessly transition the active user token into an encrypted, short lived session context key from AgentCore Runtime. This allows the microVM to securely assert a restricted, cryptographic snapshot of the user’s identity even when the user is completely offline.

Edge security: Inspect and filter traffic before it reaches the application logic, by applying the needed WAF rules, bot control, IP-based rate limiting, and so on.

Network perimeter: Restrict runtime access to a single secure, controlled network path. Traffic arriving from any unexpected origin must be rejected regardless of the token’s validity.

Content protection: Enforce the Guardrails on both incoming prompts for injection attacks and outgoing tool arguments for malicious payload before execution.

Audit and logging: Log every authentication outcome, the authorization decision on the tool invocations, and any security event to an externalized system for compliance and incident response.

These security requirements are mandatory baselines to expose any agentic workloads to users. Any missing requirement might create a potential attack vector. By applying this full set of guardrails, you help contain the impact of a potential malicious exploit to a single user, a single session and a single execution hop.

In the next section, we provide two architecture patterns that implement this propagation differently:

The first architecture validates the user’s token independently at each layer while preserving it for the runtime to verify directly.

The second architecture exchanges the user’s token at the gateway boundary for scoped machine credentials, attesting the user’s identity through verified claims. This pattern is uniquely suited for handling the session context keys required by asynchronous, unattended workloads.

Both approaches achieve the same result: the agent acts as the user rather than with elevated privileges.

The AgentCore Gateway patterns

Each of the following patterns is presented the same way: the layered controls a request passes through before reaching the agent, followed by how user identity is carried to the runtime. As you explore, please note where each pattern places the trust boundary as that difference is what drives the trade-offs summarized at the end.

Pattern A: Expose through API Gateway

We expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon API Gateway, which acts as a dedicated ingress point that terminates each client connection. Before any request reaches the agent, it must pass through layered security controls:

A Lambda authorizer: An AWS Lambda authorizer validates the Amazon Cognito-issued JSON Web Token (JWT) by verifying the signature, issuer claim and token expiration, to confirm the requester’s identity.

AgentCore Identity: Independently, AgentCore Identity performs a second validation inherent to the Lambda authorizer through its OAuth 2.0 inbound authentication flow. This helps to confirm the user’s identity before the request reaches the runtime to be processed.

Because the client-provided session ID is treated as untrusted input, the Lambda authorizer creates a composite session ID by appending the user identifier to the client-provided session ID. Even if two different users submit the same session ID, they resolve to unique composite IDs at the AgentCore Runtime level, preventing any cross-user session leakage.

To prevent denial of service attempts, we suggest using Amazon DynamoDB as a lightweight session counter. While the AWS WAF rate-based rules attached to the API Gateway stage protect against IP-level volumetric abuse, they evaluate requests before authentication. The Lambda authorizer checks and increments a per-user counter in DynamoDB after validating the user’s identity, helping prevent a single authenticated user from exhausting agent capacity, even if they connect from multiple IP addresses. This design scales cleanly by using a composite session ID. The Lambda Authorizer combines the user identifier and the client session ID, routing each user’s counter to a distinct partition. This naturally distributes write traffic and reduces the risk of hot keys.

Each session can sustain roughly 1,000 counter updates per second before reaching DynamoDB’s per-partition write limit, which is far beyond what any legitimate session would ever generate. That same limit is exactly what makes the counter an effective throttle. Meanwhile, total capacity across all users scales horizontally, growing with the number of active sessions. For high-volume production deployments, on-demand capacity mode absorbs sudden spikes automatically, and CloudWatch Contributor Insights lets you confirm traffic stays evenly distributed.

After the Lambda authorizer approves the request, as shown in the Figure 1:

API Gateway forwarding: Passes the approved request to Lambda proxy that runs within an isolated environment with no internet egress.

VPC endpoint routing: The proxy Lambda function forwards the request to AgentCore Runtime through an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) endpoint, making sure that all traffic remains strictly within the private network.

Token preservation and identity propagation: The proxy Lambda function forwards the user’s token unchanged in the authorization header; this maintains the original user identity throughout the entire flow of AgentCore Runtime.

API Gateway forwards the request to a Lambda proxy running on a private VPC with no internet egress. The role of this Lambda proxy is to relay the request to AgentCore Runtime through a VPC endpoint, so that all communication remains within the private network. The Lambda proxy forwards the user’s token (unchanged) in the Authorization header, which preserves the user’s identity all the way to AgentCore Runtime.

Figure 1: Pattern A architecture for exposing AgentCore Runtime through Amazon API Gateway

This VPC endpoint enforces a strict network perimeter using two independent controls:

Security groups: The VPC endpoint security group restricts ingress solely to the proxy Lambda function on port 443, so no other compute in the account can reach the endpoint.

Resource-based policy: The runtime resource-based policy is configured with principal "*" and a condition that allows invocations only when the request carries aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce values matching this stack’s VPC and endpoint. Authentication happens at the AgentCore Identity level, so there is no AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal to match, and the network path is the only meaningful gate and condition that remains. AgentCore Runtime rejects requests sent directly from outside the VPC with an AccessDeniedException, even with a valid JWT.

Beyond the network boundary, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails evaluates each model’s invocation for prompt injection attacks, helping catch malicious inputs even after an invocation has passed identity and network verification. This adds content protection as a defensive layer independent of identity and network controls.

Your stack logs and tracks every authorization outcome along this path as structured JSON to Amazon CloudWatch, with an INVALID_JWT alarm. The full walkthrough and a deployable AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) sample are linked at the end of this post.

Before production deployment, we recommend configuring an AWS WAF Web ACL at the API Gateway stage to inspect requests before they reach the Lambda authorizer. You should include AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet for generic OWASP Top 10 protections and known exploit patterns, AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet to catch injection signatures, a per-IP rate-based rule ahead of the DynamoDB throttle counters, and custom rules to reject oversized requests or malformed session IDs early. For a step-by-step integration guide including two deployment patterns for placing AWS WAF in front of the AgentCore Runtime, see Securing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with AWS WAF.

This first pattern satisfies the ingress security requirements discussed earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying the authentication at two independent layers, enforcing authorization through session binding and controlling traffic through per-user throttling. The architecture maintains per-hop least privilege from the API Gateway through the AgentCore Runtime while preserving end-user identity propagation by passing the user’s token through unchanged. The edge filtering is managed with AWS WAF and the network perimeter is enforced by VPC endpoint controls. The design includes the application of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content security with a tamper-proof audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. The deployable CDK sample for pattern A is available on GitHub.

Pattern B: Expose through AgentCore Gateway

With Pattern B, you expose AgentCore Runtime through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a managed service purpose-built for agentic traffic that combines ingress authentication, token exchange and Runtime routing without requiring a proxy Lambda function or custom VPC networking.

Before any request reaches the agent, it passes the following layered security controls:

Inbound authentication: A custom JWT inbound authorizer is configured on AgentCore Gateway that validates the Amazon Cognito JWT by verifying its signature, issuer, and expiration before any logic runs.

Identity extraction, session binding and guardrails: A REQUEST interceptor for Lambda, invoked directly by AgentCore Gateway, extracts the verified user identity claims from the validated token for downstream injection. For asynchronous or unattended workloads, this interceptor securely binds these claims into an encrypted, short lived session context key. This helps ensure that even if the user’s interactive session expires hours later, a secure snapshot of their identity remains intact. It mirrors the role of the Lambda authorizer in Pattern A, enforcing the same session-binding and throttling logic.

Perimeter authorization (AgentCore Policy): AgentCore Gateway uses a deterministic Cedar-based policy engine to evaluate each request against defined policies before allowing tool access. It also enforces Amazon Bedrock Guardrails through AgentCore Policy for screening prompt injection and content violations at the gateway level, before the request reaches the agent. This declarative enforcement is an advantage over the API Gateway pattern where guardrails must be invoked programmatically from within the agent code.

After the authorization succeeds, the gateway manages the outbound call to AgentCore Runtime by using a strict workload isolation mechanism as shown in Figure 2:

Token exchange: The gateway requests a machine-to-machine (M2M) token from AgentCore Identity using a dedicated Amazon Cognito M2M app client and attaches it to the request.

Workload verification: The AgentCore Runtime validates this token against the allowedWorkloadConfiguration parameter, confirming the request originated from the gateway.

On-behalf-of access: The runtime unpacks the session context key, allowlists the injected user identity passed by the interceptor and forwards it directly to the agent to enable secure, context-aware execution on behalf of the user, even during completely unattended background execution loops.

Figure 2: Pattern B architecture for exposing AgentCore runtime through AgentCore Gateway

If a client attempts to bypass the gateway by sending a valid user token directly to the runtime, the request is automatically rejected because it lacks the required workload identity.

For more operational efficiency, AgentCore Gateway integrates AWS WAF directly at the single gateway access point, protecting the entire ingress path in one place, without the need to manage separate authorizers, proxy Lambda functions or VPC endpoints.

While API Gateway also supports AWS WAF, the AgentCore Gateway pattern simplifies management by consolidating all ingress controls behind a single component.

The AgentCore Gateway also supports native rate limiting, removing the need for custom DynamoDB-based throttle tables, for your production environments. The interceptor writes a structured audit trail to CloudWatch, with an INVALID_JWT alarm to flag spikes in authentication failures.

Before production deployment, we strongly recommend that you enable AWS WAF on the AgentCore gateway with the same rule sets described in the API Gateway pattern, including the OWASP protections, SQL injection, and custom rules for oversized or malformed requests.

To summarize, this second architecture satisfies the ingress security requirements defined earlier. It achieves defense in depth by applying a managed CUSTOM_JWT authorizer directly at the entry point, enforcing authorization through interceptor-based session binding and using rate limiting to control traffic. This pattern maintains per-hop least privileges from AgentCore Gateway through to the runtime by automating M2M token exchange, while propagating user identity for on-behalf-of execution. The edge security is managed by AWS WAF, coming directly with the gateway’s single-entry point, and secure workload isolation strictly enforces the perimeter. Finally, this design applies declarative Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for early content safety, and a tamper-proof audit trail and alarms in CloudWatch. The complete CDK sample for Pattern B is available on GitHub.

Choosing your AgentCore Runtime patterns

As explained earlier, securing access to AgentCore Runtime can be achieved through two different patterns: The AgentCore Gateway pattern or the Amazon API Gateway pattern. The right choice depends on your existing AWS infrastructure, workload constraints, and operational preferences.

Choose the Amazon API Gateway pattern if:

You have existing API infrastructure: Your team already runs an established Amazon API Gateway and AWS WAF deployment

You need a single entry point: You prefer to fold agentic traffic into your existing pipelines rather than introducing a separate entry point to operate and secure.

Your security model is VPC centric: Your security and compliance teams rely on VPCs and security groups as their primary network control layer

Your agent sessions are short-lived: While API Gateway has increased its integration timeout beyond 29 seconds, long running agentic workloads with streaming tool calls might still exceed it. This isn’t a concern if your sessions are brief.

Choose the AgentCore Gateway pattern if:

You’re building a new gateway: Your organization has no existing API Gateway

You have long run workloads: Your agents use streaming or long running tool calls that require strict API timeouts

You need low operational overhead: You prefer a fully managed perimeter over manually wired infrastructure

You require advanced AI routing: You want built-in capabilities to convert APIs and Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, handle Agent to Agent (A2A) traffic and route inference across different model providers.

The following table summarizes the key elements that help you make the right architectural decision:

Consideration

API Gateway (Pattern A)

AgentCore Gateway (Pattern B)

Suited to

Teams already standardized on API Gateway

Teams starting fresh who want less infrastructure to operate.

Perimeter control

Runtime resource policy with aws:SourceVpc and VPC endpoint security group

Runtime workload lock (allowedWorkloadConfiguration).

Components to operate

API Gateway, Lambda authorizer, Amazon VPC, VPC endpoints, proxy Lambda function

AgentCore Gateway and Lambda REQUEST interceptor.

User identity to agent

User JWT forwarded unchanged (no SigV4)

Interceptor-injected verified headers (OAuth outbound M2M token).

AWS WAF

Attach directly to the API stage

Attach directly to the gateway.

Request timeout

Inherits the API Gateway integration timeout

Not subject to this limitation.

Public endpoint

Can be fully private (API Gateway PRIVATE endpoint type)

Supports AWS PrivateLink ingress and VPC Lattice egress, but keeps a public endpoint active. Access relies on the JWT authorizer and resource policy rather than removing the endpoint

Conclusion

By securing access to the AgentCore Runtime with a defense in depth, an agent can be both highly usable and secure. The two patterns in this post complete the shared responsibility model for you: they authenticate every request against the identity provider, authorize it at each step and propagate the user’s identity end-to-end from the edge through the token exchange into the isolated microVM (AgentCore Runtime) and down to the agent’s tool calls (AgentCore Gateway). Each step only holds a short-lived credential for the next one, so the agent always works within the user’s permissions rather than with broad, long-term access. If one step is ever compromised, the design limits the impact to that single step, session and user. Whether the runtime is behind API Gateway with a VPC endpoint or in front of it with AgentCore Gateway, the design verifies each request at each step.

To get started, clone the Pattern A sample or the Pattern B sample, deploy it in your account, and test it against your requirements. Both samples are provided as a starting point, not a production-ready deployment. We recommend working with your security and legal teams to adapt to the controls before going live. From there, you can extend either pattern for multi-tenant use, add observability hooks, or tighten controls for your specific compliance requirements.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

He partners with enterprise customers to architect, optimize, and deploy production-grade AI solutions using the comprehensive AWS ML stack. Christian specializes in inference optimization techniques that balance performance, cost, and latency requirements for large-scale deployments. Christian enjoys exploring nature and spending time with family and friends.

articles.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
articles.context: “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says
articles.full_text: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face. Google did not respond to The Register's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says. In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test. In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said. Next time: kill switches at the ready A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check. Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website. They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall. In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests. At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments. Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.” However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register. Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.” Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ® Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

articles.title: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
articles.context: ” Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first
articles.full_text:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

1. Start With a Presumption of Innocence–or Negligence

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

2. Look at Status Updates From Organizations That Might Be Involved

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

articles.title: Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem
articles.context: They are also available in Foundry
articles.full_text:
Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, delivered the opening keynote at Ignite in San Francisco this morning. Here is an edited version of his remarks.

This week is about two things: First is how we capitalize on new capabilities that are growing exponentially. And second is how do we build the capability to deal with the consequences of these exponentials.

At times like these, I always find it helpful to be grounded in our mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. In today’s world, that means building a frontier ecosystem. We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large.

For us, that comes down to three things: Keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring your control of your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.

And so, our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three core architectural principles.

Copilot

Copilot is the new OS for work. Copilot brings together all the new form factors of human-computer interaction, whether it is Chat, Cowork, Code or Autopilot, into one experience. It also brings together the disparate categories of knowledge work, coding and business process. That is why we have all of Office with its richness built into Copilot. And underlying it is a model system that matches the right intelligence to the right context to the right form factor to accomplish the task.

Home gives you one place to start, whether you need a quick answer or want to assign and complete complex, multi-step tasks. Code brings the power of an infinite SaaS factory to every individual. It lets you build your own custom SaaS apps, dashboards and much more. And Autopilot is an autonomous agent that keeps moving your work forward 24×7 in all the places where you and your team collaborate.

Underlying all this is Work IQ. You can think of this as the most important database for any organization, with a deep understanding of people, their relationships, documents, emails, meetings, chats and projects that make up the fabric of work.

And we are going further. We are extending Copilot for specific roles: sales, legal, finance, service. We are organizing the skills, connectors and plugins for these roles across the entire surface area of Copilot.

And that includes third-party systems, too. In fact, today we are announcing new plugins for business applications, starting with Dynamics 365. And it is not just Dynamics. We are very excited to partner with Salesforce to bring Salesforce to Copilot.

And we are going beyond that as well. Up until now, we have mostly been in a single player world of people and their agent loops and swarms. But the time has come for a true multiplayer form factor, where people, their agents and other people are all driving towards a common goal, with shared context. This is Copilot Workspaces:

YouTube Video

Click here to load media

Microsoft IQ

The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain and continuously improve its own intelligence. Essentially, we are taking the system we built underneath Copilot and externalizing it as a first-class platform that embodies your organizational intelligence as an asset that you continuously build and control.

We are bringing together all of the data you have across Fabric, Foundry and Microsoft 365. And, of course, all the third-party context too. Microsoft IQ comes with hundreds of new connectors we are announcing today, so agents can get the full enterprise context where business gets done. And all this rich context manifests as business plugins that can be shared and inherited across the organization.

Models

For us, it is about mapping intelligence to a given task, with the best economics. This is something we can uniquely do in the context of real-world tasks by tuning our products, harness and tools, and the model system, end-to-end.

And today we are thrilled to announce Microsoft-Decision-1.1, which is now generally available and ready for enterprise deployment. We have added multimodal support. And we have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster. Already, more than 4,000 customers have used it. And we ourselves are using it for core tasks like routing, data labeling, personalization, content filtering and hundreds of other use cases.

Foundry of course has all the most popular closed and open weight models, too. We are very excited to bring GPT 6.2 to Foundry. It is a great model that sets a new bar for AI in professional work. And today we are announcing that Meta’s latest models are all coming to Foundry as well.

We are also innovating at the frontier with our own MAI model family that is both compute-efficient when it comes to pre-training and token-efficient when it comes to product deployment. Our goal is to put additional points on the frontier curve informed by real world task-performance.

And we are going further. We are announcing MAI Licensed Weights, meaning our trusted customers will now be able to get access to Microsoft AI model weights through our Frontier Co.

Today, we are introducing lots of new models. But I want to highlight two in particular:

First, Code. We are introducing our new flagship family of agentic coding models: Code 2. Code 2 is at the frontier of cost-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. It excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multifile implementation, repo-wide reasoning and UI at a fraction of frontier cost.

Code 2 Flash is designed for fast, high-volume work like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and rapid iterations. It brings near-flagship quality for a much lower cost. These models are both generally available today on GitHub Copilot, both in the model picker and as part of Copilot Fusion. They are also available in Foundry.

We are taking the same approach in cyber. Cyber 2 Flash is our most capable security model yet. It is a flash-sized model that delivers performance ahead of frontier models at a fraction of the cost per task. And, just as we have done with coding, we are co-designing the model with the tools and systems where it will be used. We are integrating Cyber 2 with Perception.

Agent 365

Successfully deploying AI systems starts with making sure you have observability at every layer of the stack. That is where Agent 365 comes in. It is a control plane that extends your existing governance, identity, security and management systems to the agents in your enterprise. We already have over 50 million agents in Agent 365.

And it includes FinOps, too. As AI scales, every organization needs a clear line between what it spends and the value AI creates. That is why today we are announcing Agent 365 Business Analytics. You can think of it as your ERP system for AI usage. You can see exactly what is driving spend. You can connect spend to outcomes to drive business value. And you can optimize ROI across different scenarios.

Security

The next thing I want to talk about is how you take the environment you have set up, from Copilot to IQ to Agent 365, and secure it. And that is where Perception and our security stack comes in. We are building an end-to-end trust platform. We are helping customers both secure their AI deployments and use AI to strengthen their security posture.

Perception is a complete agentic security system with teams of red, blue and green agents that run through playbooks to deliver security outcomes at machine speed, with you always in control.

Essentially, think about it like this: red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks and green team agents fix and remediate. With Playbooks, you can compose teams of agents to tackle complex jobs and trigger them to take action autonomously.

Perception helps connect all the signals, sensors and actuators across your identity, client, cloud, apps and agents to intelligence to secure your end-to-end environments. And I am very excited to share that Perception is now generally available.

In addition to the work we have been doing across our products, we are also working across the ecosystem to ensure everyone can innovate at speed and scale, safely. Today, we can see almost everything models touch. But we cannot see what happens inside the model. And what the model tells us about itself is not independent evidence. These nested black boxes are simply unacceptable. We need to be able to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently and control what it is allowed to do.

That is why today we are also announcing the Microsoft AI Transparency Initiative.

There are three parts to this: First, we will expand our collaboration in NIST’s Agent Standards Initiative, drawing on its research to help lead the development of open, industry-wide standards for AI transparency, security and governance.

Second, we are taking a full ecosystem approach. Together, we can enable AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Already, 40 organizations are working with us on defining and applying these standards.

Third, we are working to incorporate the same standards in our products, including MAI models, Foundry and Copilot. Our ambition through our research, our product work and our ecosystem is to help establish an open industry standard that makes AI safer, more transparent and more accessible.

Cobalt 200 VMs

Underneath all of this is unbelievable silicon. We are building a heterogeneous platform working across the ecosystem to bring you all the latest innovation. We are also advancing our own hardware systems, co-designing silicon, servers and infrastructure to get more from every watt, chip and datacenter.

We just announced Maia 300, which will deliver 40 percent more tokens per watt compared with leading GPU-based systems. Azure Boost and Azure Integrated HSM move critical infrastructure and security functions into purpose-built silicon. And today we are announcing general availability of our next-generation Cobalt 200 VMs, which are our highest-performing general-purpose VMs with leading price-performance.

So, that is a quick walk through some of our news. When you look at all that is coming, it is clear that we are entering an era of ubiquitous intelligence. The key imperatives for us are to ensure human ambition, a firm’s control of its own intelligence and the diffusion of the benefits broadly. That is the promise of a frontier ecosystem. And that is what we are here to build together.

For more information on today’s announcements, check out the Book of News.

The post Ignite 2026: Building the frontier ecosystem appeared first on The Official Microsoft Blog.

articles.context: According to the complaint, roughly 1,200 agents used that unauthorized communications channel, and about 700 participated in the Hugging Face attack

In this article

AI agents escaped testing and hacked real systems

California says OpenAI lost control of agents more than 80 times

The state wants stronger safeguards and financial penalties

An AI agent doesn’t need malicious intentions to cause a cybersecurity incident. Give it a goal, tools, and enough freedom to find a shortcut, and the damage can extend well beyond the computer where it was supposed to stay.

That is the concern behind a lawsuit California Attorney General Rob Bonta filed against OpenAI on November 16. The state alleges that the company developed and tested powerful AI models without adequate safeguards, allowing experimental agents to escape their testing environments and gain unauthorized access to other organizations’ systems.

The best-known incident involved Hugging Face, the platform where developers share AI models and datasets. But California’s complaint says it was not an isolated failure: According to the filing, OpenAI acknowledged to investigators that it had lost control of autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing.

As we explained in our follow-up on the AI agent swarm, agents used a shared service as an improvised message board, exchanging information that helped others get around their restrictions. According to the complaint, roughly 1,200 agents used that unauthorized communications channel, and about 700 participated in the Hugging Face attack.

California’s complaint says the attack involved roughly 17,600 attacker actions and required two weeks of full-time remediation work by Hugging Face’s security team.

Why California decided to sue

California alleges that OpenAI had repeated warnings that its containment measures were failing and continued testing anyway.

The complaint identifies several alleged failures:

Warning signs like observed unauthorized internet access went unaddressed.

Monitoring did not match public assurances. The state alleges that OpenAI promised continuous monitoring but did not monitor models’ reasoning live in the relevant training and evaluation environments.

Reduced model safeguards were not offset by stronger containment. California says experimental models were tested without protections normally present in publicly released versions, while the surrounding infrastructure failed to keep their actions contained.

OpenAI failed to substantially comply with investigative demands for records about the incidents and its security practices.

California is suing under its Unfair Competition Law and also argues that OpenAI’s unsafe testing constitutes a “public nuisance.” In this case, that means interfering with a community’s ability to use its property safely, including computer systems. The state is seeking a court order requiring safer testing practices, along with financial penalties.

Who pays when the sandbox fails?

The lawsuit raises a question that extends beyond one company: When an autonomous system crosses a security boundary, who is responsible for keeping it in line?

The lawsuit puts responsibility back on the organization running the experiment. Whether an agent was trying to finish a benchmark or complete a research task, California’s position is that keeping it from breaking into someone else’s systems was OpenAI’s job.

For organizations using AI agents, the practical lesson is to treat them as software with the power to take actions, not simply chatbots that produce answers. Login details, network access, tools, and permissions determine how far an unexpected action can reach.

Our earlier coverage of an OpenAI agent that bypassed a government website’s access controls emphasized limiting that access and monitoring what agents actually do.

What do cybercriminals know about you?

Use Malwarebytes’ free Digital Footprint scan to see whether your personal information has been exposed online.

Using the AWS RMiT workbook and ISO Compliance Guides to support your BNM submissions
articles.context: In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services
articles.full_text:
Your next Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) notification submission needs auditable evidence of how Amazon Web Services (AWS) controls align with Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) requirements. Two resources now exist to support that work: the AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT and the compliance guides published by AWS Security Assurance Services (AWS SAS).

The AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT, available through AWS Artifact, maps each RMiT provision to AWS Control Objectives (AWS responsibilities under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model) and AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices (your responsibilities). It tells you, for every RMiT requirement, what AWS is responsible for and what you implement.

The compliance guides published by AWS SAS over the past year provide implementation guidance for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards that complements the workbook. These guides show how to implement controls that meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks using AWS services, giving your technical and compliance teams a clear path from regulatory expectation to deployed architecture.

Malaysian financial institutions can now trace from BNM regulatory requirement, through AWS control implementation, to the evidence that demonstrates it: AWS third-party attestations for AWS-side controls, and your own workload evidence for customer-side controls. BNM expects this specificity in notification documentation.

AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT

The workbook is a structured Excel document available through AWS Artifact. For each of the 394 RMiT provisions, it identifies:

Whether the requirement is an AWS responsibility or a customer responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model

The specific AWS Control Objective that addresses the requirement (where AWS is responsible)

The relevant AWS Well-Architected Framework best practice for customer implementation (where the customer is responsible)

Supporting information and references for each mapping

The following is a sample entry from the workbook:

RMiT Requirement

Responsibility

Source

AWS supporting information

10.49: A financial institution should ensure network resilience…

AWS

AWS Control Objectives

AWS Control Section: Network Security. AWS maintains redundant network connectivity with multiple tier-1 transit providers across each Availability Zone.

10.49: (Customer responsibility)

Customer

Well-Architected

REL 2: How do you plan your network topology? Implement multi-AZ deployments. Configure VPC flow logs and use AWS Network Firewall.

The workbook currently includes 394 rows across all RMiT appendix requirements, with 208 mapped to AWS responsibilities and 186 to customer responsibilities.

Why this matters now

BNM revised RMiT guidelines effective 28 November 2025, and updated them on 25 September 2026 to add requirements for National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities. Financial institutions operating under both BNM Outsourcing and BNM RMiT must demonstrate that their cloud service providers maintain controls aligned with regulatory expectations. Institutions preparing notification submissions for material cloud workloads need auditable evidence of this alignment.

The revised guidelines set higher expectations for evidence quality. Institutions submitting notifications without clear, structured control mapping evidence might face extended review cycles and requests for additional information from BNM. Workloads that could be deployed in weeks remain in governance queues for months when supporting documentation lacks the specificity regulators expect.

Compliance guides from AWS Security Assurance Services

Start with the RMiT workbook to identify which provisions AWS addresses and which you implement. Then use the following compliance guides to design and implement your customer-side controls. The guides are implementation guidance for your teams. Audit evidence comes from two places. For AWS-side controls, use AWS third-party attestations, such as ISO certificates and System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports, available in AWS Artifact. For your workload, use evidence from your own environment, including configurations, logs, and AWS Config conformance pack results. Auditors can also use the guides as a reference for how a control is typically implemented on AWS.

AWS SAS has published five compliance guides over the past year. Each guide provides control-level implementation guidance on the customer side of the Shared Responsibility Model, showing how AWS services can be configured to meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks. These guides were written by AWS SAS practicing security assessors and auditors holding Payment Card Industry Qualified Security Assessor (PCI QSA), Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM), ISO 27001 Lead Auditor, and Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certifications, drawing on experience from hundreds of cloud security assessments across financial services globally.

The following is the list of guides AWS SAS practicing auditors have published, which include control mapping information relevant to BNM RMiT:

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS (Information Security Management) – Maps Annex A controls to AWS services

ISO 31000:2018 on AWS (Risk Management) – Integrates AWS services into risk identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) – Supports institutions building responsible artificial intelligence (AI) on AWS

Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1 on AWS (Cloud Security Controls) – Maps 207 control objectives to AWS

American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) SOC 2 on AWS – Navigates SOC 2 compliance using AWS services

How these resources work together

A Malaysian financial institution preparing a BNM notification can use these resources together:

The RMiT workbook identifies which RMiT provisions are AWS responsibilities and which are customer responsibilities.

For AWS responsibilities, the workbook references the specific AWS Control Objective.

AWS third-party reports in AWS Artifact, such as the AWS ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and SOC reports, attest to those AWS Control Objectives. For customer responsibilities, the ISO compliance guides show how to implement the corresponding controls using AWS services.

The ISO 31000 guide can inform the risk management methodology you apply to your cloud workloads.

AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated, continuous monitoring of deployed controls.

Resources also supporting this approach:

The AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia examines the BNM Outsourcing and RMiT policy documents and sets out the steps to launch regulated workloads on AWS

AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated compliance monitoring through managed AWS Config rules mapped to specific RMiT controls

Compliance teams across Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) financial services have already begun referencing the AWS Guide to BNM RMiT and associated resources in their cloud risk assessment processes and BNM notification documentation.

Looking ahead: AI governance

For institutions deploying generative AI and machine learning, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) is relevant to BNM technology governance expectations. In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services. AWS passed its first surveillance audit in November 2025 with zero findings. The ISO 42001 compliance guide published in May 2026 supports institutions building their own responsible AI systems on their side of the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.

How to get started

Access the RMiT workbook through AWS Artifact and review with your compliance lead to identify which provisions apply to your material cloud workloads.

Download the relevant ISO compliance guides to plan how you implement your customer-side controls. Download AWS ISO certificates and SOC reports from AWS Artifact for AWS-side evidence.

Map your workload-specific controls using the workbook as the RMiT baseline and the ISO guides as implementation guidance.

Implement automated compliance monitoring using the BNM RMiT conformance pack for AWS Config to maintain continuous visibility over your control posture.

Engage your AWS account team or AWS SAS for additional guidance on implementing customer-side controls referenced in the workbook.

As BNM updates its regulatory expectations, AWS will update these resources to reflect revised requirements. Subscribe to the AWS Security Blog for update notifications.

articles.title: Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take  off with license data of Uber drivers
articles.context: Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7
articles.full_text: Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week. According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7. Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier. Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed. Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission. Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised. The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed. Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear. Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up. This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts. ®
