articles.title: Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident'
articles.context: In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal...
articles.full_text: Market research giant Ipsos says it's currently investigating a "cybersecurity incident," and has reported the matter to the authorities. In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal investigation is ongoing. "Upon discovery, we promptly activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident, and engaged external cybersecurity specialists to support our investigation," it said [PDF]. "The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident. We have reported the matter to the relevant authorities." Ipsos confirmed the attack had no impact on its operations or customer service delivery, however, it did not comment on the nature of the attack or whether any data was compromised. "We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously," Ipsos added. "Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly. "As the investigation is ongoing, we are not in a position to comment further at this stage." The company declined our requests for additional data, as it does not want to release unverified information to the market. Founded in France in 1975, Ipsos is one of the leading market research companies in the world, employing nearly 20,000 people and operating in 220 cities across 90 markets. It is routinely engaged by businesses for its market research data, as well as by public sector organizations for its opinion polling, often responsible for providing data regarding political views and satisfaction surveys. Tasked with procuring a wealth of data on myriad topics, Ipsos also offers data analytics services that turn the information it gathers through research, polls, and surveys into insights that inform organizations' business strategies. ®

articles.title: Facebook may have access to your entire photo gallery
articles.context: Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025
articles.full_text:
.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}

In this article

Facebook’s photo suggestions feature could access your entire gallery through a single permission

Italy fined Meta €805 million and says the privacy violation remains ongoing for some users

Check Facebook’s photo permissions to control what it can access

If you’ve given Facebook access to your phone’s photos, the app may be able to read your entire gallery, including pictures you never intended to share. Check your photo permissions if you want to limit that access.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing Android users’ entire camera rolls without specific consent or adequate disclosure. The regulator says the violation remains ongoing for some users, despite changes Meta has made.

The decision concerns Facebook’s “Get camera roll suggestions when you’re browsing Facebook” feature. Launched in 2023, the idea is to use your photos and videos to suggest potential social media posts.

You might be surprised to hear that Facebook can access every photo or video in your gallery if you’ve granted full photo access. That includes pictures of your kids, restaurant receipts, and that Wi-Fi password label you photographed awkwardly on the router behind the TV. But you might have granted that access without realizing it also enabled photo suggestions. That’s the problem, said the regulator.

Facebook’s app requested access to the camera roll through a single permission that applies across the entire app, covering multiple features with different requirements. The Garante said:

“The permission is preceded by a non-specific notice (’enable other features’) which does not make it clear to the user that they are also authorising suggestions from the camera roll.”

One permission, lots of features

Asking permission for lots of things via one request violated Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code, according to the regulator. That code is Italy’s privacy law, and its Article 122 implements the EU’s ePrivacy Directive, which protects data stored on devices such as smartphones. The Garante said access for this feature required free and informed consent.

Facebook also failed to adequately explain its use of the photo gallery, and the suggestions feature was on by default. Granting full photo access could give the app ongoing access to the entire library, the regulator said, without users being able to verify which information was actually being used.

The regulator’s investigation started in July 2025 after consumer organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti submitted a report. That prompted the Garante to conduct its own technical analysis.

Meta had asked for Ireland to handle the case. Like many other technology companies, Meta’s main EU presence is in Ireland, whose regulator handles many cross-border privacy cases. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use that system.

Meta disagrees

Meta told Reuters that users must grant device permission before the feature can operate and can change that permission in their settings.

The social media company also called the fine, which amounts to less than 0.5% of global revenues, “disproportionate.” It will appeal, it told reporters.

The Garante attributed the amount of the fine to the high number of people affected (around 20 million Android users in Italy) along with the duration of the incident, which it referred to as a breach. It also called Meta out for its “poor level of cooperation.” Changes that the company made to its app were introduced late and only applied to users who update the app, it added.

Aside from the financial penalty, the regulator has ordered Meta to request consent separately for the camera roll suggestions feature. It must get that consent after explaining to users what it will use the data for and how to disable it. The company must turn it off by default even for those who previously gave the blanket permission, it said, and if it doesn’t comply by the 60-day deadline then it must not enable the feature for users who haven’t given consent.

The regulator is preparing for a potential follow-up. It has left the door open to address the possible use of content to train AI, which Meta has denied. The Garante also “reserves the right” to assess a new feature that allows the content of the camera roll to be processed in the cloud.

Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025. It analyzes media to find memorable moments and suggests creative edits. Meta says suggestions remain private unless users choose to share them, and the feature can be turned off in Facebook’s camera roll settings.

What Facebook users can do

The Italian order does not automatically change permissions for users elsewhere, but you can review your own settings.

On Android, go to Settings > Apps > Facebook > Permissions > Photos and videos, then select Don’t allow to revoke gallery access. Depending on your Android version and the app, you may also have an option to allow access only to selected photos and videos. Menu names can vary by device.

While Italy’s decision didn’t target iPhone users, they can also review Facebook’s photo access under Settings > Privacy & Security > Photos.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

articles.title: A phishing page interested in MX records, (Tue, Nov 17th)
articles.context: Of course, MX records are publicly available, and there is nothing preventing an attacker from looking them up independently
articles.full_text:
I’ve mentioned before in some of my diaries that it can be instructive to look at what appear to be “generic” phishing messages in detail from time to time, since some of them might prove not to be as generic as they initially appear. I came across a good example of this while going over phishing messages delivered to our handler inbox over the past few weeks, when a message that, at first glance, appeared to be a fairly ordinary attempt at stealing e-mail credentials turned out to lead to a page interested in collecting a little more information than just the victim's password.

As you can see, the original message was not especially noteworthy on its own, being a spin on the usual “your password will expire today” approach…

The link pointed to an HTML page hosted on Google Cloud Storage, with the recipient's e-mail address included in the URL fragment:

hxxps[:]//storage[.]googleapis[.]com/alx2/03/1a/we.html#[recipient_e-mail_address]

After opening the link, the recipient would be presented with a generic login form, personalized using the domain part of their e-mail address. The page also attempted to use a screenshot of the legitimate website of the recipient's organization as its background, which it retrieved using the thum.io service. This didn't work quite as intended for isc.sans.edu, since the screenshot service returned an error message instead of the requested image. However, when I modified the URL to contain an e-mail address from another domain, the resulting page looked considerably more convincing.

Looking at the source code revealed a couple of layers of URL-encoding and additional JavaScript obfuscation. Once these were removed, the page turned out to contain a fairly typical credential-harvesting kit, which supported multiple languages and attempted to collect not just the submitted password, but also the visitor's public IP address, geographic location, browser information and language. This information, along with a timestamp, was supposed to be sent to the attacker using the Telegram Bot API.

Such extensive collection of information is not particularly unusual. In fact, another phishing page that I examined recently collected a similarly extensive set of information and also sent it to the attacker using Telegram. In the present case, however, one additional field included in the information sent to the attacker caught my attention – it was labeled "MX Record".

A closer look at the corresponding code revealed that the JavaScript actually performed a DNS-over-HTTPS query for MX records associated with the victim's e-mail domain, using Google's public DNS service. The relevant parts of the code (slightly simplified and reformatted for readability) looked as follows:

... const response = await fetch( "https://dns.google/resolve?name=" + domain + "&type=MX" ); const data = await response.json(); return data.Answer.map(answer => answer.data).join("\n"); ...

The retrieved records were then included in the message containing the stolen credentials:

... message += "MX Record : " + await getMXRecord(domain) + "\n"; ...

The use of MX records in phishing is certainly not new. For example, Infoblox documented a phishing-as-a-service operation called Morphing Meerkat in March 2025, which used DNS-over-HTTPS queries for MX records to identify victims' e-mail service providers and dynamically select appropriate phishing templates[1].

In the present case, however, the MX records weren't used to customize the phishing page. Instead, the lookup was performed as part of the credential collection process, and its results were included in the information sent to the attacker.

Of course, MX records are publicly available, and there is nothing preventing an attacker from looking them up independently. Nevertheless, including them with each set of stolen credentials would help the attacker automatically identify the e-mail infrastructure used by the targeted organization, which could be useful for further attacks or for prioritizing the collected credentials.

Whether the threat actor behind this particular phishing actually used the collected MX records in this (or any) way is impossible to say. Still, having the phishing page perform a little additional reconnaissance on the victim's organization, and including the results with the stolen credentials, seems like a noteworthy detail in an otherwise fairly ordinary phishing kit…

[1] https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/a-phishing-tale-of-doh-and-dns-mx-abuse/

----------- Jan Kopriva LinkedIn Nettles Consulting

articles.title: ICO Issues GTA 6 Scam Warning as Release Date Nears
articles.context: The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of...
articles.full_text:
The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6).

The much-anticipated title is set to launch worldwide on November 19, but the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) urged caution when opening messages with GTA 6 themes.

These could be crafted to steal passwords that are used to log into victims’ gaming accounts and other online accounts that share the same credentials.

The ICO said that email inboxes, financial information and other personal details could be at risk.

Read more on ICO advice: ICO Publishes Five-Step Plan to Counter Emerging AI-Powered Attacks.

“Phishing emails and other cyber vulnerabilities can be used to access people's personal information. And if you’re using the same password across multiple accounts, one mistake could give criminals the keys to much more than your gaming profile,” said ICO group director – regulatory assurance and cyber, Ian Hulme.

“Our message is simple: enjoy the game, but protect your data. Use unique passwords, switch on two-step verification for your accounts and think carefully before clicking links or sharing personal information.”

Five Steps to Protect Personal Information

The ICO’s advice for GTA 6 fans is useful best practice for any computer user. It urges individuals to:

Use different passwords across multiple accounts to reduce the blast radius of an attack if a scammer gets hold of one

Choose passwords carefully, avoiding those based on personal information such as a pet’s name or date of birth. Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, long and unique passwords

Be wary of suspicious links in unsolicited messages or emails – especially those promising free downloads, exclusive content or early access

Think before sharing personal information online, including full name, date of birth, address and account details

Check you’re using a legitimate website and understand who is collecting your data before entering personal information

Grand Theft Auto and its developer Rockstar Games have been popular targets for attack over recent years.

In 2022, Rockstar Games was hacked by an alleged member of the infamous Lapsus$ collective, with the perpetrator posting around 50 minutes of in-development footage online.

The teen responsible was also linked to a series of extortion attacks on Nvidia, Uber, BT and EE.

In June this year, it was revealed that scammers had registered a number of fake sites falsely claiming to offer early access to GTA 6 in return for crypto payments.

articles.title: Fully Autonomous Agentic Attacks Are Three Months Away, Google Warns
articles.context: ” Attacks Are Easy to Spot GTIG said the “low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits and massive scaling potential” is going to make such frameworks an enduringly...
articles.full_text:
Google expects sophisticated, fully autonomous agentic attacks to emerge in the next three to six months after observing a “paradigm shift” in the use of pen-testing frameworks like ARTEX in the past quarter.

The tech giant’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) shared the news in its latest quarterly GTIG AI Threat Tracker published on November 16.

Compiled from Mandiant incident response telemetry, global threat actor tracking and live platform defenses, the report warned that ARTEX and open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, are increasingly popular among threat actors.

Groups are also experimenting with custom-built harnesses, it added.

Read more on ARTEX: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants.

Frameworks like ARTEX effectively manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute and adapt across multiple kill chain stages including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance and lateral movement, and completion of objectives.

“While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge,” the report explained.

“These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.”

Attacks Are Easy to Spot

GTIG said the “low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits and massive scaling potential” is going to make such frameworks an enduringly popular choice for both cybercrime and nation state groups.

“Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions,” it added.

Threat actors are currently trading stealth for velocity, meaning that attacks generate plenty of forensic signals, “recognizable identifiers” and “code-level traces,” which can help defenders to detect and mitigate, the report noted. However, stealth will certainly increase going forward, it warned.

Sally Vincent, senior threat research engineer at Exabeam, argued that better behavioral monitoring by SOC teams could help to spot and block such threats by flagging unfamiliar tool use or unusual data access.

“It can also identify changes in activity volume. These changes can help expose an attack even when the attacker uses legitimate tools and valid credentials,” she added.

Google said its security operations (SecOps) team has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant has also released a hardening guide and defensive framework designed to help organizations counter the “speed and scale advantage” of AI-powered attackers.

Just last week, the FBI warned of the growing use of ARTEX in attacks, with South Korean financial institutions among the many victims.

pnpm Introduces New Lockfile Format to Reduce Git Merge Conflicts
articles.context: Incompatible tools could omit packages, misidentify resolved versions, or fail to process the dependency graph, potentially affecting vulnerability detection and other supply...
articles.full_text:
pnpm has introduced an experimental lockfile format designed to reduce Git merge conflicts by changing how dependency relationships are recorded. The new format, available starting with pnpm 12.19.0, previews changes planned for pnpm 13 and is available as an opt-in setting.

The change addresses a common frustration in JavaScript development, particularly in projects with multiple contributors or large dependency trees. Updates to dependencies can produce substantial changes in pnpm-lock.yaml, creating merge conflicts when developers work on separate branches.

The new format aims to reduce those conflicts by keeping related dependency information together and limiting the number of lines affected when peer dependencies change.

A New Structure for Dependency Relationships #

The existing v9 lockfile format uses separate packages and snapshots sections to store package metadata and resolved dependency relationships. The experimental v13 format consolidates that information into a single packages section. The top-level importers section is also renamed to projects.

Package references now use bare version numbers rather than identifiers containing peer dependency or patch suffixes. Peer dependency bindings are represented through with mappings, while optional peers use a new notation. Registry package integrity hashes also move directly onto package entries.

These changes reduce the number of entries that need to be modified when dependencies change, particularly when updating peer dependencies.

The format also introduces JSON-like syntax with tabs and trailing commas, although the file remains valid YAML. As pnpm clarified on X, the reduction in Git conflicts comes from the structural changes, not the syntax.

Experimental Support Ahead of pnpm 13 #

The new format was introduced in pnpm 12.19.0 on November 10, 2026. Subsequent releases have continued refining its behavior.

Version 12.20.0 added support for recording dependency specifiers of local directory packages and addressed issues involving peer dependency cycles. Version 12.21.0 fixed additional problems involving lockfile generation, injected workspace packages, and frozen installations.

Developers can enable the format by adding the following setting to pnpm-workspace.yaml:

lockfile: format: v13

The default remains v9. Once enabled, pnpm writes the new format when resolving dependencies or when developers run pnpm install --lockfile-only.

According to the pnpm documentation, versions supporting the setting can read both formats, regardless of which format is configured for writing.

However, older pnpm versions that predate the setting cannot read v13 lockfiles. The project also cautions that the experimental format may change before pnpm 13 is released, potentially requiring developers to regenerate their lockfiles after upgrading.

Compatibility Implications for the JavaScript Ecosystem #

The changes also affect tools that rely on lockfiles to reconstruct dependency graphs, including security scanners, software composition analysis platforms, and software bill of materials (SBOM) generators.

Although v13 remains valid YAML, tools that expect separate packages and snapshots sections, parse peer dependency information from package identifiers, or read integrity hashes from resolution objects may need updates.

Successfully parsing a lockfile does not guarantee that a tool can accurately reconstruct its dependencies. Incompatible tools could omit packages, misidentify resolved versions, or fail to process the dependency graph, potentially affecting vulnerability detection and other supply chain analysis.

The new format does not introduce additional security protections. Its primary purpose is to reduce merge conflicts, but its eventual adoption as the default in pnpm 13 will require compatible tooling across the JavaScript ecosystem.

articles.title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
articles.context: It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data...
articles.full_text: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds, telcos, retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®

articles.title: Java4Shell: Remote Code Execution in OpenJDK (CVE-2026-114938)
articles.context: Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-114938 is an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK's optimized Base64 decoder.

Denial of service is the more readily achievable impact where attacker-controlled input reaches the vulnerable decoder. Reliable remote code execution requires additional exploitation work tailored to the application and Java Virtual Machine (JVM) environment.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires the affected Java runtime to execute its AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) decoding path. Systems running on processors that lack AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected.

On affected x86-64 deployments, starting the JVM with -XX:UseAVX=2 disables the AVX-512 path and prevented out-of-bounds writes in our tests. Scope the flag to x86 deployments as native ARM64 JVMs do not recognize it and will fail to start if that flag is passed.

In a standalone test, the extra write corrupted a neighboring array's header and the JVM later crashed during garbage collection. The resulting damage depends on which objects occupy the overwritten memory.

What happened

On November 17, 2026, Oracle released a security update for CVE-2026-114938, an out-of-bounds write in OpenJDK’s optimized Base64 decoder. This vulnerability affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later and has been rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

While the vulnerability can lead to remote code execution in a worst-case scenario, it is important to stress that an attacker would have to do additional work for every application they target. There is no single, universal exploit that would work against all Java applications.

How to know if you’re affected

Oracle stated that the Java versions affected by vulnerabilities patched in this release are as below:

Java release line

Affected releases

First fixed release

Java 17

17.0.6 through versions before 17.0.21.1

17.0.21.1+4

Java 21

All versions of Java 21 before 21.0.13.1

21.0.13.1+4

Java 25

All versions of Java 25 before 25.0.5.1

25.0.5.1+4

Java 27

All versions of Java 27 before 27.0.1.1

27.0.1.1+4

In addition to running a vulnerable version of Java, the application must be running on a CPU that supports the AVX-512 VBMI decoding path. Not all systems (including modern ones) support this instruction set so it is recommended to check when prioritizing systems for patching. The following is a shell command to see if the instruction set is supported:

grep -om1 -E 'avx512[_]?vbmi' /proc/cpuinfo

If this command returns nothing, that is an indication that the CPU does not support VBMI. If the command returns avx512vbmi and/or avx512_vbmi, that is a signal that it does support VBMI and could be potentially vulnerable.

Native ARM64 Java runtimes are not affected by this vulnerability because they do not execute the vulnerable x86 AVX-512 decoding path.

An affected Java runtime and a compatible CPU are prerequisites, but the application must also pass attacker-controlled data to the vulnerable decoder. In the OpenJDK 17.0.6 build we tested, the AVX-512 path handles the basic and URL decoders returned by Base64.getDecoder() and Base64.getUrlDecoder(). The MIME decoder returned by Base64.getMimeDecoder() bypasses this path.

This distinction matters when assessing authentication and token-processing code. Base64-encoded credentials, tokens, or SAML messages expose an application only if its implementation passes the malformed value to the affected decoder. Libraries that implement their own decoding, or reject or normalize the value before calling the JDK decoder, can behave differently.

From a Java method to a native decoder

Java's Base64.Decoder supports decoding into a new array or one supplied by the caller. In both cases, it calculates the required output space before decoding. The allocating method uses that calculation directly:

public byte[] decode(byte[] src) { byte[] dst = new byte[decodedOutLength(src, 0, src.length)]; int ret = decode0(src, 0, src.length, dst); if (ret != dst.length) { dst = Arrays.copyOf(dst, ret); } return dst; }

The allocation is not the source of the overflow. Further down this call chain, HotSpot's optimizing compiler, C2, can replace decodeBlock() with a native implementation. These replacements, called intrinsics, let the JVM use specialized CPU instructions. The native implementation must respect the bounds of the Java arrays it receives.

The AVX-512 decoding routine converts each 64-byte input block into 48 output bytes. When fewer than 64 input bytes remain, a separate handler decodes the final fragment. That is where the length calculation goes wrong.

Padding produces a negative output length

Consider a value containing 128 A characters followed by one =:

value = b"A" * 128 + b"="

The first 128 characters form complete Base64 groups. The final = is invalid: Padding cannot form a group by itself. However, the initial output-length calculation does not reject this value. It counts the input and trailing padding and produces a destination length of 98 bytes.

The native routine decodes the first 128 characters into 96 bytes. It then reaches the final-fragment handler with just the = remaining.

To calculate the fragment's output size, the handler divides the remaining length by four, discards the remainder, and multiplies by three. In HotSpot's code generator, those operations are:

__ movl(output_size, length); __ shrl(output_size, 2); // Find (len / 4) * 3 (output length) __ lea(output_size, Address(output_size, output_size, Address::times_2, 0));

For a 1-byte fragment, this produces zero. The padding branch then decrements output_size for the trailing =. There is no check that the result remains nonnegative, so the count becomes -1.

The same problem occurs with other fragments containing fewer than 4 bytes.

The negative count enables a full-width store

AVX-512 supports masked stores, where individual mask bits determine which bytes reach memory. The decoder uses the output count to construct such a mask. A count of zero should permit no writes; a count of three should permit 3 output bytes.

The code starts with a 64-bit value whose bits are all set, then uses BZHI to retain the requested number of low bits:

__ movq(output_mask, -1); __ bzhiq(output_mask, output_mask, output_size);

BZHI reads its bit count from the low byte of the last operand. For -1, that byte is 255. For -2, it is 254. Both exceed the width of the 64-bit operand, so the instruction leaves all 64 bits set.

The contents of the write also follow from the implementation. The tail handler fills unused input positions with the character a before decoding the vector. Much of the excess output is consequently the repeating byte pattern 69 a6 9a. The vulnerability causes a constrained overwrite rather than a freely chosen 64-byte value.

An exception does not contain the corruption

The decoder eventually throws IllegalArgumentException for the malformed input. The Java API permits partially written output when decoding fails. Here, however, the native routine has written outside the output array altogether.

This explains why the symptom may appear far from the decoder call. A write into unused heap space can go unnoticed. A write into an object header can instead damage information that the JVM consults later, including during garbage collection. Catching the decoding exception leaves that damage in place.

Mitigation

Follow your Java runtime vendor's guidance for a fixed build. Include runtimes bundled with applications and container images in that review. After updating a container base image, rebuild and redeploy the application image. Restart affected Java processes so they use the updated runtime.

If an update cannot be deployed immediately, our tests confirmed two JVM startup options that prevented the out-of-bounds writes.

To disable the Base64 intrinsics specifically, add:

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics

Alternatively, on x86-64 deployments, disable AVX-512 execution by limiting the JVM to AVX2:

-XX:UseAVX=2

Disabling the Base64 intrinsics is the narrower workaround. Limiting AVX affects other JVM operations that use AVX-512, so assess its performance impact on your workload.

Scope UseAVX=2 to x86 deployments. Native ARM64 JVMs do not execute the vulnerable code, and they do not recognize this option. Adding it to shared startup settings can prevent ARM64 services from starting.

Apply the selected option to the application's JVM startup configuration and restart the service. Check the running process, including any bundled runtime, rather than relying on the Java installation found on your shell's path. Where jcmd is available, inspect the runtime version and effective flags with:

jcmd <PID> VM.version jcmd <PID> VM.flags -all

Confirm that the process reports UseBASE64Intrinsics = false or UseAVX = 2, depending on the workaround selected.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Live Processes provide real-time visibility into the processes running on your infrastructure. You can use it to identify Java processes running on x86-64 hosts, then filter to determine which hosts are running an affected Java runtime.

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-114938. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Conclusion

While this vulnerability can lead to remote code execution, its practical impact depends on the environment.

Applications running on processors without AVX-512 VBMI support are not affected by this vulnerability. On affected systems, denial of service is more readily achievable than reliable code execution. Attackers seeking to execute arbitrary code would need to tailor their exploits to the Java runtime and application behavior, which complicates the development of a broadly reusable exploit.

These constraints give security teams a way to prioritize their response, but affected services still need prompt attention. Follow your runtime vendor’s guidance for a fixed build, including Java runtimes bundled with applications or container images. Where an update cannot be deployed immediately, disable the vulnerable decoding path as a temporary workaround.

articles.title: Infoblox customer and staff data exposed in Sharepoint breach
articles.context: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data
articles.full_text: Networking and security firm Infoblox is investigating a third-party breach that allowed crims to access sensitive customer and staff data. "Infoblox is investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor,” a company spokesperson confirmed to The Register. According to sources, the compromised third-party data migration vendor had trusted access to Infoblox's SharePoint system, and the intruders used this vendor’s accounts and access to exfiltrate data directly from Microsoft SharePoint. This data included configuration information related to some customer's NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments. These are saved snapshots of customers’ network data, such as DNS, DHCP configurations, Grid databases, and reporting logs, that can be used to fully recover the appliance or grid in case of a system failure or faulty upgrade. The intruders also stole employee data during the break-in. According to an email CEO Scott Harrell sent to employees, which The Register has seen, compromised employee details include financial information such as direct deposit details, contact info, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Upon discovering the breach, Infoblox “immediately activated” its incident response procedures, and took steps to contain the incident, including hiring outside cybersecurity experts, the spokesperson said. “We have sent notifications about this security event and are providing support and guidance as appropriate,” the Infoblox spokesperson told us. “Based on our investigation to date, we have no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved. Our priority is to fully investigate and resolve this issue." Affected staff received a $100 "spot bonus" to buy password management services, and were warned to be "especially alert for phishing, vishing, fraud, or other suspicious communications." Infoblox also gave employees and their dependents free credit monitoring and identity protection for two years. Infoblox declined to answer our more detailed questions about the compromise, including the type of data exposed, and how many employees and customers might be affected. The Register will update this story as we learn more about the breach.®

articles.title: The Bank Outage May Have Nothing to Do With Your Bank
articles.context: ” Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were...
articles.full_text:
If you were planning to do any banking today, good luck.

Customers of many major financial institutions experienced unspecified technical issues on Monday as thousands of reports flooded the uptime-tracking website Downdetector.com from people saying that they had issues using their banks in some way.

It is currently unclear which systems are having issues. However, the problem may stem from technical difficulties at JPMorganChase, the top retail bank that holds over 10 percent of all US deposits, did identify a specific issue.

“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems—there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” says JPMorganChase spokesperson Pablo Rodriguez. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”

Rodriguez adds that the bank is not experiencing a “systemic issue” but that “other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us.” The spokesperson adds that customers “still have access to their accounts and funds” and that the bank is working to resolve the issues.

Apparent issues with the banks, credit unions, fintech apps, and credit card companies appear to begin around 9:30 am ET and peaked at around 2 pm ET. Many people also reported issues using Zelle, the peer-to-peer money-transfer system adopted by major banks. However, in a statement, Zelle denied its systems were the cause of the reported outages while acknowledging that issues at banks may impact people’s ability to use Zelle.

“Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should,” a Zelle spokesperson says in a statement. “Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds.”

US Bank spokesperson Jeffrey Shelman also says the financial institution’s systems “are not directly impacted.” Shelman adds, however, that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”

Seth Eisen, senior vice president of communications at MasterCard, says, “Our network is operating normally.” A Visa spokesperson says the company is aware of the ongoing payments issue, but that Visa’s systems are operating normally too.

According to reports on Downdetector, which is sourced to user reports rather than official statements, the issues on Monday also impacted customers of Bank of America, Capital One, Wells Fargo, TD Bank, Navy Credit Federal Union, and more. These companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: The Race to Remediation: Black October Showed that Threat Intelligence Isn’t Enough
articles.context: Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production...
articles.full_text:
In a single week in October 2026, security teams faced one serious security incident after another. A certificate authority failed, critical flaws in PHP were disclosed after a broken embargo, a popular open-source AI gateway was compromised, and developer platforms reported thefts of customer secrets. Industry insiders started calling the seemingly steady drumbeat of attacks “Black October.”

Any one of these incidents would have kept a security team busy. Collectively, they exposed a bottleneck that has little to do with any single exploit. Security teams are not short on vulnerability information. They are short on answers: what is affected in our environment, and how can we fix it – fast?

As JFrog CEO Shlomi Ben Haim put it: “A single weak link can cost far more than the fix. For LiteLLM and PHP2Shell, being caught off-guard means money, downtime, and customer trust. The companies that come through well are the ones that know exactly what they are running and can act within hours vs. days. JFrog’s role is to find the problems early, tell customers what to do, and make sure they can precisely determine their exposure.”

Three Pressures That Compound

Three forces explain why answers are getting harder to produce:

Volume: In the AI-accelerated landscape of 2026, based on our count of NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD) records, 36,952 CVEs were published in Q3 2026 alone, more than triple the 11,725 published in Q3 2025 (as of November 16, 2026).

Exploitability: A severity score does not say whether a flaw is applicable in your environment. Triage by count alone wastes scarce resources and time.

Attacker Speed: A Cloud Security Alliance survey of more than 900 security leaders found that only 9% of organizations remediate critical or high-severity production vulnerabilities within 24 hours, while 74% take between one and seven days. Meanwhile, attackers can use AI to speed up exploitation, chaining together low-severity findings and making repeated automated attempts until one unpatched system gives them an opening.

That is a different kind of weakness, and it needs a different kind of approach. A faster version of the old process will not close it. AI pushes on all three pressures: it surfaces more flaws and drafts more fixes, but maintainers cannot absorb unlimited volume.

The Disclosure Process Wasn’t Built for This

The vulnerability disclosure process was designed around human review cycles. A researcher reports a flaw, a maintainer triages it, a fix is written, and a CVE is published. That rhythm worked when exploitation was also a manual effort. It does not hold up when attackers can automate discovery and exploitation at scale.

Enterprises have also historically depended on upstream maintainers to publish patches on their own timelines, and those timelines are asynchronous with the CVE disclosure window. In an AI-powered threat landscape, that mismatch becomes an exposure gap that attackers can use.

A new ecosystem of patching vendors has stepped in to help close it. These vendors produce signed, backported fixes for the exact versions enterprises actually consume, often ahead of public disclosure.

Why Does Threat Intelligence Alone Leave a Gap?

Threat intelligence describes the outside world, not your software environment. That difference explains why teams with excellent security vulnerability feeds still lose hours after a disclosure. Two gaps open between a published threat and a confident response:

Timing: Public databases trail events. As of October 2026, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) now enriches only a subset of CVEs, and PHP2Shell was being probed days before patches shipped. A process that waits for them is structurally late.

Remediation: Even with timely, contextual intelligence, someone still has to find a trustworthy fix, apply it across every affected artifact (assuming all artifacts are even traceable), and prove it worked. This is where many teams slow from hours to days.

Know Your Exposure With JFrog Threat Hub

Finding problems early and determining exposure precisely is the first half of the job. JFrog Threat Hub, a feature of JFrog Xray, brings JFrog Security Research findings and vetted external advisories into the same single source of truth that holds your scanned artifacts, so a published threat can be matched to your own environment in one step.

Knowing your exposure only matters if you can act on it quickly, which is the second half of the job.

Fortified Defenses Start With One Source of Truth

A month like October does not call for a faster version of the old process. It calls for a different one. In our view, LiteLLM and PHP2Shell showed what separates the teams that come through well: they could see what they run, and they could fix it fast.

Know everything you run

Start with an inventory at every layer: source code, packages, container images, AI models, and agent tooling. A component you cannot see cannot be prioritized or patched. Then verify what you deploy, not only what you wrote, because malicious code can live in built artifacts while the source stays clean. JFrog Artifactory serves as that single source of truth, holding the main artifact types (binaries, containers, AI models, MCP server packages) in one system of record.

Draw on an ecosystem of fix providers

Fix providers often specialize in particular software ecosystems, so drawing on an ecosystem of providers can help broaden coverage. In our view, reducing this risk requires two critical capabilities: high-quality patches across software ecosystems and a control plane designed to automate remediation at the binary level.

Close the loop with zero-touch remediation

A patch sitting in a vendor’s repository does nothing for an artifact already running in production. Artifactory can act as the control plane that ingests each fix from supported partners. JFrog Security can then apply a selected fix according to the customer’s policy and context, and produce a signed evidence chain that can support audit reviews. The goal is a self-healing software supply chain and zero-touch remediation that aims to help customers patch in hours rather than days. For branches past their end of life, migration remains the durable fix.

Ready for the Next Black October?

When the next disclosure lands, what is affected, and can we fix it in hours rather than days? Organizations that can provide a quality answer will weather the next crowded month. Those that cannot will spend it searching.

Move From Disclosure to Fix in Hours

Patching at scale takes a single source of truth, trusted fixes from an ecosystem of partners, and a universal control plane that applies them automatically. See how zero-touch remediation and the self-healing software supply chain work in your own environment: schedule a demo, take an online tour, or start a free trial of the JFrog Platform.

articles.title: Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline
Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
articles.context: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical...
articles.full_text: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. None of the attack techniques are new, but both of these campaigns show how AI agents can boost the speed and persistence of the attacker. “The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software,” Moses added. “Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.” The FBI weighs in The FBI also hammered this message in a separate Friday alert noting “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.” The federal cops cited the August attacks against South Korean financial institutions that stole personal data belonging to about 67,000 people. The FBI also highlighted a September ARTEX campaign that targetedd ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers in a supply chain attack that ultimately compromised more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft tenants. After these security breaches became public, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October. However, forked and localized variations plus a commercial version remain, and as of November 4 internet scanning service Censys identified 1,465 hosts running an exposed ARTEX console. And the total number of deploymentsis “likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks,” according to the FBI. The feds urged all organizations – especially those operating internet-exposed applications, self-service portals, cloud infrastructure, and partner or supplier systems – to implement a series of mitigation measures outlined in its Flash alert. These include reducing external attack surfaces by restricting sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths, and moving enterprise applications behind zero-trust access policies and permissions. ®

articles.title: 'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models
‘123456’ has been the world’s most popular password for 7 out of the last 8 years
articles.context: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the...
articles.full_text: It’s been eight years since NordPass released the first edition of its most common passwords of the year list, and the world has learned nothing about password security in the meantime. NordPass’ eighth edition of its most common passwords list, as culled from data breaches, was released Monday, and it looks suspiciously like the previous ones in the worst possible way. “Once again, ‘123456’ is the most commonly used password in the world,” NordPass said in the report. “That makes it seven out of eight years this password has stood at the top of the leaderboard.” Even when 123456 wasn’t number one, it was still near the top of the heap, as the top three passwords in the list remain unchanged in the eight years NordPass has published its list: 123456, admin, and 12345678. It’s not like the rest of the most common passwords are showing any variety either. According to NordPass, the only real shuffling among the 10 most popular passwords was the entry of the worryingly short 1234 into the top ten and the migration of the ever-popular password “password” down slightly in the top 10 from 6th to 7th place. “We still have a lot of work to do to spread awareness about password safety,” NordPass concluded of that data – and there’s no more pressing time than the present. AI adoption has made password cracking an easier exercise than ever, with more credentials being sucked up in more data breaches at a faster pace. AI has also made cracking hashed passwords a snap too. In other words, if you’re reusing a password that’s been exposed in a breach, even if it’s just a hash that was exposed, you’re more likely than ever before to have another account compromised. The best advice NordPass gives is to move away from passwords toward biometric authentication or passkeys and you're insane not to enable MFA. But for the places you still have to use passwords, there are a few things to avoid – like the 200 passwords in NordPass’ list, for example. Beyond that, NordPass also recommends steering clear of pop cultural trends. “Fandoms make for terrible passwords,” NordPass notes. There are several reasons for that – namely the fact that they follow trends, meaning that “minecraft” password in the early 2000s was a simple one to add to a password stuffing dictionary, just like “skibiditoilet” in recent years. The one thing that connects all those pop-culture passwords is that “they all could be cracked in seconds,” NordPass said. We’re sure our readers are conscientious about their online habits, carefully protecting their accounts with the proper security measures and ensuring each and every password is unique, long, complicated, and random. Unfortunately for you smarties reading El Reg, the person down the hall whose security you’re responsible for may not be so disciplined, so be sure you’re enforcing good practices – Nord knows the average user just isn’t doing it despite years of begging and reminders. ®

articles.title: NoisyTCP bug gives Linux servers a remote crash problem 11 years in the making
articles.context: The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions
articles.full_text: The researcher who sounded the alarm over Dirty Frag earlier this year has uncovered another Linux kernel flaw, and this one lets attackers crash entire servers remotely without so much as a password. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, was discovered by security researcher Hyunwoo Kim, who says it affects almost all Linux distributions. The flaw dates back to October 2015 and went unnoticed until this year, when Kim found and patched it. Attackers don't need to log in or get their hands on any credentials to cause trouble. They can simply knock the server over, although there's no evidence yet that the flaw can be used to steal data or hijack a machine. The bug is buried in Linux's TCP networking code. Two parts of the kernel can trip over each other while processing incoming traffic, leaving one trying to use memory that's already been freed. When that happens, Linux can panic and take the whole machine down with it. Kim says there's no need for any special server configuration either. Services such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH can be vulnerable straight out of the box. An attacker needs access to an open TCP port on a system that processes incoming network traffic across multiple receive queues or CPUs. Perhaps more concerning for administrators running containerized workloads, the damage isn't necessarily limited to the application being attacked. Because the flaw sits in the Linux kernel, crashing a web server inside a container can take down the underlying host and anything else running on it. Kim found that the attack was particularly effective against virtual machines. During testing, he managed to crash Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running on QEMU/KVM virtual machines in between five seconds and two minutes. Physical hardware put up more of a fight. Even after tailoring his exploit to the target machine, Kim needed roughly 14 hours to crash a bare-metal server running Nginx. Kim has a knack for finding holes in Linux. Back in May, he uncovered Dirty Frag, a kernel bug that allowed local users to gain root privileges. That one caused headaches for administrators when a working exploit went public before patches were ready. His latest discovery, NoisyTCP, has another potentially nasty trick up its sleeve. Kim identified a second exploitation path involving a use-after-free condition, although pulling it off is considerably more difficult than simply crashing a server. In his advisory, Kim says he has developed a limited exploit targeting virtual machines in a lab environment but has yet to demonstrate a general-purpose remote code execution attack. For the moment, the confirmed impact is remote denial of service. A fix was committed to the upstream Linux kernel on November 3, but administrators will need to check whether their distribution has shipped an updated kernel. Red Hat has rated the vulnerability Important, assigning it a CVSS score of 7.5. For those unable to patch immediately, Kim suggests two temporary workarounds: disabling TCP SYN cookies or restricting incoming packet processing to a single receive queue. Neither is particularly appealing. Disabling SYN cookies reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, while limiting packet processing can hurt network performance. The former also needs to be applied separately to containers using their own network namespaces. Kim published the details on November 15, once the disclosure embargo was lifted. The bug had been hiding in plain sight since 2015, leaving Linux servers vulnerable to remote crashes for 11 years. Not bad for a flaw that doesn't even require a login. ®
