Typosquatters Target New Brand Domains Within 24 Hours of Registration
articles.context: “The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers...
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are impersonating big-name brands via typosquatting just one day after legitimate domains are created, according to new research from Symantec.

The active campaign, first observed in August, has seen 25 lookalike domains created which resembled authentic domain names used by companies such as Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi.

Every lookalike domain was registered within 24 hours of its authentic counterpart, often before the company even launched the new website.

“The findings highlight how attackers can exploit the period between a company's domain registration and its public launch, positioning lookalike websites to capture consumers who mistype legitimate addresses,” Symantec wrote.

Typosquatting is when malicious actors register domains that are slightly misspelled from a legitimate organization’s domain, such as one letter added or removed. This means that when a user accidently misspells a legitimate site name when typing the address by hand, they could be directed to a typosquatter’s site instead.

The fake websites are designed to closely resemble the organization they are impersonating.

These sites enable a range of follow-on malicious activity, such as directing users to scam sites, installing malware and harvesting credentials.

Attackers Focus on Campaign Sites to Maximize Effectiveness

The Symantec research, published on November 16, found that most of the malicious domains impersonated campaign sites rather than corporate home pages.

These included patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, rebates, claims portals and legal settlements.

Users are more likely to type such addresses by hand as these websites are often displayed on printed mailers, television advertisements, pharmacy leaflets and court-ordered settlement notices.

Campaign sites are also likely to ask visitors for personal information, such as names, addresses, claim numbers or health details, with visitors expecting to hand over such data upon arrival.

The typosquatting campaign focused on clients of two brand-protection registrars, Corporation Service Company (CSC) and MarkMonitor. Each time a large company registered a new domain through one of these registrars, a one-letter lookalike was registered the next day through a China-based registrar.

In one case, used car dealer CarMax registered carmaxclaims[.]com and kmxclaims[.]com through CSC on August 26. The next day, two lookalike domains were registered that removed the ‘s’ from each of the legitimate domains, carmaxclaim[.]com and kmxclaim[.]com.

Other typos used included leaving out other single letters and collapsing a double letter, for example, mywayconnect became mywayconect.

New lookalike domains were registered as recently as November 11, suggesting the campaign is ongoing.

Typosquat Domains Rapidly Monetized Through Ads and Scams

The observed typosquat domains appeared to have several purposes. Some were parked placeholder pages that earned money from pay-per-click advertising feeds, while others were deceptive search portals whose results led to scam blogs, or brand-themed blogs written around the typosquatted name and packed with ads that routed visitors to scam sites.

“This low-grade scam traffic may not be the end goal. Advertising networks of this kind can also be abused for malvertising and credential harvesting, and a domain that serves ads today could serve a fake claims form tomorrow with a single Domain Name System (DNS) or content change. Visitors who reach these domains are already primed to enter personal details,” Symantec noted.

Given the speed at which attackers published their lookalike domains following the campaign launch, the researchers believe the setup was likely automated.

“The actors’ tooling was not visible to us, but the evidence is consistent with a simple pipeline that watched new registrations, filtered on brand-protection registrars, generated a one-character variant and registered it before the next day was out,” the researchers added.

articles.title: La Poste Subsidiary Maileva Breach Exposes 22 Million People
articles.context: Read more on French cyber-attacks: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C Docaposte's statement now called what happened in mid-September "a...
articles.full_text:
A cyber-attack on La Poste-owned document-sending provider Maileva has exposed the names and postal addresses of 22 million people.

Docaposte, La Poste's digital subsidiary that owns Maileva, confirmed the breach in a November 15 statement.

Maileva sends documents such as payslips, registered letters and invoices on behalf of businesses and institutions.

The firm said that 22 million people who received mailings from Maileva’s business and institutional clients are affected by a leak of identifying information, including first name, last name and postal address.

What Maileva Data Was Exposed

Docaposte said Maileva's clients had been able to tell their customers that some of their data had been compromised, the nature of which is linked to the content of the documents sent. It did not say how many people that covered.

The content of the documents shared on its platform is not held by Maileva, rather it relates to the relationship between Maileva’s clients and the recipients of those documents.

Several thousand Maileva client companies were affected, the company told Cyberattaque.org, which first reported the breach.

Docaposte said affected clients were informed in the days after the incident was identified.

A hospital near Paris, Hôpital Foch, said an attacker could view some payment reminder letters containing invoice numbers, care dates and amounts due, but not the nature of the care or bank details. Meanwhile, a social housing provider in northern France, Flandre Opale Habitat, said exposed information could include names, contact details, client numbers, housing references and invoice amounts.

Dray Agha, senior manager of tactical response at Huntress, said in emailed comments that criminals could use the stolen names and addresses to send targeted fake invoices or payment reminders.

"I strongly advise anyone receiving an unexpected bill to verify it directly with the named organization. You must use official websites rather than the contact details provided in the suspicious letter," Agha added.

Sophisticated Cyber-Attack Hits Maileva

Maileva suspended its platform on September 23 and resumed services on September 29, a six-day outage affecting all clients. At the time, Docaposte described the event as a cybersecurity incident involving attempted unauthorized access to the platform, according to Solutions Numériques.

Cyberattaque.org reported the incident on September 24, when Maileva described attempts against some customer accounts aimed at sending fraudulent mail. No large-scale personal data leak had been announced at that point.

Read more on French cyber-attacks: France Blood Service Cyber-Attack Sends Blood Storage Temperatures to 110°C

Docaposte's statement now called what happened in mid-September "a complex cyber-attack," adding that "no data was found to have been altered or destroyed." It said France's data protection authority (CNIL) had been notified, a complaint had been filed and a judicial investigation was under way.

Docaposte did not address whether anyone had claimed the attack or whether the stolen data had been published or sold. Maileva told Cyberattaque.org that notifying affected people was the responsibility of its client organizations.

articles.title: NIST Finalizes Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance, GAO Offers a Reality Check
Hijacked by Hype: The Weaponization of GTA 6
articles.context: Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer...
articles.full_text:
Lead Analysts: Lucy Gee and Cameron Sweeney

With Grand Theft Auto 6 scheduled to launch on November 19, 2026, the 13-year wait for the most anticipated video game release of the decade is nearly over.

As legitimate marketing emails from Rockstar Games increase, video game fans are hyped. The anticipation is massive. However, this unprecedented excitement has created a perfect storm for cybercriminals.

Rockstar and its vast cult following have long fascinated threat actors, with the studio famously suffering massive network breaches and high-profile data leaks in recent years. Now, attackers are pivoting those established tactics directly toward the fanbase.

Threat actors are actively capitalizing on gamers' desperation, knowing that heightened anticipation reliably leads to lower critical thinking. By impersonating Rockstar in a massive, coordinated wave of phishing campaigns, they are weaponizing the promise of exclusive early access, fake "leaked" playable copies, or beta tester invitations to actively exploit both everyday consumers and corporate employees.

This playbook aligns directly with findings from KnowBe4’s Phishing Threat Trends Report Volume 8. That research showed planned calendar events drive the highest volume of lure-based attacks, with campaigns landing an average of 21.3 days before the actual date. On top of that, the lifespan of these planned campaigns more than doubled between 2022 and 2026, giving attackers plenty of time to tweak their angles and test out different lures.

The GTA 6 wave illustrates this dynamic in real time. Data obtained from KnowBe4 Defend shows a rapid, strategic escalation precisely within this pre-launch window:

Key Takeaways:

While GTA-themed phishing accounted for just 0.005% of threats in September, general gaming-related phishing emails have since surged by 1,300% compared to the monthly average across the previous six months (March–August 2026).

For the full week starting October 26th, 24 days before the release, GTA-related lures rapidly scaled to make up 9.6% of all phishing volume.

The First Wave: Mass-Market Noise

Predominantly, this surge is driven by high-volume, spray-and-pray commodity lures. These attacks focus on broad consumer appeal, casting a wide net across millions of inboxes in hopes of catching eager gamers off guard.

In the most widespread campaign, threat actors rely on a minimalist payload delivery to bypass security defenses: the email body is left completely blank, containing nothing more than an embedded link. By stripping away text entirely, the message circumvents basic natural language processing (NLP) filters and spam heuristics that search for suspicious gaming keywords.

To evade domain-reputation blocks, the campaign is heavily polymorphic, distributing waves of messages through constantly rotating webmail accounts with random subject lines so that blocking a single sender provides zero defense against the broader campaign.

Anatomy of the Attack

Clicking the link routes victims through a multi-stage lure that heavily borrows the official Grand Theft Auto 6 aesthetic. Initial landing pages are hosted on graph[.]org, which is Telegram’s lightweight, anonymous and login free publishing site. This allows attackers to host malicious content without registering their own infrastructure, making it easy to stand up pages that slip past filters, especially those looking at domain age.

These pages feature Vice City neon styling, AI generated imagery of characters Lucia and Jason, and prominent Rockstar Games branding. The copy leans into themed phrasing like "The wait is over," "Vice City is calling," and promises of an exclusive "$4,000 bonus" using promo code ROCKSTAR.

Once a user clicks the activate prompt, they are redirected to a fraudulent online casino or crypto platform (such as new2026[.]pro) with the promo code pre-applied. The ultimate objective is dual-pronged monetization: tricking victims into registering an account to harvest passwords they likely recycle across gaming and personal platforms, while simultaneously siphoning payment card details or cryptocurrency deposits under the guise of claiming their GTA-themed welcome bonus. While these mass-market lures lack the sophistication needed to directly compromise enterprise networks, their relentless volume acts as a smokescreen, generating endless background noise for SOC teams.

Campaign Telemetry: Commodity Attack Distribution

Top Targeted Regions: United States (47%), United Kingdom (35%), Germany (8%), France (5%), Rest of World (5%)

Primary Target Verticals: Education (39%), Technology (35%), and Finance (15%)

Campaign: 84 attacks on average per campaign, typically peaking on weekends and evenings.

While these commodity attacks lack sophistication, their sheer volume creates a smokescreen designed to overwhelm SOC teams. The real danger lies in what slips beneath the radar: advanced, targeted phishing campaigns, created to weaponize the intersection of personal interests and organizational trust.

The Second Wave: Targeting the Enterprise

Instead of directly impersonating Rockstar Games, these sophisticated attacks pose as employee benefits programs offering a "free Grand Theft Auto 6 Pre-Order" as a corporate perk. Because a free copy of a highly anticipated game is one of the few things that will convince an employee to check a work email on their days off, these campaigns are heavily weighted toward weekends, accounting for 83.2% of the attack volume. This strategy peaked over the October 31 to November 1 weekend, where GTA-related impersonations made up 42.4% of all phishing emails processed.

In this example, the attacker is combining psychological manipulation with technical evasion elements to ensure the attack lands in users’ inboxes and they’re motivated to click. Rather than impersonating Rockstar directly, which users might view with suspicion, the attacker routes the lure through a fake employee benefits program. Framing the game as a corporate perk carries significantly more weight than standard brand impersonation.

The attack also utilizes senses of urgency, claiming the offer closes in 48 hours and is strictly limited to the first 250 employees. This artificial urgency pushes the victim toward a fast, low-deliberation click. To make the attack look legitimate, the banner at the bottom of the email explicitly states that the message was sent to a verified address and does not collect payment information. This pre-answers the recipient's own suspicions, lowering their guard before they even question the email. By tying the lure directly to the real-world GTA 6 news cycle, the attack feels incredibly timely and relevant, blending seamlessly into the broader hype.

Technical Evasion

Clean Authentication Bypass: The attackers use a genuinely owned, look-alike vendor domain rather than a spoofed one. As the domain is legitimately registered to the threat actor, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass cleanly.

Unicode QR Codes: To evade traditional detection, the email uses a QR code rendered entirely out of text block characters (Unicode or HTML tables) rather than a standard image file, allowing it to bypass image QR scanners.

Device Shifting: The ultimate goal of the QR code is to shift the attack off the protected corporate network. By forcing the victim to scan the code with their personal smartphone, the attacker completely bypasses corporate web filtering and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) controls.

These sophisticated phishing emails largely followed the same distribution as the commodity attacks. Campaign sizes, however, are much smaller averaging 20 attacks per campaign.

The Corporate Risk of Personal Lures

This blurring of lines between personal interests and professional environments is exactly what makes these attacks so dangerous. While a fake GTA 6 pre-order might initially look like a standard consumer scam aimed at stealing a personal credit card, the reality is far more severe: these campaigns are explicitly designed to compromise corporate assets. When an eager employee scans a malicious QR code on their unmanaged personal phone to claim a supposed "work perk," the resulting phishing page is rarely asking for their bank details. Instead, attackers are weaponizing this gaming hype to harvest credentials; turning a momentary lapse in personal judgment into a full-scale corporate breach.

Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks

As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer excitement and corporate access. Threat actors targeted human psychology, not a software zero-day exploit. They identified an emotional blind spot of weekend relaxation and genuine excitement and used it to bypass both technical filters and common sense.

Protecting your organization against these hybrid threats requires a layered approach:

Run Contextual Simulations: Train employees on non-traditional lure types. Especially fake HR perks, vendor discounts, real-world events, and corporate benefits delivered outside typical working hours.

Validate Internal Communications: Establish a clear protocol for corporate benefits so employees know legitimate company perks will always appear on an internal intranet or HR portal, never via unsolicited external email links or urgent QR codes.

Teach the "Device Shift" Red Flag: Educate staff that any work-related email asking them to pull out a personal smartphone to scan a QR code is a deliberate attempt to bypass security perimeter controls.

Normalize Healthy Scrutiny: Remind teams that genuine corporate perks never demand urgency. If an offer says “limited to the first 250 employees,” it’s designed to shut down deliberate thinking.

Harden Quishing Defenses: Ensure your email security layer can detect QR codes, including those rendered as Unicode characters or HTML tables, not just as image files.

When real-world hype peaks, critical thinking drops. Ensuring your workforce and security stack are prepared for both the high-volume noise and the targeted signal is the best defense against turning a pop-culture milestone into a network compromise.

Where KnowBe4 Can Help

These attacks rely on natural human emotions to trick your users. Excitement. A sense of urgency. Whether it’s an invitation to click a link or scan a QR code, your users need to be aware of the varied kinds of attacks bad actors are using.

The KnowBe4 Platform and its suite of tools provides the training your users need with the technology-based defenses to help keep attacks from even reaching the inbox.

AI-Native Security Awareness Training

Hype-based attacks need a quick response to ensure your users have the resources they need to spot them. KnowBe4’s suite of AI Defense Agents (AIDA) includes the capabilities to generate custom phishing simulation templates and whole modules in minutes, helping training admins respond to the newest threats.

KnowBe4 Defend: Real-Time Behavioral AI

KnowBe4 Defend uses behavioral AI and natural language processing to analyze email content and context to clearly flag when emails look suspicious. Defend adds a warning banner directly into the email before the recipient opens it. This interrupts the illusion of legitimacy, such as phishing attacks claiming to offer internal company benefits or perks.

PhishER Plus: Automated Threat Response

Once novel threats are identified, either through machine learning or human observation, PhishER Plus uses this information to keep future users from even seeing them. It automatically categorizes threats, provides immediate feedback to reporters, and enables one-click remediation across all mailboxes. Drawing intelligence from 13+ million global users and integrations with leading security platforms, PhishER Plus delivers unprecedented visibility while providing clear decision-making transparency.

articles.title: Google Project Zero to Cut Disclosure Deadline to 30 Days by 2028
articles.context: It also argued that severity should not set disclosure timing: "A vulnerability's severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its...
articles.full_text:
Google's Project Zero has scrapped its "90 + 30" disclosure policy and will publish vulnerability details 90 days after reporting them, whether or not a fix exists, before cutting the disclosure deadline to 60 days and then 30 days.

Project Zero outlined the changes in a November 13 post and tied the changes to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

Project Zero said, "We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year."

Project Zero Replaces 90 Plus 30 Policy

Under the new policy, dubbed Full X, Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities X days after reporting them to vendors. The policy begins as Full 90, moves to Full 60 on February 2, 2027 and reaches Full 30 on January 3, 2028.

The 30-day 'soak time', the grace period and the variant policy have been removed. Three exceptions remain: vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild, bugs whose details have already been made public and cases where vendors ask Project Zero to publish the details.

Project Zero said 'soak time' was no longer meaningful because attackers can almost immediately work out bug details from a patch.

Vendors consulted by Project Zero warned that an immediate change could expose unfixed bugs, push them to fix Project Zero's reports ahead of more severe ones or lead some to stop trying.

Defenders Pressed to Close the Patch Gap

Ivan Milenkovic, VP of risk technology at Qualys, told Infosecurity that Project Zero had "removed the snooze button on responding to issues." Pointing to Project Zero's finding rate, he said: "This describes an arrival rate that most patch programmes were never built for."

For organizations, he said, patching monthly now means you're slower than disclosure. He called the vendors' objection to an immediate change to the disclosure policy "a fair response, but the alternative was letting attackers set the deadline."

Read more on vulnerability disclosure: N-able Rushes Out N-central Fixes After 33 Zero-Days Go Public

Project Zero said its new policy was intended to encourage vendors to reduce the patch gap, the period between a fix becoming available and users installing it.

It also argued that severity should not set disclosure timing: "A vulnerability's severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users."

The group said it would still track whether bugs were fixed, but that fix status would no longer decide when technical details were published.

Clive Robinson • November 16, 2026 10:17 AM

@ Bruce, Rontea, ALL,

Unfortunately as our host @Bruce notes,

“And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer.”

But the questions about “convenient” need to be asked, because as @Rontea notes,

“It’s not user error—it’s a mismatch between policy and environment.”

But consider the current “business drivers”,

“The pace, service culture, and constant demand for ultra-personalized attention create the perfect conditions for attackers to exploit.”

Questions should arise such as,

1, Will this ever change? – Probably not. 2, Will there be ways to stop attacks whilst keeping the service culture? – Put simply no.

Have a think about AI for a moment…

Not as a solution to this problem, but as an example of why you can not fix this type of vulnerability.

“Human orientated work rules” are actually,

A, Guide rails. B, Sandboxes.

Written for humans.

We know that there is proof that with AI “Guide rails” can always be subverted and by extension “Sandboxes” always broken out from.

So ask the question,

“If AI systems will provably always be open to being subverted, why should we expect human work will not be?”

The thing is anything that AI will fail at, so will humans.

articles.title: FBI Highlights Growing Abuse of AI-Driven Pentesting Framework ARTEX
articles.context: Read more about ARTEX: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses ARTEX Origins and LLM Integration ARTEX is an open-source, AI model-...
articles.full_text:
The FBI has warned of a growing number of malicious cyber intrusion campaigns leveraging the open-source, AI-powered penetration testing tool ARTEX.

In a FBI Flash notice, published on November 13, the Bureau said a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally since at least August 2026.

Targets range across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal industries.

Recent incidents have included financially motivated attacks against South Korean financial institutions which resulted in the exfiltration of personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals and a supply chain compromise affecting ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers that enabled access to more than 2250 downstream tenants.

The FBI noted that ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques and some intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.

Read more about ARTEX: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses

ARTEX Origins and LLM Integration

ARTEX is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘Autumn-27’ in July 2026.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

The FBI highlighted that ARTEX does not include its own AI model, rather it integrates with external LLM providers, including frontier models (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT) and open-source or Chinese-origin models (DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, Kimi).

“Analysis of attacker-controlled ARTEX instances shows Chinese models are most prevalent, with DeepSeek Flash family models dominating usage due to their balance of capabilities, relatively low cost and lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing,” the FBI notice read.

The original GitHub repository for ARTEX was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse. The author claimed they were not involved in the ARTEX-linked attacks and that the tool was only meant for authorized penetration testing.

Nevertheless, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO.

Key Risks: Automation, Overlooked Systems and Supply Chain Attacks

The FBI assessed that ARTEX poses several risks as threat actors adopt it.

It automates the time-consuming enumeration and exploitation phases of intrusions, allowing even small groups to run multiple campaigns at once.

It also lowers the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks.

ARTEX is particularly effective at finding and exploiting overlooked systems that receive less security attention than flagship applications, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales-support tools, legacy services and third-party integrations.

It has also demonstrated supply chain capabilities, including modifying iOS application distribution infrastructure through exposed cloud credentials. By mapping trust relationships between organizations, it can compromise weaker vendors or CI/CD pipelines and pivot into high-value enterprise networks.

Although ARTEX generates noisy traffic that may trigger alerts, its speed leaves defenders little time to coordinate a response before attackers achieve their objectives.

The FBI provided a list of recommended security controls and operational measures organizations can take to prevent and mitigate ARTEX.

The Bureau is also seeking any helpful information on ARTEX and malicious campaigns using the tool, including infrastructure artifacts, authentication and access logs, application and API activity, LLM and AI infrastructure indicators, cloud and container activity and exploitation and persistence artifacts.

Read now: ARTEX Offensive AI Tool Activity Far Exceeds Reported Campaigns, Censys Finds

Information Commissioner’s Office Receives 300+ Reports of Medical Snooping
articles.context: In May, 11 staff were sacked and 14 given written warnings after unlawfully accessing the records of victims of the 2023 Nottingham knife attacks
articles.full_text:
The UK’s data protection watchdog has written to health service leaders after receiving hundreds of reports of staff illegally accessing patient records.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) said it has asked over 200 NHS bosses across the UK to provide personal assurances that measures are in place to prevent and detect unauthorized insider access.

The letter itself details four areas that healthcare organizations must focus on: effective access controls, effective auditing and monitoring for unauthorized access, regular training for staff and consistent action when things go wrong.

“You should investigate suspected unauthorized access promptly and consistently. You should consider the impact on the person affected, including your obligations to notify the individual,” it said. “You should also consider your obligations to notify the ICO. Where you establish wrongdoing, you should take appropriate disciplinary, professional, regulatory or other action.”

The ICO said it has already received over 300 reports of unauthorized access by NHS staff, including workers looking at records with no legitimate need, and viewing or sharing the records of people they know.

Read more on NHS data leaks: ICO Cautions Healthcare Worker After Princess of Wales Incident

The letter comes on the back of several high-profile incidents impacting the health service.

In May, 11 staff were sacked and 14 given written warnings after unlawfully accessing the records of victims of the 2023 Nottingham knife attacks. A month later a Cambridgeshire hospital launched an investigation after around 40 staff accessed the records of a seriously injured child without good reason.

In June the ICO issued a former healthcare worker a formal caution after they tried to access and sell the medical records of the Princess of Wales at a private hospital.

What the ICO Wants to Know

ICO chief executive, Paul Arnold, sent out practical advice and recommendations to healthcare organizations back in June.

In his new letter, he said that NHS chief executives need the right processes, culture and behaviors in place to safeguard patient data.

“Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardise the vital trust people place in our health service,” Arnold added.

“This message goes beyond the health sector: any organization entrusted with people's most sensitive information has a duty to protect it and we will take action if they fall short. I strongly encourage leaders in every sector to ask themselves whether their safeguards would stand up to the same scrutiny.”

The ICO is now asking NHS CEOs to confirm that their organization is:

Actively and continuously managing access to patient records

Spotting suspicious access using effective monitoring and audit systems

Confident that every member of staff knows what is expected of them what the consequences are of illegally accessing medical records

Investigating suspected unauthorized access promptly and taking appropriate action if wrongdoing is established

“Senior leaders should confirm that they have reviewed their organization’s approach in these areas within the past six months,” the ICO said. “Those who have not are expected to complete a review within the next three months. The responses will help shape the regulator’s next steps to respond to this issue and help protect patient’s privacy.”

AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours
articles.context: A new report by the cybersecurity firm, Finding Critical Infrastructure Bugs with Off-the-Shelf AI, details how publicly available models can help teams working with a small...
articles.full_text:
Forescout Technologies has added its voice to the growing number urging security teams to embrace AI, revealing how the technology helped it accelerate vulnerability discovery.

A new report by the cybersecurity firm, Finding Critical Infrastructure Bugs with Off-the-Shelf AI, details how publicly available models can help teams working with a small budget unearth vulnerabilities in open source software and proprietary binaries.

The researchers used a specially built AI-assisted vulnerability research harness to find bugs in 10 popular TCP/IP stacks.

This approach reduced analysis time from around nine months to 90 hours and helped the team uncover 99 vulnerabilities, including 66 zero days, Forescout said.

Read more on AI in security: Hackers Observed Using AI to Develop Zero-Day for the First Time

After 10 hours of AI analysis, the team then spent around 80 hours manually validating the findings. Static analysis across the 10 stacks cost around $935, which means just $2.58 per finding, the report claimed.

However, it added that binary analysis was around six times more expensive and took twice as long as source-code analysis.

“AI did not eliminate the need for expert vulnerability researchers, but it dramatically compressed the work. With access to an effective AI-assisted workflow, vulnerabilities in complex embedded software can be found much faster and at a fraction of the cost, by security researchers and attackers alike,” said Daniel dos Santos, VP of Research at Forescout.

“Our research demonstrates that AI is changing the economics of vulnerability discovery and accelerating the pace at which security teams need to identify, prioritize, and mitigate cyber risk. This is especially impactful for critical infrastructure, where legacy and difficult-to-patch devices may remain in service for years.”

AI Tips for Security Teams

However, AI is not a silver bullet. Research by ReliaQuest pointed to the technology helping threat actors make attacks cheaper, faster to scale, easier to customize and harder to spot.

However, this some have warned that it can make attacks less efficient. One security expert from Proofpoint recently described AI-generated exploits as highly flawed.

To mitigate risk in this new world of AI everywhere, Forescout urged security researchers to:

Assess and prioritize risk based on reachability, exploitability, and operational impact rather than treating all vulnerabilities equally

Reduce unnecessary exposure of connected devices by disabling services such as FTP, Telnet, IPv6 and web administration interfaces

Isolate devices that cannot be patched such as those that have reached end of life

Accelerate patching timelines when fixes exist to account for a faster rate of vulnerability disclosure.

Build security into procurement by requiring suppliers to define support lifetimes, publish vulnerability disclosure policies, provide software bills of materials (SBOMs), and demonstrate ongoing security testing

articles.full_text: Email is just one of those utilities like power or water where you always expect it to just, well, to just be there. You sign up with a provider and use as much of it as you need, when you need it, and the idea of it being unavailable for any extended period of time is foreign. Microsoft's outage a few days ago was one of those exceptional circumstances, and whilst it absolutely rocked the whole internet, it's far from a reason not to decry using email for most of the things we currently apply it to. But it is a good time to look at where redundancy makes sense; maybe start with redundant channels for alerts about things that could hurt people!

articles.full_text:
By: Jacob Malimban, Intelligence Team

Cofense Intelligence has identified an active phishing campaign exploiting confusion surrounding the Microsoft November 2026 outage to deliver a credential phishing attack. The email, supposedly from Microsoft and personalized using the recipient’s organization, claims that emails are unavailable due to disruptions to Exchange Online. The recipient is instructed to click the button to “Restore Messages”. Clicking on the button, however, redirects the user to a Microsoft 365-spoofing credential phishing page.

Threat actors move quickly on big news. The first sample was seen one day into the outage. By combining the recent outage news with their phishing attacks and likely with generative AI, the threat actors have quickly created an ongoing and likely effective campaign. After this outage, people expect email problems, so a message about stuck emails matches what they already expect, and they may check emails less carefully.

Email Content

Figure 1: Held message notification used in credential phishing. (ATR 426633)

This campaign email sends a fake held message notification with a button leading to a credential phishing site. The email, as shown in Figure 1, is styled like a legitimate Microsoft notification. The email appears to come from the organization’s “Outage Notification” based on the email recipient’s company. Recipients are informed that “messages are held and will be deleted within 24 hours unless released”, because threat actors use urgency to get victims to act. Clicking on the button in the email to “RESTORE MESSAGES” will redirect the email recipient to a Microsoft 365 credential phishing site instead.

Microsoft-Spoofing Sign-In Page

Figure 2: Microsoft credential phishing page used in campaign. (ATR 426633)

In prior campaigns, threat actors were already good at creating realistic login pages. As seen in Figure 2, the Microsoft credential phishing page used in this campaign is a good mimicry of the real Microsoft login page.

When a victim first submits credentials, the phishing page will say that the credentials are incorrect. If they try a second time, the page will redirect to Microsoft to obfuscate the fact that they were on a phishing page. Although this type of phishing lure has been used before, threat actors are combining it with breaking news regarding the outage to create a dangerous attack.

Cofense Intelligence provides early warning of emerging phishing campaigns through Flash Alerts like this one, giving security teams advance notice of new tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) before they reach more inboxes. In this case, the campaign bypassed Abnormal Security, Mimecast, and Microsoft ATP. Despite the bypass of email security controls, employees trained using Cofense’s Security Awareness Training (SAT) were able to identify the phishing campaign emails like those found in ATR 426633.

articles.title: Updating our coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy timelines
articles.context: We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days...
articles.full_text:
Over the last several months, frontier models have become much better at discovering vulnerabilities. We remain optimistic that this will help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever before. However, the speed at which AI is improving has changed how we think about our own disclosure practices.

We’re shortening the disclosure window in our coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027. In-progress reports as of that date will keep their existing deadlines.

In addition to shortening the disclosure window, we are making two related changes. First, we will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to our initial vulnerability report. Second, we will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of our policy remains the same.

Finally, there are high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we reported over 90 days ago and that now exceed the deadline in our current CVD policy that have not yet been disclosed publicly. We are now notifying the maintainers of these projects that we are providing them an additional 30 days, after which time we will publish these reports on our dashboard in line with our updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

Responding to AI-enabled vulnerability discovery

Many coordinated disclosure norms, including those found in our own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities. These policies assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. Neither assumption holds today. Models can now help develop fixes, and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another. We are seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.

Some vulnerabilities still can’t be fixed quickly. Flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC can’t always be resolved in 30 or 45 days. In these cases, we will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Our seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation remains unchanged. This new policy update will not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner.

We recognize that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers. To reduce that burden, we will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible, to best enable the maintainer to confirm a finding and fix the vulnerability. We will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project.

We offer programs to help maintainers and defenders work at this new pace. Maintainers of critical open-source projects can apply to OSS Scanner, a no-cost service that periodically scans their code with our strongest models and sends them findings directly. Eligible maintainers and contributors can apply to the Claude for Open Source Program for six months of Claude Ultra at no cost. And security professionals, including open-source maintainers, can apply to our Cyber Verification Program, which tailors Claude’s safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work.

articles.title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
articles.context: Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request
articles.full_text:
By Parth Sareen and Zain Hasan (Together AI)

Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more.

This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it’s also very easy to break the prefix cache.

We come at this problem from opposite ends. Ollama works on harness integrations which means deciding what goes into each request. Together AI works on the inference engine which means deciding what happens when that request arrives. We kept finding that much of our work on each side is about protecting the cache from things the other side can do to it, so we wanted to write it all down in one place to help agent and infra builders alike!

What an agent turn looks like to a GPU

Every request goes through two phases. The first is prefill: the engine reads the whole prompt in one big parallel pass and produces the first token. GPUs are good at this because it’s a lot of math done all at once which maximizes arithmetic intensity. Prefill determines how long you wait before any new tokens appear. The second is decode: the model writes the rest of the answer one token at a time, and each new token requires reading back and attending through everything before it. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth more than by compute, and it determines how fast the text streams out.

A normal chat response spends time in both phases while an agent turn is mostly prefill, because the input is the whole session and the output is usually a short tool call. Reasoning models add thinking tokens on top of that, sometimes a lot of them, but as a session grows into the tens of thousands of tokens the input still dominates. Each turn the input gets longer, and the output stays roughly the same size — a few tool calls.

So for agents, “how fast is this model?” mostly means “how fast can it get through a long historical account of previous turns?” The way to process a task with lots of previous turns quickly is to just cache it and read it back in rather than recomputing.

Cache is king

The easiest way to picture the KV cache (or even the prefix cache, for that matter) is reading. Imagine that to read each new word on a page, you had to start again from the top. The further down the page you got, the slower you’d go, because you’d keep having to reread everything you’d already read. That’s a model with no cache. The cache solves this within a single request: the engine keeps the work it did on earlier tokens (stored as intermediate key, value pairs) and computes only the new one.

Prefix caching does the same thing across requests. Turn 7 of an agent session is turn 6 plus a bit more, so if the engine still holds turn 6’s work, it only has to process the new part.

The arithmetic is simple. If each turn adds the same amount, ten turns without caching process 1 + 2 + … + 10 = 55 units of prompt. With caching, they process 10. At a hundred turns, which isn’t unusual for a coding task, it’s 5,050 versus 100. Real turns vary in size, so treat these as idealized numbers. A cached session isn’t completely free either, since every new token still has to attend to the cached ones. But the pattern holds: without caching, the work you redo grows with the square of the session length.

The catch is that a prefix cache matches from the beginning of the prompt up to the first token that’s different, and stops there. Everything after that first difference has to be processed again.

Adding to the end of the prompt costs nothing extra. Changing anything earlier, even a single character, means re-processing everything after it. If the change is near the top, you’ve effectively thrown away the whole session and now must rebuild the cache. Almost everything else in this post follows from that one rule.

The harness decides where that first change lands. The engine decides whether the cache is still there when the next request shows up. We’ll start with the harness.

The harnesses and APIs

On the Ollama side, we shipped the ability to connect your favorite harness through the ollama launch command. So you can connect harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, Pi (and more) with open models like DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3 and maintain your existing workflows.

Connecting a harness to an API might seem easy, but there are many layers of translation and varying expectations between a harness and a model. This often is the cause of cache breakages (incurring time and monetary costs), unexplainable agent behavior, and the harness outright erroring.

Loading tools late

Harnesses carry quite a few tools now. If every definition goes into the prompt up front, you spend context on tools the task will never use, and the model gets worse at picking the right one. Newer harnesses have added a feature for tool search to alleviate this, where the tool can be loaded and used by the agent itself after searching for it.

Let’s say you have a personal assistant as an agent which has this capability. If you ask the agent to export the events you’ve starred to a calendar, and it searches for “calendar,” loads the save_calendar definition, and calls it.

For the cache, the question is where that definition goes.

The obvious approach is to add the definition to the tool list. That works, but the tool list sits near the top of the prompt, before the conversation. So if the prefix changes everything after it gets processed again. On a long session, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens. The better approach is to put the definition at the end, where new content goes anyway.

Except not every model supports that. Some chat templates don’t expect a tool definition halfway through a conversation, and the call errors out. So whether a harness can load tools late without paying for it depends on the model. Users shouldn’t have to know this, but anyone building a harness does.

Things at the top that change

The easiest way to wreck the cache is to put something in the system prompt that changes from turn to turn, like a current timestamp, the git status, or a working directory the agent keeps moving through. If the harness re-renders the system prompt with fresh values on every turn, every turn is a full re-read.

Things that are fixed for a session but differ between sessions, like the user’s name or the date the session started, don’t hurt that session. They do stop new sessions from reusing a setup that’s already cached, which we’ll get to on the engine side. Either way, the fix is the same: put that information in the task message, once, and keep the system prompt identical everywhere.

Reasoning effort

We hit this one on the Ollama side. In GLM-5.3-Flash, reasoning effort isn’t a separate setting the engine handles on the side. The chat template writes it into the very first system block, ahead of the tools and the conversation.

Let’s say you’re deep into a long task and it isn’t going well. You raise effort from low to high. That’s a reasonable thing to do, but the next request now differs from the last one almost at the first token. Which means the whole session gets processed again. On a long run, that can be hundreds of thousands of tokens spent on changing one setting.

Our advice is to pick an effort level at the start and leave it there. If you really need more thinking, it’s often cheaper to start a fresh session at the higher setting than to continue the old one, and you get a clean context out of it too. You could also compact before changing the reasoning value to decrease the amount of prompt tokens.

Big tool results

A tool’s output becomes part of the next request, and of every request after it. If the agent reads a 3,000-line file when it needed forty lines, you don’t pay for that once; you pay for it on every remaining turn (even if it is cached you lose out on the context window). To combat this, harnesses often cut tool output down. That’s the right call, but how you cut tool output matters.

Here’s a failure that’s easy to build by accident. The task is to fix a timezone bug in a calendar export. The agent reads calendar.py, and the tool returns the first 100 lines of a 640-line file without saying it stopped. The function that matters, convert_timezone, is at line 420. The model has no idea it’s missing anything.

The fix is a single line in the output, telling the model it got lines 1 to 100 of 640 and that it can search the file or request another range. With that, the model searches for “timezone,” finds line 420, and reads lines 410 to 450. Cutting output saves money. Cutting it without saying so gets you a model confidently editing code it never saw.

Subagents

Open models like Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.3-Flash are now pretty good at splitting a big task and handing pieces to subagents. How the harness starts each subagent decides how much of the parent’s cache it can reuse.

One option is for the subagent to inherit everything: the same system prompt, tools, and conversation, plus its assignment. Side chats work this way. They branch off the parent session, so the whole prefix is already cached. The other option is to send a brief: the same system prompt and tools, then only the files and instructions the subagent needs. In that case the cache covers the setup and nothing more.

Inheriting sounds strictly better, but it isn’t. A cached prefix is cheap to process, not free. Every token the subagent generates still has to read through it, and it occupies GPU memory the whole time. A reviewer that needs two files and a checklist probably doesn’t need three hundred turns of history. And if you give a subagent its own system prompt, it shares nothing with the parent at all, not even the setup.

The engine side

You can do everything above perfectly and still not benefit. The cache has to still exist, and the next request has to reach the machine that holds it.

At Together AI, we think of an inference engine as a machine for keeping GPUs busy. A single GPU costs around $50k to rent per year, so ideally it should never sit idle, and at any moment it’s serving hundreds of users who are each at a different point in their request. Agent traffic pushes on those constraints in a few specific ways.

Routing requests for optimal cache hits

A session’s cache lives on a particular node in a particular data center. If the next turn in a conversation lands anywhere else, that node has to process all earlier turns from scratch, and now two nodes are storing the same prefix. In order to route correctly we first need to pick a data center that runs the model, has capacity, and is where the session has been running. Then we need to pick a node inside it that has the previous turns cache.

There are two main ways to pick the node. The simple one is to use a key: the client sends something like prompt_cache_key with every request and then ideally we route every request with the same key to the same node. The other way is to hash the prefix and send the request to whichever node has the longest matching prefix cached, even if another session put it there.

That second option is the other reason to keep the system prompt identical. If every session of a harness starts with exactly the same system prompt and tool definitions, a brand-new session might be able to find that setup already cached. If you put unique identifiers in there then every session is guaranteed to start cold.

It also isn’t as simple as always sending the request to the warm node. Sometimes the warm node is overloaded with traffic, and then the choice is between waiting in line there or taking an idle node and paying to process the prefix again. In this load-aware routing paradigm sometimes the cache miss might be the better deal. So even a perfectly stable prompt doesn’t guarantee a hit if the inference engine on the backend is not implemented correctly.

Keeping the cache alive between turns

Routing only helps if there’s still a cache to route to. An agent will often make a tool call and then wait a couple of minutes while tests run. Keeping that session’s cache in GPU memory the whole time takes space active users need, and throwing it away means re-reading everything when the agent comes back from its tool calls. So we can also offload the cache to CPU memory while the session is idle and restore it for the next turn.

Memory is the constraint behind most of this. We can’t know ahead of time whether a response will be 30 tokens or 30,000, so instead of reserving room for the worst case max context length scenarios, we hand out cache memory in small blocks as each request needs them (PagedAttention), the way an operating system handles RAM. And we rebuild the running batch on every pass (continuous batching), so when an agent fires off five subagents at once, each new request takes a slot the moment one frees up instead of waiting for the slowest one in a batch to finish.

The upshot for anyone building a harness is that headroom for cache memory, not compute, is usually what limits how many requests a GPU can serve at once. Every oversized tool result, and every subagent carrying irrelevant history takes memory that another session’s cache could have used.

Agents also push the prefill/decode split to its extreme, with enormous prompts and tiny answers. To better optimize this we run the two phases on separate clusters. One is tuned for compute and does prefill; the other is tuned for memory bandwidth and does decode for hundreds of streams at once, with the cache shipped between them over RDMA. That way, a wave of long agent prompts doesn’t slow token streaming for everyone else.

Putting it all together: One session, both sides

Here’s what all of this looks like in a single session.

On the harness side, the agent finds the calendar tool and adds it at the end of the conversation, so nothing above it changes. It reads calendar.py, sees that it got only lines 1 to 100 of 640, searches for “timezone,” and reads the right section. Effort stays where it started. A reviewer subagent inherits the session to check agenda.ics against sessions.json.

On the engine side, every turn goes back to the node that has the session cached. While the tests run, the cache waits in CPU memory. The reviewer’s request slots into the running batch, and each turn processes only what’s new.

None of that is visible to the person using the agent; they just see it stay fast at turn ninety. But it only works if both sides do their part. A harness can keep the prompt perfectly stable and still lose the cache if the engine sends turn 7 to the wrong machine. An engine can route perfectly and still lose it if the harness changes the first line every turn.

Read more about building agents and open models on Parth’s blog and the Together AI blog.

articles.title: ESLint Ends Paid Contributor Program as AI Upends Open Source Collaboration
articles.context: In June, the Godot Foundation announced changes to its contribution policies after struggling with a growing backlog of pull requests and a limited number of qualified reviewers
articles.full_text:
ESLint is retiring its contributor pool after five years, citing growing difficulties with AI-generated contributions and disputes over whether contributors deserved payment for work produced with AI assistance.

In a November 13 announcement, ESLint creator Nicholas C. Zakas said the program had paid outside contributors more than $51,000 and helped recruit several future team members. But the increasing volume of AI-generated issues and pull requests, along with accusations about undisclosed AI use, had made the program increasingly difficult to administer.

The decision comes as open source projects across the ecosystem are reconsidering how they accept, review, and reward contributions. Some are restricting outside pull requests, others are tightening their AI policies, and several are struggling with the additional review work created by AI-assisted development.

ESLint Ends Five-Year Experiment in Paying Contributors #

ESLint introduced its contributor pool in 2022 to compensate people outside the core team for meaningful contributions to the project. The program initially allocated $1,000 per month before switching to a model that reserved 10% of monthly income for contributors. Eligible work included code, documentation, answering questions in Discord, and other activities that benefited the project.

The experiment was successful by the team's own assessment. ESLint paid outside contributors $24,680 in 2025 alone, bringing its total payouts from 2022 through 2025 to $51,180. The program encouraged repeat contributions and helped attract people who eventually joined the ESLint team.

Zakas emphasized that the decision to retire the program was unrelated to its growing expense. In his conclusion, he acknowledged how much the contributor pool had accomplished and how dramatically the circumstances surrounding it had changed.

"The contributor pool was an approach designed for a completely different time in open source. A time when we were still making human-to-human connections through a shared goal of creating great software. It worked well for a time, and we’re grateful to everyone who made a meaningful contribution to ESLint in the last five years. It introduced us to many future team members who remain with the project today."

Beginning in 2025, ESLint noticed a growing number of AI-generated issues and pull requests. The team decided that contributions produced primarily through AI tools would not qualify for payment, reasoning that asking an assistant to implement a change did not represent the kind of effort the program was intended to encourage.

Contributors were asked to disclose AI assistance in their pull request descriptions, but not everyone complied. As coding models improved, maintainers found it increasingly difficult to distinguish human-authored contributions from AI-generated work.

The situation became more contentious when people Zakas called "AI monitors" began examining pull requests and contributor payment reports, publicly accusing some contributors of undisclosed AI use. Zakas said he also received private messages warning him about accounts suspected of submitting AI-generated work.

"All of this took the joy out of the contributor pool," he wrote.

With AI-generated pull requests now dominating the project's submissions, ESLint decided to discontinue the program effective immediately rather than continue investigating the origins of individual contributions.

The decision does not prohibit AI-assisted development. ESLint's AI usage policy still allows contributors to use these tools, provided they disclose their use, review the generated work, and remain responsible for their submissions. AI-generated pull requests must also address issues that the team has explicitly accepted.

AI-Generated Contributions Are Changing Economics of Code Review #

According to GitHub's 2026 Oct overse report, more than 40% of pull requests on the platform began with an AI agent's first draft by September, up from 17% in March. GitHub reported 110 million agent-started pull requests in September alone.

Many of these submissions represent legitimate development work, and AI tools are helping experienced engineers implement changes more efficiently. For open source maintainers, however, the growing volume also complicates assumptions that have traditionally guided the contribution and review process.

In August, Rust contributor Jynn Nelson explained why five teams working on the rust-lang/rust repository had adopted new policies governing AI use. She emphasized that contributions have traditionally served a purpose beyond improving the code itself:

While the Rust project is a collection of technical artifacts, it is also a community of people who work together to build, maintain, and extend those artifacts. When we talk about 'contributing to the Rust project', we partly mean work on those artifacts, but we also mean joining that community and collaborating with the people already there.

Historically, a polished, well-tested pull request suggested that its author had invested time in understanding the codebase. Maintainers could reasonably expect that someone submitting substantial work might be interested in further contributions, making the review process an opportunity for mentorship.

AI-generated code has made those signals less reliable. A contributor can now produce an impressive-looking patch without necessarily understanding how it works, why the change is needed, or how it fits into the project's architecture.

The consequences are particularly evident at tldraw, where founder Steve Ruiz described an unusual problem in January involving AI-generated issues and the contributors attempting to resolve them.

Ruiz had created a Claude Code command that converted his rough notes about bugs and feature ideas into detailed GitHub issues. When the original instructions were sufficiently clear, the system worked well. When they were vague, the AI sometimes invented bugs or proposed solutions to problems that did not exist.

Outside contributors were then using their own AI coding assistants to implement those issues, producing pull requests that appeared technically sound but addressed problems the project never intended to solve.

Some of the submissions passed automated tests and initially looked like useful contributions. The underlying issue was that neither AI system had enough context to determine whether the work made sense. Ruiz's issue-writing assistant had generated misleading tasks, and contributors' coding assistants were implementing them without questioning the premise.

The experience led tldraw to announce that it would automatically close external pull requests, although it would continue accepting bug reports, issues, and discussions.

Ruiz questioned whether outside contributions still offered enough value to justify the review work they created:

I think this misses the point. We already accept code written with AI. I write code with AI tools. I expect my team to use AI tools too. If you know the codebase and know what you're doing, writing great code has never been easier than with these tools.

The question is more fundamental. In a world of AI coding assistants, is code from external contributors actually valuable at all?

If writing the code is the easy part, why would I want someone else to write it?

AI is changing the economics of code review. Even technically correct code can be a bad fit for a project, and maintainers still have to judge whether a change belongs, whether its author understands it, and whether anyone will take responsibility for it after it's merged.

Maintainers Are Tightening Contribution Requirements #

Several major open source projects have responded by introducing stricter rules for AI-generated work and new contributors.

In June, the Godot Foundation announced changes to its contribution policies after struggling with a growing backlog of pull requests and a limited number of qualified reviewers.

Godot said AI-generated submissions had intensified an existing problem: producing a pull request had become considerably easier, while the effort required to review one had remained largely unchanged.

The project moved to prohibit autonomous AI agents, substantial AI-generated code, and AI-generated text in discussions between contributors. New contributors with three or fewer merged pull requests must also obtain maintainer permission before proposing new features or significant refactors.

Godot's announcement raised another concern beyond the immediate review burden. Maintainers traditionally invest time helping inexperienced contributors understand the codebase, partly because those contributors may eventually become reviewers and maintainers themselves.

When feedback is passed directly into an AI coding assistant without the contributor developing that understanding, reviewers may spend considerable time on an exchange that does little to strengthen the project's future maintainer base.

LLVM has adopted a more permissive policy that allows AI-assisted contributions with human oversight, but it explicitly prohibits using AI tools to complete issues labeled good first issue. Those tasks are reserved as learning opportunities for developers getting acquainted with the codebase.

LLVM also prohibits autonomous agents from participating in project discussions or submitting changes without human approval. Its policy places responsibility on contributors to understand and review AI-generated material before asking maintainers to evaluate it.

Node.js has introduced additional requirements for pull requests exceeding 5,000 lines, addressing the difficulty of reviewing unusually large changes.

The strain on reviewers has also become apparent in the Linux kernel.

On November 10, Linux kernel developer Lorenzo Stoakes submitted changes to remove himself from several memory-management and Rust-related reviewer roles, citing the volume of AI-generated patch series.

Stoakes, an Arm engineer who remains a maintainer in his own areas of responsibility, explained that the volume of incoming work had forced him to limit his review commitments.

Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generatedseries, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offerreview except in those areas I maintain.

In the subsequent mailing-list discussion, he described encountering low-quality AI-generated submissions occasionally at first, then weekly, and eventually every few days. He estimated that such submissions now accounted for roughly half or more of the patches he encountered.

Stoakes clarified that he was primarily trying to reduce inbox noise and focus on his maintainer responsibilities. His account nevertheless offers a recent example of how the increasing volume of generated code is affecting experienced reviewers.

A Linux Foundation study published in October found that 59% of surveyed maintainers reported growing contributions associated with generative AI. Respondents estimated that 25% of incoming pull requests were low-quality AI-generated submissions.

Open Source Projects Are Reconsidering Contributor Incentives #

ESLint isn't the only project reconsidering payments to outside contributors as AI makes it easier to generate submissions in large numbers.

In January, curl announced that it was shutting down its bug bounty program after maintainers were overwhelmed by low-quality vulnerability reports, including many generated with AI assistance.

Curl creator Daniel Stenberg said the project had experienced a sustained increase in reports that required investigation but produced few actionable findings. The project ended its financial rewards and stopped recommending HackerOne as its reporting channel, directing researchers to its own disclosure process instead.

The pressure continued beyond bug bounty submissions. In July, curl temporarily suspended vulnerability reporting for an entire month to give its maintainers time to address other work.

Stenberg later described the month-long break as one of the project's best decisions in recent memory:

The effect was almost immediate. Just a few days into the bliss, my fellow curl maintainers all agreed with me that we felt a sense of relief, of vacation and that a load had been taken off our chests. We felt free, unchained, and now suddenly able to do what we wanted.

We could now spend time reviewing some of the queued up pull-requests for features and changes we like.

GitHub has also expanded the options available to repository owners in response to these issues. In February, the platform introduced settings that allow maintainers to disable pull requests or restrict them to existing collaborators, giving projects more control over which contributions they accept.

For projects that rely on outside participation, restricting contributions creates its own difficulties. New developers need opportunities to learn unfamiliar codebases, receive feedback, and develop relationships with maintainers. Those interactions have historically helped sustain open source communities, even when reviewing a newcomer's first contribution required more effort than writing the code independently.

ESLint is ending a program that successfully recruited contributors because the effort required to distinguish qualifying work has become too burdensome. Other projects are making different choices, from imposing tighter contribution requirements to changing how they fund security work or limiting access to their repositories.

Restricting outside contributions may spare maintainers from a flood of AI-generated submissions, but it also threatens one of the ways open source projects have historically recruited and developed the people who keep them running.

"Whether or not AI-powered contributions will lead to the same type of dedication as human-authored contributions is yet to be seen," Zakas said. "All I can say at the moment is that open source has changed and we need to change with it."

articles.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
articles.context: With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest...
articles.full_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.

It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.

“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”

Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.

“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”

Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.
