From Oct. 3 to Nov. 5, 2026, Amazon’s MadPot, a globally distributed network of decoy threat sensors, captured requests from AI agents that included operating memory from offensive campaigns that threat actors ran on ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework. The ARTEX agents sent these requests to MadPot sensors configured to present as popular large language model (LLM) inference APIs, and the requests carried the agents’ own records of their campaigns.

Amazon Threat Intelligence assessed threat activity referencing potentially affected AWS customers and notified them as appropriate. Because activity against other organizations could not be confirmed, this post shares the findings and indicators of compromise (IOCs) so that organizations that run the affected technologies can review their own environments.

The most prominent ARTEX campaign was a large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, organized as a self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting. Another campaign targeted cryptocurrency exchanges for know-your-customer (KYC) verification bypass using real-time deepfake injection. In aggregate, the agent records show that agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention. This post describes how these campaigns operated based on the agents’ own descriptions of the campaigns.

Attribution and instructions

Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with moderate confidence that ARTEX was used for these campaigns due to prompt references to ARTEX tooling and other technical artifacts referencing ARTEX. Threat actors instructed ARTEX agents through standing instruction prompts that set the mission objectives, targeting rules, and operational constraints. Within those instructions, the agents handled the work themselves. In one credential theft campaign, operators told the agents to work through a fixed sequence of countries, prioritize enterprise production sites over personal projects, and grade every stolen credential by whether it worked and what it could reach. Agents were directed to treat credentials exposed publicly for more than 30 days as low-value inventory.

Amazon Threat Intelligence also assess with moderate confidence these are disparate Chinese-nexus threat groups due to use of simplified Chinese language in prompts, China time-zone configurations, targeting consistent with Chinese interests, and tooling predominantly used by Chinese-nexus threats. Sample instructions included setting red lines, such as excluding mainland China targets and government domains, and required all outbound traffic to go through proxies.

How MadPot saw inside these campaigns

MadPot presents controlled services to potential attackers and records how they discover, test, and attempt to compromise or abuse them. MadPot telemetry allows Amazon Threat Intelligence to observe attacker behavior without exposing customer workloads. In this case, the MadPot sensors presented popular LLM-compatible chat-completions interfaces on various ports. Agentic frameworks sent prompts to these interfaces as part of their offensive workflows, treating them as LLM inference backends.

The resulting telemetry contained the persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and reported findings that these frameworks ordinarily send to an LLM to make operational decisions. Because agentic frameworks retain the history of past conversations, individual requests often contain the full operational history of a campaign. That history described activity that occurred before and between the captured requests, on systems MadPot does not monitor. Amazon Threat Intelligence did not observe that activity as it happened and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported, but the records show what the actors were pursuing.

Most of the activity used ARTEX to divide work among planner, worker, verification, and compression agents sharing a persistent knowledge graph. The knowledge graph acts as the operation’s shared memory: every agent reads from it, and writes its results back, so each agent picks up where the others left off. The agents’ records described reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, credential theft, cloud-privilege expansion, and cryptocurrency fraud attempts across hundreds of targets spanning AI application platforms and other workloads. These records show how threat actors are organizing persistent, financially motivated offensive operations using agentic AI frameworks.

Campaign 1: Stealing AI credentials at industrial scale

In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to steal API keys and other credentials that grant access to AI models, most likely so they could use those models while someone else paid for them. The agents’ records show stolen keys being fed into the framework’s own model gateway, where they powered the agents searching for more keys. Beyond AI model access keys, cloud credentials were treated as a doorway to more access. Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities. They prioritized access to premium frontier models over general cloud permissions.

Agents recorded use of different AI gateways, keys, and models, but they all used a shared method: find internet-exposed AI applications, extract the upstream provider keys they hold, validate those keys, and store them in a managed pool. The agents focused on applications that aggregate provider keys, because one weak management interface can expose many downstream accounts. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. A codified vulnerability playbook mapped each fingerprinted product to its known attack chain, including uninitialized installs that could be claimed, anonymous management and provider-configuration endpoints, default administrator credentials, such as the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow), CVE-2026-28797 (RAGFlow), an authentication bypass via the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, SSRF through URL-fetch features to cloud metadata services, and secrets left in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files.

To find those keys, discovery drew on internet scanning services, certificate transparency, and public code and artifact sources: GitHub repositories and event archives (targeting secrets that fell outside automated revocation), npm and PyPI tarballs, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. One parallel operation worked through a fixed country sequence, prioritizing enterprise production sites, and graded every credential: L1 for a lead, L2 for a confirmed working API call, and L3 for quantified impact, such as readable data or spendable balance. Keys exposed publicly for more than 30 days were treated as low-value inventory.

Campaign 2: Defeating identity verification with deepfakes

In this campaign, threat actors used AI agents to defeat the identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges with deepfakes. The agents’ records show generating real-time deepfake video to pass live selfie checks and forged ID document photos to pass document checks.

The records describe a methodical approach to the liveness check, which is a security method that confirms a person interacting with a digital system is a real, living human being physically present at the time of capture. The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move. Their best recorded attempt completed the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target. Even so, the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt the agents recorded. In parallel, a separate session built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. By splitting the model and avoiding unnecessary memory copies on the GPU, it reached 11.5 frames per second, close to what a live video check expects.

The agents worked on the ID document as well. Verification vendors look for signs that a document photo was edited or is a picture of a screen rather than a camera capture. To get past those checks, the agents recorded building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that re-saving an edited image would normally replace. The result is an altered image that looks, at the file level, like an untouched camera photo.

This campaign also shows how ARTEX runs several workstreams toward one goal. At least four agent sessions ran at once: one searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass. They shared findings and handed off tasks through cross-session tools.

What this means for defenders

None of the techniques in these campaigns were new. What AI agents change is the speed and persistence of the attacker. The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software. Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense.

Given the speed and persistence of the attackers, organizations should assume exposed secrets and misconfigurations will be found quickly and remediate accordingly. They should bring AI applications, model gateways, and inference endpoints under the same controls as other production systems, and they should watch for misuse of AI services through unexpected spend or unusual usage.

articles.title: ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI
Microsoft 365 Crawls Back to Life After a 24-Hour Outage
articles.context: The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page
articles.full_text:
Sorry, Margaret, your email is working again.

After a widespread outage shut down Microsoft 365 services for businesses, governments, and tens of millions of other users around the world, the essential cloud services are now (mostly) back online, according to the company’s status page.

The outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with users reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET. Within the hour, Microsoft said it was investigating reports of an outage that at the time was limited to North America. It quickly spread to impact more than 70 countries around the world.

The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page. It is also ruling out AI or AI agents playing a role in the debacle.

“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” a Microsoft spokesperson says in a statement. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

The company has promised a “full post-incident report” after it has fully reviewed what went wrong.

As Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 systems come back online, users will likely see their inboxes turn into a mess. “You're probably going to get a lot of notifications when things come back,” says Jonathan Leitschuh, an independent researcher.

Microsoft said it had increased the queue time for emails to 48 hours in an attempt to ensure that every message that people tried to send while its systems were down gets delivered. Leitschuh points out that, even with the bulk of systems restored, users may receive “a flood of notifications a few hours down the pike” as subsystems come back online.

The total impact of the Microsoft outage may never be fully known, but it’s safe to say it’s already significant. Governments from Japan to the United States reported disruptions to a bevy of functions. Airlines reported problems with their ability to communicate with customers. Many law enforcement and emergency services ground to a halt. And hospitals reported widespread interruptions to their operations.

Ultimately, the episode serves as a reminder of the risks involved when the whole world relies on a single company for a critical service. “We're very interdependent on these systems in modern life,” says Leitschuh. Next time, delayed emails may be the least of our worries.

articles.title: The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World
articles.context: “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable
articles.full_text:
In the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.

Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported issues with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his company had been brought to a standstill by the outages.

Unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.

“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”

During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.

Since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.

Patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”

Microsoft 365 Outage Set to Ramp up Security Risks to Organizations
articles.context: ), and it only takes one employee to grant access to their machine for threat actors to gain access, escalate their privileges and wreak havoc on systems,” he noted
articles.full_text:
While the global outage of Microsoft 365 services that interact with Exchange Online, significantly Outlook, is not believed to be cyber-related, security teams will need to be on high alert for threats related to the incident.

As the tech behemoth grapples with the fix, cybercriminals will be poised to take advantage of the chaos by launching a surge of convincing phishing campaigns and fake support scams designed to dupe individuals and employees desperate to reconnect to M365 services.

Marie Wilcox, VP of market strategy at digital forensics firm Binalyze, said, “Just because this outage wasn’t caused by a cyber-attack, doesn’t mean attackers won’t seize the opportunity.”

In an update on November 13, the Australian National Cyber Security Coordinator Michelle McGuiness warned people to “remain vigilant and be cautious of unsolicited contact” as cybercriminals often seek to take advantage of the uncertainty.

Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre issued an update recommending everyone exercises caution around unexpected calls and messages, especially those containing links.

It is likely that threat actors will begin to send phishing messages, claiming to be the Microsoft brand in order to trick people in this time of uncertainty.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Jake Moore, Global Cybersecurity Advisor at ESET, said that this kind of disruption is the perfect excuse for cybercriminals to hit organizations with targeted calls posing as IT support.

“Affected employees are literally waiting by the phone (or scrolling on social media!), and it only takes one employee to grant access to their machine for threat actors to gain access, escalate their privileges and wreak havoc on systems,” he noted.

Aiden Sinnott, principal threat researcher at the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, said that affected businesses like banks and shops should be particularly vigilant.

“Be aware of requests for urgent action, sharing of personal information and avoid clicking on links sent via message or email,” he said.

Microsoft is one of the brands most leveraged by threat actors for phishing campaigns. In an October update, cybersecurity firm Check Point noted that in Q3 2026 Microsoft accounted for 33% of all brand phishing attempts, up from 23% in Q2 2026 and roughly four times the share of any other brand.

Read more: Phishing Dominates as Initial Entry Method for Cyber-Attacks, as Hackers Hone Evasion Techniques

Defenders Should Treat Outage as Security Incident

Binalyze’s Wilcox said that many security teams themselves will have been locked out of tools they depend on to prevent trouble, for example Microsoft Defender XDR or important alerts pushed via Outlook.

She noted that when email services return and workers are beginning to clear the day’s backlog, this is when they will be most susceptible to trusting any messages that looks like they came from Microsoft – especially fake security updates.

During the outage period it will also be easy for suspicious activity to go unnoticed while alerts were not being monitored as usual.

“A suspicious sign-in or a new inbox forwarding rule is easy to miss when everyone is focused on getting email back,” she said.

“The wisest approach is for security teams to treat the outage window as an incident in its own right. That means going back over sign-ins, mailbox rules, account changes and endpoint activity from the hours when visibility dropped, and collecting evidence directly from devices rather than relying on the platform that was down,” Wilcox advised.

At the time of writing, Microsoft’s latest update said recovery efforts are ongoing across the impacted infrastructure. “We are seeing early signs of stabilization, but service capacity has not yet returned to normal levels and health remains variable as traffic is carefully reintroduced.”

articles.title: AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
articles.context: The last two matter more than the first
articles.full_text:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code.

AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now.

First, I want to broaden the term “hacking.”

The tax code isn’t computer code, but it is code. It’s a series of algorithms with inputs and outputs. It has vulnerabilities, which we call loopholes, and exploits, which we call tax avoidance strategies. Black hat hackers exploit them for profit. We call them accountants and attorneys.

What is a hack? One definition: “Something that a system permits, but is unanticipated and unwanted by the designers.” It’s subjective and implies novelty and cleverness. A hack follows the rules of a system but subverts its goals or intent, just as a software hack follows the logic of code while doing something its authors neither anticipated nor wanted.

All systems of rules can be hacked, including professional sports, customer reward programs, financial systems and politics. Hacks even work against our cognitive functions. A curved hockey stick is a hack, and we know the name of the man who invented it. Mileage runs were a hack. The filibuster was originally a hack in Roman times. Gerrymandering is a hack. Hedge funds and private equity are full of them.

A system is just a set of rules or norms, and the rules aren’t always formal. Even the best-designed rules will be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous. As long as people want to subvert a system’s goals, there will be hacks.

AIs are becoming hackers. After decades of slow progress, they’ve gotten very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in computer code. They do this largely autonomously, and they’re getting better scarily fast. But the implications extend far beyond software, to the tax code, financial regulations and all sorts of social, economic and political systems.

There are two distinct issues. First, someone might instruct an AI to hack one of these systems, feeding it the world’s tax codes or financial regulations to find profitable loopholes. Second, an AI might hack a system on its own, inadvertently. Both are dangerous, but the second is worse because we might never know it happened.

Now, reward hacking. AIs don’t solve problems the way people do. They stumble on solutions we never anticipated, and some subvert the intent of the system. They don’t share our context and don’t necessarily understand the implications, norms and values we take for granted.

Reward hacking is when an AI achieves a goal in a way its designers neither wanted nor intended.

Early pre-LLM examples are telling. In a two-person soccer simulation, an AI learned that kicking the ball out of bounds forced the opposing goalie to throw it in and leave the goal undefended. In a stacking simulation, an AI learned to flip a block upside down rather than stack it. In an evolution simulation where the goal was to cross a distant finish line, an AI made itself tall enough to fall over the line instead of growing longer legs or stronger muscles.

These are all hacks, the result of poorly specified goals or rewards. Today, they’d come from bad prompting.

The problem is universal. One researcher tried to teach a robot vacuum not to bump into things. Instead, it learned to drive backward, because there were no sensors in the back.

Any capable AI will find hacks wherever the rules have problems, inconsistencies or loopholes that still produce an acceptable solution. We see a hack because we understand context. The AI doesn’t, at least not in the same way.

This problem shows up often in myth.

In the story of King Midas, the god Dionysus grants him a wish: everything he touches turns to gold. Midas ends up starving when his food, drink and daughter all turn to gold. It’s a specification problem. He programmed the wrong goal.

In the Golem of Prague, a ghetto animates a clay statue to guard its residents. It guards them past all reason until they figure out how to turn it off. This is a guardrail problem. The villagers never limited the golem’s actions.

More generally, think of this as the genie problem. Genies are precise about the wording of wishes and can be maliciously pedantic when granting them. There’s no way to outsmart a genie. Whatever you wish for, he can grant it in a way you wish he hadn’t.

The reason is that in human language and thought, goals are always underspecified. We never include every caveat, exception and proviso, and we never close off every avenue for hacking. Any goal we specify will be incomplete. That’s largely fine in human interactions, because people understand context and usually act in good faith.

If I asked you to get me coffee, you’d pour a cup from the nearest coffee pot or walk to the corner shop. You wouldn’t bring me a pound of raw beans, buy a coffee plantation or snatch a cup from a stranger’s hands. I wouldn’t have to specify any of that. You’d just know.

Similarly, if I asked you to develop a technology that turns things to gold on touch, you wouldn’t build it to starve the person using it. You’d just know.

In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests. Human engineers programmed a regular computer to detect testing and behave differently during it. The cheat went undetected for years because it’s hard to tell what software is doing.

If I asked you to design engine control software that maximizes performance while passing emissions tests, you wouldn’t design it to cheat without realizing you were cheating. An AI would, because it will think “outside the box” when it has no concept of the box.

Unless programmers specify that the system must not behave differently during testing, an AI might come up with the same hack. The programmers would be satisfied, the accountants would be ecstatic, and no one would know until someone audited the code.

We can now constrain the goal to avoid that particular hack, but programmers won’t anticipate others. The lesson of the genie is that there will always be hacks programmers don’t anticipate.

We’re building AI genies: systems that take broad instructions and figure out how to carry them out, sometimes in ways we didn’t expect or intend. That’s the whole point of vibe coding. You underspecify what you want and let the AI work it out. Sometimes that produces genie behavior.

We can’t completely specify goals to an AI, and AIs can’t fully understand context. More precisely, current AIs have a shallow grasp of concepts. If we asked a current LLM to get me coffee, it would almost certainly do the right thing.

I worry about goals that aren’t well represented in training data, and about hacks that aren’t obvious, whose effects are subtle, like the Volkswagen hack.

Recommendation engines are an early example. They push people toward extreme content. No one programmed that. It emerged because that’s what people respond to. It didn’t take a bad actor. A basic automated system with feedback found the hack on its own.

We’re now seeing a second generation with today’s AI coding systems. AI researcher Simon Willison asked Fable to track down a stray scrollbar in a web app. When he returned, it had opened browsers, written its own screenshot tools, edited the framework’s internal templates to make the bug appear on cue and set up a local web server to collect measurements. It found the bug, but it also did many things he never asked for. Another researcher gave Fable a complex task, and it tried to hack its own memory limits because it needed more storage.

A new OpenAI model did something similar when it hacked into Hugging Face. It was being benchmarked on its ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. It decided the best way to reach its goal was to break out of its containment, access the internet and break into the Hugging Face network, because it thought the answers would be there.

Today’s LLMs are acting like genies, especially when powerful models are combined with sophisticated harnesses.

There are two kinds of genies. The Dionysus genie does the wrong thing. It understands your prompt literally but not correctly, and returns a mess you never intended. The Golem genie does the right thing but tramples everything in its path to get there. The paperclip maximizer is a Golem genie.

Consider some examples. Ask an AI to deal with spam calls, and a Dionysus genie might change your phone number. Ask it to book a particular flight, and a Golem genie might hack the airline database because the flight is full. Ask it to get a refund for an online purchase, and a Dionysus genie might draft a legal threat on fake letterhead and send it to the company. Ask it to buy tickets to a popular concert, and a Golem genie might discover the ticketing system is rate-limited and spin up thousands of cloud servers to hammer it. You’d know if some of these things happened, but you might never realize if others did. More detailed prompting won’t fix this. The lesson of the genie is that no amount of detail is good enough.

AI researchers aren’t surprised by any of this. Many are working on defenses against reward hacking and subtler forms of genie behavior. Some of this falls under “value alignment”: How do we teach AIs context? And how an AI satisfies a goal matters as much as whether it does. I want to build a benchmark to measure genie-like behavior, so we know where models stand and whether alignment is improving.

Think beyond LLMs and computer code. Consider specialized AIs built to find loopholes, and hacks of more general systems: the tax code, financial regulations and democratic procedures.

Financial systems are the most likely first target, because their rules are designed to be algorithmically tractable. High-frequency trading is itself a hack. Imagine giving an AI all of the world’s financial laws, plus all the news and financial data, and the goal of finding profitable loopholes. I suspect large investment banks are already doing this. The results will be novel tricks that are legal but unintended and unwanted, some of which might break the financial system.

Tax loopholes are the next likely target, for the same reasons. For a while, AIs will identify potential loopholes, and human hackers, namely attorneys and accountants, will decide which are feasible.

Further out, expect hacks of regulatory, legislative and procedural systems, and of the broader economy.

Hacking is as old as humanity. We’re creative problem solvers and loophole exploiters. We manipulate systems to serve our interests and strive for more influence, power and wealth.

Still, no human pursues their interests without constraint. Even sociopaths are limited by the complexity of society and their own contradictory impulses. They worry about their reputation and punishment, and they have limited time. These human qualities have limited hacking.

Hacking changed as everything became computerized. Computers are uniquely hackable because of their formalism and complexity. Today, nearly everything is a computer, from cars and appliances to phones. Our social, economic and political systems, including taxation, finance and elections, all involve computers.

Until recently, hacking was exclusively a human activity. Finding a novel hack required expertise, creativity, time and luck.

AI hacking will change everything again. AIs aren’t bound by the constraints that limit people. They’ll think like aliens, and they’ll change hacking’s speed, scale, scope and sophistication, sometimes at our direction and sometimes on their own.

Speed is the easiest to see. A creative process that takes a human months or years could be compressed into hours or seconds.

Scale is next. Once AI systems start discovering hacks, they can exploit them at a scale we’re not ready for. We already see this with AI-generated slop, which is rampant on social media. AI bots post around the clock, sometimes overwhelming real human discussion. It’s hard to know how much of social media is still people talking to people. What looks like boisterous political debate may be bots arguing with other bots, artificially shaping what we think and what we think others think.

Scope makes hacks more dangerous. AIs already make decisions that affect our lives, decisions we once thought belonged only to humans. As AI systems grow more capable, society will hand them more decisions, and more important ones. Hacks of these systems will do more damage.

Finally, AI hackers are more sophisticated. They can hold more variables in working memory and generate more complex hacks. What might happen if you fed an AI the entire U.S. tax code? Would it figure out, without being told, that it’s smart to incorporate in Delaware and register a ship in Panama? Consider the Double Dutch Irish Sandwich, the strategy Apple and Google used to avoid paying U.S. taxes. It involves U.S., Dutch and Irish law and an offshore tax haven. How many loopholes will an AI find that we don’t already know about? Dozens? Hundreds? Thousands? We have no idea.

These hacks will largely be perpetrated by the powerful against the rest of us. AI is fundamentally a power-enhancing technology, and so is hacking. The more power you already have, the more a hack gives you. If you or I found a tax hack, we might make a few thousand dollars. If a large investment bank found one, it and its clients could make billions.

Our societal systems for dealing with hacks were built when hackers were human, and they reflect the pace of human hacking. We have no system of governance that can handle hundreds, let alone thousands, of newly discovered tax loopholes. We won’t be able to recover from an AI finding unanticipated but legal hacks of financial systems, operating at AI speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Hacking becomes a problem society can no longer manage.

Now, defense. AIs that find software vulnerabilities help defenders as well as attackers. Vulnerabilities can be patched, removing them permanently, or turned into signatures that security systems use to detect and block attacks. In theory, AI could identify and patch every automatically discoverable vulnerability before a product ships. This is rapidly becoming routine in software development. We call it vulnops. We can imagine a future where accidental software vulnerabilities are a thing of the past.

Deliberate vulnerabilities are different. There will be an arms race. AI will craft increasingly obscure back doors, and AI will find them. It becomes a contest between the speed of creation and the speed of patching, and between obfuscation and reverse engineering.

The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.

That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.

This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.

The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.

AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?

AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.

And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.

I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.

The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.

Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.

Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.

The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.

Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.

So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.

I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.

articles.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
articles.context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
articles.full_text:
CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-114713 UnrealIRCd Improper Neutralization of Delimiters Vulnerability

CVE-2026-123039 Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

articles.title: AI Set to Revolutionize Ransomware Following “Stagnant” Few Years
articles.context: However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities...
articles.full_text:
Ransomware will be revolutionized in 2027 due to the influence of AI, with threat actors poised to become more innovative, according TrendAI’s director of cybercrime research, Bob McArdle.

“Ransomware has been pretty stagnant and boring for the past couple of years, at least if you’re a researcher like me,” he told the audience at the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11.

To date, ransomware actors have primarily used AI to enhance the speed and efficiency of campaigns. This includes the use of AI tools to identify the most important data once inside an organization’s environment, while some groups have deployed chatbots to carry out the initial negotiation stages on their behalf.

However, the overall process of ransomware attacks, from the use of initial access brokers through to the double-extortion method, have not changed.

“That’s a drop in the ocean compared to where we’re going with ransomware next,” McArdle warned.

Devaluation of the Initial Access Broker Marketplace

One expected change is around how initial access is gained to victim’s environments. In the current ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) ecosystem, initial access brokers typically sell access to affiliates through techniques like compromised vulnerabilities and stolen credentials.

However, McArdle noted that AI frameworks like Artex are removing barriers to entry for entry for initial access, by enabling attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities rapidly.

“Anything that’s connected to the internet and is misconfigured or has vulnerabilities will be compromised,” he commented.

This will devalue the initial access market and, as a result, McArdle expects brokers to adapt their business model towards offering privilege escalation to ransomware groups.

Post initial access, tools like Artex and AI agents will allow attackers to shrink down the “kill chain” to machine speed.

McArdle also observed that many organizations are centralizing their data storage, which is good for business efficiency purposes amid the growing use of AI for data processing.

However, this centralization will provide new opportunities for threat actors. This includes ransomware groups threatening to tamper with the AI orchestration around organizations’ data as a further extortion technique.

Another area in which AI will benefit ransomware groups is its ability to process data effectively, enabling actors to quickly develop datasets of high value data, which will be easier to sell on to other malicious actors. This approach will provide even more profit-making opportunities for these actors.

“Over 2027, we will start seeing an inflection point where you have extortion-based business models of ransomware living side-by-side with the actual data theft and sales models increasing every year,” McArdle explained.

Hostile Takeovers by Ransomware Groups

With AI making ransomware attacks easier to undertake, McArdle expects to see a growth in the number of ransomware groups in the next year.

This further fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem will likely lead to large groups frequently undertaking “hostile takeovers” of smaller actors.

“We will start seeing Conti and LockBit level groups effectively acquiring smaller groups for their technology or even just their affiliate networks,” he added.

articles.title: CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines: Will Your AI System Need an Independent Audit?
articles.context: These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using: Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1
articles.full_text:
Picture a customer-support chatbot at a mid-sized Indian e-commerce company. It answers questions about orders and returns. It runs on a third-party large language model. Nobody thinks of it as high-risk.

Now the product team gives it one new permission: it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 without human sign-off. It's a small feature that saves agents hours a week.

Under the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines that CERT-In issued on 4 November 2026, that one change can be enough to move the chatbot into a higher risk tier. And the tier decides how the system gets audited, how often, and by whom.

The 107-page framework scores every AI system on eight risk factors. Most coverage so far has stopped at "four risk tiers, from low to critical." This post goes further: it explains how the scoring actually works, walks through the chatbot example factor by factor, and sets out what security teams should do now.

Key Takeaways

CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines (v1.0, 4 November 2026) cover AI systems developed, procured, deployed, or operated in India, plus systems that process Indian data or serve Indian users.

Every AI system is scored from 1 to 4 on eight risk factors. The total (8–32) sets one of four tiers, and the tier sets audit depth, frequency and independence.

From Tier 2 upward, the minimum requirement includes an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation.

Giving an AI system the ability to act, such as issuing refunds or calling tools, raises its autonomy score and is a named escalation trigger.

AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, with 180-day log retention, in line with CERT-In's existing 2022 Directions.

What CERT-In Issued and Who It Covers

The Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines set a common, risk-based framework for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their full lifecycle. CERT-In lists the document on its official guidelines page under reference CISG-2026-04.

Source: CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, cover page.

The scope is deliberately wide. It covers AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated by organizations in India, as well as systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users. That brings in global AI-as-a-Service providers and SaaS platforms selling into India, not just Indian companies.

It also doesn't matter where the model came from. The guidelines say AI systems stay in audit scope regardless of model origin, ownership, or delivery mechanism. Internally built models, proprietary vendor models, open-weight models, and models consumed through an API are all covered. If you can't get evidence from your vendor, that's recorded as a scope limitation, because the absence of access is not treated as evidence of conformity.

Scope and exclusions · CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Sections 4.4–4.9

There are three narrow exclusions:

Academic research AI that doesn't make decisions about individuals and isn't in production. It enters full scope once it moves to a pilot.

Purely rule-based automation, such as traditional RPA with no machine learning. Hybrid systems that mix rules and ML are in scope.

Consumer personal use, such as an individual using a photo-editing app. The providers of those tools remain in scope.

Small companies get some relief, but only for low-risk systems. MSMEs and startups can use simplified self-assessment for Tier 1 systems. For Tier 3 and Tier 4 systems, the guidelines state there is no proportionality exemption: the full requirements apply regardless of organizational size.

Is It Mandatory?

The honest answer is: partly, and probably more so over time. The document is issued as guidelines and doesn't state a penalty or a compliance deadline. But it is written in mandatory language ("shall") and sets minimum audit requirements for each tier.

Three things give it teeth in practice:

It plugs into rules that are already binding. The six-hour incident reporting window and 180-day log retention come from CERT-In's Directions of 28 April 2022 under Section 70B of the IT Act. The new guidelines bring AI incidents squarely into that regime: AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours.

Regulators are named as intended users. The document lists RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and TRAI among the bodies it is written for. If a sectoral regulator adopts it, the tiers become obligations for banks, brokers, insurers and telecom operators.

Buyers will ask for it. Government tenders and enterprise customers already demand CERT-In empaneled audit reports for traditional systems. Expect AI audit evidence to show up in procurement questionnaires next.

For security leaders, the practical takeaway is to treat the framework as the benchmark your AI systems will be judged against, whether by a regulator, a customer or an auditor.

How the Eight-Factor Risk Score Works

Each AI system is scored from 1 (low) to 4 (critical) on eight inherent-risk factors, and the scores are added up. Organizations must score what the system can actually do, without taking credit for controls they claim to have in place.

Factor

What it asks

F1: Impact severity

How bad is the consequence of a wrong, compromised or unsafe output?

F2: Autonomy and actionability

What actions, tool calls or decisions can the AI take before a human approves?

F3: Data sensitivity

How sensitive is the data it processes, from public to biometric or classified?

F4: Scale and exposure

How many users, transactions or systems does it reach?

F5: Reversibility

How easily can the damage from a bad output or action be undone?

F6: Sector criticality

Does it support an essential, regulated or critical-infrastructure function?

F7: Adversarial exposure

Is it internal, internet-facing, or in an actively targeted environment?

F8: Complexity and auditability

How opaque is the model and its dependencies? Missing evidence can't justify a low score.

The total maps to a tier, and the tier sets the minimum audit requirement:

Score

Tier

Minimum audit requirement

8–12

Tier 1 (Low)

Self-assessment or basic internal review, reviewed annually

13–19

Tier 2 (Moderate)

Documented internal audit, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled auditing organization at least annually

20–26

Tier 3 (High)

Periodic independent third-party audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization, every six months where risk or material change warrants

27–32

Tier 4 (Critical)

Independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization with continuous monitoring

The score isn't the final word. The guidelines list escalation triggers that can push a system up a tier regardless of its total. They include AI that can autonomously execute code, transactions, or external communications; AI with privileged access to production systems or sensitive data; and AI that can't be reliably interrupted, rolled back, or placed in a safe state.

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Section 5.4, page 25.

Two more rules matter. Auditors must validate your tier independently, and where their assessment is higher than yours, the higher tier applies for scoping. And a tier can only be lowered after a documented reassessment shows a sustained drop in risk, approved by the organization's designated risk authority.

The Chatbot That Jumps a Tier

The same chatbot lands in Tier 2 when it only answers questions, and in Tier 3 once it can issue refunds. Here is an illustrative scoring using the calibration guide in Section 5.3 of the guidelines.

Version A answers questions, checks order status through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over help articles and order history, and hands refunds to human agents. Version B is the same bot, but it can issue refunds up to ₹5,000 on its own.

Factor

Version A: answers only

Version B: issues refunds

Why it changes

F1: Impact severity

2

A wrong answer or a single bad refund is still limited and recoverable

F2: Autonomy

2

3

Version B initiates consequential actions instead of advising a human

F3: Data sensitivity

2

Refunds bring payment and financial data into play

F4: Scale and exposure

3

Large-scale, customer-facing in both cases

F5: Reversibility

Money paid out to the wrong account is costly and slow to recover

F6: Sector criticality

2

An important business function, not critical infrastructure

F7: Adversarial exposure

3

Internet-facing, so anyone can send it hostile prompts

F8: Complexity

A third-party LLM is partially opaque to the deploying company

Total

19 (Tier 2)

22 (Tier 3)

Source: Illustrative scoring · tier bands and minimum audits from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Table 11

Three factor changes add three points, enough to cross from the top of Tier 2 into Tier 3.

Two things stand out.

First, even the "harmless" Version A sits at the top of Tier 2. That already means a documented internal audit, a simplified AI impact assessment, AI threat modelling and API security testing, plus an independent audit by a CERT-In empaneled organization at least annually. Many companies running customer-facing LLMs may not realize they're here.

Second, Version B doesn't just cross a score threshold. Its ability to initiate transactions is also a named escalation trigger, and an internet-facing bot that can move money is an obvious prompt-injection target. Moving to Tier 3 adds a comprehensive AI impact assessment, validation independent of the development team, a comprehensive AI security assessment with VAPT, a formal AI Governance Committee, and audits as often as every six months.

Note: This scoring is illustrative. Actual tiers depend on each system's real capabilities and context, and auditors will reach their own assessment.

What Auditors Will Test Your AI For

Section 9 of the guidelines adds dedicated requirements for generative AI, RAG, agentic, multimodal, and multi-agent systems. These are the threats auditors are told to focus on, and the ones attackers are already using:

Source: CERT-In, AI Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0, Table 16, page 63.

Source: Refund chatbot attack surface · threats from CERT-In AI Security Auditing Guidelines, Section 9.2

Mapped onto the refund chatbot, each component becomes a separate test case, and the leaked-credential risk sits outside the system entirely

CERT-In takes prompt injection seriously enough to apply it to auditors too. Audit teams using AI tools must treat auditee documents, logs and tool outputs as untrusted data and test for injection attempts designed to alter audit criteria or suppress findings.

The guidelines also expect AI threat models to draw on MITRE ATLAS, OWASP guidance, CERT-In advisories and "other relevant threat intelligence." That's where many teams have a blind spot.

Threat actors trade stolen AI API keys, discuss jailbreak and injection techniques on underground forums, and leak cloud and model credentials in breach dumps. Cyble's threat intelligence tracks this activity across the surface, deep and dark web, so security teams can build AI threat models on what attackers are actually doing rather than on assumptions.

What to Do in the Next 90 Days

The first step is the one most organizations will find hardest: knowing what AI they actually run. The guidelines treat an incomplete or missing AI inventory as a governance non-conformity in its own right.

Build your AI inventory. List every AI system in use, including vendor APIs, copilots built into SaaS tools, and shadow AI that teams adopted without approval. Record purpose, owner, model source, data processed and deployment status.

Score each system honestly. Apply the eight factors to what each system can actually do today. Flag any system that can act on its own, such as issuing refunds, sending messages, executing code or calling tools, since those are the ones most likely to sit higher than you expect.

Review permissions before you add features. Treat every new agent capability as a potential tier change. Put human approval gates on consequential actions and make sure agents run with least privilege.

Map your AI incidents to the six-hour clock. Define what an AI incident looks like, such as a successful prompt injection, data leakage through a model, or a poisoned knowledge source. Then check that you can detect, classify, and report one within six hours, with 180 days of time-synchronized logs to support the investigation.

Lock down AI secrets and watch for leaks. Move API keys and model credentials into a secrets manager and rotate them. Then monitor for those credentials turning up outside your environment. With Cyble's dark web monitoring, teams get alerts when credentials, keys or data tied to their organization appear in breach dumps, underground markets, paste sites or code repositories, so a leaked key can be revoked before it's abused.

Bring in threat intelligence for your AI threat model. Use current intelligence on attacker techniques, rather than a generic checklist, to decide what your red-team and VAPT exercises test.

Engage a CERT-In empaneled auditor early. If any system scores Tier 2 or above, start scoping the independent audit now rather than when a regulator or customer asks for the report.

How Cyble Helps You Get AI-Audit Ready

CERT-In's framework asks organizations to prove three things about their AI: that they understand the threats, that they monitor continuously, and that they can respond fast. Cyble's AI-native platform supports each of them.

That gives your AI threat model and red-team scope a grounding in real attacker behavior, as the guidelines expect.

Continuous monitoring for exposed credentials and data. Cyble's dark web monitoring watches underground forums, marketplaces, paste sites, and code repositories for leaked API keys, credentials, and datasets linked to your organization, which supports the guidelines' secrets-management and continuous-assurance controls.

Faster detection for the six-hour window. Real-time alerts on ransomware activity, data leaks, and brand impersonation help security teams spot incidents early enough to classify and report them within CERT-In's deadline.

Is your organization ready for CERT-In's AI security audits? Request a demo to see how Cyble helps you find exposure, track AI-focused threats, and respond inside the six-hour window.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines? They are a risk-based framework, issued by CERT-In on 4 November 2026, for auditing the security, governance, and resilience of AI systems across their lifecycle. Each AI system is scored on eight risk factors and placed in one of four tiers that set its audit requirements.

Do the guidelines apply to foreign AI companies? Yes. They cover AI systems that process Indian data or provide AI-enabled services to Indian users, not only organisations based in India.

Does using a third-party AI model or API take my system out of scope? No. AI systems stay in scope regardless of model origin or delivery mechanism, and lack of access to vendor evidence is treated as a scope limitation, not as proof of conformity.

Which AI systems need an independent audit? Systems scoring 13 or above (Tier 2 and higher) require an independent audit by a CERT-In empanelled auditing organisation, with frequency and depth increasing at Tier 3 and Tier 4.

How quickly must AI security incidents be reported to CERT-In? AI incidents that meet CERT-In's reportable criteria must be reported within six hours, consistent with CERT-In's April 2022 Directions, which also require 180-day log retention.

Sources

CERT-In, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines, v1.0 (PDF)

CERT-In guideline page, CISG-2026-04

Disclaimer: This article is for general information only and does not constitute legal or compliance advice. It is based on CERT-In’s AI Security Auditing Guidelines, version 1.0, dated 4 November 2026, which may be revised or supplemented by sectoral regulators. Risk scores shown are illustrative. Organizations should consult their legal advisers and a CERT-In empaneled auditing organization to determine how the guidelines apply to their AI systems.

articles.title: Shield helps technicians hand off legacy portal work with OpenAI
Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
articles.context: A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users
articles.full_text:
Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress.

LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable.

Today, we are announcing a new vulnerability disclosure policy, created with the following goals in mind:

Encourage faster vulnerability remediation

Encourage vendors to reduce “patch gap”

Allow for the policy to be automated by both Project Zero and vendors

Our new policy: “Full X”

Vulnerabilities will be disclosed X days after they are reported to the vendor.

Starting today, our policy is “Full 90”, i.e. vulnerabilities will be disclosed 90 days after they are reported to the vendor.

On February 2, 2027, we will move to a “Full 60” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 60 days.

On January 3, 2028, we will move to a “Full 30” policy where vulnerabilities are disclosed after 30 days.

We are also removing most ‘special cases’ from our disclosure policy, including grace period and variant policy. The only exceptions to our new policy are:

Vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild -- ITW vulnerabilities will be handled according to Google’s application security vulnerability disclosure policy

Public vulnerabilities -- Project Zero may make details of a vulnerability public, at our discretion, if the details have already been made public by others

Vendor request -- We will make vulnerability details public if the vendor we reported it to requests it

Why reduce remediation time gradually?

Project Zero solicited feedback from the vendors we report the most vulnerabilities to as a part of developing this new policy. An overarching concern was that immediately changing the policy could harm users by making unfixed vulnerabilities available to attackers while vendors are in the process of improving their remediation processes and technology. While the benefits of delaying disclosure are declining due to the increased probability that attackers will discover a vulnerability during the embargo period, we still feel there are benefits in the short term.

In addition, vendors mentioned two more subtle concerns. One was that an overly-aggressive disclosure policy would encourage fixing bugs reported under the new policy with more priority, even if they are less severe than other reported vulnerabilities. The other was that immediately enforcing a policy that some vendors aren’t equipped to meet might lead to a state where vendors accept that they cannot fix bugs within the deadline and don’t attempt to.

We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly.

What about severity?

While our analysis isn’t always perfect, Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities with substantial severity and demonstrated security impact in our tracker. That said, we don’t feel severity is an effective metric for making disclosure decisions, especially in the current environment. A vulnerability’s severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users.

When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances. But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.

It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bugs reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently.

What about hardware?

We encourage all vendors to consider how they would respond to imminent disclosure of a serious vulnerability, including non-patch strategies, as there is no guarantee that defenders will be the first to find a bug. That said, Project Zero has occasionally granted exceptions to our policy on rare occasions, including Spectre and Meltdown, and will continue to do so in the future.

Are you really not going to check whether bugs are fixed?

The question of whether a bug is fixed for the purposes of our policy has always been challenging and somewhat unresolved, particularly with regards to code that is not shipped directly to users and not publicly available. It is not unusual for Project Zero to communicate with vendors multiple times for each bug report to come to an agreement on whether a vulnerability is fixed. As more vendors experiment with vulnerability remediation strategies that are not patching like temporarily disabling code paths, we expect this to become even more complex.

We still plan to track whether bugs are fixed and communicate if they are not, however, this will not be a decision point in our policy. This will enable us to share technical details of how users are protected without needing to make a binary judgement with consequences for the vendor.

articles.title: ZDI-26-1009: (Pwn2Own) Synology DiskStation DS925+ C2 Identity Plugin Exposed Dangerous Method Information Disclosure Vulnerability
articles.context: Vulnerability Details This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of Synology DiskStation DS925+ devices
articles.full_text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to disclose sensitive information on affected installations of Synology DiskStation DS925+ devices. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the HomeKit Authentication service, which listens on TCP port 8080 by default. When processing crafted pairing requests, the service discloses internal information via an observable discrepancy between possible responses. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device.
