Ease of use and secure defaults in the new AWS experience
articles.context: As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate...
articles.full_text:
Starting on Amazon Web Services (AWS) is now more straightforward and more secure by default than it’s ever been. Over the past several months, we rolled out a new AWS experience that changes how you start building. It brings together a set of sensible, secure defaults, and taken one at a time, it’s easy to miss the bigger picture of what we’re building and why.

When we first built how you get started on AWS, cloud was a new concept. It was a world where RSS and APIs were the exciting new thing. Twenty years later, we’ve come a long way and learned a lot about how people start, build, and grow on AWS.

So, before I get into the recent launches, let me state the vision plainly: Make AWS straightforward to start on without giving up the depth, the pricing, or the security that make it the right place to grow. You shouldn’t have to choose between getting started quickly and staying secure. The rest of this post builds out this idea and highlights the defaults that make it real.

What developers told us

For years, developers have told us a version of the same thing. They knew AWS was where they wanted to grow, but they wanted to start fast, not plan for scale on day one. The same depth that lets AWS grow with you also meant more to set up on day one. There’s a payment method to enter before you can start, a console built for experienced administrators to get oriented in, and permissions to configure before your app can run. That feedback is fair, and it’s a big part of why we keep building a better AWS. The new experience is our answer to that, and most of it comes down to sensible, secure defaults.

The secure defaults behind the new experience

The new AWS experience sets secure defaults for you, so your setup starts secure instead of something you harden later. The defaults are sensible ones, drawn from what we’ve learned about how people start on AWS. Here are a few and what they do:

Builder ID sign-in, with two-factor protection built in. In the early days of AWS, you signed in as the account’s root user. You could set up separate identities for everyone, but that took real effort, so sharing one login was often the path of least resistance. We’ve learned a lot since then. AWS Builder ID is a personal identity that represents you as an individual, and you use it to sign in with email and password or through a social login like Google or Apple. When you start working with others, each person signs in with their own Builder ID rather than sharing one set of credentials, so access is tied to a person, not passed around. It’s the straightforward path rather than the hard one. In addition to that, you can register multi-factor authentication (MFA, an authenticator app or security key) that applies to whichever sign-in method you choose. This used to require deliberate setup. Now it’s there from the start.

A managed organization with AWS Organizations doing the heavy lifting behind the scenes. The starting flow is straightforward: you sign up and land in a project where you can start building right away. What I find interesting is what’s happening underneath. A project is more than an account. It pairs an account with its own spend limit and its own set of collaborators, so each project is a self-contained boundary with access scoped to just the people you invite. Rather than dropping you into a bare account, AWS creates and manages an organization for you, with your project as a member account inside it, and sensible guardrails already in place. As you grow, you add more projects—each its own member account—when you have work that needs its own budget or collaboration boundary, like a personal experiment kept separate from the beta you’re putting in front of your first users. This is the structure experienced teams land on eventually, usually after learning the hard way that putting resources with different budget or collaboration boundaries in the same account is tough to unwind later. The difference is we create the organization that enables this best practice for you from the start, so you’re set up for success well beyond day one without having to design or operate any of it yourself. When you’re ready for full control, you can activate advanced features in a single step and take over the organization directly, with no migration or downtime.

A data perimeter that grows with you. This is another default that I really want people to notice. You start with a foundational data perimeter already in place, restricting access to your resources from principals outside your organization. It’s a secure starting point rather than the complete, multi-dimensional data perimeter a larger organization would eventually build out. But the direction is that your security boundary should grow with you as you succeed on AWS, and here a brand-new developer gets that baseline automatically, without knowing the term or writing a line of policy.

A single AWS Region by default. Your resources run in one home Region to start, assigned when you sign up (aside from the handful of AWS services that are global by nature). That keeps your footprint simple and predictable: a smaller surface to secure and reason about, and a clear answer to where your data lives. When you need to operate more broadly, you can activate advanced features.

Spend limits that put you in control. You can set a hard spend limit on a project, starting at $20 a month, with notifications as you approach it. If a project reaches its limit, AWS pauses it rather than letting charges keep climbing, and you decide whether to raise the limit and resume. For an individual developer or a small team, that means no surprise bills: you set the ceiling, and no charges accrue past it without your say-so. You stay in control, and you can think big knowing the guardrails are already in place. A spend limit can also serve as an early signal. Unexpected spend is a classic indicator of inappropriate access or a runaway process, and because the project pauses at the ceiling you set, it also caps how far a cost surprise can go.

Roles set up for you, so IAM isn’t step one. As a new developer, you want to spend your early days building and experimenting, not wiring up IAM permissions. IAM Role Manager is on by default in the new AWS experience, so it creates and attaches the IAM roles your app needs as you build. Those roles start with the permissions an app typically needs to call other AWS services, enough to get you moving, not meant to last forever. As your app matures and tightening permissions matters, you take those roles over and right-size them, and by then you’ll know exactly what it needs. You focus on your app, AWS handles the plumbing.

Why the foundation matters

Starting from a secure base changes things in two ways. For you, it means the environment you start in is the one you keep. When you’re ready to scale, you grow it rather than building a new one. For us, it means secure by default is something we can keep extending, because a structured, secure starting point gives us a place to add to. We’re able to turn on additional governance controls as a natural part of the experience. One example we’re already working on is setting account-level Amazon S3 Block Public Access protections for newly created environments. I’m not going to put a timeline here, but I want to be clear about the trajectory.

Building for security and ease of use

Ease of use and strong security are too often framed as opposites. Everything we’ve shipped here is an argument that they don’t have to be. You can give someone the fastest possible path to building something real and have that path be secure and cost-safe by default. The same experience makes the easy things easy, like connecting your coding agent in a single step or inviting a collaborator by email, without extra setup. Each of these is useful on its own, but they were all designed around the same idea, that the easy path and the secure path should be the same path.

If you’ve tried the new experience, I’d genuinely like to hear what resonated and what you’d want next, including how we can make activating advanced features feel more managed over time. If you haven’t yet, the fastest way to see these defaults in action is to create an account and start your first project. We’re listening.

Keshav Narsipur

Keshav is Vice President of Identity, Cloud Governance, and Certificate Trust Services at Amazon Web Services. Keshav leads a global organization of engineers, product managers, and security professionals operating hyper-scale services that handle over 2 billion requests per second. His teams bridge the gap between developer velocity and enterprise security. Keshav’s organization is currently focused on pioneering new identity and governance capabilities to secure the generative AI era.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.context: The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with ransomware groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: Gang Exposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

articles.title: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns
articles.context: Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools
articles.full_text:
Three China-nexus intrusion clusters across Latin America, Asia and Europe have been linked through shared malware and infrastructure to a possible common supplier of hacking tools.

Check Point Research (CPR) detailed the findings in a November 10 report, linking the clusters through shared infrastructure features and code similarities within the Sparrow framework.

The year-long investigation covered campaigns targeting several dozen high-profile organizations across the three regions. CPR called the suspected supplier behind the framework 'CopperDragon.'

Three Clusters Share Sparrow Framework

The three clusters are tracked by CPR researchers as SilentDelivery, OceanGate and DarkWire.

SilentDelivery, observed since early 2026, has compromised legitimate websites, mainly in government, shipping and IT or research sectors.

Visitors were shown a fake Chrome certificate warning that prompted them to install a "Certificate Fix" utility, with targets mainly in the Czech Republic, Germany, France, Taiwan, Nepal, Hong Kong and Indonesia. The fake utility delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant, giving the attackers an initial foothold.

OceanGate was observed during 2025 and 2026 and mainly targeted government organizations and critical infrastructure in Asia. CPR said attackers entered through an internet-facing Linux server before moving into Windows environments and conducting extensive credential theft, lateral movement and exfiltration of sensitive operational information.

DarkWire, first identified in mid-2025, initially concentrated on Latin America but more recent intrusions suggested expansion. The cluster has targeted telecom operators, including at least three major providers in the region, as well as foreign affairs and justice bodies.

CopperDragon May Sit Behind Multiple Groups

CPR described CopperDragon as "a potential digital quartermaster supporting China-nexus threat actors" and the Sparrow framework's "possible developer and supplier." It also assessed that CopperDragon is involved in maintaining and supplying variants of the Melofee backdoor.

The report links the framework to FamousSparrow, first identified in 2021 and known for using the SparrowDoor backdoor. CPR said Earth Estries, TropicTrooper and UAT-9244 use a shared toolset "potentially supplied by the same entity," and noted that FamousSparrow was previously also linked to Salt Typhoon, though the details of that relationship remain unclear.

Read more on FamousSparrow: FamousSparrow Swaps SparrowDoor For New SparroWocky Backdoor

For DarkWire, CPR said it did not identify direct code similarities with the CopperDragon toolset. The link instead rests on infrastructure tied to a previously reported FamousSparrow domain.

Shared malware and infrastructure "can blur the boundaries between operators and campaigns," CPR wrote, presenting its findings as a basis for tracking activity long grouped under FamousSparrow more precisely.

articles.title: Hardening Self-Hosted Artifactory for Agentic Workloads
articles.context: This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat...
articles.full_text:
OpenAI has published a focused follow-up to its July report on the Hugging Face intrusion. This one covers a smaller event from the same month: on July 19, agents running in two ExploitGym evaluation runs reached parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure that sat outside the scope of their assigned targets. The earlier Hugging Face incident has already been analyzed at length by several research teams. The new report is narrower, and focuses on details regarding how agents coordinated and how techniques spread between them.

OpenAI’s self-hosted Artifactory is mentioned as the internal on-prem instance agents use so they could install packages during their runs. That makes the report a useful case study for anyone operating a binary repository inside an environment where autonomous agents run with real credentials and real network access. The lessons are about the permissions, the network, and the hosts around the repository. This post walks through what the report describes and what we recommend for teams using self-managedArtifactory in similar settings.

What the report describes

Two conditions in the Open AI hosting environment, unrelated to the repository, made the July 19 events possible:

Agents granted with read and write permission on a repository while they only needed to have read access.

The machine hosting that repository ran a kernel with a publicly known exploit and had a network path toward the research cluster.

Everything else in the OpenAI report follows from those two facts.

Excessive permissions. We recommend customers to manage and enforce zero-trust access policies to the repository. In this event, the agents’ workspaces needed only to pull packages, a read-only operation against a pull-through cache. The deployment environment, however, allowed agent identities to also upload due to having over-privileged write permissions. According to the OpenAI report they used that to turn the repository into a message board, encoding short messages in directory names and leaving longer ones in files. Later agents found credentials, scripts, and technical leads there, and a network bypass spread the same way. Without write access there is no board, and each technique that moved between agents would have had to be rediscovered by every agent on its own.

An exposed host. OpenAI hosted the repository on infrastructure adjacent to the research cluster. One agent adapted a public kernel exploit to gain root on the machine hosting an Artifactory container, a route earlier agents had sketched on the board. From that foothold, and through scripts recovered from CI job logs, five agents ran jobs with root privileges inside workloads on OpenAI’s research cluster. When the agents’ reasoning refers to “[container-management]” APIs reachable through internal DNS, that is the cluster’s Kubernetes control plane, which one agent names directly when it eventually declines to continue. The entry point was never the repository software but the kernel beneath it and the network around it.

Neither incident turned on a single component. In the Hugging Face runs, agents relied in part on previously unknown exploits against the product, which we fixed and disclosed at the time. In the July 19 report no product vulnerability was involved, and the route ran through the host and the network. Read together, the two make one point: a repository that agents can reach is a high-value target, and the controls that contain damage live in the surrounding environment: identity, permissions, network segmentation, and host hardening.

Guidance for self-hosting Artifactory in agentic environments

Self-hosted software, no matter the vendor, has always been a partnership between provider and customer. JFrog builds the platform, supports it and stands behind it. Self-hosted customers run it on the hardware and operating system of their choice, apply updates, set the guardrails, monitor it, and implement the policies and permissions that fit their business. With JFrog SaaS, JFrog runs the platform for you and takes responsibility for the environment security and for hardening of the underlying systems.

Agents behave like a large, fast, and creative population of users. OpenAI’s report shows with unusual candor how agents behave when they find gaps in the environment, and its value is that customers can close those gaps before agents go looking.

The controls below are standard practice for any self-hosted instance and are provided as guidance to our thousands of customers. In an environment where agents hold credentials, they stop being optional.

Apply zero trust to agentic writes and anonymous access. A pull-through cache does not require upload rights, and an identity that cannot write cannot leave a message, a script, or a credential for the next agent to find. Grant agent identities read permission on the specific repositories they need and nothing more. Disable anonymous access unless there is a concrete reason for it.

Harden the full hosting environment. The route to root ran through a kernel exploit on the host, not through the repository. Keep hosts patched, run the service with minimal privileges in a dedicated namespace, segment it from the research cluster and from CI workers, and restrict its outbound network access. The repository should not be a hop toward the control plane, and the control plane should not be reachable back from a workload that only needs to serve packages.

Isolate repositories between tenants when writes are genuinely needed. If agents must publish artifacts, give each run, team, or tenant its own repository with permissions scoped to that tenant. Cross-tenant reads should be a deliberate decision, not a default. This limits what one compromised or misbehaving agent can pass to another.

Audit for unusual repository activity. Watch for directory names that look like text, bursts of small uploads, repeated failed writes, and identity or token activity that does not match the expected pull pattern. OpenAI’s monitors first flagged the incident through unusual identity-related API calls tied to Artifactory roles. Repository logs and access events are a strong signal, and they should feed the same detection pipeline as the rest of the environment.

Scan binaries for embedded credentials. The agents uploaded exploit files, and in at least one case command output containing internal secrets left the infrastructure. Secrets scanning on everything that lands in a repository, with blocking policies on findings, catches both careless leaks and deliberate staging of credentials for later use.

Fully offline runs

OpenAI reports that its frontier reinforcement learning runs now browse and search an offline collection of web content instead of the live internet. That solves the web half of the problem. Agents that build software still need packages, and an offline web corpus does not serve a pip install or a Maven resolve. We assume the current runs bundle only a handful of packages into the sandbox image, which works until an agent needs a dependency that was not anticipated.

The package counterpart is an air-gapped Artifactory, pre-populated before the run. Curate the set of packages the evaluation needs, continuously scan them, promote them into the isolated instance, and give agents read-only access. Nothing new enters during the run, nothing leaves, and the repository cannot become a conduit to any other system because there is no other system to reach. For high-sensitivity evaluations this is the configuration we recommend. It also gives the operator an exact record of every dependency the agents had available, which is useful evidence when a run is later reviewed.

The repository is part of the threat model

The July 19 report is a careful account of how agents share what they learn, and it is worth reading on those terms. For operators, the practical lesson is that a binary repository inside an agent environment is infrastructure the agents will study, probe, and use for their own purposes if it lets them. Scoping permissions to reads, isolating tenants, auditing activity, scanning what is stored, and hardening the hosts around the service are the measures that keep it serving packages and nothing else. We are happy at JFrog to work with OpenAI and other research labs on reference configurations for providing a fully secure setup that gives agents the packages they need without giving them a path to anything else.

articles.title: NCSC scheme will help critical organisations test their cyber defences
articles.context: A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape
articles.full_text:
The NCSC has launched a new Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme.

The scheme is designed to help strengthen national cyber resilience, supporting the UK's most critical organisations, as well as overseeing bodies.

The scheme assures suppliers of cyber adversary simulation services, helping organisations identify trusted providers to test their defences and their ability to prevent, detect and respond to realistic simulated cyber attacks.

Like all NCSC Industry Assurance schemes, CyAS draws on the NCSC’s expertise as the UK’s National Technical Authority for cyber security. Commercial providers are assessed against an NCSC-defined standard, giving organisations confidence that they are buying services that meet recognised requirements.

A key feature of the CyAS methodology is that providers conduct reconnaissance to understand the customer’s technology, exposure and threat landscape. This is then used to develop realistic, customer-specific attack plans. Testers adopt an adversarial mindset and use appropriate tools and techniques to achieve agreed objectives, rather than being driven by commercially procured threat intelligence or constrained by documented tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs).

The scheme complements other NCSC frameworks that support cyber regulation, including the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) and the associated Cyber Resilience Audit (CRA) scheme. Together, these frameworks will help organisations - particularly larger organisations, those operating in critical national infrastructure and government - build a clearer picture of their cyber security and resilience.

They also give Cyber Oversight Bodies a trusted way to gather evidence of resilience across the sectors they oversee. This supports consistency, shared learning and a stronger understanding of cyber risk.

Speaking at the launch, the NCSC’s Chief Technology Officer Ollie Whitehouse said:

You cannot improve what you do not know. That is why I am delighted to see the launch of the Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme. By enabling rigorous, realistic end to end assessments by the very best adversary simulation experts, CyAS will help organisations build a clearer picture of how they would stand up to genuine cyber attacks and take action to strengthen their security and resilience.

“Ultimately, stronger resilience across the UK helps prepare the country for crisis by protecting the essential services we all rely on every day from the most pressing threats.

NCSC Deputy Director Chris Ensor added:

Moving beyond traditional pen testing and auditing of controls, the CyAS service enables organisations to practically test their cyber defences, ensuring they are able to protect, detect and respond to cyber attacks.

CyAS has been developed in partnership with Cyber Oversight Bodies, including regulators and Lead Government Departments, to establish a common core standard and a more consistent approach to demonstrating cyber resilience.

The scheme will initially operate as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), enabling the NCSC to test demand, refine the methodology and build confidence before moving towards a fuller operating model.

You can find a full list of assured service providers on the schemes ‘Find a Provider’ page.

articles.title: OT Incidents Hit a Third of Industrial Organizations, SANS Finds
articles.context: Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and...
articles.full_text:
A third of organizations running OT or industrial control systems (ICS) recorded at least one cyber incident over the past year, according to new data from SANS Institute.

The cybersecurity training and research specialist polled nearly 700 IT and security professionals to compile its 2026 State of ICS/OT Security Survey Insights report.

It revealed the biggest ever single-year leap in incidents, from 22% last year to 34% of responding organizations in 2026.

The impact of incidents was also more severe. The share of respondents who said an incident affected safety increased from 8% to 13% in the period, and the share reporting theft of IP surged from 6% to 31%.

Shared IT/OT credential and identity compromise (31%) and ransomware (31%) were the most frequently cited incident types this year.

Read more on ICS threats: ICS Operators Warned of AI-Driven Attacks on Siemens PLCs

Poor visibility into systems appears to be a contributing factor to the rise in incidents and the severity of their impact.

Just 13% of respondents claimed to have full IT/OT visibility across the cyber kill chain, with budget (43%) cited as the most common barrier to improved detection.

Early detection is key to minimizing the impact of incidents. Nearly three-quarters (72%) of respondents said these led to facility or system downtime.

Only 15% of respondents said they are fully capable of sustaining critical operations in manual mode for more than 48 hours, while two-fifths (40%) don’t know if they could. In the longest case reported, a shutdown lasted a year.

Risk is arguably greatest in the supply chain. If their primary automation vendor disappeared, 58% of respondents said they would shut down or be unable to operate within a year. Yet only a fifth (20%) have a fully functional third-party risk management program.

A Plan to Build OT Resilience

Staff are another potential point of failure: 68% of organizations said that the loss of one or two key individuals would delay or severely risk ICS/OT security and incident response. A third (33%) are deploying AI or automation tools to overcome potential staff shortages, with real-time threat and anomaly detection (42%) the most common investment.

There are plenty of lessons to be learned from the report. Nearly half (46%) of organizations that test their business continuity and disaster recovery plans at least annually and build ICS/OT into them can bring their most critical facility or system back online within the first day, versus 27% of all respondents.

Yet only 16% of respondents have fully integrated cyber resilience into those programs.

The recent cyber-attacks on supermarket OT equipment across Europe highlight the potential for significant operational disruption and financial damage.

With this in mind, SANS Institute recommended a three-point plan to build resilience:

Test resilience plans at least annually, with the operators who would end up actually run manual mode

Integrate ICS/OT cyber resilience into existing BC/DR programs

Map people and vendor-related dependencies

Jason Christopher, SANS Principal Instructor and author of the report, argued that the most resilient organizations are also the ones that known their ICS/OT systems best.

“Industrial security has come a long way over the past decade, and the data this year shows how much is still left to do,” he added.

“What happens after the alarm comes down to rehearsal: who runs the plant by hand, who holds the knowledge that is not written down, and what the fallback is if a vendor is unavailable. Most of the industry has not answered those questions yet.”

articles.title: Microsoft Fixes 1235 Flaws in Another Record Patch Tuesday
articles.context: The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes
articles.full_text:
Microsoft has issued updates to fix over 1200 vulnerabilities in its products, a new record.

The tech giant’s November Patch Tuesday contained fixes for 1235 flaws, including one zero-day being actively exploited in the wild.

It makes this month the fourth this year in which Microsoft has issued a record number of patches, following previous milestones passed in July, September and October.

The zero-day vulnerability is CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Microsoft Outlook, exploited in attacks to steal NTLM account hashes.

“An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and gets the user to open it. Outlook then connects to a network location the attacker controls, but it skips the usual warning about external content,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.

“That quiet connection can leak the user's NTLMv2 hash, a scrambled form of their login secret, which the attacker can use to sign in as that person. It affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024.”

Read more on patching: Exploited Vulnerabilities Typically Take Three Months to Patch, Moody’s Finds

Although the zero-day is rated “moderate,” sysadmins should prioritize it, Bicer advised.

“Attackers are already exploiting it, it needs only one click on an email file, and it hits Outlook, which nearly every organization runs,” he added. “A stolen hash can open doors far beyond the inbox. Push the Office update to every Outlook user now, starting with administrators and high-value accounts.”

The majority (536) of CVEs patched this month are elevation of privilege (EoP), followed by remote code execution (296) and information disclosure (157).

A total of 66 are rated critical, most of these being remote code execution flaws.

SAP Patch Volumes Hit New Highs

Microsoft wasn’t the only software giant to release a record-breaking number of security updates yesterday. SAP’s November Patch Day was the biggest ever, with 43 vulnerabilities addressed, including 12 Hot News Notes and 13 High Priority.

“Hot News” is the highest priority ranking given to SAP security updates (Notes).

The patch load was twice the size of the average for 2026 and included four with a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, according to Onapsis.

These were:

CVE-2026-89103 (SAP Security Note #3798345), a broken access control vulnerability in SAP Gateway dubbed “ProxyGate”

CVE-2026-76964 (SAP Security Note #3778530), a memory corruption flaw in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP (Internet Communication Manager)

CVE-2026-89126 (SAP Security Note #3778556), a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP Web Dispatcher

CVE-2026-120017 (SAP Security Note #3849308), a missing authentication (SAML2 authentication bypass) vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform (SAML2 Service Provider)

articles.title: CVE-2026-118383: Use-after-free vulnerability in MongoDB
articles.context: Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into
articles.full_text:
Key points and observations

CVE-2026-118383 is a critical use-after-free in MongoDB Server's primary catch-up process, with a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5. It affects replica set members, including those used by shards and config servers. Standalone mongod instances are unaffected.

Remote unauthenticated exploitation is possible, but only during a specific window that the attacker does not have visibility into.

We reproduced a crash (segmentation fault) on MongoDB Server 8.0.34.

An unauthenticated client can set up the crash with two ping requests, because vulnerable servers accept ping before login. Turning on authentication does not prevent this.

Upgrade every affected replica set member to a fixed release. Restricting network access can reduce exposure while you upgrade.

What happened

MongoDB announced a security update on November 10. The company said it found the vulnerability internally and was not aware of exploitation attempts at the time of its announcement. The advisory describes a use-after-free when a newly elected replica set primary completes catch-up. During catch-up, the member applies operations it missed before accepting writes as primary.

The vulnerability affects ordinary replica set members. It also affects the replica set members used by shards and config servers in sharded clusters. A standalone mongod does not perform replica set primary catch-up and is not affected by this vulnerability. The advisory rates the issue Critical and says the server may terminate unexpectedly or, under certain conditions, execute arbitrary code in the server process.

How to know if you are affected

The issue affects replica set members, including shard and config server replica set members in sharded clusters. Standalone mongod instances are not affected.

The MongoDB fix releases are:

MongoDB Server branch

First fixed release

9.0

9.0.7

8.3

8.3.16

8.0

8.0.37

7.0

7.0.48

6.0

6.0.30

5.0

5.0.35

4.4

4.4.32

Upgrade to the fixed release for your branch, or use a distributor package that includes the fix. Verify the version running on every member after the upgrade, including members in containers and any members that were offline during maintenance. MongoDB says Atlas clusters are upgraded automatically during maintenance. It urges customers who defer maintenance to apply the upgrade promptly.

Until you can upgrade, restrict network access to MongoDB to the specific systems that need access to it. This limits who can send the unauthenticated requests, but it does not fix the use-after-free.

Exploitation window and likelihood

When a replica set member wins an election, it first catches up on writes it missed, then starts accepting new ones. The bug is in the cleanup at the end of that catch-up step. Before any election happens, an attacker can leave two stale “waiters” on a member. A waiter is a pending notification MongoDB creates when a request asks to wait until replication reaches a certain point. Planting them does not crash the server by itself. The diagram below traces an election timeline and marks where the crash fires.

Plant during steady state: The attacker sends two unauthenticated ping requests that include a readConcern.afterOpTime value to a reachable, vulnerable replica set member. The waiters don't expire. They stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back, or steps down from primary.

Reach catch-up: Later, the same member has to win an election while it is behind another member. The attacker can't cause the lag or the election. Both have to happen on their own, for example during maintenance or an outage.

Crash when catch-up ends: When catch-up finishes, the new primary runs its cleanup twice, uses memory it has already freed, and crashes before it accepts any writes. Once the first two steps are in place, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race.

We created the lag and the failover ourselves, so the roughly 40 seconds our lab run took is not an estimate of how quickly a real attack would work. After the crash, our test cluster had no primary. Another deployment might elect a new primary and keep running.

What we reproduced

We built a four-member replica set from MongoDB's official Linux x86_64 binaries and created the two conditions an attacker can't control: one member falling behind on replication, and a failover that makes that member the new primary. Setting this up took admin access to the lab, to pause and stop mongod processes and to write data with an authenticated client. The attacker's part, the two ping requests, used no credentials, and we confirmed that the same unauthenticated client could not write to the database.

We ran the same failover three times, changing only the MongoDB version and whether we sent the two requests:

Run

Server

Unauthenticated waiter requests

Observed result

A

8.0.34

Both timed out after about 1.5 seconds with MaxTimeMSExpired

The target member exited catch-up twice, logged SIGSEGV, and the mongod process crashed

B

8.0.34

None sent

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

C

8.0.37

Both rejected immediately with Unauthorized

The target member exited catch-up once, became writable, and remained running through the observation window

The video below shows run A from start to finish: the two unauthenticated requests, the failover we triggered, and the new primary crashing.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

In run A, MongoDB's log shows the new primary leaving catch-up mode twice within the same millisecond, followed by “Invalid access at address: 0” and “Got signal: 11 (Segmentation fault).” The backtrace points to CatchupState::abort_inlock(). Runs B and C went through the same failover, logged a single catch-up exit, and kept running.

Run C shows that the patched server refuses the requests. It does not test the other half of MongoDB's fix, which stops the double cleanup even when waiters are already in place; MongoDB's own regression tests cover that case. Our results show that the crash can be set up without credentials in this lab setup. They don't tell us how often it would succeed in other topologies, and we did not achieve code execution.

How to detect exploitation attempts

Start with MongoDB's structured server logs. In our vulnerable run, each planted request appeared as a COMMAND “Slow query” event (ID 51803). The useful fields were:

attr.command.ping

attr.command.readConcern.afterOpTime

attr.command.maxTimeMS

attr.errName (MaxTimeMSExpired)

attr.durationMillis

attr.remote

Look for an unauthenticated command with unusual operation-time values and an expired wait.

Also check the logs for the sequence that preceded a crash: a member enters primary catch-up (ID 21359), exits catch-up twice (ID 21363) in one transition, and then logs a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock(). A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not identify this CVE. The requests may arrive before the failover. Review earlier logs from the same member, not just events around the crash.

Whether these request fields appear in the logs depends on your logging settings. MongoDB documents that client operations enter the diagnostic log when they exceed the slow-operation threshold or when command verbosity is at least one. Check whether your logs retain the command object. Slow-operation sampling or a log pipeline may drop it. The attr.remote field may contain a loopback address rather than the original client IP.

How Datadog can help

Datadog Cloud Security Management reports findings for CVE-2026-118383. Check the vulnerability findings for affected hosts and container images.

Datadog Cloud Security Management also flags security groups that allow inbound MongoDB access from the internet, through the rule Inbound MongoDB access should be restricted. Use it to find exposed replica set members to patch first. Datadog Cloud SIEM detections for CVE-2026-118383 are currently being evaluated, and we will update this post when they are available.

Conclusion

CVE-2026-118383 affects MongoDB replica set members when a newly elected primary finishes catch-up. We reproduced a crash after two unauthenticated requests left abandoned waiters. The patched release rejected those requests. The vendor also identifies arbitrary code execution as a possible impact under certain conditions; our tests did not demonstrate it. Upgrade every affected member to a fixed release, verify the running versions, and investigate unusual readConcern.afterOpTime requests alongside catch-up and crash events.

articles.title: November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs
Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
articles.context: This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers,...
articles.full_text:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

Finally, Payment by Bank Transfer Comes to Have I Been Pwned
articles.context: That left only two options for orgs in this situation: Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢 Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢 The problem with the first option is obvious
articles.full_text:
Presently sponsored by: Not every rogue agent is an attack. In a live webinar on Nov 17, Researcher Tyler Holmwood walks through cases of agents going off course.

This is simultaneously the most boring yet exciting blog title I've written in a long time. How you pay for services isn't exactly a sexy topic, but it solves a problem that's been a massive bugbear for a long time.

Here's a brief history of the issue: many organisations have policies that make it extremely hard to purchase goods and services with a credit card. I wrote about this more than two years ago now, where I referred to "Neville" in the procurement department who, because "reasons", demanded an invoice in advance and payment via electronic funds transfer (EFT) only. That ultimately means the world's most popular way to make online payments is out of reach for them. Unfortunately, until today, that was the only way we could take payment via Stripe, which processes all our online HIBP purchases. That left only two options for orgs in this situation:

Don't use Have I Been Pwned at all 😢

Buy a subscription via a reseller 🤢

The problem with the first option is obvious. The second option "solved" the first problem by allowing a company to pay a reseller by EFT, who then paid us by card. The reseller would then mark the price up (often significantly), slow the whole process down, log countless tickets with us (despite the existence of a dedicated portal for them), and frankly, just be a pain in the arse for everyone. It's hard to express the level of disdain I have for most resellers, and I even still have a 1,381-word draft blog post titled "That's it - Resellers are now Banned from Have I Been Pwned", which I held back from posting. Why? Because I've walked in the shoes of the folks trying to purchase our services who are just trying to get their job done, and Neville has told them they can't pay by card. That was me in a previous life, and it sucked. We kept resellers solely to support those people.

But today, HIBP's subscription page has something all new on it:

Stripe has given us early access to EFT payments in Australia. They've been available in the US for a while, but as an Aussie company and with global financial systems being what they are (i.e. not always the most flexible), we just didn't have that option. Until now. So, we've added EFT as a payment method to our Pro and High RPM plans and kept the entry-level Core ones on card only, as there's some additional overhead on our end. You'll see these every time you go to purchase an eligible subscription:

When you choose to pay by bank transfer, you're given a form for your company details (this is how we calculate any applicable taxes), then a Stripe payment link which loads something similar to the following:

The first thing is that, being an Aussie company with an Aussie bank account, we need to reflect EFT payments in AUD rather than USD. It makes sense when you think about it: we do USD for all the existing products paid for by card, and whatever the FX conversion gods decide is the corresponding Aussie amount eventually lands on our end. But that's a model where the card is charged, and access is granted immediately. For EFT, funds flow through the wires, do FX conversion for non-Aussie purchasers, land in the target account and then Stripe webhook magic enables the service. We need that exact amount to land on our end, so we can't be rolling the dice on what exchange rate we're going to get; hence, Stripe requires us to charge in the target currency. The products are exactly the same price based on the rate we currently see via Stripe purchases today (about 69 American cents per Aussie dollar), we'll just have to see if that's revised in the future with any major currency fluctuations.

Next are the banking details. Pretty straightforward, and I'm sure we've all made payments to an account like this before. The main thing is that the account number is a virtual one, which is how Stripe reconciles money that comes in from a previously raised invoice. When you sell a very limited number of products and a bunch of customers are buying the same one, this is how Stripe is then able to reconcile who has paid for what. If you really want to geek out on bank payments, Stripe has a dedicated EFT explainer page.

And finally, subscriptions in HIBP begin as soon as the invoice is raised, but access to the service only begins when payment is made. You can see the problem if we didn't do it this way: bad guy spins up the service and immediately starts using it then just never pays. But this all ties into the quote ecosystem in the existing HIBP dashboard, so it's easy to generate a quote, go flick it to Neville, get it approved, then raise and pay the invoice straight away.

As I said in the opening, it's not the most exciting topic, but it's a major thing for us and the customers who were left with only bad options if they genuinely couldn't pay by card. In the aforementioned draft blog post on binning resellers, I'd written about how we'd seen markups of up to 131% (so yes, more than double the price!), with absolutely zero value add (i.e. they don't do any product support, that remains entirely on us). But the burden resellers really put on us is the support they require to make purchases; in that same draft post, I calculated that resellers accounted for 0.86% of all sales but 43% of all support tickets. That's just nuts, especially for such a small team (although Bruce has helped enormously).

We hope this makes life easier for a bunch of people who were previously stuck between a rock and a hard place, and that includes all the "Nevilles" out there too. This is all now live and accessible via the pricing page. If you run into any issues, Bruce is standing by in the support portal.

The penultimate month of 2026 bring with it the usual storm of patches from Microsoft and Adobe. I’ve been prototyping some new ways to display this data, but as always, I’m open to suggestions. Seriously – hit me up on Bluesky if you have any ideas.If you’d rather watch the full video recap covering the entire release, you can check it out here:

Adobe Patches for November 2026

For the first part of the November release, Adobe released nine bulletins addressing 110 unique CVEs in Adobe Connect, Experience Manager, After Effects, Audition, Dimension, Photoshop, Media Encoder, Premiere, and Content Credentials SDK.

Obviously, if you need to prioritize, the Connect patch is the biggest and most severe bulletin this month: 24 CVEs, 18 of them Critical, with a top CVSS of 10.0. It’s Priority 2, and Adobe is not aware of any exploits in the wild. Each of the CVSS10 bugs are reachable over the network with no authentication or user interaction, and each changes scope. The other Critical-rated update for this month is in Experience Manager. It addresses 14 CVEs, which includes four Critical bugs with a CVSS 9.9 rating. Two are incorrect-authorization bugs and two are code injections. All give arbitrary code execution over the network. Each needs a low-privileged account but no user interaction, and each changes scope.

Besides the bugs already mentioned, all other patched from Adobe are a Deployment Priority 3. None of the other Adobe bugs receiving patches this month are listed as publicly known or under active attack at the time of release.

Microsoft Patches for November 2026

Well, at least it’s not a new record for Microsoft. As always, the overall count is a bit confusing, but I see about 1,090 new CVEs released today. At this point, does the exact number actually matter? Regardless of the actual count, it’s huge but less than the 1,400 or so released last month. That’s two months in a row that have exceeded all previous years from Microsoft. As for the products affected by this release, we have Windows and Windows components; Office and Office Components; Windows networking and remote access; Windows graphics, media and printing; Windows storage file systems and drivers; .NET and Visual Studio; Windows Security and identity; Azure, cloud and identity; Exchange Server; Microsoft Dynamics; and Xbox. We’ll see how close I came to matching Microsoft’s “Cohorts” list.

Interestingly, there is only one bug under active attack, and none are publicly known this month. While this is encouraging, it does not mean we’re seeing less exploitation in the wild. It does mean we are seeing fewer 0-days exploited in the wild. This makes sense, as AI is better at reversing patches than it is at finding and exploiting bugs in closed-source software.

Let’s begin by covering some of the more severe and interesting patches released this month.

- CVE-2026-124194 - Microsoft Outlook Spoofing VulnerabilityThis is the one bug under active attack this month. It’s labeled spoofing, but the impact is bigger than the name suggests. An attacker sends a specially crafted message file and convinces a user to open it. Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, which discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash. The attacker can use that hash to authenticate as the user. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector, and the CVSS is only 6.5, so don’t let the score lull you. Microsoft marks it as exploited, so this one goes to the top of the list.

- CVE-2026-116928 - Windows Search Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityWe start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server. This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month.

- CVE-2026-119958 - Windows LDAP - Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction. Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly.

- CVE-2026-119990 - Azure OpenAI Elevation of Privilege VulnerabilityUPDATE: Microsoft has revised this bulletin to indicate there is no customer action needed.This is an odd duck. The bulletin says “Customer Action Required: Yes” for this bug, but nothing in the advisory tells customers what to do. There are no mitigations, workarounds, or customer steps. The FAQ says an unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted request over the internet to an affected Azure OpenAI service, with no account or user interaction. The impact is access to orchestration information, workflow changes, or service disruption. Hopefully, Microsoft adds some direction here soon.

- CVE-2026-119952 - Windows Schannel Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityThis flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit arbitrary code over a network without user interaction. Microsoft rates this bug as “Exploitation More Likely”. It is one of only a few Critical-rated patches with that rating. They also list the attack complexity as high, which is why the CVSS score is lower than the others. I would still put this near the top of my list.

- CVE-2026-95962 - Windows Virtual Filtering Platform (VFP) Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityI include this one because it’s in a little-documented component. It’s not the first CVE in VFP, but it appears to be just the second. It’s a use-after-free that allows an unauthenticated attacker to get code execution on affected targets by sending a specially crafted packet to the affected service over the network. No authentication or user interaction is needed. There is a race condition here, but we see those overcome all the time at Pwn2Own. This should be an interesting component to watch.

- CVE-2026-112967 - Windows Xbox Live Networking Service Remote Code Execution VulnerabilityYou don’t see a lot of Xbox Live bugs, but here we are with a CVSS 9.8. This bug is a heap overflow that doesn’t need authentication or user interaction. Microsoft states the attacker can “gain remote code execution via an in-network attacker calling arbitrary endpoints.” Is this really likely? Probably not, but it’s fun to think of Xbox Live exploits in the wild.

On to those that are Wormable…

Last month saw 59 bugs that fit this definition. This month, it’s a bit less. A total of 30 of the November CVEs fit my definition of wormable. Specifically, 17 contain the advisory language describing an unauthenticated attacker executing code over the network with no authentication or user interaction required. The other 13 use variant wording or have no FAQ, but their summaries and CVSS vectors (AV:N/PR:N/UI:N) describe the same thing.

These bugs are as follows:

Message Queuing (5): CVE-2026-116710, 119963, 119964, 109459, 119967

DNS (4): CVE-2026-81384, 96092, 96177, 88218

Two each (8): Color Management (CVE-2026-96067, 96078), DHCP Server (CVE-2026-88243, 72998), DirectMusic (CVE-2026-95882, 95901) and Xbox (CVE-2026-112967, 66801)

One each (13): Exchange Server (CVE-2026-116928), LDAP (CVE-2026-119958), Schannel (CVE-2026-119952), CredSSP (CVE-2026-119962), Deployment Services (CVE-2026-119951), IIS (CVE-2026-119961), NAT (CVE-2026-113862), RPC Runtime (CVE-2026-118737), Media Foundation (CVE-2026-96157), iSCSI (CVE-2026-88234), Virtual Filtering Platform (CVE-2026-95962), eSCL Scanner (CVE-2026-95956) and Modern Device Management (CVE-2026-119945)

I may be wrong about some of these, since a few advisories are light on detail. As always, I recommend testing and deploying these patches quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange
